"...you conquered in the lovely contest of God. Remember him whom you raised, blessed martyr, and grant me a conversation, just as you 8) used to do 9) before."

1. Of those three 10) who were called by the name of Ignatius in ancient times and were eminent for the holiness of their lives, we are here dealing with the Bishop of Antioch.

In the *Martyrdom* <note>A hagiographic account of a saint's death</note> found in Symeon Metaphrastes <note>A 10th-century Byzantine author famous for rewriting lives of saints</note>, chapter 1, and in the Greek *Menaia* <note>Eastern Orthodox liturgical books containing the lives of saints</note> found in Bollandus 11), it is recorded that Ignatius was that tiny child whom the Savior, having lifted him in His own hands, presented to the Apostles to commend simplicity and integrity 12). The origin and beginning of this narrative seems to have been an erroneous way of writing the epithet *Theophoros* <note>original: "Θεόφορος" (God-bearer) vs "Θεόφορος" (God-borne). The shift in accent changes the meaning from one who carries God to one who was carried by God</note>, which occurs frequently in his Letters. Where and from what place he originated is not established; for this reason, various authors have piled up different conjectures without much critical effort, though with much and profound confidence. Gregory Abulpharagius <note>Also known as Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century Syrian scholar</note> calls him "Nuranian" 13), which some understand as referring to Nura in the island of Sardinia, or to Cappadocia. Tillemont <note>A 17th-century French ecclesiastical historian</note> thinks he was of Syrian origin rather than Greek. Another 14) derives the name from "fire," saying Ignatius is the same as "fiery" <note>A reference to the Latin "ignis"</note>.

The author of the *Acts of the Martyrdom of Ignatius*, chapters 1 and 3 (first edited by Ruinart) and Metaphrastes in chapter 2, along with several of the ancients 15), assert that he enjoyed the companionship of John the Apostle along with Polycarp. Gregory the Great 16) also writes that he was instructed by the Apostle Peter. Moreover, Ignatius was appointed as the prelate of the metropolis of Antioch, where the name "Christian" had recently originated; whether he was the first or the second is ambiguous; nor do we have it for certain whether Peter or Paul ordained him. The author of the *Apostolic Constitutions* (VII, 46) writes that Evodius was appointed head of the church of Antioch by Peter; Jerome says 17): "Ignatius, the third Bishop of the Church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter." The same order of succession is found in Nicephorus 18) and Metaphrastes in the *Acts of the Martyrdom*, chapter 1, and in our own edition from Vatican Codex 866. But the same author of the *Constitutions* in the place cited shows Ignatius as having been appointed prelate of that same church by Paul; Chrysostom 19) contends that it was done by Peter. According to the opinion of Theodoret 20), Ignatius succeeded Peter. To reconcile the discrepancy of the earlier tradition, some think that Evodius, appointed by Peter, died while Peter himself was still living, and thus Ignatius, who succeeded Evodius, was ordained by the Apostle. Another way of settling the dispute is indicated by Baronius 21) and also by Natalis Alexander 22), namely that because of—

<page-num>XXIII</page-num>
<header>IGNATIUS.</header>

Because of the dispute between the Jews and the Greeks <note>The early Christian community in Antioch was split between Jewish converts and Gentile converts</note>, some believe that Evodius and Ignatius presided over the church of Antioch at the same time—one for the Jews and the other for the Gentiles. When this tension was finally smoothed over, they believe Ignatius yielded to Evodius, and after Evodius's death, Ignatius once again ruled, and did so alone.

*The Acts of his Martyrdom* <note>original: "Acta eius Martyrii"; these are early accounts, often embellished, describing a saint's trial and execution</note> declare clearly enough that Ignatius performed this duty with singular care.<sup>23)</sup> These same records relate that while Emperor Trajan was staying in Antioch, about to wage war against the Armenians and Parthians, Ignatius was condemned to the wild beasts because of his excessive zeal for Christ and was sent to Rome to undergo the ultimate punishment. The ship that carried him under military guard put in at Smyrna, where he happened to visit and greet Bishop Polycarp and the delegates of the neighboring churches. From here, he sent letters to the faithful of Christ in Ephesus, Magnesia, Tralles, and Rome.

Then, heading for Rome, he was carried to Troas, from where he sent letters to the Philippians, the Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp. He was led away to Neapolis, then to Philippi, and having traveled through Macedonia, he boarded a ship at Epidamnus (Dyrrhachium) <note>A major port on the Adriatic, modern-day Durrës in Albania</note>. After crossing the Adriatic Sea, he entered the Tyrrhenian Sea with his guard. When they docked at Puteoli, he himself desired to leave the ship and proceed to Rome by land, following the example of the Apostle Paul. But because a storm arose and they were driven into the deep sea, they had to pass that town by. He entered the Roman Port <note>The harbor of Portus, near Ostia</note>, where brothers from Rome had come to greet him. From there, he was led by the guards into the City and was torn to pieces by two lions in the amphitheater; his remains were gathered by the faithful and carried back from Rome to Antioch.

These same *Acts* relate<sup>24)</sup> that Ignatius was crowned with the crown of martyrdom in the tenth year of Trajan—that is, on the 20th of December in the year 107. Since this corresponds poorly with historical records, and the hand of an interpolator <note>Someone who later inserts or alters text in a manuscript</note> has undoubtedly inflicted wounds upon the *Acts* here and there, different scholars have attempted different ways of reconciling the dates. But unless I am mistaken, they have "lost both their work and their oil," as the saying goes <note>original: "operam et oleum... perdiderunt"; a Latin idiom meaning to waste time and effort on a fruitless task</note>. For it is well established that Emperor Trajan crossed into Asia in the year 114 to move his arms against the Armenians and Parthians, that he wintered in Antioch, and began his expedition in the following year. Consequently, G. Lloyd,<sup>25)</sup> Pearson,<sup>26)</sup> Pagi,<sup>27)</sup> Grabe,<sup>28)</sup> Noris,<sup>29)</sup> J. Eckhel,<sup>30)</sup> easily the leader among numismatists <note>Experts who study coins and medals</note>, and recently H. Francke,<sup>31)</sup> have all determined that Ignatius was condemned by Trajan in the year 115, while the Emperor was established in his winter quarters at Antioch. It must then be said that the martyr died in the eighteenth year of that reign: a date which hardly fits the time indicated in the *Acts*. Those who believe that the *Acts* should be trusted instead must invent a double expedition of Trajan against the Armenians and Parthians, though they do so without certain or firm historical witnesses. Among their number is Tillemon—

...Tillemont<sup>32)</sup> and E. Corsinus,<sup>33)</sup> whom Eckhel refuted in his *Study of Ancient Coins*, Part II, Vol. VI (Vienna, 1796), pages 448–454. To me, it seems that the *Acts* <note>The "Acts of the Martyrdom," historical or hagiographical records of a saint's trial</note> which have now been published in Greek for the first time from the Vatican Codex 866, offer a timely remedy for this disagreement. They begin as follows:

<note>original Greek: Ἐν ἔτει πέμπτῳ τῆς βασιλείας Τραϊανοῦ καίσαρος...</note> "In the fifth year of the reign of Trajan Caesar, and the second year of the consulship of Atticus, Suberinus, and Marcellus, Ignatius—bishop of the Church of God in Antioch and the second to follow the Apostles—having succeeded Evodius under a most diligent military guard, was sent from Syria to the city of the Romans because of his testimony for Christ."

These records are entirely silent regarding Ignatius being condemned by Emperor Trajan at Antioch, as they instead report that his capital trial was conducted before Trajan and the Senate in Rome.

2. The passages from Ignatius cited by the ancient Church Fathers, although they refer to the same subjects, frequently differ in their wording and meaning in a surprising way. Regarding the letters that have come down to us under his name: if you exclude those three written in Latin (two to the Apostle John and one to the Blessed Mary) and likewise the five Greek letters (to Mary of Cassobola, the Tarsians, the Philippians, the Antiochenes, and Hero) which are considered forgeries,<sup>34)</sup> there remain seven written in Greek to the same churches mentioned earlier. However, these seven differ so much among themselves that one version seems to be the original of the other. These are the letters to the Ephesians, Magnesians, Trallians, Romans, Philadelphians, Smyrnaeans, and to Polycarp. 

Almost all critics, as far as I know, agree that the shorter version is to be preferred over the longer, expanded one. The arguments put forward by Karl Meier<sup>35)</sup>—in which he tried to prove from the longer versions that the shorter ones were merely the work of an abridger—carry no weight and have already been refuted by others.<sup>36)</sup> But although we also believe the shorter version is preferable to the longer one, we frankly confess that we have never doubted that an editor has inflicted "wounds" <note>This refers to "interpolations," or later unauthorized changes to the text</note> upon both versions. Indeed, the longer we have occupied ourselves with studying them, the more we are persuaded, along with others,<sup>37)</sup> <note>original Greek: τὸ ἐντὸς βλέπειν καὶ φυσιογνωμονεῖν</note> "to look within and judge the character" of the matters treated there and the manner in which they are handled.

3. Not a few of the ancient writers testify that Ignatius wrote several letters. Let the following be brought forward:

a) Polycarp, *Letter to the Philippians*, chapter 13 (found in Eusebius, *Church History*, III, 36):<sup>38)</sup>

<header>IGNATIUS.</header>

...by this [letter]; from which you will be able to be greatly benefited. *For they <note>Referring to the collection of Ignatius's letters</note> contain faith and endurance and every kind of edification that pertains to our Lord.*

b) Also, the records of the martyrdom from the Vatican Codex 866 <note>A significant medieval manuscript containing lives of saints</note> assert near the end: **"And Polycarp, the bishop of the congregation of Smyrna, also makes mention of these [letters], saying..." etc.** Irenaeus^39) transmitted this more clearly than the master, citing these words from Ignatius's *Letter to the Romans*, chapter 4: "**As one of our own said, having been condemned to the wild beasts because of his testimony toward God: 'I am the wheat of God, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found to be pure bread.'**"

> Almost the same is found in the records of the martyrdom from the Vatican Codex 866: **Irenaeus, the bishop of Lyons, knows of his martyrdom, and mentions his letters, saying thus: "One of our own said, having been delivered to the wild beasts because of his testimony for God, 'I am the wheat of my God, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may become pure bread.'"**

Regarding the *Letter of Polycarp to the Philippians* itself, the same Irenaeus says:^40) "**There is also a letter of Polycarp written to the Philippians, etc.**"

c) Lucian of Samosata, that famous mocker of Christians, in his dialogue *On the Death of Peregrinus*, seems to have criticized Ignatius in no uncertain terms.^41) In section 1.42, Peregrinus is described as **unfortunate** <note>original Greek: κακοδαίμων</note>, just as Ignatius is in the *Martyrium* <note>The account of his martyrdom</note>, chapter 2. Peregrinus is a bishop in section 11, and more specifically in section 18: **having been bound in Syria.** He [Lucian] asserts in section 13 that the Christians sent funds to their captive, a story which seems to have arisen from the fact that churches near Ignatius's route sent faithful people to congratulate him on his suffering. However, Lucian's words: "**And they say he sent letters to almost all the famous cities... and for this purpose he appointed some of his companions as ambassadors, calling them 'messengers of the dead' and 'underworld-runners'**" <note>original Greek: νεκραγγέλους καὶ νερτεροδρόμους; these are satirical titles Lucian used to mock Christian ecclesiastical terms</note> (§ 41) seem to have come from the pen of a writer who had Ignatius's *Letter to the Smyrnaeans*, chapter 11, and his *Letter to Polycarp*, chapter 7, before his eyes.

d) Origen (in his *Preface to the Song of Songs*)^42) transcribed these words from Ignatius's *Letter to the Romans*, chapter 7: "I remember one of the saints saying—Ignatius by name—concerning Christ: 'But my Love has been crucified.'"

e) Eusebius (in *Church History* III. 34)^43), discussing Ignatius's journey and his various letters, transcribed some portions from the letter to the Romans (chapter 5) and to the Smyrnaeans (chapter 3): "**And Ignatius, who is even now famous among most people, was the second to be allotted the bishopric in the succession of Peter at Antioch. The story goes that he was sent from Syria to the city of the Romans to become food for wild beasts because of his testimony for Christ...**"

<page-num>XXVI</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

Thus, having arrived in Smyrna, where Polycarp was, he writes one letter to the church in Ephesus, mentioning its shepherd, Onesimus; another to the church in Magnesia by the Maeander, where again he makes mention of Bishop Damas; and another to the church in Tralles, whose leader at that time he records as being Polybius. In addition to these, he also writes to the church of the Romans, to whom he offers an exhortation, so that they might not, by pleading for his life <note>original Greek: παραιτησάμενοι, meaning to beg off or avert the martyrdom</note>, deprive him of the hope he longed for. Now follow those things which correspond exactly to Chapter 5 of the *Letter to the Romans*, and specifically to the shorter version of it. After those things: "Now having already gone beyond Smyrna, from Troas he again communicates through writing to those in Philadelphia, and to the church of the Smyrnaeans, and individually to its leader Polycarp; whom, knowing well as an apostolic man <note>A term for early church leaders who were direct disciples of the Apostles</note>, he commends to him the flock in Antioch, as a genuine and good shepherd, asking him to have diligent care for it." Having stated these, Eusebius adds half of Chapter 3 of the *Letter to the Smyrnaeans* from the shorter version: "For I [saw him in the flesh even after the resurrection] ........ and they believed."

f) Athanasius also (in *On the Councils of Ariminum and Seleucia*, no. 47) <gloss>44)</gloss> is a witness, as one who had the letters of Ignatius at hand. For from the *Letter to the Ephesians*, chapter 7, some things are found in these [writings] of his: "Ignatius, therefore, who was established as bishop in Antioch after the Apostles, and became a martyr of Christ, writing about the Lord, said: 'There is one Physician, both fleshly and spiritual, begotten and unbegotten, God in man, true life in death, both from Mary and from God.'" <note>This is a foundational statement of early Christology, balancing the human and divine natures of Jesus.</note>

g) Jerome (in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 16), following the lead of Eusebius, recorded: "Ignatius, the third bishop of the church of Antioch after the Apostle Peter, when Trajan was stirring up persecution, was condemned to the wild beasts and sent bound to Rome. And when, while sailing, he had come to Smyrna, where Polycarp, a student of John, was bishop, he wrote one letter to the Ephesians, a second to the Magnesians, a third to the Trallians, and a fourth to the Romans; and departing from there, he wrote to the Philadelphians and to the Smyrnaeans, and specifically to Polycarp, commending to him the church at Antioch; in which [letter] regarding the Gospel, which was recently translated by me <note>Jerome likely refers here to the *Gospel according to the Hebrews*</note>, he places testimony concerning the person of Christ, saying" (to the Smyrnaeans, chapter 3): "'But I truly saw him in the flesh even after the resurrection, and I believe that he exists. And when he came to Peter, and to those who were with Peter, he said to them: "Behold, touch me and see, that I am not an incorporeal spirit" <note>original Latin: daemonium incorporale; in this context, "demon" refers to a ghost or bodiless phantom</note>.' And immediately they touched him and believed." "It seems worthy, since we have made mention of such a great man, to also place a few things from his letter which he writes to the Romans" (chapter 5). <page-num>XXVII</page-num>
<header>IGNATIUS.</header>

[...I am ground] by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found to be pure bread." <note>original Latin: "tibus bestiarum molar, ut panis mundus inveniar." A famous quote from Ignatius’s *Letter to the Romans*, chapter 4, expressing his desire for martyrdom.</note> "He suffered in the eleventh year of Trajan’s reign." <note>Trajan was Roman Emperor from 98 to 117 AD; the eleventh year would be roughly 108 AD.</note> See the testimonies of Jerome and later writers which Pearson collected in his *Vindication*, Part I, chapters 2 and 9.

4. We have already hinted above (in section 3) that neither version of the Ignatian Epistles appears to us to be untainted <note>The author is referring to the "Long" and "Short" versions of the letters that circulated in the early modern period.</note>. The art of criticism in such matters does not require a display of vast knowledge, nor does it need that collection of favored opinions summoned from near and far to support a cause. Rather, it requires above all else an open mind and an honest interpretation from the reader. One who brings such a mind to the reading of the Ignatian Epistles, as they exist in Greek, will a hundred times be struck by the excess of individual words and commands of every kind. To be sure, Ignatius’s mind—filled with the heat of Christian charity—is very similar to that passion which so graphically distinguishes the Apostle Paul; but Ignatius is himself a "son of Asia" <note>Meaning his writing style reflects the "Asianic" school of rhetoric, which was known for being ornate, emotional, and wordy.</note>. Yet even this cannot excuse all the things that are held against a writer of apostolic simplicity. Therefore, the Epistles of Ignatius, as they have come down to our own times, are hardly in every respect the same ones that Polycarp recommended to the Philippians in chapter 13 of his own work. I would call them a "painted tablet" by a very ancient author, restored by hands that were not always pious, and here and there edited with a specific purpose: namely, not to give birth to the <term>episcopal system</term> <note>The hierarchy of the church led by bishops.</note>, but to recommend that system once it had already been created. From this it happens that the manner of speaking smells of the "style of the Curia" <note>The administrative and legal language used by the central government of the Church.</note>, which mandates, ordains, and commands—a new kind of speaking indeed for the age in which Ignatius lived, and one quite foreign to the diplomacy of the early church.

5. Learned men differ on how much genuine and how much forged material is preserved within these letters. Salmasius, Blondel, and especially Jean Daillé (Dallaeus)—men endowed with marvelous insight and a wealth of learning—were the first to doubt their authenticity. Daillé did so in 1666 in his book: *On the writings circulated under the names of Dionysius the Areopagite and Ignatius of Antioch.* Against him rose John Pearson with his *Ignatian Vindications* (Cambridge, 1672), which was included in Le Clerc’s editions of the *Apostolic Fathers* (1698, 1700, 1724), and recently reprinted by William Cureton in Oxford, 1852: *A Vindication of the Epistles of St. Ignatius, by John Pearson, Bishop of Chester. A new edition with notes and a preface adapted to the current state of the controversy.*

But Pearson’s *Vindication* did not enjoy universal applause from learned men. It was challenged by Matthieu de Larroque, Samuel Basnage, Casimir Oudin, and others. Responding from the other side were Nicolas Nourry⁴⁵), Rémi Ceillier⁴⁶), Tommaso Maria Mamachi⁴⁷), and Lumper⁴⁸)—all of whom venerated the authority of tradition perhaps too much, or rather defined its internal meaning according to their own understanding. Doubts about their integrity were also raised by Neander⁴⁹) and Netzius⁵⁰). In our own time, Baur⁵¹)...

<page-num>XXVIII</page-num>
<header>PROLEGOMENA.</header>

A Professor of the University of Tübingen <note>Referring to Ferdinand Christian Baur (1792–1860), a famous German theologian who founded the "Tübingen School" of biblical criticism.</note> believed that the Ignatian Epistles were forged in the second century by some counterfeiter in Rome, intended to recommend the office of the bishop by using the illustrious name and authority of Ignatius. To this view, Schwegler and Hilgenfeld have agreed, with only slight differences in their reasoning.

Following the lead of Rothe, Johann E. Huther, Friedrich Düsterdieck, and Gerhard Uhlhorn—I shall remain silent regarding the <term>petty critics</term> <note>original Greek: μικρολόγους (*mikrologous*). These are scholars who focus on trivial details rather than the substance of the argument.</note> who, leaning on no real weight of evidence, flow away with dripping and slippery words, for their arguments are well-regarded as being born on the lips and not in the heart—Hefele has very recently attempted to address the matter of Ignatius again and again. However, he has more often declared war on the opposing parties than he has actually defeated them. We praise his diligence, yet we do not marvel at the sharpness of his judgment.

6. In the year 1839, Henry Tattam found a manuscript in a Syrian monastery in Nitria <note>The Nitrian Desert in Egypt was a major center for early Christian monasticism and a treasure trove for ancient manuscripts.</note>. It was written, it is believed, before the 6th century, and it preserved a Syriac version of Ignatius's *Letter to Polycarp*. On a second journey three years later, he purchased many other manuscripts from the same monastery; among them was an ancient Syriac version of three Ignatian Epistles—to the Ephesians, the Romans, and to Polycarp—dating, it is said, to the 6th or 7th century, along with several fragments of other Ignatian letters. William Cureton had also discovered a Syriac fragment of the *Acts of Ignatius's Martyrdom* among the treasures of the British Museum. Aided by these manuscripts, he published: "The ancient Syriac version of the epistles of saint Ignatius to St. Polycarp, the Ephesians, and the Romans: together with extracts from his epistles, collected from the writings of Severus of Antioch, Timotheus of Alexandria, and others, edited with an English translation, and notes. Also the Greek text of these three epistles, corrected according to the authority of the Syriac version. By William Cureton, M. A. London: Rivingtons. Berlin: Asher et Comp. 1845."

Cureton left no stone unturned to prove that this Syriac version alone was genuine, and that all those passages which occur more frequently in the shorter Greek version were false. To persuade himself and others of this more firmly, he was moved not only by the nature of the version itself but also by the fact that, after those two manuscripts he used earlier, a third was available, containing the same short Syriac version of those same three Epistles. Having compared this one as well, Cureton published the *Corpus Ignatianum*: a complete collection of the Ignatian epistles, genuine, interpolated, and spurious; together with numerous extracts from them, as quoted by ecclesiastical writers down to the tenth century; in Syriac, Greek, and Latin: an English translation of the Syriac text,

<page-num>XXIX</page-num>
<header>IGNATIUS. XXIX</header>

...with copious notes, and an introduction, by William Cureton, M. A. F. R. S. Chaplain in ordinary to her Majesty the Queen. London 1849. Berlin, same year." The author primarily attacks Hefele, who had already judged as follows in his third edition of the *Apostolic Fathers* <note>original Latin: "PP. App." referring to *Patres Apostolici*.</note>: "Cureton attempts to persuade us that this Syriac version corresponds most accurately to the 'genuine' text of Ignatius, and that all the additional material found in our Greek text was added and introduced by others. However, we are so far from agreeing with him that we can only consider the Syriac version to be an <term>epitome</term> <note>A summary or condensed version of a larger work.</note> of the Ignatian epistles, composed by a certain Syrian monk for his own private pious use, especially since the same manuscripts discovered by Tattam contain several other 'excerpts' from the Ignatian letters as well as other ascetic booklets, as Cureton himself admits. Furthermore, it often appears from the fact that the flow of thought in the Syriac version is less tight-knit that this monk acted not so much as a translator, but as an abridger." Nor was Hefele led to renounce his previously formed opinion <note>original Latin: "ut nuntium mitteret," literally "to send a messenger," a classical idiom for breaking off a relationship or opinion.</note> in his fourth edition of the *Apostolic Fathers* by those arguments which Cureton’s *Corpus Ignatianum* sets forth more extensively against him. 59)

Along with Cureton, Christian Karl Josias Bunsen awarded the palm to the Syriac version over the Greek Epistles of Ignatius, explaining and defending his opinion learnedly and shrewdly, as is his custom. 60)

And as for us, regarding the opinion leveled by Hefele against Cureton and those who side with him, we cannot help but say that the weight of the arguments on which he relies is quite slight. For if someone is reducing a work to a summary for their own pious use, what, I ask, is he doing with the full greeting formulas of the Epistles, which relate only to those to whom the letters were written? Therefore, the very opening of the Epistles would be <term>vain talk</term> <note>original Latin: "vaniloquium."</note> in a summary. I pass over other matters of no small importance already pointed out by Cureton 61). In short: if the author of the Syriac version is an abridger, he must be called the <term>lowliest</term> <note>original: "postremissimus." The author references Tiberius Gracchus to imply he is the most incompetent or "last" of his kind.</note> of all abridgers, since he would have produced a work without external or internal consistency, and without any certain purpose or goal, even if "private pious uses" were the purpose themselves. Indeed, the variety itself—and truly, a manifold variety of subjects even in the Syriac Epistles of Ignatius—is to me a guarantee of the law and condition by which the Syriac version was made; I mean the law of the Epistles. Yet it is not my intention to go entirely over to Cureton’s side. For the Syriac version seems to present genuine material mixed with forgeries just as much as the Greek original does. Which of the two should be granted the primary place certainly cannot be determined unless new witnesses, more effective than those surviving, are found for one side or the other. However, a second copy of the same Syriac revision of the three Epistles is not to be valued so highly, because it may belong to the same "family," as they say.

<meta>This page continues the technical history of the publication and scholarly debate surrounding the Ignatian epistles. It moves from the criticism of Cureton’s Syriac discovery to the evaluation of Julius Heinrich Petermann’s work on the Armenian version, and then provides a chronological history of the early printed editions of the letters.</meta>

<page-num>XXX</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

...edited it and added critical notes, Julius Heinrich Petermann." He has served the cause of textual criticism <note>original: "re critica"</note> most excellently. But an undue love for Armenian literature, which he holds in high regard, seems to have clouded the judgment of a man who valued the Armenian version of the thirteen Epistles of Ignatius so highly. For that version contains not only those seven shorter letters, but also the six so-called spurious <note>original: "supposititias," referring to works falsely attributed to an author</note> ones (Mary of Cassobola to Ignatius, Ignatius's Letter to Mary of Cassobola, and Ignatius’s letters to the Tarsians, the Antiochians, to Hero, and to the Philippians). That is to say, it presents the same letters commonly called "interpolated" <note>original: "interpolatas." In textual criticism, an interpolation is a passage inserted into a text by a later hand.</note>, and I would even dare to say it is very similar to them. This fact will be grasped without much effort by anyone who carefully reads through the letters as we are now publishing them, corrected from manuscript codices. Petermann therefore concluded (p. XXVI):
> 1) "Our version was made in the fifth century AD from that Syriac version of which Cureton published a copy. 2) That Syriac version originally comprised not only three, but thirteen epistles attributed to Saint Ignatius; and these were not shortened, as they are read in that edition, but were arranged just as our author Petermann presented them. From this it appears that the conclusions drawn by Bunsen based on that version cannot stand."

I would not think so. Perhaps the following is more correct:
> 3) "The Armenian version was interpolated and corrupted in various places by later scribes (or readers) who compared it with the Greek text, and editors completely lacking in critical judgment inserted these interpolations and corruptions into the text."

Bunsen, in his work *Hippolytus and His Age* (1852), Volume I, p. 46 and Volume II, p. VII following, replied to Petermann. Ritschl (*The Origin of the Early Catholic Church*, Bonn 1850, pp. 418, 577 ff.) and Weiss (in *Reuter’s Repertorium* 1852) took the side of Cureton and Bunsen. Along with Baur (*The Ignatian Epistles and Their Latest Critic: A Polemic against Mr. Bunsen*, Tübingen 1848), the very learned Hilgenfeld (*The Apostolic Fathers*, Halle 1853, p. 188 ff.) doubts the authenticity of both the Greek and Syriac Epistles attributed to Ignatius.

7. Of the Epistles said to be by Ignatius, the first three were written in Latin (two to the Apostle John and one to the Blessed Virgin) and were published in Paris in the year 1495.

Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>original: "Iac. Faber Stapulensis"</note> in 1498, omitting those three, published eleven others in Paris from an old Latin version. Symphorien Champier of Lyon <note>original: "Symphorianus Champerius Lugdunensis"</note> increased this number by adding the three rejected by Lefèvre, and added a fourth to Mary of Cassobola, which he was the first to make known. Thus, fifteen Epistles had then become known under the name of Ignatius, but only in Latin; these were later reprinted several times. We have used the text of the rare and corrected Venetian edition of 1546.

From a codex in the Augsburg Library, Valentin Fried <note>original: "Valentinus Hartungus Frid (Pacaeus)." Fried used the Greek-derived pseudonym Pacaeus, from 'pax' (peace).</note> was the first to publish twelve of them in Greek in 1557 at Dillingen, omitting those three written in Latin. In 1558, there were published in Paris by Guillaume Morel: *The Epistles of Saint Martyr Ignatius, Archbishop of Antioch (Greek and Latin)*. Morel says to the reader on page 147:
> "Since Valentin Fried was the first to publish these Greek epistles of the Blessed Ignatius, and they were greatly desired by our people because a sufficient supply of copies did not remain, men of the highest learning and piety easily persuaded me to print them—men who [desired] such pious authors..."

<header>IGNATIUS.</header>

...I could not hope for a better edition <note>original: "editionem exoptem, ut nihil supra"</note> than this. Therefore, I reread the book as diligently as possible and compared it with Latin copies, so that I do not regret my labor. For through that comparison and the advice of a most learned man, I seem to have restored certain passages in such a way that I believe no good man, if he wishes to weigh the matter with an open mind, would fail to admit that much has been contributed to their understanding." Andreas Gesner oversaw the printing of these same twelve Epistles in Greek with the Latin interpretation of Johann Brunner from the Manuscript <term>Codex</term> <note>A "codex" is an ancient manuscript in book form rather than a scroll.</note> of the Library of Caspar von Niedbruck at Zurich in 1559; he was the first to do so, as he himself believed, being unaware of Pace's edition. Seven of these are said to be interpolated <note>original: "interpolatae," meaning they were expanded or altered by later editors</note>, and five are spurious <note>original: "supposititiae," meaning they were falsely attributed to Ignatius</note>. Of this same version <note>original: "recensionis"</note> are: *The Epistles of the Holy Martyr Ignatius, Archbishop of Antioch* (XII), in Greek and Latin, Antwerp, from the workshop of Christopher Plantin, 1566; — *The Epistles of the Holy Martyr Ignatius, Archbishop of Antioch*. Now at last published, revised, and illustrated with notes, with the Latin interpretation placed alongside the Greek. Edited by Martial Maestraeus, Doctor of Theology. Paris, 1608; — The edition of James Ussher in Greek and Latin, Oxford, 1641. He consulted five *Manuscript Codices*, about which he himself wrote in his Annotations on page 4: "...I diligently compared two Oxford *Manuscripts* (the older one sought from the library of Balliol College, the more recent from Magdalen College) with the printed books. And when I learned that another very ancient copy was preserved in the Library of the distinguished Alexander Petau, Senator of Paris and son of Paul, I followed the benefit of the most kind Claude Sarrau, likewise a Senator of Paris... To this I joined another ancient Interpretation, hitherto unpublished, made more correct by the mutual comparison of two Manuscript Codices."

Isaac Voss was the first to publish in Greek six shorter Epistles of Ignatius (to the *Smyrnaeans, Polycarp, Ephesians, Magnesians, Philadelphians, Trallians*) from the *Medicean Codex 7 Shelf LVII*, with an ancient Latin translation corresponding to the new text, which James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, had published from two manuscripts in 1644 at Oxford. The Letter to the Romans, which was missing in the Greek Manuscript, Voss attempted to restore by following his own ingenuity <note>original: "ingenio duce," suggesting he used his scholarly intuition to fill gaps</note> based on Ussher's ancient Latin version and the longer Greek version; he published it in Amsterdam in 1646: "*The Genuine Epistles of St. Ignatius the Martyr, which now for the first time see the light from the Florentine library. Added are the Epistles of St. Ignatius as they are commonly circulated. To these is added the Epistle of St. Barnabas. An ancient translation has been added to all.*" I am uncertain to whom the glory should be attributed for discovering the shorter version <note>original: "recensionem"</note> in the Medicean Codex—Lucas Holstenius or Isaac Voss. For the former seems to have transcribed it before Voss and translated it into Latin. His autograph <note>a manuscript in the author's own handwriting</note> can be seen in the Barberini Library in Rome. Finally, Thierry Ruinart found the Greek Letter to the Romans corresponding to the ancient Latin version, inserted into the *Acts of the Martyrdom of Ignatius* which are called "sincere" <note>original: "sincerae," meaning authentic or original records</note>, contained in Manuscript 1451 of the Royal Library of Paris (formerly *Colbert Codex 460*); he was the first to publish it in Paris in 1689 in the "*Sincere Acts of the Martyrs*."

An index of editions of the shorter version exists in Jacobson (*Apostolic Fathers*) p. LXIX. The more outstanding among these are those which, following Thomas Smith (Oxford 1709), J. L. Frey prepared after him (Basel 1741),

### THE ACTS OF THE MARTYRDOM OF IGNATIUS.

1) The Acts of the Martyrdom of Ignatius which have become known so far are these:
a) The Acts published in Latin by Ussher from the Caius College Manuscript <term>Codex</term> <note>A "codex" is an ancient manuscript in book form.</note> in 1647.

2) The Ignatian Acts first published by Ruinart are considered genuine by the general consensus of learned men. Smith <gloss>2)</gloss> <note>Thomas Smith, an 18th-century scholar</note> may speak for all:

> "These Acts, which ought to be reprinted, seem to me to be clearly genuine and sincere: although perhaps—though I would hardly affirm it—they may have some blemish mixed in toward the end. However, the Ancient Version, which Lord Ussher of Armagh <note>James Ussher, a famous 17th-century Irish Archbishop</note> published from the Caius codex, as will easily be clear to anyone from a slight comparison, agrees most closely with the Greek Colbert manuscript. Having removed the errors of both, which have crept in here and there, we now give a far more complete edition, since they provide mutual light to one another. Many things in the Acts themselves testify most clearly <gloss>3)</gloss> and place it beyond all doubt that they were described by the companions of Saint Ignatius, who accompanied him from Antioch all the way to Rome, and were present at his final and most glorious struggle; and indeed, they were written not long after his consummation <note>his death/martyrdom</note>, and in the very next year, as seems most likely, while the events and the account of the whole journey remained fresh in the memory of the faithful. That these companions were Philo and Agathopus—whom the most holy Martyr mentions in the *Epistles to the Smyrnaeans* and *to the Philadelphians*, the latter being a Deacon of the Church of Antioch and the former of the Tarsian Church—can or should hardly be doubted by anyone."

Before and after Smith, the same was held by Ussher, Dodwell, Ruinart, Grabe, Tillemont, Pearson, Cotelerius, Mamachi, Galland, Lumper, and, following others, Hefele, who set out to refute the doubts moved against their authenticity since the time of Daillé, Oudin, Heumann, Hilgenfeld <gloss>4)</gloss>, and especially by Uhlhorn <gloss>5)</gloss> <gloss>6)</gloss>. # IV.
## POLYCARP.

1) In the Vatican Library’s Royal Codex 81, after the "Praise of Heron"—or a prayer, if you prefer to call it that—the Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians follows in Latin. This is followed by things pertaining to the life and deeds of Polycarp, composed by an anonymous author from the writings of Irenaeus and Jerome. Since these are the source of everything that has come down to us regarding Polycarp, and since they occasionally depart from the commonly published text of the writers I mentioned, it is pleasing to transcribe them from that source:

> "Polycarp ¹), a disciple of John the Apostle, and ordained by him as bishop of Smyrna, was the leader of all Asia, since he had as teachers and saw several of the Apostles and those who had seen the Lord. He, on account of certain questions concerning the day of **Passover** <note>original: "die Paschae"</note>, during the reign of Emperor Antoninus Pius, while Anicetus was governing the church in the City <note>meaning Rome</note>, came to Rome, where he brought back many of the believers—who had been deceived by the persuasion of Marcion and Valentinus <note>famous early Christian heretics</note>—to the faith. And when Marcion had by chance met him and said: 'Do you recognize ⁵) us?' he replied: 'I recognize the firstborn of the devil.' Later, however, during the reign of Marcus Antoninus and Lucius Aurelio Commodus, in the fourth persecution after Nero ⁶), at Smyrna—while the Proconsul sat in the amphitheater and the whole crowd shouted against him—he was handed over to the fire. He wrote ⁷) to the Philippians a very useful Epistle, which is read today in the assembly of Asia."

<page-num>XXXV</page-num>

-># POLYCARP.<-

"Now, as for this Polycarp—who, praising and confirming the faith of the aforementioned ⁸) Ignatius, exhorts the Philippians to follow it—his outstanding disciple Irenaeus, the illustrious bishop of the most noble city of Lyons <note>original: "Lugdunensis"</note> in Gaul, testifies that he is a witness to the truth and that he always handed down to the church those things which he himself had learned from the Apostles. In his book *Against Heresies* ⁹), Irenaeus writes the following about him": "Polycarp," he says, "was not only instructed by the Apostles and lived among many who had seen the Lord, but he was also appointed Bishop of the Church of Smyrna by the Apostles themselves. We also saw him in our early youth. For he remained in this life a long time, and having reached a very great age, he departed this life through a most glorious and noble martyrdom. He always taught those things which he had learned from the Apostles, which he also handed down to the Church, and which alone are the true teachings. All the churches in Asia bear witness to these things, as do those who have succeeded Polycarp down to the present day. This man is a much more reliable and steadfast witness to the truth than Valentinus and Marcion <note>Valentinus and Marcion were prominent 2nd-century leaders whose teachings were later condemned as heretical by the orthodox Church</note> and the rest of those of perverse mind. He even traveled to Rome during the time of Anicetus <note>Bishop of Rome, approx. 155–166 AD</note> and converted many from the aforementioned heretics back to the Church of God, proclaiming that he had received from the Apostles this one and only truth which he handed down to the Church."

"He lived during the times of the bishops of the Roman Church—namely Clement, Evaristus ¹⁰), Alexander, Sixtus, Telesphorus, Hyginus, Pius ¹¹) and Anicetus—under whom he also suffered his passion <note>meaning his martyrdom</note> in the 6th year of Marcus Aurelius ¹²), four years after the persecution of Nero. That this Irenaeus was truly a listener of this same Polycarp during his childhood, he himself shows most clearly in his own words when writing to a certain arch-heretic <note>original: "haeresiarchen"</note> named Florinus, saying ¹³)": "These dogmas, Florinus, which you assert (I say this with confidence) are not of sound judgment; these dogmas are not in harmony with the faith of the Church. These dogmas not even those heretics who were expelled from the Church could ever bring themselves to commend. These dogmas teach impiety; those holy elders who were before us, and who saw the Apostles (whom you also knew), never handed these down. For I saw you, while I was still a boy, in Asia with Polycarp; you were then faring prosperously within the royal court, yet you were striving to be well-regarded by Polycarp. For I remember the events of that time much more vividly than recent ones—since what we learn as children grows with the soul itself and becomes united to it. Thus, I can even describe to you the very place where the blessed Polycarp sat while he spoke, and his gait, and his face, and his way of life, and even the physical appearance of his body; and also the discourses he gave to the people, and his familiarity with John <note>Referring to John the Apostle</note>, as he used to recount it, as well as with the others who had seen the Lord; and how he remembered their words, and what he had heard from them concerning the Lord—"

<page-num>XXXVII</page-num>

<header>POLYCARP</header>

"...Eusebius <note>A 4th-century church historian</note> copied it, and there can be no doubt about it, unless we also doubt the entire letter at once without any reason."

"You will easily perceive that the arguments which Dallaeus <note>Jean Daillé, a 17th-century French Protestant scholar known for criticizing the authenticity of early church writings</note> brings forward from the letter itself against its integrity are of no importance."

a) "This critic contends that a most fitting conclusion to the letter is found in chapter 12, and therefore the remaining parts were added later. But St. Paul and Clement of Rome also used conclusions of this kind *before* the end of the entire letter: compare Romans 15:33; Ephesians 3:21; and the First Epistle of Clement to the Corinthians, chapters 20, 38, 45, 50, and 58."

b) "If you listen to Dallaeus, the 'imposter' <note>the supposed later forger</note> speaks in such a way as to suggest that Ignatius was still alive at the time these words were written. In chapter 13, he says: 'Concerning Ignatius himself, and those who are with him, let us know whatever you have learned more certainly.' However, the author of the first part of the letter (chapter 9) most clearly affirms that Ignatius was already dead. This is a futile argument. For if those words in chapter 13—which are accused of being a lie—still existed in the original Greek (<note>original: "καὶ περὶ Ἰγνατίου καὶ περὶ τῶν μετ' αὐτοῦ"</note>—'and concerning Ignatius and those with him'), surely no one would contend that they signify or hint that Ignatius was 'still alive.'"

"Most recently, Dr. *Ritschl* (*The Old Catholic Church*, Bonn 1850), in a different manner than Dallaeus, attempted to bring many passages of this letter from various chapters into suspicion of interpolation <note>unauthorized later additions</note>—especially those passages that speak of St. Ignatius and his letters. He relies not on 'arguments,' but on 'arbitrary conjectures.' Dr. *Denzinger* responded to him well and at length in the *Tübingen Theological Quarterly*, 1851, pages 399–409."

---

4. It seems to be hinted at the beginning of chapter 13 that **Polycarp's** Epistle to the Philippians was written not long after the death of Ignatius. However, since nothing but a fragment is preserved in Greek in the manuscripts, it is not sufficiently clear how much trust should be placed in the old Latin version or the Greek text provided by Eusebius (*Church History* III, 36) when it comes to judging the authority and integrity of the original archetype. In the form it is held today, it does not appear entirely free from the pen of an Interpolator, although I would consider such blemishes to be traces of glosses <note>brief marginal explanations that were accidentally copied into the main text by later scribes</note> rather than deliberate, forged interpolations.

*Jacobus Faber* (Stapulensis) <note>Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples, a pioneering French humanist scholar</note> was the first to publish the old Latin version of the entire Epistle in Paris in the year 1498. Among the later editions of this version that I have seen, the *Venetian* edition of 1546 (containing the Epistles of St. Ignatius, Polycarp, Martial, and Anthony the Great) is more accurate.

From a transcript by *Franciscus Turrianus* <note>Francisco Torres</note>, which was granted to *Sirmond* by **Halloix**, the latter first published the Epistle in both Greek and Latin at Douai in 1633. *James Ussher* <note>The famous Irish Archbishop known for his biblical chronology</note> prepared a new and more emended edition in London in 1647. He used another copy derived from *Andreas Schott’s* transcript, which had been described by *Claude Salmasius* in his own hand and shared by *Isaac Vossius* himself along with other papers; Ussher also compared this with the Halloix edition. In the 1672 edition of the *Apostolic Fathers* (page 1019), **Cotelerius** repeated it, adding a new Latin translation. After *Thomas Smith's* 1709 edition, **G. Jacobson**, in addition to our Vatican manuscript 859 and the Florentine 21 (Pluteus VII), used the Parisian Codex 937 (on paper, 16th century) and Codex 20 (Pluteus XXIII, Medici Library, on parchment, 15th century) for his version...

# ACTS OF THE MARTYRDOM OF POLYCARP.

1. The details about Polycarp which we placed above—compiled by an anonymous author from the works of *Irenaeus* <note>A 2nd-century bishop and student of Polycarp</note> and *Jerome* <note>A 4th-century scholar famous for translating the Bible into Latin</note>—make mention of his martyrdom. But a more illustrious testimony is preserved in the Encyclical Letter <note>A circular letter intended for distribution among many churches</note> written in the name of the church of the *Smyrnaeans* concerning this same event. *Eusebius* <note>A 4th-century historian known as the Father of Church History</note> held it in high regard, inserting the greater part of it into his *Ecclesiastical History*.<sup>1</sup>) Nor is the praise for this monument of the past lacking in the judgments of learned men of later times, such as *Valesius* (*the translator of Eusebius*)<sup>2</sup>), *Smith*<sup>3</sup>), and others.

2. Chapter 18 informs us that it was written in the first year after Polycarp's martyrdom. For there, the first *Birthday* of the martyr <note>original: 'Natalis'; in the early church, this term referred to the anniversary of a martyr's death—their 'birthday' into heaven</note> appears not to have been celebrated previously. Its author, near the end of chapter 20, identifies himself as *Evarestus*; in the same place, a certain *Marcus* (called *Martianus* by the *Ancient Interpreter*) is indicated as having delivered the Letter to the people of Philomelium. Because *Irenaeus* possessed a copy of this encyclical, *Gaius*, his disciple, transcribed it, and later so did *Socrates of Corinth* and a certain *Pionius*.<sup>4</sup>)

3. Both those who piously venerate tradition and those who believe that only sound reason should be used as a guide in deciding such matters are convinced that the core of the Letter of the *Smyrnaean* church exists without the stain of interpolation <note>Later unauthorized additions to a text</note>.<sup>5</sup>) However, it seemed to *Heumann* and others that certain brief fragments—especially that little story about the dove<sup>6</sup>) <note>original: 'columba'; a legendary detail claiming a dove emerged from Polycarp's body when he was stabbed</note>—were added at a later time. Nor would I reject the opinion of *Hefele*<sup>7</sup>), who judges another passage thus: "For my part, I consider the final portion of chapter 22, which speaks of *Pionus*, to be spurious and composed by the one who, with evil intent, joined those forged acts of *St. Polycarp* (falsely ascribed to *Pionius*) to the genuine letter of the *Smyrnaeans*. For with the words 'as I shall show in the following [parts]' <note>original: καθὼς δηλώσω ἐν τῷ καθεξῆς</note>, the *Pseudo-Pionius* indicates that he will declare in 'what follows' (that is, in the *Forged Acts* he added) those things which Polycarp manifested to him through a revelation."

4. *Thomas Smith*, when he visited Smyrna, reported the following concerning that amphitheater where Polycarp was consumed by fire, and concerning his tomb<sup>8</sup>): "By the sides of the other gate of the citadel, which faces the East, there still..."

<page-num>XXXIX</page-num>
<header>ACTS OF THE MARTYRDOM OF POLYCARP. HERMAS.</header>

> ...two eagles are seen, the insignia of the Romans, quite large and beautifully drawn. From here, while descending, we entered a large amphitheater toward the Southeast <note>original: 'Notapeliotem'; a term for the South-East wind or direction</note>, where St. Polycarp was crowned with martyrdom, though the stone steps were taken from there by the Turks to decorate their houses. In its sides, two caverns, in which the lions were enclosed, face each other. The tomb of St. Polycarp, which is still preserved on the side of the mountain facing the South-Southeast, is solemnly visited by the Greeks on his feast day, consecrated to his memory, according to the custom that prevails among them. It is situated in a certain small shrine <note>original: 'aedicula'</note>, perhaps a chapel of a church, adjacent to another through which one must pass to get there. In the restoration of this monument—whether it be damaged or profaned by the elements, by the Turks, or by Western Christians who carry away fragments of marble as if they were so many relics—their laudable work is displayed; an earthenware pot is also placed there, into which almost everyone, out of the veneration felt toward the Great Martyr <note>original: 'τὸν Μεγαλομάρτυρα'; a title for high-ranking saints who suffered significant torture</note> who endured death for Christ with invincible presence of mind, is led to throw a few small silver coins <note>original: 'aspros'; the 'asper' or 'akçe' was a silver coin of the Ottoman Empire</note>, so that it may endure for all time.”

Among our own scholars, Constantine Tischendorf <note>A famous 19th-century biblical scholar and manuscript hunter</note> went to see the tomb of Polycarp during his journey to Asia.⁹) He himself testifies that it is not far from the town on the side of the mountain called "Mustasia."

5. The first edition <note>original: 'editio princeps'</note> of the letter from the church of the Smyrneans was published in Greek (incomplete) and Latin by Pierre Halloix in the *Lives of the Oriental Fathers*, Volume I, at Douai in 1633. Of the two ancient versions that survive, you might consider one to be a paraphrase. James Ussher <note>An Irish Archbishop and scholar famous for his biblical chronology</note> published the complete Encyclical Letter in London in 1647 from a certain Baroccian manuscript containing a Greek Menologium <note>A church calendar containing lives of the saints</note>. Cotelerius included it in his 1672 edition of the *Apostolic Fathers*, Thierry Ruinart in the *Authentic Acts of the Martyrs* in 1689, and Smith in his 1709 edition of the *Letters of Ignatius and Polycarp*. William Jacobson, aided by the Baroccian Codex 238 (parchment), the Parisian Codex 1452 (parchment), and the very ancient and highly regarded Imperial-Viennese Codex III of Greek Ecclesiastical History (parchment), deserved well for correcting its text in his 1838 edition of the *Apostolic Fathers* and those following.

## HERMAS.

1. Origen¹) however, guesses that he is that Hermas who is greeted by Paul along with others in the Epistle to the Romans, chapter 16:14, writing: “I think, however, that this Hermas is the writer

<page-num>XL</page-num>
<header>PREFACE.</header>

...of that little book called *The Shepherd*, a writing that seems very useful to me, and, as I think, divinely inspired, and <note>original Latin: "si tamen cui placet, huiusmodi scripturam recipere"</note> "if indeed it pleases anyone to accept such a writing..." In the works of Eusebius <note>A 4th-century bishop and the "Father of Church History"</note> we read almost the same thing: <note>original Greek: "Ἐπεὶ ὁ αὐτὸς Ἀπόστολος..."</note> "Since the same Apostle [Paul], in the greetings at the end of the letter to the Romans, has made mention of Hermas among others, to whom they say the book of the Shepherd belongs." But Eusebius, departing from Origen’s view, adds a little later: "It should be known that this book has been disputed by some, because of whom it cannot be placed among the universally accepted books." Jerome <note>The 4th-century translator of the Vulgate Bible</note> reports it in much the same way as Origen, stating: "They assert that Hermas (whom the Apostle Paul mentions when writing to the Romans: 'Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermas, Patrobas, Hermes, and the brothers who are with them') is the author of the book called *The Shepherd*; and it is already read publicly in certain churches of Greece. It is truly a useful book, and many of the ancient writers have used testimonies from it; but among the Latins, it is almost unknown." Subsequent writers maintained this opinion of the ancients regarding the author of *The Shepherd*. A scribe, seemingly for the sake of recommendation, even placed Jerome's words at the beginning of *The Shepherd* in the 14th-century Vatican Codex 3848, and wrote at the conclusion of the Tenth Similitude:

->“Here ends the book of the Shepherd, the disciple of the blessed Apostle Paul.”<-

There is, however, a monument of ecclesiastical history from approximately the year 170, commonly called the Muratorian Fragment <note>The oldest known list of New Testament books</note>, in which these things are told: "But Hermas wrote *The Shepherd* very recently, in our own times, in the city of Rome, while his brother Pius the bishop was sitting in the chair of the church of the city of Rome. And therefore it ought indeed to be read, but it cannot be published <note>i.e., read officially during liturgy</note> to the people in the church, neither among the Prophets, whose number is complete, nor among the Apostles at the end of times."

Pseudo-Tertullian <note>An anonymous author writing in the style of Tertullian</note> says similar things:
> "And now in the ninth place Hyginus took the chair,
After him then Pius, whose brother by birth was Hermas,
The angelic shepherd, who spoke the words entrusted to him."

The *Book of the Pontiffs* <note>original: 'Liber Pontificalis'; a collection of papal biographies</note> says no differently: "During the episcopate of this man (Pius I), his brother Hermas wrote a book in which a mandate is contained, which the angel of the Lord commanded him when he came to him in the clothing of a shepherd, so that the holy Passover should be celebrated on the Lord’s Day [Sunday]."

2. Anyone who has thoroughly examined the internal condition and doctrine of *The Shepherd* will hardly attribute the work to the Hermas mentioned in the Epistle to the Romans (chapter 16, verse 14). Hence Gratzius states: "The purpose for which this entire work was written can hardly be reconciled with that Hermas at all. Indeed, having looked through..."

<page-num>XLI</page-num>
<header>HERMAS.</header>

In this book, anyone will easily perceive that the author directed his efforts primarily toward the controversy that first arose in the second century. He establishes that even for the most serious sinners—both adulterers and those who have renounced their faith <note>original Latin: *apostatis*</note>—repentance <note>original Latin: *poenitentia*</note> remains available, though only once. It seems truly strange that so little attention was paid to this purpose, which the author clearly reveals; if this observation had been used as a guide, determining the age of the writer would have faced no difficulty. Furthermore, from the very logic and arrangement of this book, it seems clear to us that the author of *The Shepherd* intended to target Montanus <note>the founder of Montanism, a 2nd-century prophetic movement that practiced strict discipline</note> and his followers. For while Montanus, along with his companions Priscilla and Maximilla, boasted of divine revelations which established what they deemed most desirable in Christian discipline, our author intended to oppose them with other revelations given by God." This inquiry is supported by the prologue of the Vatican Codex 3848, where it is written:

### The book of the shepherd, the messenger of repentance. <note>original Latin: *Liber pastoris nuntii poenitentiae*</note>

To which Hermas, however, *The Shepherd* should be attributed is a matter that Hefele <note>Karl Joseph von Hefele, a 19th-century church historian</note> believes we are taught by the Muratorian Fragment <note>the oldest known list of New Testament books, dated to roughly 170 AD</note> and the previously cited passage of Pseudo-Tertullian. He does not doubt that the brother of Pius I, Bishop of Rome, wrote our book.
But Gratz brought forth a heavy argument against that opinion, saying:¹¹) "If the author had indeed been a member of the Latin church and joined to the Roman pontiff by the bond of kinship, his book surely would have been better known to the Latins than to the Greeks."
But indeed: how do we know for certain that the Muratorian Fragment and the passage cited from Pseudo-Tertullian refer to the specific writing that still exists today, and not some other work with the same subject and title? The name of the author is not to be placed by chance, but by a certain internal force and logic of the character or nature of the booklet: **names are not by convention, but by nature.** <note>original Greek: οὐ θέσει τὰ ὀνόματα, ἀλλὰ φύσει</note>
And as for us—to whom Hefele seems to have attributed *The Shepherd* to the brother of Pius I more out of partisan zeal than necessity or strong arguments—we do not hesitate to take the side of Hilgenfeld. For he,¹²) based on the character of the work, was able to define with certainty that the book was written by a layman who favored the "Judaizing" parties <note>Christians who believed in maintaining Jewish customs</note> and who, at the beginning of the second century, sought to reform or renew the church by preaching repentance.
3. *The Shepherd* of Hermas has been divided into three books by its editors. The manuscripts we have seen do not recognize that division. They do, however, present **Visions**, **Mandates**, and **Similitudes** among themselves, though not divided into an equal number of parts.
4. The booklet seems to have been named *The Shepherd* because someone dressed in pastoral clothing acts as the messenger of repentance, addressing Hermas in the **Mandates** and **Similitudes**. Others, following Jachmann,¹³) wish to argue that the ethical character of the work gave rise to that title, just as three of the Apostle Paul’s letters were called "Pastoral."
5. Regarding the authority of *The Shepherd* in theological matters and its ultimate goal, Jachmann (in *The Shepherd of Hermas*, Königsberg 1835) and Hilgenfeld (in *The Apostolic Fathers*, p. 165 ff.) have provided the best discussions.

<page-num>XLII</page-num>
<header>INTRODUCTION.</header>

6. Up until our own day, the Greek text of *The Shepherd* was known only from fragments. These were found scattered and in pieces in the writings of Clement of Alexandria, Origen, and especially in the *Doctrine for Prince Antiochus* <note>A work attributed to Athanasius of Alexandria, though likely by a later author</note>, in the works of Eusebius, and among the works falsely attributed to Athanasius published by Montfaucon. This loss was somewhat compensated for by a complete, ancient Latin version <note>Often called the "Vulgata" or common Latin version of Hermas, not to be confused with the Vulgate Bible</note>, which is more faithful than it is elegant, yet is overflowing in some places with errors and in others with corruptions. We do not know who the translator was. Tertullian, in his own time in Africa, seems to indicate that it was already very well known.

Jacques Lefèvre d'Étaples <note>Original Latin: *Iac. Faber (Stapulensis)*, a pioneering French humanist and theologian</note> was the first to publish *The Shepherd* in Paris in the year 1513, and indeed he did so quite accurately. For although Cotelier <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier, a 17th-century scholar of early Christian texts</note> consulted three manuscripts for his 1672 Paris edition of the Apostolic Fathers, his work must often be considered inferior to the first edition in its critical analysis.<note>*) Cotelier states in his preface: "The Shepherd of Hermas comes forth more corrected and purified from three manuscript codices: first, from the library of Saint-Germain, which is older than the others, of good faith and great authority, but mutilated; second, a more recent one and so different from the printed books that the reader might suspect it contains a different translation from the one commonly published—this is held in the library of Saint-Victor. The third, neither as similar to the first edition as the first manuscript nor as different as the second, I found later among the Discalced Carmelites of the Suburb."</note> Fabricius provided a more corrected version of Cotelier’s edition in his *Codex of the New Testament Apocrypha*, Volume III, published in Hamburg in 1719.

We were the first to bring to light a second Latin translation of *The Shepherd*, and a complete one at that, from the Palatine Codex 150 (dating to the 14th century). It deviates for the better from the common version in a hundred places and is almost always superior in ambiguous cases.

Nevertheless, because both Latin versions are such that the intended meaning can hardly be untangled from the corruption of the text, there remained a great longing to find the Greek text after so many centuries of oblivion. This happened, as it certainly seems, beyond all hope. Indeed, Constantine Simonides <note>A controversial 19th-century Greek paleographer and dealer of manuscripts</note> recently brought *The Shepherd* <note>Original Greek: *τὸν ποιμένα*</note> from Mount Athos to Leipzig, and it was published shortly thereafter: *"The Shepherd of Hermas in Greek. First edited by Rudolph Anger. With a preface and index added by Wilhelm Dindorf. Leipzig, 1856."*

In his Preface (page v and following), Rudolph Anger writes the following regarding the external condition of the Codex: "The source from which we have most recently drawn is twofold: three leaves of a codex recently found in Greece, and a transcript <note>Original Latin: *apographon*</note> of the remaining parts of that same codex. All of these were brought to Leipzig by Constantine Simonides. After their authenticity was carefully investigated, they were acquired for the use of the university library by the illustrious Gersdorf and most generously granted to me for the preparation of this edition."

"In these combined materials, therefore, the entire book of Hermas is contained up to the beginning of chapter 30 of the Ninth Similitude <note>Similitudes, or Parables, are the third major section of the book</note>; nor is anything missing from the entire little work except for the end of this chapter and the final seven chapters. Specifically, those three leaves of the codex itself contain the end of the Mandates <note>The second major section of the book</note> and the greater part of the Similitudes—that is, the material printed from page 51, line 21, to page 75, line 29, and from page 96, line 22, to the end. If these are compared with the scope of the whole book, it appears that the complete codex consisted of ten leaves, with four leaves preceding the Leipzig leaves,"

It focuses specifically on the "Codex Lipsiensis" (Leipzig Codex) and the scholarly debate regarding the reliability of the Greek text discovered in the 19th century compared to older Latin translations.</meta>

<page-num>XLIII</page-num>
<header>HERMAS. XLIII</header>

<note>The following is likely a continuation of a quote describing the physical manuscript</note> "...two intermediate leaves, one placed after the last leaf of the Leipzig manuscript, in which those parts that are now missing would have been written out, barely exceeding the space of a single page."

"Now indeed, those three leaves (which we shall call by the name 'Leipzig Codex') are made of paper, in octavo format <note>A book size resulting from folding a sheet of paper three times to form eight leaves</note>, and written in a larger hand in the beginning or middle of the 15th century."

But concerning the critical value of this same manuscript, G. Dindorf <note>Wilhelm Dindorf (1802–1883), a preeminent German classical scholar known for his editions of Greek authors</note> judges in his second Preface (page XXVI) that its authority should by no means be considered perfect in every respect, especially if you compare it with the Latin translation or measure one against the other. 

> "For (he says), although the Greek text which we are now publishing for the first time <note>original: "editio princeps"</note> is in places more complete than the Latin translation, there is a far greater number of passages in the Greek codex that are either corrupted or lacking. These can be restored to their original state with the help of the Latin translator, who used a Greek copy many centuries older than our own."

These, then, were the editors of the first edition of the Greek Hermas. Now, however, C. Tischendorf <note>Constantine von Tischendorf (1815–1874), the biblical scholar famous for discovering the Codex Sinaiticus</note>, who has served our book most excellently, will not only add the entire Greek text—skilfully recovered by his own labor from the sources—to our Latin texts, but will also demonstrate in a brilliant dissertation what is to be concluded regarding the authority of this Greek text discovered by Simonides <note>Constantine Simonides (1820–1867), a controversial figure who "discovered" many manuscripts, some of which were later accused of being forgeries</note>.

# ON THE GREEK HERMAS OF LEIPZIG.

It is well known among learned men that two manuscripts in particular were recently brought forward in Leipzig by Simonides of Symi <note>Constantine Simonides (1820–1890) was a brilliant but notorious forger of ancient manuscripts who deceived many of the era's greatest scholars</note> which excited much admiration: one was a palimpsest <term>palimpsest: a manuscript page from which the original text has been scraped or washed off so that the parchment could be reused for a new document</term> of Uranius, and the other was of the so-called "Shepherd of Hermas." 

Regarding the former (the Uranius), it was prepared with no small amount of artifice so that it might, for a time, deceive those less skilled in ancient Greek script on parchment and in the whole science of palaeography <term>palaeography: the study of ancient writing systems and the deciphering and dating of historical manuscripts</term>. As soon as we were able to see it, we showed without any doubt that it was a forgery, owing to the poorly mixed forms of the letters and the nature of the parchment, which differed in a strange way from the oldest palimpsest books. This conclusion by us—who alone of all people have searched out and studied with zeal the vast majority of surviving ancient Greek codices and palimpsests throughout the world—could not have happened otherwise; nor, in my opinion, does it deserve great praise <note>Tischendorf is being characteristically confident in his own expertise here</note>. 

In the case of the Hermas, however, that great craftsman from Symi employed a different method of fraud. For while he had brought a smaller portion of this text—three paper leaves from about the fourteenth century—from Mount Athos, he had copied the larger part in his own hand on that same mountain. When asked to sell and hand over both of these precious Greek remains of a most valuable book for publication, he indeed consented. However, he did not hand over anything except those three ancient leaves, neither to the buyer nor the editor, except for what he had transcribed again in Leipzig with incredible treachery from his own copy made on Mount Athos. 

He had two main reasons for this conduct. First, he was seeking material for forging a **new** palimpsest manuscript of Hermas, which he indeed brought to light shortly after with almost equal success and audacity. Second, he thought he should provide against the suspicion raised by the most learned Rudolph Anger: that the Greek of his manuscript was actually translated back from the Latin versions. Therefore, he freely "corrected" whatever seemed likely to confirm such a suspicion. He reworked passages already quoted in Greek by ancient writers—such as Clement, Origen, or the author of the *Doctrine for Antiochus*—so that his text would conform to those ancient fragments. Finally, he filled the gaps in the Greek text (found by comparing it to the Latin) by translating the Latin itself back into Greek, and changed many other things with wonderful boldness. 

Regarding these matters, pertaining both to the fake Uranius and the falsified Hermas—and especially how it came to pass that the long-infamous Simonides was given the opportunity for such great and manifold deception—enough has been explained elsewhere, both by us (having been provoked by his strange insolence) and by Alexander Lycurgus, a learned young man of great promise and the offspring of a most celebrated hero¹). # XLVI

### ON THE SOURCE OF THE GREEK HERMAS OF LEIPZIG.

Beyond those whose duty it is to repair the first edition <term>editio princeps: the first printed edition of a work</term>, we must briefly state why we ourselves took up this cause. For when we were urging a highly esteemed Leipzig bookseller to undertake the printing of an edition of the Apostolic Fathers—prepared over a long time by the most learned Albert Dressel, a man who has served sacred literature well through his investigation of the treasures of Roman libraries—we gave our word, just a few days before the first Greek edition of Hermas appeared, that a Greek text of Hermas would be included in Dressel’s book through our own efforts. We kept this promise all the more gladly because the difficulty of reading the text—which was not sufficiently mastered in various places, neither in the three ancient leaves nor in Simonides’s transcript <note>original: "apographo"</note>—prompted us, being accustomed to handling ancient and unpublished Greek books,³) to provide a text to learned men that had been examined as faithfully as possible. Indeed, it has been clearly proven in many places by a diligent comparison that this accuracy was not achieved even in those parts of the text that could be drawn from the three ancient leaves themselves, with the additional use of Simonides’s transcript.⁴)

# XLVII

### ON THE SOURCE OF THE LEIPZIG GREEK HERMAS.

Now, as I reviewed this Greek text of *The Shepherd of Hermas*—which the first editor <term>editio princeps: the first printed edition of a work</term> believed was an authentic piece of very early Christian writing, even though it came mostly from the forged papers of Simonides—I quickly discovered elements that were deeply troubling. These issues raised a suspicion: while Simonides "found" these Greek passages (and surely did not invent them himself, for was he even capable of reading the manuscript properly?), they likely originated in the Middle Ages rather than the second century. It seemed this was not the original text used by the ancient Latin translator, but rather a later attempt to reconstruct the lost Greek by translating the Latin version back into Greek.

Given the weight of the matter, I felt compelled to share my observations with the first editor, a highly esteemed man. I also pointed out the clarity brought to the question by Albert Dressel’s new revision of the Latin text, which he drew from the Palatine Roman manuscript. The first editor, unsure of how to explain the discrepancies and aware of how much the true text differed from Simonides’s forged copy, did consider my observations significant—the authority of which was greatly increased by the now-famous history of the Simonides fraud in Leipzig <note>5)</note>. Nevertheless, he did not yield to my view. He pushed back using other evidence—such as the word "to dash down" <note>original: "ῥᾶξαι" (rhaxai)</note> in Mandate X, 1 compared to "to break" <note>original: "ῥῆξαι" (rhêxai)</note> found in Clement of Alexandria <note>6)</note>—and pointed to the remarkable agreement between the text brought to us from Mount Athos and the ancient Greek fragments of Hermas cited by the Church Fathers. After carefully weighing these points, I could not be moved to change my opinion. Since the question of the sources and reliability of the Greek text found by Simonides is the most critical issue in this entire case, and since our view differs so significantly from that of the first editor (who sought to prove the ancient origin of that text through a curious and eloquent explanation, believing he had proven it "more than sufficiently"), we shall briefly state our primary arguments—as much as our time allows while currently buried under a mountain of printer's proofs <note>7)</note>.

Looking at the arguments with which the most learned Anger defended the text—
