### XVII. The Saints, especially Abraham, Job, and Moses, as examples of humility.

Let us also become imitators of those who wandered about in goatskins and sheepskins, preaching the coming of Christ; we mean Elijah and Elisha, and also Ezekiel, the prophets; and besides these, those who have been well-attested. Abraham was greatly attested, and was called the "friend of God," and he says, looking intently at the glory of God in humility: "But I am earth and ashes." And furthermore, concerning Job it is thus written: "Job was righteous and blameless, true, god-fearing, keeping himself from all evil." But he, accusing himself, said: "No one is clean from filth, even if his life be but for one day." Moses was called "faithful in all his house," and through his service God judged Egypt through their plagues and torments; but even he, though greatly glorified, did not use boastful words, but said, when an oracle was given to him from the bush: "Who am I, that you send me? I am feeble-voiced and slow-tongued." And again he says: "I am but smoke from a pot."

### XVIII. David as an example of humility.

And what shall we say of David, who was well-attested? To whom God said: "I have found a man after my own heart, David the son of Jesse, in eternal mercy I have anointed him." But he himself says to God: "Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy, and according to the multitude of your compassions blot out my transgression. ## XIX. Imitating these examples, let us seek peace.

The humility¹ and the submissiveness² through obedience of so many and such great men who have thus been attested, has made not only us, but also the generations before us better—even those who received³ His oracles⁴ in fear and truth. Having therefore participated⁶ in many great and glorious deeds, let us run back to the goal of peace delivered to us from the beginning, and let us look steadfastly to the Father and Creator of the whole world, and let us cleave to His magnificent and surpassing gifts of peace and His benefits.⁷ Let us behold Him in our mind, and let us look with the eyes of our soul into His long-suffering will. Let us consider how free from anger⁸ He is toward all His creation.

## XX. The harmony of the world and the order of nature demonstrate that peace and concord are loved by God; from which many benefits flow to us.

The heavens, moving by His management, are subject to Him in peace. Day and night accomplish the course assigned by Him, in no way hindering one another. The sun and the moon, and the choirs of stars, according to His appointment, roll on in harmony without any deviation through the limits assigned to them. The fruitful earth, according to His will, brings forth in its proper seasons an abundance of food for men and beasts and all the living creatures that are upon it, [never] failing...

<header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XX. XXI.</header>

See the philological discussion in the marginal notes regarding whether this refers to "judgments," "regions," or "waves."</note> of the lower worlds are held together by the same ordinances. The basin of the boundless sea, gathered together by His creative action into its reservoirs, does not pass beyond the barriers placed around it, but just as He commanded it, so it acts. For He said: "Thus far you shall come, and your waves shall be broken within you." <note>A reference to Job 38:11.</note> The ocean, impassable for men, and the worlds beyond it <note>original: οἱ μετ᾽ αὐτὸν κόσμοι. The seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter give way to one another in peace. The stations of the winds fulfill their service without hindrance at the proper time; and the ever-flowing springs, created for enjoyment and health, offer their breasts of life to men without fail. Even the smallest of living creatures hold their gatherings in peace and harmony. All these things the great Creator and Master of all commanded to exist in harmony and peace, doing good to all, but most abundantly to us who have fled for refuge to His mercies through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and majesty forever and ever. Amen.

**XXI.** Let us obey God, rather than the authors of sedition, lest His countless benefits turn to our condemnation. Exhortations.

See to it, beloved, that His many benefits do not turn into a judgment for us all, if we do not live worthily of Him and do what is good and pleasing in His sight with harmony. For it says somewhere: *The spirit of the Lord is a lamp searching the hidden chambers of the belly.* <note>Proverbs 20:27.</note> Let us see how near He is, and that nothing escapes Him of our thoughts or the reflections which we make. It is right, therefore, that we should not desert our post from His will. Let us rather offend foolish and senseless men who exalt themselves and boast in the arrogance of their speech, than offend God. Let us reverence the Lord Jesus Christ, whose blood was given for us; let us respect those who lead us; let us honor our elders; let us instruct the young in the discipline of the fear of God; let us direct our women toward that which is good. Let them exhibit a character of purity worthy of love; let them demonstrate a sincere will of gentleness; let them make the moderation of their tongue manifest through their voice; let them bestow their love not according to personal preferences, but equally to all who holily fear God. Let your children partake of the discipline that is in Christ; let them learn how much humility prevails with God, what [pure] love [can do]...

The mass of the immense sea, gathered into heaps by His arrangement, does not pass the barriers placed around it, but just as He commanded it, so it does. For He said: "Thus far you shall come, and within yourself your waves shall be broken." The ocean, impassable to men, and the worlds that are beyond it, are governed by the same dispositions of the Lord. The seasons of spring, summer, autumn, and winter succeed one another in peace. The stations of the winds perform their service without hindrance at their proper time; the perennial springs also, made for use and health, offer their breasts without fail to sustain the life of men; and even the smallest animals form their gatherings in peace and harmony. All these things the great Creator and Lord of all commanded to be done in harmony and peace, doing good to all, but most abundantly to us who have fled for refuge to His mercies through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and majesty forever and ever. Amen.

XXI. Let us obey God, not the authors of sedition, lest His innumerable benefits turn to our condemnation. Exhortations.

See, beloved, lest His benefits, which are many, turn to the condemnation of us all, unless we live worthily of Him and do what is good and pleasing in His sight with harmony. For it is said in a certain place: "The spirit of the Lord is a lamp searching the hidden chambers of the belly." <note>Proverbs 20:27</note> Let us consider how near He is, and that nothing of our thoughts or the conversations we have is hidden from Him. It is right, therefore, that we should not be deserters from His will. Let us rather offend foolish and senseless men, who are lifted up and boasting in the pride of their speech, than offend God. Let us reverently worship the Lord Jesus Christ, whose blood was given for us; let us respect those set over us; let us honor our elders; let us instruct the young in the discipline of the fear of God; let us direct our wives toward that which is good. Let them show forth their lovely habits of purity, demonstrate the pure and sincere will of their gentleness, make the moderation of their tongue manifest by their voice, and exhibit their charity without partiality to all who holily fear God. Let your children be partakers of the discipline of Christ; let them learn how much humility prevails with God, what chaste love can do with God, how the fear of Him—

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XXI. XXII. XXIII.

[Purity] is powerful before God, and how the fear of Him is good and great and saves all those who live holily within it with a pure mind. For He is a searcher <note>original: "Ereunētēs"</note> of thoughts and desires; His breath is in us, and when He wills, He shall take it away. <note>original: "anelei"</note>

## XXII. These exhortations are strengthened by Christian faith, which proclaims the misery of sinners.

And all these things the faith in Christ confirms; for He Himself, through the Holy Spirit, thus invites us: "Come, children, listen to me, I will teach you the fear of the Lord. Who is the man that desires life, loving to see good days? Keep your tongue from evil, and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil, and do good. Seek peace, and pursue it. The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and His ears are open to their prayer; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy the memory of them from the earth. The righteous cried out, and the Lord heard him, and delivered him out of all his troubles. Many are the scourges of the sinner, but mercy shall encompass those who hope in the Lord."

## XXIII. Be humble. Believe that Christ is coming.

The merciful in all things and beneficent Father has compassion <note>original: "splangchna," literally 'bowels' or 'inner organs,' the seat of deep emotion</note> upon those who fear Him, and kindly and lovingly bestows His favors upon those who approach Him with a sincere mind. Therefore, let us not be double-minded, <note>original: "dipsychōmen"</note> nor let our soul be deceived <note>original: "endallesthō"</note> by His surpassing and glorious gifts. Let this scripture be far from us, where it says: "Wretched are the double-minded, those who doubt in their soul, who say: 'These things we heard even in the days of our fathers, and behold, we have grown old, and none of these things has happened to us.'" O foolish ones! Compare yourselves to a tree; take a vine. First it sheds its leaves, then a shoot comes, then a leaf, then a flower, and after these a sour grape, then the ripened cluster. You see that in a short time the fruit of the tree reaches maturity. In truth, quickly and suddenly shall His will be perfected, the Scripture also bearing witness: "For He shall come quickly, and shall not delay; and suddenly the Lord shall come to His temple, even the Holy One whom you expect."

->I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XXIV. XXV. XXVI. XXVII.<-

XXIV. God continually shows us the future resurrection in nature. <note>original Latin: "Futuram resurrectionem Deus continue nobis in natura ostendit."</note>

Let us consider, beloved, how the Master <note>Greek: *despotes*, a term for God emphasizing absolute authority</note> continually proves to us that there will be a future resurrection, of which He made the Lord Jesus Christ the first-fruits by raising Him from the dead. Let us look, beloved, at the resurrection that occurs according to the seasons. Day and night show us a resurrection: the night falls asleep, the day rises; the day departs, and night comes on. Let us behold the fruits: in what manner does the sowing of a seed take place? The sower went forth and cast it into the earth, and when the seeds were cast—which fall into the earth dry and bare—they dissolve. Then, out of their dissolution, the majesty of the Master's providence raises them up, and from the one seed many grow and bring forth fruit.

XXV. The Phoenix is an image of our resurrection. <note>original Latin: "Phoenix resurrectionis nostrae imago."</note>

Let us behold the strange sign that occurs in the eastern lands, that is, in the regions near Arabia. For there is a bird which is called the Phoenix. This creature, being the only one of its kind, lives for five hundred years; and when it draws near the time of its dissolution in death, it makes for itself a coffin of frankincense and myrrh and other spices, into which, when its time is fulfilled, it enters and dies. But as the flesh decays, a certain worm is engendered, which, being nurtured by the moisture of the dead creature, puts forth wings. Then, having grown strong, it takes up that coffin where the bones of its predecessor are, and carrying them, it journeys from the land of Arabia as far as Egypt, to the city called Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in ancient Egypt</note>. And in the day-time, in the sight of all, it flies onto the altar of the sun and places them there, and then starts back on its return. The priests then inspect the records of the dates and find that it has come when the five hundredth year is completed.

XXVI. We shall rise again, therefore, as the Holy Scripture also witnesses. <note>original Latin: "Resurgemus igitur, quod et S. Scriptura testatur."</note>

Do we then think it a great and wonderful thing if the Creator of all things shall bring about the resurrection of those who have served Him holily in the confidence of a good faith, when He shows us the greatness of His promise even through a bird? For He says in a certain place: *And You shall raise me up, and I will confess to You.* And again Job says: *And You shall raise up this flesh of mine, which has endured all these things.*

XXVII. In the hope of resurrection let us cleave to God, the almighty and all-knowing. <note>original Latin: "Spe resurrectionis adhaereamus Deo, omnipotenti et omniscienti."</note>

With this hope, then, let our souls be bound to Him who is faithful in His promises and righteous in His judgments. He who commanded—

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XXIV. XXV. XXVI. XXVII.
<page-num>73</page-num>

XXIV. *God continually shows us the future resurrection in nature.*

Let us consider, beloved, how the Lord continually shows us the future resurrection, of which He made the Lord Jesus Christ the first-fruits <note>original: "primitias"; a biblical term referring to the first harvest offered to God, signifying more is to come</note> by raising Him from the dead. Let us look, beloved, at the resurrection that occurs at all times. Day and night show us a resurrection; the night lies down to sleep, the day rises; the day departs, the night sets in and follows. Let us look at the fruits of the earth; how the sowing of the grain takes place. The sower went forth and cast the seed into the earth, and once the seeds—which fell into the earth naked and dry—are cast, they dissolve. Then, from that dissolution, the great power of divine providence raises them up, and from one, many grow and produce fruit.

XXV. *The Phoenix is an image of our resurrection.*

Let us contemplate the marvelous sign that happens in eastern regions, namely in Arabia and the neighboring lands. There is a bird called the Phoenix. Being the only one of its kind, it lives for five hundred years, and when it is time for it to be dissolved by death, it builds itself a casket out of frankincense, myrrh, and other spices, into which it enters when its time is fulfilled, and lays down its life. As its flesh decays, a certain worm is born, which, nourished by the moisture of the dead animal, grows feathers. Later, when its strength has increased, it carries the casket in which the bones of its parent are stored, and bearing them, it completes the journey from the Arabian region to Egypt and the city called Heliopolis <note>The "City of the Sun" in ancient Egypt</note>. And while all are watching during the day, it flies down and places them upon the altar of the Sun, and then returns to where it came from. The priests then inspect the records of the dates and find that it has returned exactly when the five hundredth year was completed.

XXVI. *We shall rise again, therefore, as Holy Scripture also testifies.*

Shall we then consider it a great and wonderful thing if the Creator of all things makes those rise again who have served Him religiously in the confidence of good faith, when He reveals the magnificence of His promise to us even through a bird? For He says in one place: "You shall raise me up, and I will praise You;" and: "I laid down and slept; I awoke, because You are with me." <note>original: "quia tu mecum es"; a variation of Psalm 3:5</note> And again Job says: "And You shall raise up this flesh of mine, which has endured all these things."

XXVII. *By the hope of resurrection, let us cling to God, the almighty and all-knowing.*

Therefore, let our souls be bound by this hope to Him who is faithful in His promises and just in His judgments. He who forbade lying is much less—

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XXVII. - XXVIII. XXIX.

<note>original: "ψεύδεσθαι" (to lie)</note> not to lie, much more will He Himself <note>original: "αὐτὸς"</note> not lie; for nothing is impossible with God, except to lie. Who <note>original: "Τίς"</note> shall say to Him: "What have You done?" or who shall withstand the might of His power? Day unto day pours forth speech, and night unto night proclaims knowledge; and there are no words or speeches whose voices are not heard.

## XXVIII. God sees all things, therefore let us flee from sins.

Since all things, then, are seen and heard, let us fear Him and leave behind the foul desires of evil works, so that by His mercy we may be shielded from the coming judgments. For where can any of us flee from His mighty hand? And what world shall receive any of those who desert from Him? For the Writing <note>original: "γραφεῖον" - likely referring to the Hagiographa or the Psalms</note> says somewhere: "Where shall I go, and where shall I be hidden from Your face? If I ascend into heaven, You are there; if I go to the ends of the earth, there is Your right hand; if I make my bed in the abysses, there is Your Spirit." Where, then, shall one go, or where shall one run away from Him who encompasses all things?

## XXIX. And let us approach God in holiness of heart.

Let us therefore approach Him in holiness of soul, lifting up pure and undefiled hands to Him, loving our gentle and compassionate Father, who made us a portion of His choice <note>original: "ἐκλογῆς"</note> for Himself. For so it is written: "When the Most High divided the nations, as He scattered the sons of Adam, He set the boundaries of the nations according to the number of the angels of God. His people Jacob became the Lord's portion, and Israel the cord of His inheritance." And in another place He says: "Behold, the Lord takes for Himself a nation from the midst of nations, just as a man takes the first-fruits of his threshing floor; and from that nation shall come forth the Holy of Holies."

<header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XXX. XXXI. XXXII.</header>

<header>XXX. Let us do what is pleasing, and flee what is displeasing to God, so that we may be blessed.</header>
Being therefore a portion of the Holy One, let us do all things that pertain to holiness, fleeing slanders, foul and impure <note>original: "anagnous"</note> embraces, drunkenness and innovations <note>likely referring to social or religious upheavals</note>, and abominable lusts, detestable adultery, and loathsome pride <note>original: "hyperēphaniān"</note>. For God, it says, "resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." Let us therefore cleave to those to whom grace has been given by God. Let us clothe ourselves in harmony <note>original: "homonoian"</note>, being humble-minded and self-controlled, keeping ourselves far from all whispering and slander, being justified <note>original: "dikaioumenoi"</note> by works and not by words. For He says, "He who speaks much shall also hear much in return; or does the talkative man think he is righteous? Blessed is the one born of woman who is short-lived. Do not be wordy among us." Let our praise be in God, and not from ourselves; for God hates those who praise themselves. Let the testimony of our good deeds be given by others, just as it was given to our righteous fathers. Boldness, arrogance, and audacity belong to those cursed by God; but gentleness, humility, and meekness are with those blessed by God.

<header>XXXI. Let us see by what means we may obtain the divine blessing.</header>
Let us therefore cleave to His blessing, and let us see what the ways of blessing are. Let us unroll the records of what has happened from the beginning. For what reason was our father Abraham blessed? Was it not because he wrought righteousness <note>original: "dikaiosynē"</note> and truth through faith <note>original: "pisteōs"</note>? Isaac, with confidence, knowing what was to come, cheerfully became a sacrifice. Jacob with humility departed from his own land because of his brothers, and went to Laban and served, and there was given to him the twelve-sceptered <note>original: "dōdekaskēptron"; referring to the twelve tribes</note> sovereignty of Israel.

<header>XXXII. Not through ourselves nor through our works, but through faith are we justified.</header>
If anyone considers these things with sincerity, one by one, he will recognize the magnificence of the gifts given by Him. For from him <note>Jacob/Israel</note> come all the priests and Levites who minister at the altar of God; from him comes the Lord Jesus according to the flesh; from him come kings and rulers and leaders, through Judah; and his other scepters <note>tribes</note> are in no small glory, as God promised: "Your seed shall be as the stars of heaven." All these, therefore, were glorified and magnified, not through themselves or their own works, or the righteous doing which they performed, but through His will. And we...

XXX. Let us do what is pleasing, and flee what is displeasing to God, so that we may be blessed.

Since we are therefore a portion of the Holy One, let us do all things that pertain to holiness, avoiding slanders, impure and unchaste embraces, drunkenness, the pursuit of innovations <note>original: "novarum rerum studia" — often implying political agitation or social upheaval</note>, abominable lusts, detestable adultery, and cursed pride. For God, it says, resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble. Let us therefore cling to those to whom grace has been granted by God. Let us clothe ourselves in harmony, being humble and self-controlled, keeping far from all whispering and slander, justifying ourselves by works and not by words. For it says: "He who speaks much shall also hear much in return; or does a talkative man think himself to be righteous? Blessed is the one born of woman who is short-lived; do not be excessive in words." <note>A paraphrase of Job 11:2-3 from the Septuagint version</note> Let our praise be in God, and not from ourselves; for God hates those who praise themselves. Let the testimony of our good actions be rendered by others, just as it was rendered to our fathers, who were righteous. Rashness, arrogance, and audacity are cursed by God; but moderation, humility, and gentleness are for those blessed by God.

XXXI. Let us see by what means we may obtain the divine blessing.

Let us therefore adhere firmly to His blessing, and let us see what the ways of blessing are. Let us recall to mind the things that have happened from the beginning. For what reason was Abraham our father blessed? Was it not because he wrought righteousness and truth through faith? Isaac, with confidence, as if knowing what was to come <margin>Wocher prefers to read <note>original Greek: "as one knowing"</note></margin>, willingly became a sacrifice. <page-num>78</page-num>
# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. CHAPTERS XXXII. XXXIII. XXXIV.

Therefore, having been called through His will in Christ Jesus, <note>original: "διὰ θελήματος αὐτοῦ ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ κληθέντες"</note> we are not justified through ourselves, nor through our own wisdom or understanding or piety or works which we have wrought in holiness of heart, but through faith, <note>Clement emphasizes that even "holy" works do not earn salvation; it is a gift of God's sovereign will.</note> through which the Almighty God has justified all those from the beginning; to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## XXXIII. We must not truly abandon good works and love. God Himself is the example to us of good works.

What then shall we do, brothers? Shall we become idle from doing good, and shall we abandon love? May it never be! May the Master <note>original: "δεσπότης" (Despotēs) — a term for God emphasizing absolute ownership and authority.</note> never allow this to happen to us, but let us hasten with intensity and readiness to accomplish every good work. For the Creator and Master of all things Himself rejoices in His works. For by His most mighty power He established the heavens, and by His incomprehensible understanding He set them in order; and He separated the earth from the water surrounding it, and fixed it upon the secure foundation of His own will; and the animals that roam upon it He commanded to exist by His own decree; having pre-fashioned the sea and the creatures within it, He enclosed them by His own power. Above all, with His holy and faultless hands, He formed man, the most excellent and greatest in terms of intellect, the very impress of His own image. For thus God says: "Let us make man according to our image and according to our likeness; and God made man, male and female He made them." Having finished all these things, He praised them and blessed them and said: "Increase and multiply." We see, then, that all the righteous were adorned with good works, and the Lord Himself, having adorned Himself with works, rejoiced. Having this pattern, <term>hypogrammon: a writing-copy or model used by students to trace letters</term> let us approach His will without hesitation; with all our strength let us work the work of righteousness.

## XXXIV. Great is the reward with God for good works. Joined in harmony, let us pray for it from the Lord.

The good laborer receives the bread of his work with boldness; the slothful and careless one does not look his employer in the eye. It is necessary, therefore, that we be eager in well-doing, for from Him are all things. For He foretells to us: "Behold, the Lord, and His reward is before His face, to render to each according to his work." He exhorts us, therefore, with all our heart toward Him,

->I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XXXII. XXXIII. XXXIV.<-

We therefore, having been called through His will in Christ Jesus, are not justified through ourselves, nor through our own wisdom or understanding or piety or the works which we have wrought in holiness of heart, but through faith, through which the Almighty God has justified all from the beginning; to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

XXXIII. *But let us not abandon good works and charity. God Himself is the example of good works to us.*

What then shall we do, brothers? Shall we cease from good works, and abandon charity? May the Lord by no means permit this to happen among us, but let us hasten with diligence and eagerness of mind to accomplish every good work. For the Creator <note>original: "opifex"</note> and Lord of all things Himself exults in His works. For by His supreme and greatest power He established the heavens, and by His incomprehensible wisdom He adorned them; He also separated the earth from the water which surrounds it, and firmly established it upon the immovable foundation of His own will; and the animals which move upon it, He commanded to exist by His word; the sea also, and the animals that live within it, having first created them, He enclosed by His power. In addition to these, He formed man—the most excellent being and the highest in dignity of intellect, the very stamp of His own image—with His sacred and untainted hands. For thus God says: "Let us make man according to our image and likeness; and God created man, male and female He created them." Therefore, when He had finished all these things, He praised and blessed them, and said: "Increase and multiply." Let us see how all the righteous have been adorned with good works; even the Lord Himself, adorning Himself with works, rejoiced. Having this example, therefore, let us approach His will without hesitation, and with all our strength let us work the work of righteousness.

XXXIV. *A great reward for good works is with God. Joined in harmony, let us pray for it from the Lord.*

The good laborer receives the bread of his labor with a good spirit; but the sluggish and remiss one does not dare to look at his employer <note>original: "locatorem"</note>. It is necessary, therefore, for us to be prompt in spirit toward doing good; for all things are provided by God. For He foretells to us: "Behold the Lord, and His reward is before Him, to render to each according to his work." Therefore, by exhorting us, He turns us to Him with our whole heart, so that we may not be sluggish or lazy toward any work...

How blessed and wonderful are the gifts of God, beloved. ### XXXVI. All blessedness is bestowed upon us through Christ.

## XXXVI. All blessedness is bestowed upon us through Christ.

This is the way, beloved, in which we find our salvation: Jesus Christ, the High Priest <term>pontificem; the chief priest or mediator</term> of our offerings, the protector and helper of our weakness. Through him we look upward to the heights of heaven; through him we behold as in a mirror his spotless and exalted face; through him the eyes of our hearts are opened; through him our foolish and darkened mind buds forth anew into his admirable light; through him the Lord willed that we should taste immortal knowledge; who, being the brightness of the majesty of God, is so much greater than the angels as he has inherited a more excellent name. # I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XXXVII. XXXVIII. XXXIX.

...they perform the things commanded of them in a submissive manner. Not all are generals <note>original: "ἔπαρχοι" (eparchoi) - high-ranking officials or governors, here used in a military sense</note>, nor commanders of a thousand, nor commanders of a hundred, nor commanders of fifty, and so on; but each one in his own rank performs the things commanded by the king and the leaders. The great cannot exist without the small, nor the small without the great; there is a certain mixture in all things, and in these there is a practical use. Let us take our own body as an example. The head is nothing without the feet, and likewise the feet are nothing without the head; even the smallest members of our body are necessary and useful to the whole body. Rather, all parts work together <note>original: "συμπνεῖ" (sympnei) - literally "breathe together," implying a harmonious conspiracy of action</note> and use a single subjection for the preservation of the whole body.

## XXXVIII. Let the members of the church submit themselves, and let no one exalt himself; for we have received all good things from God.

Therefore, let our whole body be saved in Christ Jesus, and let each be subject to his neighbor, according to the special gift <term>charisma: a spiritual gift or grace bestowed by God</term> placed upon him. Let the strong not neglect the weak, and let the weak respect the strong; let the rich provide for the poor, and let the poor give thanks to God, because He gave him someone through whom his need might be supplied. Let the wise man manifest his wisdom not in words, but in good works; let the humble-minded man not bear witness to himself, but let him allow himself to be witnessed to by another. Let him who is pure in the flesh <insert>remain so</insert> and not be boastful, knowing that it is another who provides him with his self-control. Let us consider, brothers, from what matter we were made, who and what kind of creatures we were when we entered into the world, as if from a grave and from darkness. He who made and fashioned us brought us into His world, having prepared His benefits for us before we were even born. Having all these things from Him, we ought to give thanks to Him for everything; to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

## XXXIX. There is no reason for us to be exalted.

"Foolish, senseless, stupid, and uninstructed men mock and deride us, wishing to exalt themselves in their own conceits. For what can a mortal do? Or what is the strength of one born of the earth? For it is written: 'There was no shape before my eyes, but I heard a breeze and a voice: What then? Shall a mortal be pure before the Lord? Or is a man blameless in his works? If He does not trust His own servants, and has noticed some crookedness in His angels? Even the heaven is not pure in His sight; how much less those who dwell in houses of clay, of which we ourselves are made from the same mud. He struck them like a moth, and from morning until evening they no longer exist; because they could not help themselves, they perished. He breathed on them, and they died, because they had no wisdom.' But call out, if anyone [shall answer] you..."

### XL. Let us preserve the order in the church established by God.

Since these things are clear to us, and we have looked into the depths of the divine knowledge <note>original: "theia gnosis"</note>, we ought to do all things in order, whatever the Master <note>original: "despotes," a term for God as absolute ruler</note> has commanded us to perform at appointed times. ### XLI. Continuation.

Those, therefore, who do anything contrary to the fitting of His will, have death as their punishment. See, brothers, by as much as we have been deemed worthy of greater knowledge, by so much more are we subject to danger.

### XL. Let us keep the order established by God in the church.

Since, therefore, these things are manifest to us, and we have looked into the depths of divine knowledge, we ought to do all things in order, which the Lord has commanded us to perform at appointed times. Specifically, He commanded that the offerings and sacred offices be performed, and not to be done thoughtlessly or in disorder, but at appointed times and hours. Where and by whom He wishes them to be celebrated, He Himself has defined by His own supreme will, so that all things, being done religiously according to His good pleasure, might be acceptable to His will. Those, therefore, who make their offerings at the assigned times are accepted and blessed; for following the commands of the Lord, they do not go astray. Those, therefore, who do anything contrary to what is agreeable to His will, are punished with the penalty of death. You see, brothers, by how much greater knowledge we have been deemed worthy, by so much the more are we exposed to danger.

# FIRST EPISTLE OF CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. CHAPTERS 42, 43.

[The Apostles received the Gospel for us] from God, and the apostles from Christ; both, therefore, came in due order by the will of God. Having therefore received their instructions, and being fully assured <note>original: πληροφορηθέντες</note> through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and established in the word of God, with the full assurance of the Holy Spirit, they went forth preaching the good news that the kingdom of God was about to come. Preaching then through countries and cities, they appointed <note>original: καθίστανον</note> their first-fruits—having tested them by the Spirit—to be bishops <note>term: episcopos; literally "overseers," the early title for church leaders</note> and deacons <note>term: diaconos; "servants" or "ministers"</note> of those who were to believe. And this was no new thing; for indeed, for a long time it had been written concerning bishops and deacons. For thus says the Scripture in a certain place: "I will appoint their bishops in righteousness, and their deacons in faith." <note>A free citation of Isaiah 60:17</note>

## XLIII. Moses of old settled a contention that arose concerning the priestly dignity.

And what wonder is it, if those in Christ who were entrusted by God with such a work, appointed the aforementioned persons? Since even the blessed Moses, "a faithful servant in all his house," noted down in the sacred books all the things commanded him; and the rest of the prophets followed him, bearing witness together to the laws enacted by him. For when a jealousy arose concerning the priesthood, and the tribes were quarreling as to which of them should be adorned with that glorious name, he commanded the twelve tribal leaders to bring him rods, inscribed with the name of each tribe. And taking them, he bound them, and sealed them with the rings of the tribal leaders, and deposited them in the Tabernacle of Witness upon the table of God. And having closed the Tabernacle, he sealed the keys, as he had the rods, and said to them: "Brethren, the tribe whose rod shall blossom, this one has God chosen to be priests and to minister to Him." And when morning came, he called together all Israel, the six hundred thousand men, and showed the seals to the tribal leaders, and opened the Tabernacle of Witness and brought out the rods. And the rod of Aaron was found not only to have blossomed, but also to be bearing fruit. What do you think, beloved? Did not Moses know beforehand that this would happen? He certainly knew it; but that there might be no disorder <note>original: ἀκαταστασία</note> in Israel, he acted in this way, so that the name of the true and only God might be glorified, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XLII. XLIII.

This was done; and both things occurred in an orderly manner according to the will of God. Therefore, having received their commands and being fully convinced through the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, and confirmed by the word of God, they went forth with the certain confidence of the Holy Spirit, announcing the coming of the kingdom of God. Preaching through regions and cities, they appointed their first converts—having tested them by the Spirit—to be <term>bishops</term> <note>overseers</note> and <term>deacons</term> <note>ministers/servants</note> of those who were to believe. ## XLIII. Moses of old settled the contention that arose concerning the priestly dignity.

When he had received them, he bound them into a bundle, sealed them with the rings of the leaders of the tribes, and deposited them in the <term>tabernacle of testimony</term> <note>the portable earthly dwelling place of God</note> upon the table of God. He certainly knew it; but so that sedition might not arise in the people of Israel, he acted in this way, so that the name of the "true and only God" <note>John 17:3</note> might be glorified, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen!

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XLIV.

**XLIV. The institution of the Apostles, so that no contention should arise concerning the priestly office.**
**He has wickedly cast out from their office those who were lawfully elected and living rightly.**

And our Apostles knew through our Lord Jesus Christ that there would be strife over the name of the office of bishop. <note>original: "ἐπισκοπῆς" (episkopēs). In this early period, the terms for "bishop" and "elder" were often used interchangeably.</note> For this reason, therefore, having received perfect foreknowledge, they appointed those mentioned before and afterwards gave a codicil <note>original: "ἐπινομή" (epinome). A difficult term here translated as a legal provision or rule for succession.</note> so that, if they should fall asleep, other approved men might succeed to their ministry. Those, therefore, who were appointed by them, or afterwards by other eminent men with the consent of the whole Church, and who have ministered blamelessly to the flock of Christ with humility, quietly and without vulgarity, and who have been well-reported of by all for a long time—these men we consider to be unjustly removed from their ministry. For it will be no small sin for us if we cast out from the office of bishop those who have blamelessly and holily offered the gifts. <note>original: "τὰ δῶρα" (ta dōra). Likely referring to the elements of the Eucharist or the prayers of the congregation.</note> Blessed are those elders <note>original: "πρεσβύτεροι" (presbyteroi).</note> who have gone before, who had a fruitful and perfect departure; for they do not fear that anyone should remove them from the place established for them. For we see that you have removed some who were conducting themselves well from the ministry which they had honored blamelessly.

Chapter XLIV. 1) <note>original: "In Ms. siglum XY = Χριστοῦ"</note> In the manuscript, the abbreviation XY stands for "of Christ."
2) That is, either concerning the episcopal dignity, so that the "name" signifies the "rank"; or concerning the thing itself, the office of the Apostles, denoting the matter by the name. — Hammond.
3) This means the Bishops and Deacons. The Apostles appointed overseers and ministers for those who were to believe, equally in the Roman and Corinthian Churches as in others. In which matter it should be observed in passing that Peter's part and authority were no greater than the others'; for Clement commemorates "any" Apostles and calls them "our" Apostles. — Gul. Burton. Compare above, chapter 42.
4) "Afterwards" <note>original: "μεταξὺ" (metaxy)</note> = "thereafter," as used later, and in Acts 13:42, Epistle of Barnabas ch. 13, note 9, and elsewhere.
5) "Epinome" <note>original: "Ἐπινομή"</note>, derived from "nemo" <note>original: "νέμω" (to distribute)</note>, is used among the ancients regarding the right of pasturing on another's land and the spreading of fire [Stephanus's Thesaurus]. But that word can perhaps also be derived from "nomos" <note>original: "νόμος" (law)</note>, so that it signifies a precept or ordinance. Hammond and Wotton translated it: "series" or "mode of succession"; relying on the fact that the word "epinemo" <note>original: "ἐπινέμω"</note> sometimes signifies "to enroll," i.e., to add to a catalogue. To Hesychius, "Epinomos" <note>original: "Ἐπίνομος"</note> = "heir" <note>original: "κληρονόμος"</note>, supported by which Rothe (Anfang. p. 374 ff.) renders it: "testamentary disposition," as if the Apostles, by the power of a testament, had ordained for themselves (the Apostles) that upon their death <note>original: "ἐὰν κοιμηθῶσιν"</note> the duty of choosing elders and deacons (bishops in the broader sense) ought to pass to other approved and excellent men (i.e., Bishops in our sense). For Rothe dreams that only shortly before their death did the Apostles institute the order of the Episcopate, whereas previously there existed only Elders (who were also called Bishops) and Deacons. But we do not care to agree with the learned man, as is clear from our Latin version. Nolte conjectures: "they gave a law further." In a fragment of an old Latin version in Pitra, vol. 1, it is read: "holding this form," where "epinome" = "form" = "precept." In the 4th edition, Lipsius exploded the fictions of Rothe's opinion, explaining the passage thus: "Clement relates that elders and deacons were appointed by the apostles as soon as they laid the first foundations of the church; then, lest internal contentions should arise concerning the new office, the same apostles added a precept that other approved men should succeed these elders and deacons." From this very fact, that the ecclesiastical office draws its origin from the apostles, it clearly appears to be a sin if anyone [removes] those who were appointed either by the apostles themselves or by other approved men at the command of the apostles.

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS XLIV.

XLIV. The institution of the Apostles, so that no contention should arise concerning the priestly office. You have unjustly cast out from their ministry those who were lawfully elected and living uprightly.

Our Apostles also knew through our Lord Jesus Christ that there would be strife over the title of Oversight <note>original: "Episcopatus"; referring to the office of a bishop or overseer</note>; for this reason, therefore, being endowed with perfect foreknowledge, they appointed the aforementioned persons, and subsequently gave an order <note>original: "ordinationem"</note> so that, when they should die, other approved men might succeed to their ministry. Those, therefore, who were appointed by them, or afterwards by other eminent men with the consent of the whole church, and who have blamelessly served the flock of Christ with humility, quietly, and not meanly, and who for a long time have received a noble testimony from everyone—these men we think are being unjustly cast out from the oversight <note>original: "episcopatu"</note>, though they have offered the gifts <note>referring to the elements of the Eucharist</note> holily and without reproach. Blessed are the elders <note>original: "presbyteri"</note> who have finished their course before now, who have obtained a fruitful and perfect departure; for they do not fear that anyone should remove them from the place appointed for them. For we see that you have removed some who were living honorably from the office which they were performing blamelessly and with honor.

From this interpretation even those differ but little who recently judged that the word **succession** <note>original Greek: "ἐπίνομην"</note> ought to be changed. <header>I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XLV. XLVI.</header>

<header>XLV. It is the way of the wicked to vex and cast down the just.</header>

Be contentious, brothers, and zealous about things that do <insert>not</insert> lead to salvation. <note>original: "Φιλόνεικοι... περὶ [μὴ] ἀνηκόντων εἰς σωτηρίαν." Clement is likely using irony here, or the "not" is a later correction to suggest they are wasting energy on trivial disputes.</note> Look deep into the scriptures, the true utterances of the Holy Spirit. You know that nothing unjust or forged has been written in them. You will not find that righteous men were ever cast out by holy men. The righteous were indeed persecuted, but by the lawless; they were imprisoned, but by the unholy; they were stoned by the rebellious; they were killed by the vile and those who had taken up an unjust jealousy. These things they endured gloriously. For what shall we say, brothers? Was Daniel cast into the lions' den by those who feared God? Or were Ananias, Azarias, and Misael <note>These are the Greek/Hebrew names for Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.</note> shut up in the furnace of fire by those who practiced the magnificent and glorious worship of the Most High? Far be it from being so! Who then were the ones who did these things? The hateful and those full of all wickedness were stirred up to such a pitch of fury that they inflicted torture upon those who served God with a holy and blameless purpose; they did not know that the Most High is the champion and defender of those who serve His all-virtuous name with a pure conscience; to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen. But those who endured in confidence inherited glory and honor; they were exalted and made beautiful by God in their memorial, forever and ever. Amen.

<header>XLVI. Let us cleave to the righteous. Your dissension is pernicious.</header>

Therefore, we also must cling to such examples, brothers. For it is written: "Cleave to the holy, for those who cleave to them shall be made holy." And again in another place it says: "With the innocent man you shall be innocent, and with the chosen you shall be chosen, and with the crooked you shall be perverse." <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 18:25-26.</note> Let us therefore cleave to the innocent and the righteous; for these are the chosen of God. Why are there strifes, and angers, and dissensions, and schisms, and war among you? Do we not have one God and one Christ? And one Spirit of grace poured out upon us, and one calling in Christ? Why do we tear apart and rend the members of Christ, and revolt against our own body, and reach such a point of madness that we forget we are members of one another? Remember the words of Jesus our Lord. For He said: "Woe to that man! It would have been better for him if he had not been born, than that he should cause one of my chosen to stumble; it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around him and he be sunk in the sea, than that he should corrupt one of my little ones." Your schism has perverted many, has brought many to despondency, many to doubt, and all of us to grief. And yet your rebellion continues.

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XLV. XLVI.

### XLV. It is the way of the wicked to harass and cast down the righteous.

You are contentious, brothers, and burning with zeal for things that contribute very little to salvation. Look closely at the Scriptures, which are the true oracles of the Holy Spirit. Observe that nothing unjust or perverse is written in them. For you will not find that righteous men were ever rejected by holy men. The righteous have suffered persecution, but it was at the hands of the iniquitous; they were cast into prison, but by the impious; they were stoned by the lawless; they were killed by the wicked and by those carried away by an unjust zeal. While suffering these things, they bore them gloriously. For what shall we say, brothers? Was Daniel cast into the lions' den by those who feared God? Or were Ananias, Azarias, and Misael <note>These are the Hebrew names for Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego from the Book of Daniel.</note> shut into the furnace of fire by those who observed the magnificent and glorious worship of the Most High? Far be it from us! Who then were the ones who perpetrated these things? Men who are abominable and full of all malice reached such a pitch of fury that they subjected those to torments who served God with a holy and blameless will. They were ignorant that the Most High is the champion and defender of those who worship His name, full of virtue, with a pure conscience—to whom be glory forever and ever, Amen! But those who endured patiently in confidence became heirs of glory and honor; they were exalted by God and rendered gracious in their memory forever and ever, Amen!

### XLVI. Let us cling to the righteous. Your dissension is ruinous.

Therefore, brothers, it is necessary for us to cling to such examples. For it is written: "Join yourselves to the holy, because those who cling to them shall be sanctified." <note>original: "Sanctis vos adiungite, quia, qui illis adhaerent, sanctificabuntur." This specific phrasing is not found directly in the Bible; Clement may be quoting an oral tradition or an apocryphal source.</note> And again in another place: "With an innocent man you will be innocent, and with the perverse you will be perverted." <note>original: "cum viro innocente innocens eris, et cum cum perverso perverteris." A reference to Psalm 18:25-26.</note> Therefore let us join ourselves to the innocent and the righteous; for these are the elect of God. Why are there contentions, angers, dissensions, schisms <term>schismata: formal divisions or splits within a group</term>, and war among you? Do we not have one God and one Christ? Is there not one Spirit of grace poured out upon us, and one calling in Christ? Why do we tear apart and mangle the members of Christ, and stir up sedition against our own body? Have we reached such a point of madness that we forget we are members of one another? Remember the words of Jesus our Lord. For He said: "Woe to that man! It would have been better for him if he had not been born, than that he should cause one of my elect to stumble; it would be better for a millstone to be placed around him and for him to be drowned in the sea, than that he should cause one of my little ones to stumble." <note>Clement here combines several sayings of Jesus found in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke.</note> Your schism has perverted many, has cast many into dejection of soul, many into wavering, and all of us into sadness; and yet your sedition persists.

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XLVII. XLVIII. XLIX.

## XLVII. Your recent discord is worse than the former, which occurred in the time of Paul.

Take up the epistle <note>original: "ἐπιστολὴν"</note> of the blessed Paul the Apostle. What did he first write to you at the beginning of the Gospel? <note>original: "εὐαγγέλου"</note> In truth, he wrote to you by the Spirit concerning himself and Cephas <note>The Aramaic name for Saint Peter.</note> and Apollos, because even then you had formed partialities. <note>original: "προσκλίσεις"; refers to taking sides or favoring specific leaders.</note> But that partiality brought less sin upon you; for you were then partial to apostles of high reputation and to a man approved by them. But now, consider who they are that have perverted you and diminished the glory of your renowned brotherly love. <note>original: "φιλαδελφίας"</note> It is shameful, dearly beloved, yes, very shameful, and unworthy of Christian conduct, <note>original: "ἀγωγῆς"</note> to hear that the most steadfast and ancient church of the Corinthians, because of one or two persons, is in rebellion against its elders. <note>original: "πρεσβυτέρους"</note> And this report has not only reached us, but also those who differ from us; <note>original: "ἑτεροκλινεῖς"; likely referring to non-believers or those hostile to the faith.</note> so that blasphemies are brought upon the name of the Lord because of your folly, <note>original: "ἀφροσύνην"</note> and you create danger for yourselves.

## XLVIII. May you return to the pursuit of brotherly love.

Let us therefore remove this quickly, and let us fall down before the Master <note>original: "δεσπότῃ"</note> and weep, imploring him that he may be merciful and be reconciled to us, and restore us to the honorable and pure conduct of our brotherly love. For this is the gate of righteousness <note>original: "δικαιοσύνης"</note> opened unto life, as it is written: *Open to me the gates of righteousness; I will go into them and give thanks <note>original: "ἐξομολογήσομαι"</note> to the Lord. This is the gate of the Lord; the righteous shall enter into it.* While many gates are opened, <note>original: "ἀνεῳγυῖα"</note> this gate in righteousness is the one in Christ, in which all are blessed who enter and direct their way in holiness <note>original: "ὁσιότητι"</note> and righteousness, performing all things without confusion. Let a man be faithful, let him be able to utter knowledge, let him be wise in the discernment of words, let him be pure in his deeds; for the more he seems to be great, the more he ought to be humble-minded, <note>original: "ταπεινοφρονεῖν"</note> and to seek the common good <note>original: "κοινωφελὲς"</note> of all, and not his own.

Who can explain the bond <note>original: "δεσμὸν"</note> of the love of God? Who is sufficient to tell, as it ought to be told, the majesty of its beauty? <note>original: "καλλονῆς"</note> The—

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XLVII. XLVIII. XLIX.

### XLVII. Your recent discord is worse than the first, which occurred in the time of Paul.

Take up the epistle of the blessed Paul the Apostle. What did he first write to you at the beginning of the Gospel? <note>original: "principio Evangelii"; this refers to the early days of Paul's preaching among them.</note> Certainly, inspired by God, he wrote to you concerning himself, and Cephas <note>The Aramaic name for Peter.</note>, and Apollos, because even then you had formed factions and partisan leanings. But that factionalism brought less sin upon you; for you were then leaning toward Apostles who were distinguished by excellent testimony, and toward a man <note>Apollos.</note> approved by them. But now, consider who those people are who have led you astray and diminished the glory of your renowned brotherly love. It is shameful, brothers, very shameful indeed, and unworthy of a Christian way of life, for us to hear that the most steadfast and ancient church of the Corinthians, because of one or two persons, is moving in sedition against its elders <term>presbyters</term>. And this report has not only reached us, but also those who are estranged from us; so that because of your folly, blasphemies are brought upon the name of the Lord, and danger is created for yourselves.

### XLVIII. May you return to the pursuit of brotherly love.

Let us therefore remove this quickly; let us fall at the feet of the Master, and weeping, let us humbly implore him that he may be merciful and be reconciled to us, and restore us to our former honorable and pure conduct of brotherly love. For this way of life is the gate of righteousness opened unto life, just as it is written: “Open to me the gates of righteousness; entering into them, I will praise the Lord; this is the gate of the Lord, the righteous shall enter into it.” <note>original Latin: "Ps. 117, 19. 20."; traditionally Psalm 118 in modern Bibles.</note>
Since, therefore, many gates are open, the gate of righteousness is that same one which is in Christ; blessed are all those who have entered through it, and have directed their path in holiness and righteousness, performing all things without disturbance. Let a man be faithful, let him be powerful in explaining higher knowledge, let him be wise in the discernment of words, let him be pure in his works; yet he ought to be so much more humble as he seems to be greater, and he ought to seek what is useful for all, and not only for himself.

### XLIX. The praise of love.

He who has love <note>original: "charitatem"</note> in Christ, let him keep the commandments of Christ. Who can describe the bond of the love of God? Who is capable of speaking of the magnificence of its beauty, as is fitting? The height to which love elevates us is—

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. XLIX. L.

The height to which love leads is beyond description. Love joins us to God; love covers a multitude of sins; love bears all things, is patient in all things. There is nothing vulgar in love, nothing arrogant. Love has no schism, love does not rebel, love does all things in harmony. In love all the elect of God were perfected; without love nothing is pleasing to God. In love the Master took us to himself; because of the love he had for us, Jesus Christ our Lord gave his blood for us, by the will of God, and his flesh for our flesh, and his soul for our souls.

->L. *Let us pray, that we may be deemed worthy of love.*<-

You see, beloved, how great and wonderful love is, and of its perfection there is no explanation. Who is capable of being found in it, except those whom God shall deem worthy? Let us therefore pray and ask from his mercy, that we may live in love, without human partiality, blameless. All the generations from Adam until this day have passed away, but those perfected in love, according to the grace of God, have a place among the godly; they will be made manifest in the visitation of the kingdom of Christ. For it is written: “Enter into your chambers for a little while, until my anger and wrath pass away, and I will remember a good day, and will raise you up from your graves.” <note>This is a paraphrased reference to Isaiah 26:20 and Ezekiel 37:12.</note> Blessed are we, beloved, if we perform the commandments of God in the harmony of love, so that our sins may be forgiven us through love. For it is written: “Blessed are those whose iniquities are forgiven, and whose sins are covered. Blessed is the man to whom the Lord shall not impute sin, and in whose mouth there is no deceit.” <note>Quoting Psalm 32:1-2.</note> This blessing was upon those chosen by God through Jesus Christ our Lord, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. 51. 52. 53.

### 51. *Those participating in the discord, especially the leaders, should confess their sin.*

Whatever we have transgressed through any of the wiles of the adversary <note>original: "tou antikeimenou." Clement refers to the spiritual opponent or "Adversary" as the source of the conflict in the church.</note>, let us ask for forgiveness. And those who were the leaders of the rebellion and discord ought to look toward the common hope. For those who live with fear and love would rather experience suffering <note>The manuscript originally read "houses" (oikiais), but scholars correct it to "suffering" or "torture" (aikiais) to fit the context.</note> themselves than see their neighbors suffer; they would rather bring condemnation upon themselves than upon the harmony which has been handed down to us so well and justly. For it is better for a person to confess their transgressions than to harden their heart, just as the hearts of those who rebelled <margin>Numbers 16</margin> against Moses, the servant of God, were hardened. Their judgment was made manifest; for they went down into Hades alive, and death swallowed them up. Pharaoh <margin>Exodus 14</margin> and his army, and all the leaders of Egypt, with their chariots and their riders, were submerged in the Red Sea and perished for no other reason than that their foolish hearts were hardened, after signs and wonders had been performed in the land of Egypt through Moses, the servant of God.

### 52. *Such confession is pleasing to God.*

The Master <note>original: "despotēs." A title for God emphasizing His absolute sovereignty and ownership over creation.</note> of all things, brothers, is in need of nothing; He requires nothing from anyone, except that they confess to Him. For the elect David says: "I will confess to the Lord, and it will please Him more than a young calf that has horns and hooves; let the poor see it and be glad." And again he says: "Sacrifice to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High; and call upon me in the day of your trouble, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. For a broken spirit is a sacrifice to God."

# I. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS. 51. 52. 53.

### 51. *Those participating in the discord, especially the leaders, should confess their sin.*

Whatever we have transgressed through any of the suggestions of the adversary <note>original: "adversarii." Clement refers to the devil or the spiritual "opponent" as the source of the conflict in the church.</note>, let us implore forgiveness and indulgence. Indeed, those who stood out as the leaders of the rebellion and discord ought to consider the common hope. For those who spend their lives in fear and love would rather that they themselves fall into sufferings <note>original: "cruciatus." This reflects the early Christian value of self-sacrifice for the sake of the community.</note> than their neighbors; and they would rather bring blame upon themselves than upon the harmony which has been handed down to us so beautifully and justly. For it is better for a man to confess his sins than to harden his heart, just as the hearts of those who stirred up rebellion against Moses, the servant of the Lord, were hardened—whose condemnation was made manifest. For they went down into the underworld <note>original: "infernum." Referring to the biblical account of Korah, Dathan, and Abiram from Numbers 16.</note> alive, and death swallowed them up. Pharaoh and his army, and all the leaders of Egypt, with their chariots and those standing in them, were submerged in the depths of the Red Sea and perished for no other reason than that their foolish hearts were hardened, even after so many signs and miracles had been shown through Moses, the servant of God, in the land of Egypt.

### 52. *Such confession is pleasing to God.*

The Lord of all, brothers, is in need of nothing; he desires nothing from anyone, except that confession be made to him. For the chosen David says:

> "I will confess to the Lord, and it will please him more than a young calf that grows horns and hooves; let the poor see and be glad."

And again he says:

> "Offer to God a sacrifice of praise, and pay your vows to the Most High. And call upon me in the day of your trouble; I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me. For a broken spirit is a sacrifice to God." <note>These quotations combine several Psalms (69, 50, and 51) to emphasize that God values a repentant heart over ritual animal sacrifice.</note>

### 53. *The love of Moses toward his people.*

For you know, beloved—and you know right well—the sacred Scriptures, and you have looked deeply into the divine oracles. Recall them to your memory. When Moses had ascended the mountain and had spent forty days and forty nights in fasting and humility, the Lord said to him:

> "Moses, Moses, go down quickly from here, because your people, whom you brought out of the land of Egypt, have committed iniquity; they have quickly turned aside from the way which you commanded them, and have made for themselves molten images."

And the Lord said to him:

> "I have spoken to you once and twice, saying: I have seen this people, and behold, it is a stiff-necked people; let me destroy them, and I will blot out their name from under heaven; and I will make you into a great and wonderful nation, more numerous than this one."

But Moses said:

> "By no means, Lord; forgive this people their sin, or else blot me out also from the book of the living."

Oh, great love! <note>Moses offers his own salvation to save his rebellious people, serving as a model for the leaders in Corinth to put the needs of the church before their own status.</note>

## 54. *He who is full of love undergoes every loss, provided the peace of the church is restored.*
<note>original Latin heading: "Qui charitate plenus est, omne damnum subit, dummodo pax ecclesiae restituatur."</note>

Who then among you is noble? Who is compassionate? Who is filled with love? Let him say<gloss>1</gloss>: "If because of me there is rebellion, and strife, and schisms, I withdraw; I depart wherever you wish, and I do what is commanded by the community; only let the flock of Christ be at peace with the appointed elders." <note>term: "elders" (Greek: presbyteroi). These were the leaders of the early church whom the rebellion sought to oust.</note> He who does this will earn for himself great glory in the Lord, and every place will receive him. Clement uses the metaphor of "citizenship" to describe the Christian way of life.</note> of the kingdom of God, which brings no regret, have done and will continue to do.

Not less<gloss>6</gloss> did the perfect-in-faith Esther also cast herself into danger, so that she might rescue the twelve tribes of Israel when they were about to perish. For through her fasting and her humiliation she besought the all-seeing Master, the God of the ages; and He, seeing the humility of her soul, rescued the people for whose sake she had encountered danger.

...to accept, beloved. The admonition which we give to one another is good and exceedingly useful; for it binds us to the will of God. For the holy word says: "The Lord has disciplined me severely, but he has not given me over to death." <note>Psalm 118:18</note> "For whom the Lord loves he disciplines, and he scourges every son whom he receives." <note>Proverbs 3:12; Hebrews 12:6</note> "For," it says, "the righteous man shall discipline me in mercy and reprove me, but let not the oil of sinners anoint my head." <note>Psalm 141:5. Clement uses these scriptures to show that correction is a sign of God's favor, not his rejection.</note> And again it says: "Blessed is the man whom the Lord has reproved; and do not reject the admonition of the Almighty. For he causes pain, and again he restores; he has struck, and his hands have healed. Six times he shall deliver you from necessities, and in the seventh, evil shall not touch you. In famine he shall save you from death, and in war he shall release you from the power of the sword. From the scourge of the tongue he shall hide you, and you shall not be afraid when evils come. You shall laugh at the unrighteous and the lawless, and you shall not be afraid of wild beasts; for wild beasts shall be at peace with you. Then you shall know that your house shall be at peace, and the way of life in your tent shall not fail. You shall know that your seed is great, and your children shall be like the grass of the field. And you shall come to the grave like ripe grain harvested in its season, or like a heap on the threshing floor gathered in at the proper time." <note>Job 5:17–26. This passage illustrates the protective nature of accepting God's discipline.</note> You see, beloved, that there is protection for those who are disciplined by the Master; for being good, God disciplines us so that we may be admonished through his holy discipline.

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the document traditionally known as the Second Epistle of Clement. While the previous page concluded the First Epistle (a genuine letter from the church at Rome to Corinth), this text is actually an early Christian sermon—the oldest surviving complete Christian homily outside the New Testament—likely written in the mid-2nd century.</meta>

# CLEMENT

## THE SECOND EPISTLE^1

### I. *We must think magnificently of Christ, who called us to salvation.*

Brothers, we ought to think of Jesus Christ as of God, as the judge^2 of the living and the dead; and we should not think small things concerning our salvation^3. For when we think small things about him, we also hope to receive small things. And those of us who listen as if to small things^4 are doing wrong, not knowing from where we were called, and by whom, and to what place, and how much Jesus Christ endured to suffer for our sake. What recompense, then, shall we give to him, or what fruit worthy of that which he has given to us? And how many holy things^5 do we owe him? For he has granted us the light; he has addressed us as a father addresses his sons; he saved us when we were perishing. What praise, then, shall we give to him, or what payment^6 in return for what we have received? We were blind in our understanding, worshipping stones and wood and gold and silver and copper, the works of men; and our whole life was nothing else but death. Therefore, being wrapped in darkness and filled with such a mist in our vision, we have recovered our sight, having laid aside that cloud which surrounded us by his will. For he had mercy on us, and in his compassion he saved us, seeing in us much error and destruction, and that we had no hope of salvation except that which comes from him. For he called^7 us when we were not, and willed that from non-existence we should come to be.

### II. *The Church, formerly sterile, becomes wonderfully fruitful through the calling of the Gentiles.*

"Rejoice,^1 O barren woman who does not bear; break forth and shout, you who are not in labor, for many are the children of the desolate, more than she who has a husband." <note>This is a quotation from Isaiah 54:1, also cited in Galatians 4:27, interpreted here as the growth of the Gentile church.</note> When he said, "Rejoice, O barren woman who does not bear," he spoke of us; for our Church was barren before children were given to her. And when he said, "Shout, you who are not in labor," he means this: [offering] our prayers

<meta>This page marks the beginning of the document traditionally known as the Second Epistle of Clement. While titled an "epistle," scholars have identified this text as the oldest surviving complete Christian sermon (or homily) from the early church, likely dating to the mid-2nd century. It serves as an exhortation to the congregation to live worthily of their salvation.</meta>

ST. CLEMENT OF ROME, EPISTLES II. IV. V.

# CLEMENT
## THE SECOND EPISTLE

---

### I. ***We must think highly of Christ, who called us to salvation.***

Brothers, you ought to think of Jesus Christ as of God, as the judge of the living and the dead; and it is not fitting for us to think small things about our salvation. For when we think small things about him, we also hope to receive small things. And those of us who listen to these things as if they were of little account^5 <note>original: "negligenter haec audimus... quasi tenuia sint." The text warns against treating the gospel as trivial or unimportant.</note> are doing wrong, not knowing from where we were called, and by whom, and to what place, and how much Jesus Christ endured to suffer for our sake. What recompense, then, shall we give to him, or what fruit worthy of that which he has given to us? Truly, how many benefits^6 do we owe him? For he has granted us the light; he has addressed us as a father addresses his sons; he saved us when we were perishing. What praise, then, shall we give to him, or what payment in return for what we have received? We, who were weak in our understanding, worshipping stones and wood and gold and silver and copper—the works of men; and our whole life was nothing else but death. Therefore, being wrapped in darkness and having our vision filled with such a mist, we have recovered our sight, laying aside that cloud which surrounded us by his will. For he had mercy on us, and in his compassion he saved us, seeing in us much error and destruction, and that we had no hope of salvation except that which comes from him. For he called^7 us when we did not exist, and willed that from nothingness we should come to be.

### II. ***The Church, formerly barren, is now wonderfully fruitful through the calling of the nations.***

> “Rejoice, O barren woman, you who do not bear^1; break forth and cry out, you who do not travail; for the children of the desolate are more than those of her who has a husband.” <note>original: "Laetare sterilis..." quoting Isaiah 54:1 and Galatians 4:27</note>

When he said, “Rejoice, O barren woman, you who do not bear,” he was referring to us; for our church was barren before children were given to her. But when he said, “Cry out, you who do not travail,” he means this: that we should offer our prayers to God with sincerity—

Regarding the phrase “of small things,” *Bois* reads: “And if we listen to the things concerning Christ as if they were small”; *Wotton* reads: “And we who listen to these things as if they were small”; *Birrius* reads: “And those who disregard them as small,” the sense of which the **Latin version renders**. *Nolte* conjectures: “And those of us hearing.”

7) Romans 4:17; Hosea 2:23; Romans 9:25.

->II. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS II. III. IV. V.<-

...simply to offer our prayers to God, and not to grow weary like women in labor <note>original: "μὴ ὡς αἱ ὠδίνουσαι ἐκκακῶμεν." There is a scholarly debate here—some read it as "not to cry out like those in labor," while others read it as "not to lose heart."</note>. For He said: "The children of the desolate are many, more than those of her who has a husband"; since our people seemed to be desolate and abandoned by God, but now that we have believed, we have become more numerous than those who seemed to have God <note>original: "πλείονες ἐγενόμεθα τῶν δοκούντων ἔχειν Θεόν." This refers to the growth of the Gentile church compared to the Jewish community of that time.</note>. And another Scripture says: "I did not come to call the righteous, but sinners." This means that it is necessary to save those who are perishing. For it is a great and wonderful thing to support not the things that stand firm, but the things that are falling. So also Christ willed to save the things that were perishing, and He saved many, coming and calling us who were already perishing.

### III. Let us confess Christ by doing His commandments and honoring Him from the heart.

Since, then, He has shown such mercy toward us—firstly, that we who are living do not sacrifice to dead gods, nor do we worship them, but through Him we have known the Father of truth. What is this knowledge toward Him, if not to refuse to deny Him through whom we have known the Father? And He Himself says: "He who confesses Me before men, I will confess him before My Father." This, then, is our reward, if we confess Him through whom we were saved. But in what way do we confess Him? By doing what He says, and not disobeying His commandments, and honoring Him not only with our lips, but with our whole heart and with our whole mind. And He says also in Isaiah: "This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me."

### IV. Who truly confesses Christ.

Let us not, therefore, merely call Him Lord, for this will not save us. For He says: "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' shall be saved, but he who does righteousness." So then, brothers, let us confess Him in our works, by loving one another, by not committing adultery, nor speaking against one another, nor being envious, but being self-controlled, merciful, and good; and we ought to have sympathy for one another, and not be lovers of money. By these works let us confess Him, and not by the opposites. And we must not fear men rather than God. For this reason, if we do these things, the Lord said: "If you are gathered with Me in My bosom, and do not keep My commandments, I will cast you out, and will say to you: 'Depart from Me, I know not where you are from, you workers of iniquity.'"

### V. Let us despise the world and strive for the happiness of the next life.

Therefore, brothers, leaving behind our sojourning in this world, let us do the will of Him who called us, and let us not fear to depart—

->II. CLEMENT TO THE CORINTHIANS II. III. IV. V.<-

...not—like those in labor—to grow weary <note>original: "non — parturientium instar — deficientes." The author uses a metaphor of a woman in labor to describe the intensity of prayer or the spiritual struggle.</note>. For He said: "For the children of the desolate are many, more than those of her who has a husband"; He said this because our people seemed to be desolate and forsaken by God, but now that we have believed, we have become more numerous than those who were thought to possess God. ### III. *Let us confess Christ by doing His commandments and honoring Him from the heart.*

Since, then, He has shown such great mercy toward us—firstly, that we who are living do not sacrifice to dead gods nor worship them, but through Him we have known the Father of truth—what is the knowledge that leads to Him, if not to refuse to deny Him through whom we have known the Father? For He Himself says: "He who confesses Me before men, I will confess him before My Father." This, then, is our reward, if we confess Him through whom we were saved. But in what way shall we confess Him? By doing what He says, and not disregarding His commandments, and by honoring Him not only with our lips, but with our whole heart and our whole mind. For He says in Isaiah: "This people honors Me with their lips, but their heart is far from Me."

### IV. *Who truly confesses Christ.*

Therefore, let us not only call Him "Lord," for that will not save us. For He says: "Not everyone who says to Me, 'Lord, Lord,' will be saved, but he who does what is right." Therefore, brothers, let us confess Him in our works, by loving one another, by not committing adultery, nor slandering one another, nor being jealous, but by living in self-control, mercy, and goodness; and we ought to be led by mutual compassion, not by the desire for money. In these works let us confess Him, and not in their opposites; and we should not fear men, but rather God. For this reason, if we do these things, the Lord said: "If you are gathered with Me in My bosom and do not keep My commandments, I will cast you out and say to you: Depart from Me, I do not know you or where you are from, you workers of iniquity." <note>This quote is not found in the canonical Gospels; it may come from a lost apocryphal source like the Gospel of the Egyptians.</note>
