### II. Do not rescue me from martyrdom.

For I do not wish you to please men, but to please God, just as you indeed do please Him. For I shall never again have such an opportunity to attain to God; nor will you, if you remain silent, ever be credited with a better work. For if you remain silent about me, I shall become a word of God; but if you love my flesh <note>meaning his physical life or survival</note>, I shall again be a mere runner <note>original: "trechōn." This implies he would have to restart the race of faith rather than finishing it.</note>. Grant me nothing more than to be poured out <term>spondīsthai: to be offered as a drink-offering or libation</term> to God, while an altar is still prepared; so that, forming a choir in love, you may sing to the Father in Christ Jesus, because God has deemed the bishop of Syria worthy to be found at the setting of the sun, having summoned him from its rising. It is good to set from the world toward God, so that I may rise in Him.

### III. Rather, pray to God that He might supply me with strength for martyrdom.

You have never envied anyone; you have taught others. And I wish that those things which you enjoin when teaching may remain firm. Only ask for strength for me, both within and without, that I may not only speak, but also truly will; that I may not only be called a Christian, but also be found to be one. For if I am found to be one, I can also be called one, and then I can be faithful when I am no longer visible to the world. Nothing that is visible is good. "For the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal" <note>A quotation from the apostle Paul in 2 Corinthians 4:18.</note>. For our God, Jesus Christ, being in the Father, is more clearly seen. Christianity is not a work of silence alone, but of greatness.

### IV. Allow me to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts, that I may be found as the bread of Christ.

I am writing to all the churches, and I command everyone that I die willingly for God, if only you do not hinder me. I appeal to you,

### II. *Do not rescue me from martyrdom.*

For I do not want you to please men, but to please God, just as you indeed do please Him. For I shall never again have such an opportunity to attain to God; nor will you, if you remain silent, ever be credited with a better work. For if you remain silent about me, I shall belong to God; but if you love my flesh <note>meaning his physical survival</note>, I shall have to run the race all over again. Grant me nothing more than to be sacrificed to God while an altar is still prepared; so that, having become a choir in love, you may sing to the Father in Christ Jesus, because God has deemed the bishop of Syria worthy to be found, summoning him from the East to the West <note>original: "ab Oriente in Occidentem," referring to his journey from Antioch to Rome</note>. It is good to set from the world toward God, so that I may rise in Him.

### III. *Rather, pray to God that He might supply me with strength for martyrdom.*

You have never envied anyone; you have taught others. And I wish that those things which you enjoin when teaching may remain firm. Only ask for strength for me, both inward and outward, that I may not only speak, but also truly will; that I may not only be called a Christian, but also be found to be one. For if I am found to be one, I can also be called one, and then I can be faithful when I am no longer visible to the world. Nothing that is visible is good. "For the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal." <note>A quotation from 2 Corinthians 4:18</note> For even our God Jesus Christ, now that he is again in the Father, is more clearly shown. Christianity is not a matter of silence alone, but of greatness.

### IV. *Allow me to be ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found as the bread of Christ.*

I am writing to all the churches, and I charge them all that I die willingly for God, provided that you do not hinder me. I beg you, not to show an untimely... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; Ignatius is about to ask them not to show "untimely kindness" by trying to save him.</note>

---

5) This passage from 2 Corinthians 4:18, having been translated, is missing in the ancient Interpreter, the first Syrian version, the Syrian fragments, and the first and second Armenian versions. *H.* <note>referring to editor Hefele</note> included it in brackets in the fourth edition.

6) Christ, since the time he returned to the Father, becomes more manifest through the spirit of the new creation, and appears gloriously through his working.

7) Thus says the *Codex Colbertinus*, whose meaning (if you listen to Clericus) is that the Christian religion is not something that should be suppressed in timid silence, but must be accompanied by "magnificent speech" (which Ignatius intends by the word "greatness"), as can be observed in the preceding and following words. Using the reading of the manuscript, Smith and Ruchat (following Vossius and the ancient Interpreter) reconstruct it thus: *The Christian is not a work of persuasion, but of greatness, especially when he is hated by the world.* <note>original: "Οὐ πεισμονῆς τὸ ἔργον, ἀλλὰ μεγέθους ἐστὶν ὁ Χριστιανός, μάλιστα ὅταν μισῆται ὑπὸ κόσμου."</note> Symeon the Metaphrast has: *The Christian is not a work of persuasion, but of greatness; when he is hated by the world, he is loved by God.* <note>original: "φιλεῖται παρὰ Θεοῦ"</note> Toupius emends too boldly and yet not successfully, writing in the margin of his copy: "I read *not a work of sitting still, nor of delay*," <note>original: "οὐχ

<column-break/>

ἕδρας ἔργον, οὐδ' ἀμβολᾶς"</note> perhaps as a reference to Bacchylides and the ancient Interpreter's "sitting." Indeed, you have this praised expression from Dionysius of Halicarnassus in the book *On the Arrangement of Words* (page 234, Upton edition), and also from Athenaeus (Book 14, 30 and Book 5, 289, Schweighäuser edition). Wake translates strangely: "A Christian is not a work of opinion, but of greatness of mind, (especially when he is hated by the world.)" Wocher does better: "Christianity does not consist merely in being quiet, but in (spiritual) greatness." *Iac.* <note>Jacobson</note> The Interpolator <note>the later, expanded version of the letters</note> writes: "The Christian is not a work of persuasion, but of greatness." The Metaphrast omitted this sentence in our codices A, E, and N. The ancient Interpreter, the first Syrian, and the second Armenian versions seem to read: *Christianity is not a work of persuasion, but of greatness, when it is hated by the world.* In Timothy’s book against the Council of Chalcedon (compare Cureton, page 42), it is translated: *This is not a work of persuasion, but the Christian is of greatness, when he is held in hatred by the world.*

<columns>
...do not become an untimely kindness to me. Let me be food for the wild beasts, through whom it is possible to attain God. I am the wheat <note>original: "Sitos." Ignatius uses the imagery of grain being ground into flour to describe his martyrdom as a preparation for a sacred meal.</note> of God, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found to be the pure bread of Christ. Rather, coax the wild beasts, so that they may become my tomb, and leave nothing of my body behind; thus, when I have fallen asleep, I shall not be a burden to anyone. Then I shall truly be a disciple of Jesus Christ, when the world shall not even see my body. Beseech Christ on my behalf, that through these instruments <note>the wild beasts</note> I may be found a sacrifice. I do not command you as Peter and Paul did <note>original: "Petros kai Paulos." This suggests Peter and Paul had a specific historical authority over the Roman church that Ignatius, as a visiting bishop, does not claim.</note>. They were Apostles, I am a condemned man; they were free, but I am a slave until now. But if I suffer, I shall become a freedman of Jesus, and I shall rise up free in Him. Now, in my chains, I am learning to desire nothing worldly or vain.

### V. I long to die.

From Syria <note>Ignatius's home province</note> all the way to Rome I fight with wild beasts, by land and sea, by night and day, bound to ten leopards <note>original: "leopardois." This is a very early use of the word "leopard" to describe the fierce Roman soldiers guarding him.</note>—that is, a company of soldiers—who only become worse when they are treated well. But in the midst of their wrongdoings, I am becoming more of a disciple; yet "I am not thereby justified." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 4:4</note> May I enjoy the wild beasts that are prepared for me! I pray that they may be found ready for me; I will even coax them to devour me quickly, unlike some whom they were too afraid to touch. And if they are unwilling and refuse, I will compel them. Bear with me; I know what is to my advantage. Now I begin to be a disciple. Let nothing visible or invisible envy me, so that I may attain Jesus Christ. Let fire and cross, gatherings of wild beasts, cuttings, tearings, scatterings of bones, mangling of limbs, the grinding of the whole body, and the wicked punishments of the devil come upon me, provided only that I attain Jesus Christ.

---

**Chapter IV.** 1) These noble sentiments, written by Ignatius and later spoken aloud during his final struggle, exist in various readings. You may find these variations—which do not alter the core meaning—collected from the Later Editor, the Translators, the *Acts of Ignatius*, the Greek *Menaion* (liturgical book), as well as from Irenaeus (Book V, 28), Eusebius (Church History III, 36), and Rufinus’s translation of the same. Jerome writes: "And when he had already been condemned to the beasts, in his ardor for suffering, when he heard the roaring lions, he said: 'I am the wheat of Christ, I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, that I may be found pure bread.'" <note>original: "Frumentum Christi sum, dentibus bestiarum molar, ut panis mundus inveniar."</note> (From *On Illustrious Men*, ch. 16). — Cotelerius.
2) "Rather..." according to the Angelicus Manuscript (A).
3) Gallicciolli: "by such means." Graziani: "by means of these instruments."
4) Ignatius mentions Peter and Paul for this reason: among all the disciples and followers of Christ, they stood out for preaching and teaching the Gospel, and were thus distinguished by a certain authority over the rest. Therefore, I am surprised that Jacobson writes that Ignatius mentions them simply because they were the only Apostles who had been among the Roman Christians.

<column-break/>

5) That is, set free from the chains of the weaknesses of this age.
6) Compare 1 Corinthians 7:22.
7) "To desire anything worldly or vain" is the reading in the Colbert Manuscript and the Later Editor (also Manuscripts B, F, O, V). The words "worldly or vain" seemed they should be excluded according to the ancient Latin, the first Syriac, and the first and second Armenian versions. Vossius correctly identified this on p. 300.

**Chapter V.** 1) This entire section is cited by Eusebius (Church History III, 36) and Jerome in his *Catalogue of Ecclesiastical Writers*. From Jerome's Latin translation, his translator Sophronius composed a new Greek version. These things are also produced by Gildas in the *Epistle* where he chastises the British clergy, though he uses Rufinus’s version of Eusebius. — Ussher. The author of the *Epistle to the Tarsians* (circulated under Ignatius's name) imitated this passage in his opening.

### V. I long to die.⁶

From Syria all the way to Rome I fight with wild beasts², by land and sea, by night and day, chained to ten leopards³, which is a company of soldiers; who only become worse when they are treated well⁴. However, I am more instructed <note>in discipleship</note> by their injuries, though I am not justified because of this⁵. May I enjoy the wild beasts prepared for me, and I pray they are found ready for me; I will even coax them to devour me quickly—not like some whom, out of fear, they did not touch⁷. If they are unwilling and refuse, I will compel them by force. Grant me this pardon⁸; I know what is for my benefit. Now I begin to be a disciple⁹. Let nothing visible or invisible envy me, that I may attain Jesus Christ. Let fire and cross, packs of wild beasts, butcherings, tearings apart, the wrenching of bones, the mangling of limbs, the crushing of the whole body, and the cruel tortures of the devil come upon me; only let it be that I attain Jesus Christ¹⁰.

2) Compare 1 Corinthians 15:32, where "I fought with beasts at Ephesus" <note>original: "ἐθηριομάχησα ἐν Ἐφέσῳ"</note> is also to be explained as a struggle against beast-like men. —Jacobson.

3) The word "leopard" <note>original: "λεόπαρδος"</note> was found objectionable by Basnage, Baur, and others, who denied that the term existed before the age of Constantine. But Pearson (*Vindiciae Ignatianae* II, p. 92) has clearly demonstrated that before the time of Constantine, this word was in use not only among the Latins, but also among the Greeks. The close connection of the provinces of the Roman Empire caused many Latin words to be adopted by the Greeks. Compare Ignatius, *To Polycarp*, ch. 6; Huther... and Düsterdieck... See also Stephen’s *Greek Thesaurus*, ed. Hase. —Hefele. Cotelerius has gathered more evidence here to defend the use of this word by Ignatius.

4) If you listen to Wocher, these "benefits" refer to gifts given to the soldiers by Christians who hoped to make them milder toward Ignatius through bribes. —Jacobson.

6) Chrysostom, in his *Eulogy of Ignatius* (ch. 5): "Hearing that this manner of punishment awaited him, he said, 'May I have joy of those beasts.'" Jerome, in his *Life of the Same*: "May I enjoy the beasts." —Ussher. Pearson reads it differently: "I would rather possess the beasts than these leopards."

7) The word "I shall pass by" <note>original: "παραβήσομαι"</note>, which I find in Codex E, is not unpleasing.

10) The words "butcherings" and "tearings" <note>original: "ἀνατομαὶ, διαιρέσεις"</note> do not appear in Eusebius or Jerome when they quote this passage, nor are they translated by the Syrian or the old Latin interpreter. However, they are present in all our later, longer Codices and the Armenian 2; Armenian 1 has "tearing" without the preceding "butcherings."

<header>THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE ROMANS. VI. VII.</header>

### VI. Through my death, I shall attain the true life.

The ends of the world <note>original: "ta perata tou kosmou"</note> will profit me nothing, nor will the kingdoms of this age. It is better for me to die for Christ Jesus than to rule over the ends of the earth. *For what does it profit a man, if he gains the whole world, but loses his own soul?* <note>A quotation from the Gospel of Matthew 16:26.</note> I seek Him who died for us; I desire Him who rose for our sake. The pangs of birth <note>original: "toketos," which can mean both "birth" and "financial interest/usury." Ignatius uses it here to describe the painful "labor" of entering eternal life.</note> are upon me. Forgive me, brothers; do not hinder me from living, and do not wish for me to die. Do not hand over to the world one who desires to belong to God, nor deceive me with material things. Allow me to receive the pure light; when I have arrived there, I shall be a true human being of God. Permit me to be an imitator of the passion of my God. If anyone has Him within himself, let him understand what I desire, and let him sympathize with me, knowing the things that constrain me.

### VII. I desire to die, for my love has been crucified.

The ruler of this age <note>A reference to Satan or the worldly powers opposing the spirit.</note> wishes to seize me and corrupt my mind which is directed toward God. Therefore, let none of you who are present help him; rather, be on my side—that is, on the side of God. Do not speak of Jesus Christ while you still desire the world. Let no envy dwell among you. Even if I myself, when I arrive, should entreat you, do not be persuaded by me; rather, believe these things that I write to you now. For though I am alive as I write to you, I am in love with dying. My earthly desire <note>original: "eros," referring here to physical or worldly passion.</note> has been crucified, and there is no fire of material longing within me; but there is water, living and speaking within me, saying from deep inside: "Come to the Father." I find no pleasure in the food of corruption, nor in the delights of this life. I desire the bread of God, the heavenly bread, the bread of life, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was born in later times from the seed of David and Abraham; and I desire the drink of God, which is His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.

Chapter VI. 1) So it is found in the Interpolated version, the old Latin Interpreter, and the 1st and 2nd Armenian versions; but the Colbert Codex and the Metaphrast read **delights** <note>original: "terpna"</note>. The 1st Syriac version translates nothing from this chapter except the words: **the pangs of birth are upon me**, and connects them to those beautiful words in the following chapter: **my love is crucified**, etc.

2) Previously the word was **good** <note>original: "kalon"</note>, and in the translation "bonum," which is a style of speaking taken from the Hebrew language and is not uncommon. But we have followed the Greek and interpret **rather** <note>original: "mallon"</note> as a matter of greater importance. *Clericus* favors the 2nd Armenian version. Nevertheless, along with the old Latin version, all our recent interpolated Codices, the Metaphrast, and a fragment in Timothy of Alexandria (which presents these and the immediately following words in Syriac until the end of the chapter), and the 1st Armenian, the reading **good** seems preferable.

### VI. Through my death, I shall attain the true life.

The farthest reaches of the world will profit me nothing, nor will the kingdoms of this age. It is better for me to die for Jesus Christ than to rule over the ends of the earth. "For what does it profit a man, if he gains the whole world, but suffers the loss of his own soul?" <note>original Latin: "Quid enim prodest homini, si universum mundum lucretur, animae vero suae detrimentum patiatur?" — A quotation of Matthew 16:26.</note> I seek Him who died for us; I desire Him who rose for our sake. This gain is set before me. Forgive me, brothers! Do not hinder me from living <note>Ignatius views his earthly existence as a kind of death and his martyrdom as the beginning of true life.</note>; do not wish for me to die; do not hand over to the world one who desires to belong to God. Do not deceive me with material things. Allow me to receive the pure light; when I have arrived there, I shall be a true human being of God. Grant me to be an imitator of the passion <note>the suffering and death</note> of my God. If anyone has Him within himself, let him understand what I desire, and let him sympathize with me, knowing the things that constrain me.

### VII. I desire to die, for my love has been crucified.

The ruler of this age <note>The "Princeps huius seculi," referring to the devil or the worldly spirit that opposes God.</note> wants to seize me and corrupt my will toward God. Therefore, let none of you who are present help him; rather, be on my side—that is, on the side of God. Do not speak of Jesus Christ while you still desire the world. Let no envy dwell among you. Even if I were there in person and begged you otherwise, do not believe me; instead, believe these things I am writing to you. For I write to you while living, yet desiring to die. My Love has been crucified <note>original: "Amor meus crucifixus est." This famous phrase likely refers to Christ being his "Love," or that his earthly desires have been put to death.</note>, and there is no fire in me that loves material things. Instead, there is a living and speaking water within me, saying deep inside: "Come to the Father." I take no pleasure in corruptible food, nor in the delights of this life. I want the Bread of God, the heavenly bread, the bread of life, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who in later times was born of the seed of David and Abraham; and I want the drink of God, His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.

### VIII. *Grant me this favor.*

I no longer wish to live according to human standards. This will be possible, if you so desire. Desire it, so that you also may be desired <note>The Greek "thelethete" is a passive form of "desire," suggesting that if the Romans accept God's will for Ignatius, God will look favorably upon them.</note>. I ask this of you in few words; believe me. Jesus Christ will reveal to you that I speak the truth; He is the mouth that cannot lie, through which the Father has truly spoken. Pray for me, that I may succeed <note>That is, succeed in reaching his goal of martyrdom.</note>. I have not written to you according to the flesh, but according to the will of God. If I suffer, it is because you willed it; if I am rejected <note>original: "apodokimasthe"—referring to the possibility of being spared from execution, which Ignatius views as a rejection of his sacrifice.</note>, it is because you hated me.

### IX. *Pray for the church in Syria. Greeting.*

Remember in your prayers the church in Syria, which now has God as its shepherd in my place. Jesus Christ alone will oversee it—He and your love. But I am ashamed to be counted among them; for I am not worthy, being the least of them and like "one born out of due time." <note>original: "ektroma"—a term used by the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:8 to describe his own late and sudden calling.</note> Yet I have received mercy to be someone, if I reach God. My spirit greets you, along with the love of the churches that received me in the name of Jesus Christ, not as a mere passerby. For even those churches that were not on my physical route <note>meaning the churches not directly on the road to Rome</note> went before me from city to city to welcome me.

### X. *Conclusion.*

I write these things to you from Smyrna by the hand of the Ephesians, who are most worthy of blessing. Crocus is also here with me, along with many others—a name very dear to me. Regarding those who went before me from Syria to Rome for the glory of God, I believe you have met them; let them know that I am near. For they are all worthy of God and of you; it is fitting for you to refresh them in every way. I have written this to you on the ninth day before the Kalends of September <note>In the Roman calendar, this is August 24th, though the text includes a gloss specifying the 23rd.</note> [that is, the twenty-third of August]. Farewell until the end, in the endurance of Jesus Christ. Amen.

**Chapter VIII.** 1) The Syrian translator did not translate the eighth chapter and the larger part of the ninth.

2) A manner of speaking very familiar to the Apostle Paul. Compare Romans 3:5; 1 Corinthians 9:8; Galatians 3:15.

3) The Old Latin Interpreter, Metaphrastes, and the updated interpolated Manuscripts B, F, O, and V read "desire" [thelete]. Only in the margin of the Ottobonian manuscript is "you might desire" [thelesetai], changed to "you may desire" [thelesete]. "Desire, then, so that you also may be desired."

4) Compare Galatians 6:11; Letter to Polycarp, ch. 7. Regarding the following word "I ask" [aitoumai], the scholar Vossius thinks Ignatius undoubtedly wrote "I exhort" [parakalo].

5) Manuscript A has "will reveal" [phanerosei] with the "oi" vowel written above. The optative mood <note>expressing a wish or prayer: "May He reveal"</note> is preferable.

6) "If I become a castaway," if I am rejected (Mark 8:31) — Pearson. "If I am delivered from death, as if I were a rejected thing, and entirely unworthy of this honor which I seek with such fervor of soul" — Smith.

Therefore, the Interpolator <note>A later editor who added to the original text.</note> is incorrect to have: "to the Lord, who said, 'I am the good shepherd.'" By this unnecessary explanation, he weakens the testimony concerning the Divinity of Christ which Saint Ignatius inserts everywhere in these Letters — Smith. Graziani translates: "Remember in your prayer the church in Syria, which now has God as its shepherd in my place."

2) A Pauline phrase. Compare 1 Corinthians 15:8, 9.

4) That is, not as a stranger passing through those churches on a hasty journey, but with such love and zeal [as to provide a full welcome]...

### VIII. Grant me this favor.

I no longer wish to live according to human standards. This will be possible, if you so desire. I pray that you do desire it, so that you also may find benevolence. I ask this of you in few words: believe me. Jesus Christ will reveal to you that I speak the truth; He is the truthful mouth through which the Father has truly spoken. If I suffer, it is because you willed it; if I am rejected <note>original: "apodokimasthe"—referring to the possibility of being spared from execution, which Ignatius views as a rejection of his sacrifice.</note>, it is because you hated me.

Remember in your prayers the church in Syria, which now has God as its shepherd in my place. Jesus Christ alone will oversee it—He and your love. But I am ashamed to be counted among them; for I am not worthy, being the last of them and like "one born out of due time." <note>original: "ektroma"—a term used by the Apostle Paul in 1 Corinthians 15:8 to describe his own late and sudden calling.</note> Yet I have received mercy to be someone, if I reach God. My spirit greets you, along with the love of the churches that received me in the name of Jesus Christ, not as a mere passerby. For even those churches that did not lie on my physical route accompanied me from city to city.

### X. Conclusion.

I am writing these things to you from Smyrna via the Ephesians, who are most worthy to be called blessed. With me also is Crocus, a name very dear to me, along with many others. Regarding those who went before me from Syria to Rome for the glory of God, I believe you have come to know them; tell them that I am near. For they are all worthy of God and of you, and it is fitting for you to refresh them in all things. I have written this to you on the ninth day before the Calends of September <note>original: "ante diem IX Calendas Septembris"—in the Roman calendar, this corresponds to August 23rd.</note>. Farewell, stay strong until the end in the endurance of Jesus Christ. Amen.

...as if I were their bishop. <note>This refers to a comment by the scholar Smith.</note> The words "Not as a passerby" <note>original: "Ouch hōs parodeuonta"</note> are not translated by the first Syriac version; they are found in the first and second Armenian versions.

5) Pearson understands the "churches" mentioned here to be those under Ignatius’s own jurisdiction. Gallicciolli also translates: "those which do not belong to me in a fleshly way." However, the passage is more correctly explained as referring to churches located far from the road through which they were traveling. Graziani expresses this: "While those which were not adjacent to me on the road that I took according to the flesh, accompanied me from city to city." I do not believe, as Ruchat does, that the phrase "according to the flesh" <note>original: "te kata sarka"</note> is a later addition by a scribe. Rather, it serves to contrast with the "way according to God" or the spiritual path, just as "the things seen" and "the things unseen" are set against each other. These words are supported by the first Syriac and second Armenian versions. Frequently, the word "to lead forward" <note>original: "proagein"</note> is used for "to escort" <note>original: "propempein"</note>, as seen in the Letter to Titus 3:13.

<column-break/>

Chapter X. 1) We have noted in the appropriate place that the Syriac translator attached the fourth and fifth chapters of the preceding *Letter to the Trallians* to the ninth chapter of *Romans*. After those, the Syriac version ends with the final sentence of the tenth chapter: "Farewell until the end in the endurance of Jesus Christ [your God]."

2) The Christians had sent Crocus from Ephesus to meet and greet Ignatius when he approached their borders. Compare the *Letter to the Ephesians*, chapter 2.

3) The phrase "[that is, the twenty-third of August]" <note>original: "toutestin Augoustou eikadi trite"</note> is recognized neither by the ancient Translator nor by the Interpolator. It is a "gloss" <note>A later explanatory note added to the text.</note> that should be removed. Such an explanation was hardly necessary for someone writing to the Romans. It is, however, found in the first Armenian (August 22) and second Armenian (August 24) versions.

4) The word "Amen" certainly did not come from Ignatius’s own pen; it is not found at the end of any of the shorter recensions of the Letters. Therefore, I would say it is an addition by another hand.

### TO THE PHILADELPHIANS: IGNATIUS.<sup>1</sup>

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>The name "Theophorus" literally means "God-bearer." In the early church, it was a title Ignatius used to emphasize his spiritual union with Christ.</note>, to the church of God the Father and of the Lord Jesus Christ, which is in Philadelphia of Asia,<sup>2</sup> which has found mercy and been established<sup>3</sup> in the concord of God, and rejoices in the passion of our Lord without wavering,<sup>4</sup> and<sup>5</sup> in His resurrection, being fully assured in all mercy; which I greet in the blood<sup>6</sup> of Jesus Christ; which is an eternal and lasting joy, especially if they are at one with the bishop and the elders and deacons who are with him, who have been appointed by the mind<sup>7</sup> of Jesus Christ, whom He established and confirmed according to His own will by His Holy Spirit.

---

->I. *Praise of the bishop.*<-

Whom<sup>8</sup> I have known to be your bishop, obtaining this ministry which belongs to the community not of himself, nor through men, nor for the sake of vainglory, but in the love of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ; I am struck by his kindness, for by remaining silent<sup>11</sup> he has more power than those who speak vanities. For he is as harmoniously tuned<sup>12</sup> to the commandments as a lyre is to its strings. Therefore my soul blesses his mind toward God, recognizing it to be virtuous and perfect,<sup>13</sup> and his stability and lack of anger in all the kindness of the living God.

<columns>2</columns>

1) The name IGNATIUS <note>original: "ΙΓΝΑΤΙΟΣ"</note> appears first in Codices C and L. However, both mark it as *to the Magnesians and the Philadelphians. Ignatius:* — Any observer can see that the first part of this inscription belongs to the preceding Letter. — After leaving Smyrna, Ignatius reached Troas, from where he wrote to the Philadelphians of Mysia <note>The commentator notes the geographical region.</note>, whose town he had passed through on his journey (chapters 11, 3, 6, 7). He extols their bishop with praise, noting that he must be obeyed everywhere, and likewise that divisions must be avoided (chapters 1—3). Penitents are to be received, unity must be observed through the worship of God, and Judaism must not be mixed with the Gospel, since there is only one High Priest, Jesus Christ (chapters 3—9). He asks the Philadelphians to send an envoy to Antioch, thanking them by name for certain individuals (chapters 10, 11).

2) That is, in Lydia. This same church is mentioned in Revelation 1:11 and 3:7.

3) *found mercy and been established* <note>original: "ἠλεημένῃ καὶ ἡδρασμένῃ"</note> (with the smooth breathing mark) in Code C, and according to Heyse—disagreeing with Jacobson—also in Code L, though without the iota subscript; *pitied and established* <note>original: "ἐλεημένῃ καὶ ἑδρασμένῃ"</note> in the Voss manuscript.

<column-break/>

8) *Whom* <note>original: "ὅν"</note> in Code C and Holstenius's copy: it had previously occurred to Jacobson to use *Of whom* <note>original: "Ὧν"</note>, asserting: “This word has neither a breathing mark nor an accent in the manuscript, where the vowels 'o' and 'omega' are very often swapped.” But Pietro del Furia is my witness, contrary to Jacobson, that *Whom* <note>original: "ὅν"</note> stands out distinctly in Code L. Therefore, nothing should be changed. It refers back to the bishop mentioned just before. In the original manuscript, there was no separation between the greeting and the first chapter.

# TO THE PHILADELPHIANS.

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>The name "Theophorus" literally means "God-bearer."</note>, to the church of God the Father and of the Lord Jesus Christ, which is in Philadelphia in Asia, which has obtained mercy and is established in harmony with God, rejoicing inseparably in the passion of our Lord, and fully instructed in all mercy through his resurrection; which I greet in the blood of Jesus Christ. ### *THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE PHILADELPHIANS.

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus, to the Church of God the Father and of the Lord Jesus Christ, which is in Philadelphia in Asia, having obtained mercy and being established in the harmony of God, and rejoicing in the passion of our Lord without hesitation, and firmly believing in His resurrection in all mercy; which I greet in the blood of Jesus Christ, which is an eternal and lasting joy, especially if they are one with the Bishop and the Elders and Deacons joined with him, appointed according to the mind of Jesus Christ, whom they confirm in stability by His holy spirit according to His own will.

## I. *Praise of the bishop.*

I have known this bishop, who obtained the ministry of ruling the assembly not of himself, nor through men, nor for the sake of empty glory, but by the love of the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I have greatly admired his modesty; he is more powerful by his silence than those who speak empty things. For he is as in tune with the commandments as a lyre is to its strings. Therefore, I declare his soul to be blessed, knowing it to be devoted to God, adorned with virtues and perfect, and I admire his steadiness and his lack of anger, patterned after the gentleness of the living God.

* I. I have known this Bishop to have attained this ministry, which belongs to the community, not from himself nor through men, nor through empty glory, but in the love of God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ. I was struck by his modesty; for in his silence he is more capable than others who speak empty things. Indeed, he is equipped with the divine commandments just as a lyre is with its strings. For this reason, my soul calls him blessed because of his disposition toward God, which I know to be devoted to virtue and perfect, as well as his stability and gentleness, living as he does in all the mildness of God.

<header>THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE PHILADELPHIANS. II. III. IV.</header>

II. *Maintain unity with the bishop, and flee from wicked doctrines.* <note>original Latin: "Tenete unionem cum episcopo, et fugite pravas doctrinas"</note>

Therefore, as children of light and truth, flee from division and wicked teachings; where the shepherd is, there follow as sheep. For many wolves, who appear trustworthy, lead captive those <term>running God's race</term> <note>Greek: "theodromous," describing Christians as athletes in a spiritual race</note> by means of evil pleasure; but in your unity, they shall find no place.

III. *Flee from schismatics.* <note>original Latin: "Fugite schismaticos"</note>

Keep yourselves from those evil weeds which Jesus Christ does not cultivate, because they are not a planting of the Father. It is not that I found division among you, but rather a <term>filtering</term> <note>Greek: "apodiulismon." Ignatius uses a wine-making metaphor: the community hasn't just split, it has been strained or purified of impurities.</note>. For as many as belong to God and Jesus Christ, these are with the bishop; and as many as shall repent and come into the unity of the church, these also shall belong to God, so that they may live according to Jesus Christ. Do not be deceived, my brothers: if anyone follows a schismatic, he does not inherit the kingdom of God; if anyone walks in a foreign opinion, he does not align himself with the <term>Passion</term> <note>Ignatius often uses "the Passion" to refer to the suffering and death of Christ as the central truth of faith.</note>.

IV. *Use one Eucharist.* <note>original Latin: "Utamini una Eucharistia"</note>

Take care, therefore, to participate in one <term>Eucharist</term> <note>The central Christian ritual of sharing bread and wine</note>; for there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup for the unity of His blood, and one altar, just as there is one bishop, together with the council of elders and the deacons, my fellow-servants; so that, whatever you do, you may do it according to God.

2) "And" was omitted in the Vossian edition.

3) I have written "where indeed" according to Manuscript C; Manuscript L reads "but where," which Tischendorf also attests, and which all editors following Voss have printed.

5) The word "trustworthy" <note>Greek: "axiopistoi"</note> is taken not only to mean those who are worthy of faith, but also those who appear to be so. Voss. Compare the Letter to the Trallians, chapter 6; and to Polycarp, chapter 3.

6) Manuscripts C and L read "they lead captive"; Hefele reads the same based on Cotelier. Compare II Timothy 3:6.

Following this, Manuscripts C and L and Holsten's copy read "planting" <note>Greek: "phytian"</note>, as did Voss.

### II. *Maintain unity with the bishop, and flee from wicked doctrines.* <note>original Latin: "Tenete unionem cum episcopo, et fugite pravas doctrinas"</note>

Therefore, as children of light and truth, flee from division and wicked teachings; where the shepherd is, there follow as sheep. For many wolves, who are considered trustworthy, capture those running to God with deadly pleasures; but in your harmony, they will find no place.

* II. Wherefore, as children of the light of truth, flee from dissension and perverse doctrines. But where the shepherd is, follow there as sheep. For many enticing wolves lead captive those running in <term>God's racecourse</term> <note>original Latin: "in Dei stadio," a metaphor for the Christian life as an athletic competition</note> with the lure of deadly pleasure; but in your harmony, no place will be given to them.

### III. *Flee from schismatics.* <note>original Latin: "Fugite schismaticos." A schismatic is one who creates a split or division within the church.</note>

Abstain from the harmful weeds, which Jesus Christ does not cultivate, because they are not the Father’s planting. This is not because I found division among you, but rather a <term>purification</term> <note>original Latin: "defaecationem." Ignatius suggests the community has been "filtered" or "strained" of its impurities rather than simply split.</note>. For as many as belong to God and Jesus Christ, these are with the bishop; and as many as return to the unity of the church, led by repentance, these also shall belong to God, so that they may live according to Jesus Christ. Do not be deceived, my brothers. If anyone follows a <term>schismatic</term>, he does not obtain the inheritance of the divine kingdom; if anyone walks in a foreign doctrine, he does not agree with the <term>Passion</term> <note>original Latin: "passioni," referring to Christ’s suffering and death.</note>.

* III. Abstain from harmful weeds, which Jesus Christ does not tend, because they are not the Father's planting. This is not because I found dissension among you, but a pure and filtered spirit. For as many as are of God and Jesus Christ, these are with the Bishop, and as many as return to the unity of the Church, led by repentance, these shall be of God, that they may live according to Jesus Christ. Do not be deceived, my brothers. If anyone follows the author of a dissension, he does not inherit the kingdom of God. If anyone walks in a false opinion, he stands against the Passion.

### IV. *Use one Eucharist.* <note>original Latin: "Utamini una Eucharistia"</note>

Strive, therefore, to partake in one Eucharist; for there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup for the unity of his blood, one altar, just as there is one bishop, along with the <term>presbytery</term> <note>The council of elders or priests.</note> and deacons, my fellow servants; so that, whatever you do, you may do it according to God.

* IV. Wherefore, give your effort to using one Eucharist: for there is one flesh of our Lord Jesus Christ, and one cup for the union of his blood, one altar, just as there is one Bishop with the Presbytery and Deacons, my fellow servants: so that, whatever you do, you do according to God.

V. *Pray for me, who takes refuge in the Gospel and the Apostles. Honor also the prophets of the Old Testament.* <note>original Latin: "Orate pro me, qui confugio ad Evangelium et Apostolos. Honorate etiam prophetas V. T."</note>

My brothers, I am overflowing with love for you, and in my great joy I watch over you for your safety—yet it is not I, but Jesus Christ, in whom I am bound, and so I am the more afraid, as I am still <gloss>1</gloss> being carried away <note>Greek: "anarpastos," referring to being snatched away or dragged off as a prisoner.</note>. But your prayer to God will perfect me, so that I may attain that lot by which I have received mercy, taking refuge in the Gospel as the flesh of Jesus, and in the apostles as the council of the church. <gloss>2</gloss> And let us also love the prophets, because they too announced the Gospel, and hoped in Him, <gloss>3</gloss> and waited for Him; in whom they also believed and were saved, in the unity of Jesus Christ, being saints worthy of love and admiration, witnessed to by Jesus Christ, and numbered together in the Gospel of our common hope.

VI. *Do not, however, admit Judaism.* <note>original Latin: "Nec tamen Iudaismum admittite."</note>

But if anyone interprets Judaism to you, <gloss>1</gloss> do not listen to him. For it is better to hear about Christianity <gloss>2</gloss> from a man who is circumcised than to hear about Judaism <gloss>3</gloss> from one who is uncircumcised. But if neither of them speaks about Jesus Christ, they are to me like monuments and tombs of the dead, <gloss>4</gloss> upon which only the names of men are written. Flee therefore the evil arts and snares of the prince of this world, lest at any time, being oppressed by his influence, you grow weak <gloss>5</gloss> in love. But all of you, come together with an undivided heart. I thank my God that I have a good...

<columns>2</columns>

**Chapter V.** 1) The manuscript "p" reads "as he is," while manuscript "C" reads "as yet." Next, manuscripts "C" and "L" read *anarpastos* (snatched away), while the Interpolated version, the Old Interpreter, and the Armenian read *anapartistos* (imperfect/incomplete); this latter reading could easily have arisen from the following word "perfect" (*apartisei*). Vossius and Pearson have shown that the word *anarpastos* fits Ignatius well. The ancients called those *anarpastous* who were called out from the provinces and led away from their homeland and kin by force. Thus Josephus in *Antiquities of the Jews* (XIV. 8, 4): "And he rightly said that Aristobulus had been snatched away (*anarpaston*) to Rome." Gallicciolli translates: "I fear more, as if I were not yet dragged away." Perhaps, following the Casanatensian Codex, it should be written: "being as he is one snatched away."

2) H. A. Niemeyer, in *Fries and Schroeter's Opposition Journal* (I, 2. p. 14), explains this passage thus: "Gospel" = the sum of the life and deeds of Jesus; "Apostles" = the narratives of the Apostles about Christ. The sense: I cling to those things which Christ preached and did, as if He Himself were still living; and I cling to the narratives of the Apostles, as if they themselves still constituted the council of the church as they once did. But also—

<column-break/>

—I accept the Prophets of the Old Testament, since they announced Jesus. Compare also Rothe (*Anf.* p. 732) and Gieseler (*Attempt on the Origin of the Written Gospels* p. 157), who, before Niemeyer, had advised that the "Gospel" in our passage should not be understood as a written book. Lessing (Works, ed. Lachmann, Vol. XI, p. 567) thinks it should be written: "taking refuge in the bishop as the flesh of Jesus Christ, and in the elders of the church as the apostles." Others understand "Gospel" as the written Gospels, "Apostles" as the written Apostolic works, and "Prophets" as the written Prophets or the Old Testament. Eichhorn mistakenly dreams of the "Prophets" being New Testament teachers or Christian doctors. —H.

3) The Old Interpreter translates: *and hope in Christ.*

**Chapter VI.** 1) Manuscript "C" and "L" read "to us," for which Vossius correctly gave "to you."

2) Question: whether, just as the name "Christian" was first used at Antioch, so also the word "Christianity" (*Christianismos*) was first used by Ignatius, the Bishop of Antioch? —Pearson.

3) Manuscript "C" in the margin, by a more recent hand: *Against the Rabbis.*

V. *Pray for me, who takes refuge in the Gospel and the Apostles. Honor also the prophets of the Old Testament.* <note>original Latin: "Orate pro me, qui confugio ad Evangelium et Apostolos. Honorate etiam prophetas V. T."</note>

\* V. My brothers, I am exceedingly poured out in love for you, and exulting beyond measure in joy, I fortify you; yet not I, but Jesus Christ, in whom I am bound, and so I fear more, as being still imperfect: but your prayer to God will perfect me, so that I may attain the lot to which I have been called, taking refuge in the Gospel as the flesh of Jesus, and in the Apostles as the council of the Church. But we also love the Prophets, for the reason that they also proclaimed the Gospel, and hoped in Jesus himself and waited for him; in whom they also believed and obtained salvation, in the unity of Jesus Christ, holy and worthy men, whom we should love and admire, having received witness from Jesus Christ, and being numbered in the Gospel of our common hope.

Therefore, flee the evil arts and traps of the ruler of this world, lest you should ever be oppressed by his cunning and grow weak in love. But be all united with an undivided heart. ...I have behaved among you, and no one can boast, neither secretly nor openly, that I have been a burden<sup>6</sup> to anyone in small or great things. And for all those to whom I spoke, I pray that they do not use it as a testimony<sup>7</sup> against themselves.<sup>8</sup>

->VII. *Driven by the Holy Spirit, I have exhorted you to unity.*<-

For even if some desired to deceive me according to the flesh, yet the Spirit is not deceived, being from God. For it knows<sup>1</sup> from where it comes and where it goes, and it exposes secret things. I cried out while I was among you, speaking with a loud voice:<sup>2</sup> "Pay attention to the bishop, the council of elders <term>presbytery</term>, and the deacons." Now, some suspected<sup>3</sup> me of saying these things because I knew beforehand of the division among certain people. Rather, the Spirit preached, saying<sup>4</sup> these things: "Do nothing without the bishop; keep your flesh as the temple of God;<sup>5</sup> love unity; flee divisions; be imitators of Jesus Christ, as He also is of His Father."

->VIII. *Strive for unity. Christ is the place of all records.*<-

I, therefore, did my part as a man prepared for unity. For where there is division and anger, God does not dwell. Therefore, the Lord forgives all who repent, if they return to the unity of God and the council of the bishop. I trust in the grace of Jesus Christ, who will release every bond<sup>1</sup> from you. ->IX. *The Old Testament is good, but the New Covenant is better.*<-

The priests <note>original: "οἱ ἱερεῖς"</note> are good, but the High Priest <term>High Priest: referring here to Jesus Christ as the ultimate mediator between God and humanity</term> is greater, to whom alone the "Holy of Holies" <note>The inner sanctum of the Tabernacle and later the Temple in Jerusalem</note> has been entrusted, and who alone has been entrusted with the secret things of God. He is the door of the Father, through which Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the prophets, the apostles, and the church enter. All these things lead to the unity of God. But the Gospel has something uniquely excellent: the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, His suffering, and the resurrection. For the beloved prophets announced Him; but the Gospel is the fulfillment of immortality. All things together are good, if you believe with love.

---

->X. *Rejoice with those in Antioch over the end of the persecution.*<-

Since, according to your prayer and the compassion you have in Christ Jesus, it has been reported to me that the church in Antioch of Syria is at peace, it is fitting for you, as a church of God, to appoint a deacon <term>Deacon: a recognized minister or servant within the early church hierarchy</term> to go there as God's ambassador, to rejoice with them when they are gathered together, and to glorify the Name. Blessed in Jesus Christ is he who shall be found worthy of such a ministry; and you also shall be glorified. This is not impossible for you if you are willing, for the sake of God’s name; just as the nearest churches have sent bishops, and others elders and deacons.

---

Chapter IX. 1) The priests = Jewish priests = the old dispensation; the High Priest = Christ = the new covenant. Rothe (Anf. p. 731 sq.) thinks differently, taking "priests" to mean the Christians of the Philadelphian church, explaining: *your prayers for me are good, but the prayers of Christ are much better*. However, the flow of thought does not favor Rothe's explanation. The word for "greater" appears as "superior" in the Interpolated version.

2) Alludes to the Holy of Holies of the ancient temple. Compare Hebrews 2:17, 9:25.

3) "Being" <note>original: "ὢν"</note> is found in manuscripts C and L. I believe Voss’s "would be" is an error. Compare John 10:7, 9.

4) The arrangement of the Old and New Testaments looks toward the restoration of humanity with God.

5) The Interpolated version uses "Savior" instead of "Lord"; the old translation renders both: *the presence of the Savior our Lord Jesus Christ*; The Armenian version reads: *But excellence exists in the gospel, the advent of the Savior our Lord Jesus Christ.*

<column-break/>

6) That is, through the Gospel, the kingdom of God <note>original: "ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note> and eternal life in this kingdom are established. Heringius explains this passage differently: a perfect doctrine that will always remain, after which nothing more will be revealed. In the margin of manuscript C, a second hand wrote the sentence: *the Gospel is the completion of immortality.*

7) Gallicciolli: *All these things together are beautiful, if you believe them in charity.* <note>original Italian: "Tutte insieme queste cose sono belle, se in carità le crediate."</note>

8) So read C and L; the old translation uses the indicative "you believe," which was followed by Voss and those who copied him.

Chapter X. 1) "Since" <note>original: "ἐπειδὴ"</note> in C and L; Cotelerius, Smith, and others followed Voss in reading "But after." The next "and" was added by Jacobson from L, now supported by C. The article "the" before "compassion" was omitted in the third and fourth editions by Hefele.

2) Before Ignatius left Asia, it became known to him that the persecution stirred up against the Christians in Antioch had ceased. This is clear from this passage and from the Letter to the Smyrnaeans, ch. 11 (compare Letter to Polycarp, ch. 7).

### IX. *The Old Testament is good, but the New Covenant is better.*

The priests <note>original: "sacerdotes"</note> are indeed good, but the High Priest <term>High Priest: referring here to Jesus Christ as the ultimate mediator between God and humanity</term> is more excellent, to whom the "Holy of Holies" <note>The inner sanctum of the Temple; here used metaphorically for the deepest mysteries of God</note> has been entrusted, and to whom alone the secret things of God have been committed. He Himself is the door of the Father, through which Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, the prophets, the apostles, and the church enter. All these things lead toward union with God. But the Gospel possesses something unique: the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ, His suffering, and His resurrection. For the beloved prophets announced Him; but the Gospel is the fulfillment of eternal life. All things together are good, provided you believe with love.

\* IX. The priests are certainly good; but the High Priest is better, to whom the Holy of Holies has been entrusted: who alone has the secrets of God committed to Him. He is the door to the Father, through which Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob enter; likewise the Prophets, the Apostles, and the Churches: all these lead to the unity of God. But the Gospel has something exceptional, namely the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and His passion and resurrection. For the beloved Prophets announced things concerning Him: but the Gospel is the perfection of incorruptibility <note>original: "incorruptibilitatis", suggesting the eternal, unchanging nature of the soul in Christ</note>. All things together are good, if you believe in love.

---

### X. *Congratulate those in Antioch on the end of the persecution.*

Since it has been reported to me that, through your prayer and the compassion you feel in Christ, the church at Antioch in Syria has obtained peace; it is fitting for you, as a church of God, to choose a deacon <term>Deacon: a recognized minister or servant within the early church hierarchy</term> to fulfill a divine embassy there. He should rejoice with them when they are gathered together and should glorify the Name. Blessed is he in Jesus Christ who shall be found worthy of such a ministry; and you also shall be glorified. To you who are willing, this is not impossible for the sake of God’s name, just as some neighboring churches have sent bishops <term>Bishop: an overseer or senior leader (Episcopos)</term>, and others have sent priests <term>Priest: an elder or presbyter (Presbyteros)</term> and deacons.

\* X. Since indeed, through your prayer and the deep affection <note>original: "viscera", literally "the bowels," a common metaphor for deep-seated compassion</note> you have in Christ Jesus, it has been reported to me that the Church of Antioch in Syria is at peace, it is fitting for you, as the Church of God, to choose a Deacon to undertake God's embassy there, so that being joined together in one place, you may rejoice with them and glorify the name of God. Blessed is he in Jesus Christ who shall be worthy to perform this ministry: and you also shall be glorified. If you are willing, this is not difficult for the sake of God's name, just as neighboring Churches have sent, in some cases, Bishops, and in others, Priests and Deacons.

<header>IGNATIUS’S LETTER TO THE PHILADELPHIANS XI. TO THE SMYRNAEANS I.</header>

**XI.** I give thanks to you, because you kindly received my companions. The brothers in Troas greet you.

As for Philo, the deacon from Cilicia, a man of renown who even now serves me for the sake of God, together with Rheus Agathopus, an elect man who accompanies me from Syria, having renounced this life <note>original: "vitae renuntians" — likely referring to leaving behind worldly affairs or status to serve the church</note>; they also give a good testimony of you. I myself give thanks to God for you, because you received them, just as the Lord received you. May the grace of Christ forgive those who treated them with dishonor. The love of the brothers in Troas greets you, from where I also write to you by the hand of Burrhus, who was sent with me by the Ephesians and Smyrnaeans as a mark of honor. May the Lord Jesus Christ honor them—He in whom they hope in flesh, soul, faith, love, and harmony. Farewell in Christ Jesus, our common hope.

* XI. Furthermore, concerning Philo the Deacon from Cilicia, a man who bears a good testimony, and who even now serves me in the word of God, along with Rheus and Agathopus, an elect man who has followed me from Syria since he renounced his own life; they also bear testimony of you. I myself give thanks to God on your behalf, because you welcomed them, just as the Lord welcomed you. But as for those who treated them with insult, may they be delivered through the grace of Jesus Christ. The love of the brothers who are in Troas greets you, from where I also write to you through Burrhus, who was sent to me by both the Ephesians and the Smyrnaeans for the sake of honor. The Lord Jesus Christ will reward them—He in whom they hope in flesh, soul, faith, love, and harmony. Farewell in Christ Jesus, our common hope.

---

### III. *Christ was in the flesh even after the resurrection.*

For I know and believe that He was in the flesh even after the resurrection. And when He came to those who were with Peter <note>original: "tou peri Petron"</note>, He said to them: "Take, handle me, and see that I am not a bodiless demon." <note>original: "daimonion asomaton." This famous line does not appear in the four canonical Gospels, leading scholars to debate its source.</note> And immediately they touched Him and believed, being united <note>term: "krathentes" — literally "blended" or "mixed," suggesting a profound physical and spiritual union</note> with His flesh and spirit. Because of this, they also despised death, and were found to be beyond the reach of death. Moreover, after the resurrection, He ate and drank with them as a being of flesh, although spiritually He was united with the Father.

### IV. *Beware of these heretics. If Christ did not truly suffer, neither would I.*

I am advising you of these things, beloved, though I know that you yourselves hold these same beliefs. But I am guarding you against those beasts in human form <note>Ignatius uses "beasts" to describe false teachers whose doctrines he considers spiritually predatory</note>, whom you must not only refuse to receive, but if possible, not even meet. You should only pray for them, if perhaps they might repent—which is difficult. However, Jesus Christ, our true life, has the power to bring this about. For if these things were done by our Lord only in appearance <note>original: "to dokein" — the root of the word "Docetism," meaning to "seem" or "appear"</note>, then I am also bound only in appearance. Why then have I given myself up to death, to fire, to the sword, to the beasts? But to be near the sword is to be near God; to be among the beasts is to be among God; only let it be in the name of Jesus Christ. I endure all things so that I may suffer with Him <note>note: original: "sumpathein," echoing the language of the Apostle Paul in Romans 8:17</note>, as He who became the perfect man strengthens me.

### V. *The danger of the Docetists’ error.*

Whom some, being ignorant, deny—or rather, they have been denied by Him—since they are advocates of death rather than of the truth. These are people whom neither the prophecies—

### III. *Christ was in the flesh even after the resurrection.*

For I know and believe that He was in the flesh even after the resurrection. And when He came to Peter and those with him, He said to them: "Take, handle me, and see that I am not a bodiless demon." <note>original: "daemonium incorporale." Ignatius is likely quoting a non-canonical source here, perhaps the Gospel of the Hebrews or the Preaching of Peter, to prove that Jesus had a solid, physical body after rising.</note> And immediately they touched Him and believed, being united <note>term: "mixti" — literally "mixed" or "blended," used here to describe a deep, inseparable union of the disciples with Christ's physical and spiritual reality</note> with His flesh and spirit. Because of this, they also despised death and were found to be victors over death. Moreover, after the resurrection, He ate and drank with them as a physical being, although spiritually He was united with the Father.

* III. Indeed, I knew Him in the flesh even after the resurrection, and I believe He is still in the flesh. For when He came to Peter and his companions, He said to them: "Take, handle me, and see that I am not an incorporeal demon." And at once they touched Him and believed, joined to His flesh and spirit. Therefore, they also looked down upon death; for they were found to be superior to death. After the resurrection, He truly ate and drank with them like a man of flesh, even though He was spiritually one with the Father.

### IV. *Beware of these heretics. Unless Christ truly suffered, neither would I.*

I am warning you of these things, beloved, although I know that you hold the same convictions. But I am guarding you in advance against beasts in human form, whom you must not only refuse to welcome, but if possible, you should not even meet them. You should only pray for them, in case they might somehow repent—which is very difficult. However, Jesus Christ, who is our true life, has the power to grant this. For if these things were done by our Lord only in appearance <note>original: "ad apparentiam." This refers to the Docetist heresy (from the Greek "dokein," meaning "to seem"), which claimed Christ only *seemed* to suffer.</note>, then I am also a prisoner only in appearance. Why then have I given myself up to death—to fire, to the sword, to the wild beasts? But the one who is near the sword is near to God; the one who is with the beasts is with God; provided it is in the name of Jesus Christ. That I may suffer together with Him, I endure all things, as He who became a perfect man strengthens me.

* IV. I remind you of these things, dear friends, knowing that you feel the same way. But I protect you against beasts who carry a human shape; you should not only not receive them, but you should avoid even encountering them, if possible. Pray only for them, if perhaps they may be led to repentance, which is a hard thing. But Jesus Christ, our true life, alone has the power over that. For if those deeds were done by our Lord only in opinion, then I am a prisoner only in opinion. Why then have I offered myself to death—to fire, to the sword, to wild animals? But he who is close to the sword is close to God; he who is surrounded by beasts is surrounded by God: only let it be in the name of Jesus Christ, so that I may suffer with Him. I endure everything because He comforts me, who was born a perfect man.

...the prophecies, nor the law of Moses, <note>original: "νόμος Μωσέως"</note> nor even the Gospel until now, nor our own personal sufferings. For they think the same thing about us. <note>These heretics believe that if Christ only "seemed" to suffer, then the martyrs' actual physical pain is also an illusion or is worthless.</note> For what does it profit me if someone praises me, but blasphemes my Lord, not confessing Him to be a flesh-bearer? <note>term: σαρκοφόρος (sarkophoros) — "flesh-bearer." Ignatius uses this to emphasize that Jesus truly carried a human body.</note> But he who does not say this has completely denied Him, being himself a corpse-bearer. <note>term: νεκροφόρος (nekrophoros) — "corpse-bearer." A biting wordplay by Ignatius: if you deny Christ’s life-giving flesh, you are just a living dead man carrying your own corpse.</note> But their names, being those of unbelievers, I have not seen fit to record. May it not even happen that I remember them, until they repent regarding the passion, which is our resurrection.

### VI. *Whoever does not believe in the blood of Christ will be judged, even if he were an angel. These heretics even lack virtues.*

Let no one be deceived. Even heavenly beings, and the glory of the angels, and the rulers visible and invisible, if they do not believe in the blood of Christ, judgment awaits them too. "Let him who can receive it, receive it." <note>This is a quote from the Gospel of Matthew 19:12.</note> Let position puff no one up; for the whole is faith and love, to which nothing is preferred. But consider those who hold heterodox opinions <note>term: ἑτεροδοξοῦντας (heterodoxountas) — literally "other-thinking," the root of the word "heterodox."</note> regarding the grace of Jesus Christ which has come to us, how contrary they are to the mind of God. They have no concern for love, nor for the widow, nor for the orphan, nor for the afflicted, nor for the prisoner or the one released, nor for the hungry or thirsty.

### VII. *These heretics abstain from the Eucharist, denying that it is the flesh of Christ. Let us stay away from them.*

They abstain from the Eucharist and prayer, because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father, in His goodness, raised up.

...neither the law of Moses, nor the Gospel until this day, nor our individual sufferings. For they hold the same opinion about us. For what does it benefit me if someone praises me, but blasphemes my Lord, denying that He assumed flesh? But he who does not profess this has completely denied Him, himself carrying a corpse. <note>original: "funus portans" — This mirrors the "corpse-bearer" pun from the previous page.</note> Their names, since they belong to unbelievers, I did not think it right to write down. And far be it from me to make mention of them, until they return to the passion of Christ, which is our resurrection.

<note>The following paragraph is a parallel Latin translation of the same passage above, often found in early modern scholarly editions to show textual variations.</note>

...[to] persuade, neither the Mosaic law, nor the Gospel itself until now, nor our tortures which we individuals endure: for they think the same about us. For what does it profit me, if someone praises me, but blasphemes my Lord, not confessing Him to be clothed in flesh? But he who does not say this has utterly denied Him, carrying around a cadaver. Furthermore, their names, since they belong to unbelievers, I did not wish to insert into these letters. But far be it from me to make mention of them, until they come to their senses regarding the passion, which is our resurrection.

### VI. Whoever does not believe in the blood of Christ will be judged, even if he were an angel. These heretics even lack virtues.

Let no one be deceived. Even the heavenly beings, and the glory of the angels, and the rulers visible and invisible, if they do not believe in the blood of Christ, they too will be judged. "Let him who can receive it, receive it." <note>A reference to Matthew 19:12.</note> Let position puff no one up; for the whole is faith and charity, <note>In this context, "charity" (caritas) refers to Christian love in action.</note> than which nothing is more excellent. But consider those who hold a different opinion regarding the grace of Jesus Christ which has come to us, how contrary they are to the divine will. They have no care for charity: no care for the widow, no care for the orphan, no care for the oppressed, no care for the prisoner or the one released, no care for the hungry or the thirsty.

* VI. Let no one be deceived; even heavenly things, and the glory of Angels, and rulers visible and invisible. If we do not believe in the blood of Christ, there is judgment even for them. "He who takes it, let him take it": let position inflate no one: for the whole and the principal thing is faith and charity, than which nothing is more excellent. But consider those who think differently about the grace of Jesus Christ which has reached us, how they oppose the mind of God regarding love: they have no care for the widow, nor for the orphan, nor for the afflicted, nor for the prisoner, nor for the freeman, nor for the hungry or thirsty.

### VII. These heretics abstain from the Eucharist, denying that it is the flesh of Christ. Let us stay away from them.

They abstain from the Eucharist and prayer, because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father in His goodness raised up. Those therefore...

* VII. They abstain from the Eucharist and prayer, because they do not confess that the Eucharist is the flesh of our Savior Jesus Christ, which suffered for our sins, and which the Father in His goodness raised up.

-># THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE SMYRNAEANS. VII. VIII. IX.<-

Therefore, those who speak against the gift of God perish while they engage in disputes.<sup>3</sup> It would be better<sup>4</sup> for them to love,<sup>5</sup> <note>The Greek verb *agapan* can mean "to love" or "to celebrate the Agape feast."</note> so that they might also rise again. It is proper, therefore, to keep away from such people, and not to speak about them either privately or publicly; instead, give heed<sup>6</sup> to the prophets, and especially to the Gospel, in which the passion has been revealed to us and the resurrection has been perfected.<sup>7</sup> But flee from divisions as the beginning of evils.<sup>8</sup>

## VIII. Let nothing be done without the bishop.

All of you, follow the bishop, as Jesus Christ follows the Father; and follow the council of elders <note>original: "presbyterion"</note> as you would the apostles; and respect the deacons as the commandment of God.<sup>1</sup> Let no one do anything relating to the church without<sup>2</sup> the bishop. Let that be considered a valid Eucharist which is celebrated under the bishop, or by one whom he appoints.<sup>3</sup> Wherever the bishop appears, let the congregation be there; just as wherever Jesus Christ is, there is the **Catholic**<sup>5</sup> **Church**. <note>This is the earliest known use of the phrase "Catholic Church" in Christian literature, meaning the "universal" or "whole" church.</note> It is not permitted without the bishop either to baptize or to hold a love-feast; <term>Agape</term> <note>A common meal shared by early Christians, often associated with the Eucharist.</note> but whatever he approves, this is also pleasing to God, so that everything you do may be secure<sup>6</sup> and valid.

## IX. Honor the bishop. You have refreshed me in all things.

It is reasonable, finally,<sup>1</sup> for us to return to soberness and, while we still have time,<sup>2</sup> to repent toward God. It is good to recognize both God and the bishop. He who honors the bishop has been honored by God; he who does anything secretly from the bishop serves the devil. — Therefore, let all things abound for you in grace, for you are worthy. You have refreshed me<sup>3</sup> in all things, and may Jesus Christ refresh you. You have loved me whether I was absent or present. May God repay<sup>4</sup> you, for whose sake you endure all things, and so you will attain Him.

those who speak against this gift of God perish in their disputing. It would be beneficial for them to love, so that they might also rise again. It is fitting, therefore, to abstain from such people, and not to speak of them either in private or in public conversation; but rather to give heed to the prophets, and especially to the Gospel, in which the passion is shown to us and the resurrection is perfectly demonstrated. But flee from divisions, as the beginning of all evils.

Whoever, therefore, speaks against the divine gift, perishes in their searching. But love would be advantageous to them, so that they might also rise again. It is fitting, then, to abstain from such things, and not to speak of them privately or publicly; but to give heed to the Prophets, and most of all to the Gospel, in which the passion is placed before our eyes and the resurrection is perfectly explained to us. Flee from separation, as the source of evils.

### VIII. *Let nothing be done without the bishop.*

All of you, obey the bishop as Jesus Christ obeyed the Father; and the council of elders <note>original: "presbyterio"</note> as you would the apostles; and revere the deacons as the command of God. Let no one do anything relating to the church apart from the bishop. Let that be considered a valid Eucharist which is performed under the bishop, or under one to whom he has granted permission. Wherever the bishop appears, let the congregation be present; just as wherever Christ Jesus is, there is the **Catholic Church**. <note>original: "catholica est ecclesia." This is the earliest recorded use of the term "Catholic" (meaning universal or whole) to describe the Church.</note> It is not permitted without the bishop either to baptize or to celebrate the love-feast; <term>Agape</term> <note>A communal meal shared by early Christians to express their fellowship and love.</note> but whatever he approves, this is also well-pleasing to God, so that everything that is done may be firm and valid.

\* VIII. All of you, follow the Bishop as Jesus Christ followed the Father, and the college of Presbyters as if they were Apostles; and revere the Deacons as a divine precept. Without the Bishop, let no one do anything of those things which pertain to the Church. Let that Eucharist be held as certain which is under the Bishop or to whom he himself has granted it. Wherever the Bishop appears, there let the multitude be: just as where Christ is, there is the Catholic Church. It is not lawful without the Bishop either to baptize or to celebrate the love-feast; but whatever he shall have approved, this will also be pleasing to God, so that whatever is done may be firm and certain.

### IX. *Honor the bishop. You have refreshed me in all things.*

Moreover, it is reasonable for us to return to a sober mind, and while we still have time, to return to God through repentance. It is good to honor both God and the bishop. He who honors the bishop is honored by God; he who does anything secretly from the bishop serves the devil. — Now may grace be supplied to you abundantly in all things; for you are worthy. You have refreshed me in every way, and Jesus Christ has refreshed you. You have loved me both when I was absent and when I was present. May God reward you, for whose sake you endure all things, and so shall you attain unto Him.

\* IX. It is thereafter consistent to become wise again, and while we still have time, to be converted to God through repentance. It is good to recognize God and the Bishop. He who honors the Bishop is honored by God; he who does anything secretly from the Bishop performs service for the devil. Therefore, let all things be done for you with grace; for you are worthy. You have refreshed me in all things: so may Jesus Christ refresh you. You have loved me while absent and while present; may God reward you, for whom you endure all things, and you shall possess Him.

->THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE SMYRNAEANS. X. XI.<-

### X. *You have kindly received my companions; your reward will not fail.*

You did well in receiving Philo and Rheus Agathopus <note>original: "Ῥέον Ἀγαθόπουν"</note> as servants of Christ God, for they followed me for the sake of the Word of God. They also give thanks to the Lord on your behalf, because you refreshed them in every way. Nothing you have done for them will be lost to you. My spirit is a sacrifice for you <note>original: "Ἀντίψυχον ὑμῶν," meaning a ransom or a substitute for your souls</note>, as are my chains, which you did not despise nor were you ashamed of. Neither will the perfect faith, Jesus Christ, be ashamed of you.

### XI. *Send an envoy to the people of Antioch for the sake of the peace restored there.*

Your prayer has reached the church in Antioch of Syria. From there, bound in these most godly chains, I greet everyone. I am not worthy to be from there, being the very last of them; yet by the will [of God] I was deemed worthy—not by my own conscience <note>meaning his own merit or awareness of worthiness</note>, but by the grace of God. I pray that this grace may be given to me in perfection, so that through your prayer I may attain to God. Therefore, so that your work may be perfect both on earth and in heaven, it is fitting for your church, for the honor of God, to appoint a "God-envoy" <note>original: "θεοπρεσβύτην," a sacred ambassador</note> to go as far as Syria to rejoice with them, because they are now at peace, have regained their proper stature, and have had their own corporate body <note>original: "σωματεῖον," referring to the restoration of their communal organization</note> restored to them. It seemed to me, therefore, a worthy thing to send one of your people with a letter, so that he might join in glorifying the [peace]...

Chapter X. 1) **Rheos** in both manuscripts. Vossius observes: "I read **Rheus**. Rheus Agathopus was the name of this good man whom Ignatius praises. However, interpreters have wrongly formed two names from it. Not content with this error, they substituted *Gaius* and *Gavius* for Rheus. But you can see in Ussher <note>Latin: "Armachanum," referring to James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh</note> how variously the name of Agathopus has been corrupted. # THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE SMYRNAEANS. X. XI.

### X. *You have kindly received my companions; your reward will not fail.*

You have kindly received my companions; your reward will not fail you.

In receiving Philo and Rheus Agathopus, who followed me for the sake of God, as ministers <note>original: "ministros," referring to those who serve the church</note> of Christ God, you have done well. They also give thanks to the Lord on your behalf, because you refreshed them in every way. None of these things will be lost to you. In return, may my spirit and my chains—which you did not despise and of which you were not ashamed—be a refreshment for you. Nor will the perfect faith, Jesus Christ, be ashamed of you.

* X. You did well in receiving Philo, Rheus, and Agathopus as my companions in the word of God, just as you would receive ministers of Christ God. They also give thanks to the Lord for you, because you revived them in every possible way. Nothing of your benefit to them will perish; for I, in turn, am ready to offer my spirit and my chains for your soul <note>original: "pro anima vestra," suggesting a spiritual sacrifice or dedication</note>, which you did not look down upon, nor did you blush because of them. Therefore, our perfect faith, Jesus Christ, will not be ashamed of you either.

### XI. ->*Send an envoy to the people of Antioch for the sake of the peace restored there.*<-

I pray that this grace may be given to me in perfection, so that through your prayer I may attain to God. So that your work may now be made complete before God and men, it is fitting for the honor of God that your church elect a sacred envoy <note>original: "sacrum legatum," a representative of the church</note> who, when he arrives in Syria, may congratulate them that they have achieved peace, and have regained their greatness, and that their corporate body <note>original: "corpus," referring to the organized structure of the local church</note> has been restored to them. Therefore, it seemed a worthy thing to me that you should send someone of your own with a letter, who might join them in glorifying the tranquility which, according to God’s will—
