I do not command these things as an apostle; for who am I? Or what is my father’s house <note>A biblical expression of humility, famously used by King David in the Old Testament.</note>, that I should call myself equal in honor to those men? Rather, I am your fellow-soldier, holding the rank of a prompter <note>original: *ὑποφωνητοῦ* (hypophōnētou); one who suggests words to a speaker or an assistant in a choir.</note>.

V. My brothers, I am overflowing with love for you, and in my great joy, I watch over your safety—though not I, but the Lord Jesus through me. Being bound in Him, I am the more afraid, for I am still incomplete <note>Ignatius uses "incomplete" to mean he has not yet achieved his goal of martyrdom, which he viewed as the perfection of his faith.</note>. But your prayer to God will complete me, so that I may attain the lot to which I was called, having fled to the Gospel as to the flesh of Jesus Christ, and to the apostles as to the presbytery <note>The council of elders or priests.</note> of the Church. And I love the prophets also, because they announced Christ, and because they participated in the same Spirit as the apostles. For just as the false prophets and the false apostles drew to themselves one and the same wicked, deceitful, and people-misleading spirit; so also the prophets and the apostles received from God, through Jesus Christ, one and the same Holy Spirit, who is good, sovereign, true, and instructional. For there is one God of the Old and New Testaments; one mediator between God and men, for the creation of things intellectual and things perceptible, and for a fitting and suitable providence; and there is one Comforter <note>original: *Παράκλητος* (Paraklētos); the Holy Spirit.</note>, who worked in Moses, the prophets, and the apostles. All the saints, therefore, were saved in Christ, hoping in Him and waiting for Him; and through Him they obtained salvation, being saints worthy of love and admiration, having been witnessed to by Jesus Christ in the Gospel of our common hope.

VI. If anyone preaches that there is one God of the Law and the prophets, but denies that Christ is the Son of God, he is a liar, even as his father the devil is; and such a person is a false Jew of the "lower circumcision" <note>A derogatory reference to physical circumcision without spiritual faith.</note>. If anyone confesses Jesus Christ the Lord, but denies the God of the Law and the prophets, saying that the Father of Christ is not the Creator of heaven and earth, such a person does not stand in the truth, even as his father the devil does not; such a person is a disciple of Simon Magus <note>A figure from the Book of Acts who was traditionally viewed by early Christians as the first heretic and the father of Gnosticism.</note>, and not of the Holy Spirit. If anyone says that there is one God, and confesses Jesus Christ, but thinks the Lord is a mere man <note>original: *ψιλὸν ἄνθρωπον* (psilon anthrōpon); the heresy that Jesus was only human and not divine.</note>, and not the only-begotten God, and Wisdom, and the Word of God, but supposes Him to consist only of a soul and body, such a person...

For there is one God of the Old and New Testaments; one Mediator <note>A go-between; here referring to Christ connecting God and humanity.</note> between God and men, for the creation of both spiritual <note>original: *intelligibilium*; things understood by the mind.</note> and physical <note>original: *sensibilium*; things perceived by the senses.</note> things, who exercises providence over all. There is also one Paraclete <note>The Holy Spirit, often translated as Comforter, Advocate, or Helper.</note>, who worked in Moses and the prophets and the apostles. For all the saints were saved in Christ, hoping in Him and awaiting Him; and through Him they obtained salvation, being worthy of love and praise, sanctified by Jesus Christ, and bearing witness in the Gospel of our common hope.

If anyone preaches that the God of the Law and the Prophets is the only God, but denies that Christ is the Son of God, he is a liar, just as his father the Devil is; and such a person is a "False-Jew" of the inferior circumcision. But if anyone confesses Christ Jesus as Lord, yet denies that the God of the Law and the Prophets is the Father of Christ, he does not stand in the truth, just as his father the Devil does not; and such a person is a disciple of Simon Magus <note>A figure from the Book of Acts who tried to buy spiritual power; he was later considered the "father of all heresies" by early church writers.</note> and not of the Holy Spirit. <header>THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE PHILADELPHIANS. VI. VII.</header>

He is a serpent, preaching deceit and error for the destruction of men. Such a person is poor in his understanding, just as he is called <term>Ebion</term> <note>The name Ebion comes from the Hebrew word for "poor." Ignatius is making a wordplay: the Ebionites, who viewed Jesus as merely a man, are "poor" in their spiritual insight.</note>. If anyone confesses these things <note>referring to the core tenets of the faith mentioned previously</note> but calls lawful union <note>marriage</note> and the procreation of children "corruption" and "defilement," or finds certain foods to be detestable, such a person has the apostate dragon dwelling within him. If anyone confesses the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, and praises the creation, but says that the <term>incarnation</term> <note>original: "ensomatosis," the act of taking on a body</note> was merely an appearance <note>This refers to Docetism, the belief that Jesus only "seemed" to have a physical body and did not truly suffer.</note> and is ashamed of the passion, such a person has denied the faith no less than the Christ-killing Jews. If anyone confesses these things, and that God the Word dwelt in a human body—being the Word within it as a soul is in a body, because it was God inhabiting it, but not a human soul <note>This specific view—that Jesus had a divine soul instead of a human one—was later known as Apollinarianism, though the author here presents it as an orthodox defense against other heresies.</note>—yet says that unlawful unions are a good thing and places the goal of happiness in pleasure, such as the falsely-named <term>Nicolaitan</term> <note>A group mentioned in the Book of Revelation, often accused by early church writers of promoting sexual immorality.</note>, this person can be neither a lover of God nor a lover of Christ. Rather, he is a corrupter of his own flesh, and for this reason, he is empty of the Holy Spirit and a stranger to Christ. All such people are but pillars and tombs of the dead, upon which only the names of dead men are written.

Flee, therefore, the evil arts and snares of the spirit that is now at work in the sons of this age, lest you ever become weakened in love by being oppressed. Instead, all of you come together in an undivided heart and a willing soul, being of one mind, always thinking the same things about the same matters, both in times of ease and in dangers, in sorrows and in joys. I give thanks to God through Jesus Christ that I have a good conscience among you, and no one can boast, either secretly or openly, that I was a burden to anyone in matters small or great. And for all those to whom I have spoken, I pray that they do not possess that speech as a testimony against themselves.

VII. For if some people wanted to lead me astray according to the flesh, yet my spirit is not led astray; for I have received it from God. For it knows from where it comes and where it goes, and it exposes secret things. For I cried out, while I was speaking among you, with a loud voice: "This is not my word, but God's: Attend to the bishop, and to the presbytery, and to the deacons." But if you suspect me of saying these things because I had prior knowledge of the division of certain people, He is my witness, for whose sake I am in chains, that I did not learn this from the mouth of any man. Rather, the Spirit preached to me, saying: "Do nothing without the bishop; keep your flesh as the temple of God; love unity; flee divisions; be imitators of Paul and the other apostles, just as they also were of Christ."

### VII.

For even if some people wanted to lead me astray according to the flesh, my spirit is not led astray; for I received it from God. For it knows where it came from and where it is going, and it exposes secret things. For I cried out with a loud voice among those to whom I was speaking—bringing forth not my own word, but the word of God: "Pay attention to the <term>Bishop</term>, and to the <term>Presbytery</term> <note>The council of elders or priests within a local church.</note>, and to the <term>Deacons</term>." ### VIII.

I, for my part, did what was my own duty, as a man set apart for the sake of unity; and I add this also: where there is division of opinion, and anger, and hatred, God does not dwell. Therefore, God forgives<gloss>1</gloss> all who repent, if they run together into the unity of Christ and the council<gloss>2</gloss> of the bishop. I have faith in the grace of Jesus Christ, that He will loosen every bond of injustice from us<gloss>3</gloss>. I exhort you, then: do nothing out of selfish ambition<gloss>4</gloss>, but according to the learning of Christ<gloss>5</gloss>. <note>The Greek text here uses a play on words between "chrestomatheia" (good learning) and "christomatheia" (the learning of Christ), suggesting that true education is found in following Him.</note> For I heard some people saying, "If I do not find the Gospel in the archives,<gloss>6</gloss> I do not believe it." <note>The "archives" here refer to the Old Testament scriptures. Ignatius is addressing people who refused to accept any Christian teaching that wasn't explicitly spelled out in ancient Hebrew prophecy.</note> To such people I say that, for me, the "archives" are Jesus Christ; to disobey Him is manifest destruction. My authentic<gloss>7</gloss> archive is His cross and His death, and His resurrection, and the faith which is through these; by which I desire, through your prayers, to be justified. He who does not believe the Gospel, disbelieves everything at once; for the archives of the Spirit are not to be preferred above it<gloss>8</gloss>. It is hard to kick against the pricks, hard to disbelieve Christ, and hard to reject the preaching of the Apostles.

### IX.

The priests<gloss>1</gloss> and the ministers of the word are indeed good; but the High Priest is superior<gloss>2</gloss>, for He has been entrusted with the Holy of Holies, and He alone has been entrusted with the secrets of God. The ministering<gloss>3</gloss> powers of God are good. But<gloss>4</gloss> the Comforter is holy, and the Word is holy, the Son of the Father, through whom the Father has made<gloss>5</gloss> all things and provides for the whole universe. He is the Way that leads to the Father, the Rock, the Fence, the Key, the Shepherd, the Sacrifice, the Door of knowledge, through which Abraham and Isaac and Jacob entered, as did Moses and the entire choir of the prophets, and the pillars of the world—the Apostles—and the bride of Christ, for whose sake, as a dowry, He poured out<gloss>6</gloss> His own blood so that He might redeem her. All these things lead toward the unity of the one and only true God. But the Gospel has something surpassing: the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, His passion, and the resurrection itself. For what the prophets were announcing<gloss>7</gloss>, saying, "Until<gloss>8</gloss> He comes, for whom it is reserved, and He is the expectation of the nations," <note>A reference to the messianic prophecy in Genesis 49:10.</note> these things have been fulfilled in the Gospel: "Go and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit." All things, therefore, are good when taken together—the Law, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the whole assembly that has believed through them—provided that we love one another.

### VIII.

I indeed did what was my part, as a man made perfect in unity; and I add this also: where there is dissension of mind and anger and hatred, there God does not dwell. Therefore, God forgives all who repent, if they run together to the unity of Christ and to the consensus of the Bishop <term>Bishop: from the Greek *Episcopus*, the head of the local Christian community</term>. He who does not believe the Gospel, does not believe all things <gloss>8: to men in the Palatine manuscript</gloss> at once, because the antiquity <gloss>9: by antiquity in the Palatine and Regius manuscripts</gloss> of the spirit is not judged beforehand. For "it is hard to kick against the goad" <gloss>10: Acts 9:5 and 26:14</gloss>; it is also hard not to believe in Christ; it is also hard to despise the preaching of the Apostles.

### IX.

For the priests <gloss>1: For the priests are good in the Regius manuscript</gloss> and the ministers of the word are good; but the High Priest <note>Latin: *Pontifex*. Ignatius uses this title to describe Christ as the ultimate mediator between God and humanity</note> is better, to whom the Holy of Holies has been entrusted, to whom alone the secrets of God have been committed. Also good are the offices of God's power <gloss>2: the Lord's in the Palatine manuscript</gloss>; good also <gloss>3: also and in the Palatine manuscript</gloss> is the Holy Spirit, who is the holiest of all holy things <gloss>4: "holy" omitted in the Regius manuscript</gloss>, and the minister of the word. But more holy than all the holy is the High Priest, 

<column-break/>

and the Prince of Priests <gloss>5: The words "High Priest, and" are not read in the Palatine or Regius manuscripts</gloss> <gloss>6: "Priests of God" in the Palatine; "of the Priests" in the Regius</gloss>; who is the ambassador and minister of the Father, and the prince of the legions of the heavenly host <gloss>7: the legion of the heavenly host in the Palatine manuscript</gloss>; through whom the Father made <gloss>8: makes in the Palatine. All these things, therefore, are in the unity of the one and only-begotten true God. But what does the Gospel have that is special? The presence of the coming of our Savior Jesus Christ, His passion, and indeed His resurrection itself. For the things which the Prophets announced, saying: "Until He comes, for whom it is reserved <gloss>15: "are reserved" (plural) in the Palatine and Regius manuscripts. Therefore, all things together are good: the Law, the Prophets, the Apostles, and the whole congregation which has believed through them. It only remains that we love one another <gloss>17: that we might love one another in the Regius manuscript</gloss>.

<summary>Ignatius argues that Jesus Christ is the fulfillment and the "archive" of all ancient prophecy, asserting that faith in Christ's resurrection is the only path to justification. He portrays Christ as the High Priest and the spiritual door through which all patriarchs, prophets, and apostles must enter into unity with God.</summary>

<header>IGNATIUS'S EPISTLE TO THE PHILADELPHIANS. X. XI.</header>

### X.

Since, in accordance with your prayer and the deep compassion <note>original: *σπλάγχνα* (splanchma), literally "inner parts" or "bowels," a Greek idiom for the seat of mercy and affection</note> which you have in Christ Jesus, it has been reported to me that the church at Antioch in Syria is now at peace, it is fitting for you, as a church of God, to appoint a bishop <note>Ignatius likely means a delegate or envoy acting with official authority</note> to go there as God's ambassador, so that he may congratulate them when they are gathered together and may glorify the name of God. Blessed is he in Christ Jesus who has been deemed worthy of such a ministry; and if you are diligent, you too shall be glorified in Christ. Now, for those of you who are willing, this is not impossible to do for the sake of God’s name; just as the nearest churches have already sent bishops, and others have sent presbyters <term>Presbyter: an elder or priest within the early church hierarchy</term> and deacons.

### XI.

Concerning Philo the deacon, a man from Cilicia of proven character, who even now serves me in the word of God along with Gaius and Agathopus—an elect man who has followed me from Syria, having renounced this worldly life—they also bear witness to you. And I myself thank God on your behalf, because you received them; may the Lord also receive you! But as for those who treated them with dishonor, may they be redeemed by the grace of Jesus Christ, who does not desire the death of the sinner, but rather his repentance. The love of the brothers at Troas <note>A port city in Asia Minor where Ignatius stopped on his way to Rome; it is the site from which he is writing this letter</note> greets you; from there I write to you by the hand of Burrhus, who was sent along with me by the Ephesians and Smyrnaeans as a mark of honor. The Lord Jesus Christ will reward them, in whom they hope in flesh, soul, spirit, faith, love, and harmony. Farewell in Lord Jesus Christ, our common hope, in the Holy Spirit.

### X.

Since, in accordance with your prayer and the compassion which you have in the Lord Jesus, it has been reported to me that the Church at Antioch in Syria is at peace, it is fitting for you, as a Church of God, to appoint a Bishop to be sent there as a Godly embassy <note>original Latin: *visitationem*, implying an official visit or mission of oversight</note>; to allow those gathered there to glorify the name of God. Blessed in Christ Jesus is he who shall be found worthy of such a ministry; and you yourselves, by being diligent in this, shall be glorified in Christ. Now, if you are willing, this is not impossible for you to do for the sake of God’s name, just as the neighboring Churches have already been accustomed to do—some sending Bishops, and others Presbyters and Deacons.

### XI.

Concerning Philo the deacon, a religious man from Cilicia, who now ministers to me in the word of God, along with Gaius and Agathopus <note>original Latin: *Agathopo*. Variants in the manuscripts suggest different spellings, such as Chatopus</note>, an elect man who has followed me from Syria, having renounced the world and taken upon himself the completion of martyrdom: I bear witness to you concerning them. And I give thanks to God on your behalf, praying that you may receive them in the Lord, just as the Lord Jesus Christ may receive you. As for those who slandered them, may they be redeemed by the grace of Jesus Christ, who **does not desire the death of a sinner, but rather his repentance.** <note>A reference to Ezekiel 33:11 and 2 Peter 3:9</note> The love of the brothers who are in Troas greets you, from where I also write to you by the hand of Burrus <note>original: *Burgum*. Burrus was a deacon from Ephesus who served as Ignatius's scribe</note>, who was sent to me by the Ephesians and Smyrnaeans as a mark of honor. May the Lord Jesus Christ reward them, in whom they hope in flesh and soul, in spirit and faith, in love and concord. Fare well in the Lord Jesus Christ, our common hope, and in the Holy Spirit.

<header>IGNATIUS'S EPISTLE TO THE SMYRNAEANS. I. II.</header>

# THE EPISTLE OF THE SAME MAN TO THE SMYRNAEANS.¹
<note>original: "ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ ΕΠΙΣΤΟΛΗ ΠΡΟΣ ΣΜΥΡΝΑΙΟΥΣ." This refers to Ignatius, whose previous letters appear earlier in the collection.</note>

Ignatius, who is also called Theophoros <note>meaning "God-bearer"</note>, to the Church of God the Father Most High and of His beloved Son Jesus Christ; a church which has been mercifully blessed with every spiritual gift, filled² with faith and love, lacking in no gift, most God-befitting and holy-bearing; to the Church which is in Smyrna <note>modern-day Izmir, Turkey</note> of Asia, in a blameless spirit and the word of God: abundant greetings.

I. I glorify the God and Father of our⁴ Lord Jesus Christ, who through Him⁵ has made you so wise. For I have perceived that you are perfected in an immovable faith, as if you were nailed to the cross of our⁶ Lord Jesus Christ, both in flesh and in spirit, and established in love by the blood of Christ. You are fully convinced,⁷ truly, regarding our⁸ Lord Jesus Christ: that He is the Son of God, the firstborn of all creation, the God-Word, the only-begotten Son; that He is of the lineage of David according to the flesh, born of Mary the Virgin, baptized by John so that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him; that He lived⁹ holily without sin, and under¹⁰ Pontius Pilate and Herod the tetrarch was truly nailed [to the cross] for us in the flesh. From this fruit we exist—from His divinely blessed passion—so that He might raise a standard <term>sussēmon: a military banner or signal-flag</term> for all ages through His resurrection, for His saints and faithful people, whether among Jews or Gentiles, in the one body of His church.

II. For He suffered¹ all these things for our sake; and He truly suffered,² and not in appearance only <note>Ignatius is attacking "Docetism," a heresy claiming Jesus only *seemed* to have a physical body or suffer</note>, just as He truly rose again. It is not as some unbelievers say—those who are ashamed of the formation of man, the cross, and death itself—that He suffered only in appearance, and did not truly take a body from the Virgin. They forget the one who said: **The Word became flesh**; and, **Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up**; and, **If I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw⁴ all people to myself.** Therefore, the Word dwelt in flesh; for Wisdom built a house for herself. The Word raised up⁵ His own temple on the third day after it had been destroyed by the Jews who fought against Christ. When His flesh was lifted up, like the bronze serpent in the desert, the Word drew all people to Himself for eternal salvation.

<header>IGNATIUS'S EPISTLE TO THE SMYRNAEANS. I. II.</header>

### THE EPISTLE OF THE SAME MAN TO THE SMYRNAEANS. FROM TROAS.

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>meaning "God-bearer"</note>, to the Church of God the Father most high and of His beloved Son Jesus Christ; a church which has obtained mercy and is filled with grace, founded in faith and love, and most worthy of God in every gift; to the holy church which is in Smyrna <note>modern-day Izmir, Turkey</note>, blameless in spirit and the word of God: abundant greetings.

I. I glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who through Himself has so enlightened you. For I have recognized that you are perfected in an immovable faith, as if you were fixed with nails to the cross of the Lord Jesus Christ, in both flesh and spirit, and confirmed in love by the blood of Christ. You are truly and fully instructed in our Lord Jesus Christ: that He is the Son of God, the firstborn of all creation; <note>original Latin: "primogenito totius creaturae," a reference to Colossians 1:15</note> the God-Word, the only-begotten Son, who is of the lineage of David according to the flesh, and born of the Virgin Mary; baptized by John so that all righteousness might be fulfilled by Him. Having lived holily without sin, He was truly nailed [to the cross] for us in the flesh under Pontius Pilate and Herod the Tetrarch. From this fruit we exist—from His divinely blessed passion—so that through His resurrection He might raise up a sign <note>The Latin implies a gathering or lifting up</note> for all ages, for His saints and faithful ones, whether among Jews or Gentiles, into the one body of His Church.

II. For He suffered all these things for our sake. And He truly suffered; not in appearance only, but truly, just as He also truly rose again. But it is not as some unbelievers say, who are ashamed of the physical formation of man, the cross, and death itself. They claim that He took a body from the Virgin only in appearance <note>original: "putative," referring to the Docetic heresy which claimed Christ only "seemed" to have a physical body</note> and not in truth, and that He suffered only in appearance. These people are unmindful of Him who said, "The Word was made flesh and dwelt among us." And again, "Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up." And in another place, "When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself." Therefore, the Word dwelt in the flesh. "For Wisdom built a house for herself." Therefore, the Word raised up His own temple which had been destroyed by His adversaries on the third day. Truly, the Word, having exalted His own flesh—just like that bronze serpent in the desert—drew all to Himself for eternal salvation.

### III. For I know and believe that He existed in the flesh even after the resurrection. And when He came to those who were with Peter, He said to them: "Take, handle me, and see that I am not a bodiless demon <note>original: δαιμόνιον ἀσώματον; Ignatius uses this phrase where the Gospel of Luke uses 'spirit'</note>; for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having." And He said to Thomas: "Bring your finger here <gloss>to the place of the wounds</gloss> into the print of the nails, and bring your hand, and put it into my side." And immediately he believed that it was Christ Himself. Therefore, Thomas also said to Him: "My Lord and my God!" Because of this, they also despised death—or rather, to put it mildly, they despised insults and beatings. Furthermore, after showing Himself to them, He proved that He had truly been raised, and not merely in appearance <term>Docetism: from the Greek 'dokeo', meaning 'to seem'. A heresy claiming Christ's body was an illusion</term>. And He ate and drank with them for forty full days; and thus, while they were looking on, He was taken up in the flesh to the One who sent Him, and He shall come again with that same flesh in glory and power. For the scriptures say: "This same Jesus, who was taken up from you into heaven, shall come in the same way as you saw Him going into heaven." But if some say He comes without a body at the end of the age, how shall they look upon Him, "those who pierced Him," and how shall they recognize Him and beat their breasts? For those without bodies have neither form, nor distinct character, nor the shape of a living being, because of the simplicity of their nature <note>A philosophical argument that pure spirits lack physical dimensions or recognizable features</note>.

### IV. I advise you of these things, beloved, knowing that you also hold these views. But I guard you against those beasts in human form, whom you must not only turn away from, but even flee. Only pray for them, if by any means they might repent. For if the Lord existed in the body only in appearance, and was crucified only in appearance, then I am also bound in appearance <note>Ignatius is currently a prisoner in chains; he argues his suffering is meaningless if Christ's was not real</note>. Why then have I given myself up to death—to fire, to the sword, to wild beasts? But it is not in appearance, but in truth, that I endure all things for the sake of Christ, that I may suffer along with Him, as He Himself strengthens me; for I do not have such strength on my own.

### V. Some, in their ignorance, have denied Him, and advocate for the lie rather than the truth. They have not been convinced by the prophecies, nor the law of Moses...

### III.

But I know that He was not only^1 born and crucified in the body, but I also know and believe that He existed in the flesh even after the resurrection. And when He came to those who were with Peter, He said to them:

> “Handle me, and see, for I am not^3 a bodiless demon <note>original: "daemonium incorporeum." This reflects the Greek "daimonion asomaton." Ignatius uses this phrase to emphasize that Jesus had a physical, solid body after rising from the dead.</note>. For a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see me having.”^4

And to Thomas He says:^5

> “Place your finger in the print of the nails, and bring your hand, and put it into my side; and be not faithless, but believing.”

And immediately they believed, because it was Christ Himself. Because of this, Thomas also said to Him:^6

> “My God, and my Lord.”

Therefore, they despised death, considering it a small thing^7 to endure insults and beatings and many other things for His sake. For even after He showed Himself to them—proving that He had truly risen and not just in appearance^8—He ate and drank with them for forty days. And so, while they were watching, He was taken up^9 in the flesh to the One who sent Him. In that same flesh He is to come again^10 with glory and power, according to what was said by the Angels to the Apostles:

> “This Jesus,^11 who was taken up from you into heaven, shall come in the same way as you saw Him ascending into heaven.”^12

If, therefore, they say He is to come without a body at the end^13 of the age, how will those who pierced Him see Him, and recognizing Him, mourn among themselves? For^14 of things that have no body, there is neither shape nor figure, nor indeed^15 can any likeness of a living form be held in which the print^16 of the nails or the hole of the spear might appear, because of the simplicity of their nature <note>The "simplicity of nature" refers to the philosophical idea that pure spirits lack physical parts or dimensions.</note>.

### IV.

Now, I warn you of these things, my dear friends, knowing that^1 you also hold these views. But I am guarding you in advance against beasts in human form^2: whom you must not only avoid, but even flee from. Only pray for them, that^3 perhaps they might repent. For if the Lord was in a body only in appearance, and was crucified only in appearance, then I too am bound^4 only in appearance. Why then have I surrendered myself^5 to death, to fire, to the sword, to the beasts? But it is not in appearance, but in truth that I endure all things^6 for the sake of Christ, so that I may suffer along with Him—He Himself strengthening me, for such power is not mine.

### V.

Indeed,^1 certain ignorant people^2 have denied Him, and they agree with lies rather than the truth. Neither the Prophets nor the Law have persuaded them...

## VI.

Let no one be led astray. Unless one believes that Jesus Christ lived in the flesh, and confesses His cross, and His passion, and the blood which He shed for the salvation of the world, he shall not attain eternal life, whether he be a king, a priest, a ruler, a private citizen, a master or a slave, a man or a woman. <meta>This page continues Ignatius’s instructions to the church at Smyrna. Having previously warned against the Docetists—who denied Christ’s physical reality—Ignatius now pivots to the practical remedy for heresy: strict adherence to church hierarchy (Bishops, Presbyters, and Deacons) and the authorized celebration of the sacraments. He argues that unity with the Bishop is the only safeguard against spiritual error.</meta>

...the faith of the apostles, which the Jewish multitude stirred up against the Lord, and which even now works in the "sons of disobedience," whom the Lord Jesus Christ shall deliver—He who prayed that the faith of the apostles might not fail, not as though He were not sufficient to preserve it, but as one rejoicing in the pre-eminence of the Father. ### VIII.

But flee from those ill-named heresies and those who create divisions, as the beginning of evils. All of you follow the bishop, as Jesus Christ follows the Father; and the <term>presbytery</term> <note>The council of elders or priests who advised the bishop.</note> as you would the apostles; and respect the deacons as the commandment of God. Let no one do anything belonging to the church without the bishop. Let that be considered a valid <term>Eucharist</term> <note>The ritual of Holy Communion or 'Thanksgiving'.</note> which is celebrated by the bishop, or by one whom he appoints. Wherever the bishop appears, let the multitude of people be there; just as wherever Christ is, the whole heavenly host stands by, as the <term>Chief Captain</term> <note>original Greek: 'archistrategos', a military term for a supreme commander.</note> of the Lord’s power and the distributor of every intellectual nature. It is not permitted without the bishop either to baptize, or to offer, or to present the **sacrifice**, or to celebrate a <term>love-feast</term> <note>original: 'dochen', referring to the communal meal or 'agape' that often accompanied early Christian worship.</note>; but whatever he approves is also well-pleasing to God, so that everything you do may be safe and valid.

But I say: Honor God as the cause and Lord of all things; and the bishop as high priest, bearing the image of God—representing God in his rule, and representing Christ in his priesthood. He who honors the bishop shall be honored by God; just as he who dishonors him shall be punished by God. For if anyone who rises against kings will be justly punished, as one who dissolves public order; how much worse punishment do you think he deserves who chooses to do anything without the bishop, tearing apart harmony and confusing the good order? For the priesthood is the [highest] of all...

All of you must follow the Bishop, as Jesus Christ follows the Father; and the **Presbyters** <note>The council of elders or priests who advised the bishop.</note> as you would the Apostles; and respect the **Deacons** as those ministering by the command of God. ...above all good things among men. # X.
You did well in welcoming Philo and Gaius and Agathopus as deacons of Christ, for they followed me for the sake of God’s word. Nothing you have done for them shall be overlooked; may the Lord grant you to find mercy from the Lord on that day. My spirit and my bonds are a <term>Ransom</term> <note>original: "antipsychon"; literally "a soul for a soul," expressing Ignatius’s total devotion and sacrifice for the church</note> for you—bonds which you did not look down upon¹ nor were you ashamed of. # XI.
Your prayers have reached the church of the Antiochians, and it is now at peace;¹ from there I greet you all in my bonds, though I am not worthy, being the least among them. Yet by the will of God² I was deemed worthy—not because of my own conscience, but by the grace of God. I pray that this grace may be given to me in perfection, so that through your prayers I may attain to God. Therefore, so that your work may be perfect on earth and in heaven, it is fitting, for the honor of God, that your church appoint a "God-ambassador" <note>original: "theopresbytes"</note> to go into Syria to rejoice with them that they are at peace, and have recovered their proper greatness, and their own small body <note>Likely referring to the local church community</note> has been restored to them. It seemed worthy to me to send someone from among you with a letter, so that he may join in glorifying the calm³ that has come to them according to God’s will,⁴ and because I have reached a safe harbor, Christ, through your prayers. Since you are perfect, think perfect thoughts; for to those of you who wish to do well, God is ready⁵ to provide.

If anyone dishonors it, he dishonors God, and the Lord Jesus Christ, the firstborn of all creation <note>A reference to Colossians 1:15</note>, and the only one who is by nature the high priest of God. Let all things be done in good order by you, as they were commanded in Christ. Let the laity be subject to the **Deacons**; the deacons to the **Presbyters**; the presbyters to the **Bishop**; and the bishop to Christ, just as He is to the Father. Even as you have refreshed me, brothers, so may the Lord Jesus Christ refresh you. You have loved me whether I was absent or present; God will reward you, for whose sake you showed such great kindness to His prisoner. And although I am not worthy, yet your devotion is great. "For if anyone honors a prophet in the name of a prophet, he will receive a prophet's reward." <note>Matthew 10:41</note> It is clear that he who honors a prisoner of Jesus Christ shall receive the reward of the martyrs.

### X.

You did well to receive Philo, Gaius, and Agathopus, who follow me in the word of God and are ministers of Christ, as ministers of God. They also give great thanks to the Lord on your behalf, because you refreshed them in every way. Nothing of what you spent on them will be counted as sin against you. May the Lord grant you to find mercy with the Lord on that day. <note>Referencing 2 Timothy 1:18</note> For the sake of your souls, let my spirit and my bonds be a <term>Ransom</term> <note>original: "antipsychon"; a term suggesting a spiritual exchange or pledge of one's life for others</note>, which you did not despise and of which you were not ashamed. This is the perfect hope in Christ Jesus.

### XI.

Your prayers have reached the Church at Antioch, with which you are at peace. From there, I, a prisoner, greet everyone. From there, I am not worthy to be the last of them; but according to the will of God, I have been made worthy—not by my own foresight, but by the grace of God. I wish for this grace to be given to me in perfection, so that through your prayers I may deserve to attain God, and that my work might be perfect in heaven and on earth. It is fitting, therefore, for the honor of God, that you care for the Church in Syria, which is worthy of God, and congratulate them because they are at peace, and have regained their greatness, and their own body <note>Referring to the congregation or the physical restoration of the church community</note> has been restored to them. It seemed good to me to send someone from among you there with a letter, so that they may glorify the tranquility which has come to them according to God, and their rest. I have indeed earned a most safe harbor in Christ through your prayers. Since you are perfect, think of perfect things, be wise, and be of one mind. For even when you wish to do well, God is ready to provide for you.

->### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE SMYRNAEANS. XII. XIII.<-

### XII.
The love of your brothers who are in Troas greets you. It is from here that I write to you through Burrhus, whom you sent with me along with the Ephesians, your brothers. He has refreshed me in every way. Would that all might imitate him, for he is a <term>Pattern</term> <note>original: "exemplarion"; a model or standard for others to follow</note> of God’s ministry. The grace of the Lord will reward him in all things. I greet your bishop Polycarp, who is worthy of God, and your God-befitting <term>Presbytery</term> <note>the council of priests or elders</note>, and the Christ-bearing <note>original: "christophorous"; a favorite term of Ignatius, suggesting the faithful carry Christ within their hearts</note> deacons, my fellow-servants. I also greet each of you individually and all of you together, in the name of Jesus Christ and of His flesh and blood, His passion and resurrection, both physical and spiritual, in the unity of God and of you. Grace to you, mercy, peace, and endurance forever in Christ.

### XIII.
I greet the households of my brothers, along with their wives and children, and the <term>Virgins</term> <note>original: "aeiparthenous"; literally "ever-virgins." In this context, it refers to a group of women who had dedicated themselves to a life of celibacy within the church</note> and the widows. Farewell to you in the power of the Spirit. Philo, the fellow-deacon who is with me, greets you. I greet the house of Gavia, and I pray that she may be firmly established in faith and love, both physically and spiritually. I greet Alce, a name very dear to me, and the incomparable Daphnus, and Eutecnus, and all of you by name. Farewell in the grace of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ, being filled with the Holy Spirit and with divine and sacred wisdom.

-># THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. I. II. III.<-

### BY THE SAME AUTHOR TO POLYCARP, BISHOP OF SMYRNA. <note>original: "ΤΟΥ ΑΥΤΟΥ" (Of the same). This refers back to Ignatius, identifying him as the author of the preceding letters in the manuscript.</note>

Ignatius, who is also called Theophorus <note>The Greek "ὁ καὶ μάρτυς" (the witness/martyr) appears in this transcription, though many manuscripts use "Theophorus," meaning "God-bearer."</note>, bishop of Antioch and witness of Jesus Christ, to Polycarp, bishop of the church of the Smyrnaeans, or rather, one who is himself "overseen" <note>Ignatius uses a wordplay here: Polycarp is an *Episkopos* (Overseer/Bishop), but he is *episkopēmenō* (overseen) by God the Father.</note> by God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ: abundant greetings.

I. Because I welcome your godly mind, which is fixed as if upon an unmovable rock, I exceedingly glorify God that I have been counted worthy to see your irreproachable countenance—may I have joy in it in God! I exhort you, by the grace with which you are clothed, to press forward in your course and to exhort all people so that they may be saved. Uphold your office with all diligence, both in fleshly and spiritual matters. Pay attention to unity, for nothing is better than this. Bear with all people, even as the Lord bears with you. Endure all in love, just as you are already doing. Devote yourself to unceasing prayers. Ask for more understanding than you currently have. Be vigilant, possessing a spirit that does not sleep. Speak to each person individually, following the manner of God. Bear the infirmities of all like a <term>perfect athlete</term> <note>In the early church, "athlete" was a common metaphor for a Christian, especially a martyr, who trains the soul to endure suffering for a prize.</note>, just as the Lord bears the infirmities of all. For it is said: *He took our infirmities and bore our diseases.* <note>Quoting Isaiah 53:4 / Matthew 8:17.</note> Where the labor is greater, the gain is much more.

II. If you love only the "good" students, you deserve no credit; rather, subdue the more troublesome ones with gentleness. Not every wound is healed by the same plaster. Soothe the "paroxysms" <note>Used here to mean sharp fits of temper or outbreaks of trouble.</note> with moist applications. Be wise as a serpent in all things, and always harmless as a dove. For this reason, you are composed of both soul and body—fleshly and spiritual—so that you may correct the things that appear before your face, and that you may ask for the invisible things to be revealed to you, so that you may lack nothing and abound in every spiritual gift. The present time requires you to pray. For just as a pilot needs the wind, and as a storm-tossed ship needs a harbor for safety, so do your prayers help you to reach God. Be sober, as God’s athlete; the prize is incorruptibility and eternal life, of which you are already convinced. In all things, I am your "ransom" <note>original: "ἀντίψυχος" (antipsychos). A term of deep affection meaning "I give my life for yours."</note>, as are my chains, which you have loved.

III. Do not let those who seem trustworthy but teach strange doctrines dismay you. Stand firm like an anvil when it is struck. It is the mark of a great athlete to be bruised and yet to conquer. Especially for God’s sake, we must endure all things, so that He may also endure us in His kingdom. Increase your zeal even more than you have. Run more intensely. Observe the times; as you are here, be victorious. For here is the—

### THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. I. II. III.

### TO POLYCARP, BISHOP OF THE SMYRNAEANS. CONCERNING THE ENLIGHTENED.<sup>1</sup> <note>original: "De Illuminatis." In the early church, "enlightened" was a common term for those who had been baptized or were undergoing final instruction.</note>

->Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, who is also a martyr of Jesus Christ, to Polycarp, Bishop<sup>2</sup> of the Smyrnaeans.<-

I. Welcoming your godly mindset as if it were established upon an unmovable rock, I exceedingly desire to be worthy of seeing your irreproachable face, which I have gained<sup>4</sup> in the Lord. I exhort you, by the grace with which you are clothed, to press forward in your course, and to exhort all people that they may be saved<sup>5</sup> in Christ. Defend<sup>6</sup> your position with all spiritual diligence. Have a care for unity, for nothing is better than this. Support everyone, just as the Lord also supports you.<sup>8</sup> Endure all in love. Devote yourself to unceasing prayers: ask for a greater wisdom than you already possess. Be vigilant, possessing a spirit that does not sleep: speak according to the help of God. Bear the infirmities of all like a perfect athlete: just as the Lord of all does. 

> "For he himself," it says,<sup>9</sup> "bore our infirmities, and took away our sicknesses." <note>A quotation of Isaiah 53:4, also found in Matthew 8:17.</note>

For where the labor is great, there<sup>10</sup> also the gain is greater.

II. If you love only the good disciples, you deserve no credit; rather, subdue the more troublesome ones with gentleness. Not every wound is healed with the same bandage. Soothe sharp pains with compresses.<sup>1</sup> <note>original: "embroche." This refers to a medicinal lotion or fomentation applied to a wound.</note> Be shrewd as a serpent, and simple as a dove.<sup>2</sup> For this reason you are composed of soul and body,<sup>3</sup> of flesh and spirit, so that you may correct the things that are shown to your face: but as for the things that are<sup>4</sup> invisible, ask that they may be revealed to you,<sup>5</sup> so that you may lack nothing, but may abound in every gift. The time demands you, just as a pilot requires a fair wind, or a storm-tossed ship requires a safe harbor. So it is with you, God’s athlete, that you may receive incorruption and eternal life: in which things you also place your trust. In all things, I am your substitute—and my bonds, which you have loved.

III. Let those who seem to be worthy of trust, yet teach different doctrines, not dismay you; but stand firm like an anvil<sup>1</sup> that is struck. For it is the part of a great athlete to be beaten and yet to conquer. Especially for God’s sake, we must endure all things, so that He may also endure us in His kingdom. Increase your haste; run continuously: recognize the times, so that in them you may—

### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. III. IV. V. VI.

...the arena, and there are the crowns. Wait for Christ, the Son of God, who is beyond time yet in time, invisible by nature but visible in the flesh; intangible and untouchable as one without a body, yet for our sake tangible and touchable in a body; impassible <term>impassible: incapable of suffering or pain</term> as God, yet for our sake passible <term>passible: capable of suffering</term> as a man, who endured in every way for our sake.

<note>original Latin: "per vincas..." This paragraph is a Latin translation of the Greek text immediately preceding it.</note>
...that you may overcome. For here is the arena, there the crown. Wait for Christ the Son of God, the timeless in time, invisible by nature, visible in the flesh, impalpable and untouched, as one incorporeal; but for us made corporeal and touchable; impassible as God, but for us passible as man, sustaining all things in every way for our sake.

IV. Let not widows be neglected; after the Lord, you must be their guardian. Let nothing be done without your consent, nor should you do anything without God's consent—as indeed you do not; stand firm. Let gatherings be held more frequently; seek out everyone by name. Do not look down on male or female slaves; but neither let them be puffed up with pride, but let them serve even more for the glory of God, so that they may obtain a better freedom from God. Let them not desire to be set free at the public expense <note>Literally "from the common [fund]," suggesting the church treasury.</note>, lest they be found to be slaves of their own desires.

V. Flee from evil arts, or rather, do not even speak of them. Tell my sisters to love the Lord and to be content with their husbands in both flesh and spirit. Likewise, charge my brothers in the name of Jesus Christ to love their wives as the Lord loves the Church. If anyone is able to remain in purity <note>original: "hagneia" — here referring to a state of celibacy or virginity</note> to the honor of the flesh of the Lord, let him remain so without boasting. If he boasts, he is lost; and if his vow becomes known to anyone except the bishop, he is corrupted. It is right for men and women who marry to form their union with the consent of the bishop, so that the marriage may be according to the Lord and not according to lust. Let all things be done to the honor of God.

VI. Pay attention to the bishop, so that God may also pay attention to you. I am a ransom <note>original: "antipsychon" — literally "a soul for a soul"; a term of deep devotion and sacrifice</note> for those who are subject to the bishop, the presbytery <term>presbytery: the council of elders or priests</term>, and the deacons; may it be my lot to have a portion with them before God. Labor together with one another, strive together, run together, suffer together, sleep together, and rise together as God's stewards, assistants, and servants. Please Him under whom you serve, from whom you also receive your wages. Let none of you be found a deserter. The...

### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO POLYCARP. VI. VII. VIII.

Let your baptism remain as your armor; your faith as your helmet; your love as your spear; your patience as your <term>panoply: a complete suit of armor</term>. Let your deposits be your works, so that you may receive your <term>receipts: Ignatius uses the Latinism "accepta," referring to wages or rewards</term> worthy of God. Therefore, be long-suffering with one another in gentleness, and God will be with you. May I have joy of you always.

VII. Since the church in Antioch of Syria is at peace—as has been made known to me—through your prayer, I also have become more cheered in a God-given freedom from care, if only I may attain to God through suffering, so that I may be found a disciple through your petition. It is fitting, O Polycarp, most blessed of God, to convene a most God-becoming council and to appoint <note>literally "ordain" or "elect by show of hands"</note> someone whom you hold very dear and who is untiring, who can be called "God's courier." Authorize this man to go to Syria, so that by arriving in Syria he may glorify your untiring love, to the glory of God. A Christian has no authority over himself, but is at leisure for God. This is the work of God and of yours, when you have completed it. For I trust in the grace that you are ready for a good work belonging to God. Knowing your brevity regarding the truth, I have exhorted you through these few words.

VIII. Since, therefore, I was not able to write to all the churches because of my sudden sailing from Troas to Neapolis—as the divine will commands—you shall write to the churches ahead, as one possessing the mind of God, so that they also may do this: those who are able should send foot-messengers, and others letters through those sent by you, that you may be glorified in an eternal work, as being worthy. I greet everyone by name, and the wife of the Governor <note>original: "Epitropos," a title for a steward or provincial official</note> with her whole house and children. I greet Attalus my beloved. I greet the one who is about to be deemed worthy to go to Syria; grace shall be with him always, and with Polycarp who sends him. I bid you farewell always in our God Jesus Christ, in whom may you remain in the unity and oversight of God. I greet Alce, a name very dear to me. Amen. May the grace of God be with you. Farewell in the Lord.

<meta>This page begins a new letter from Ignatius, moving from his personal correspondence with Polycarp to a letter addressed to the church in Antioch. Having just secured peace for that community, Ignatius now writes to them from his captivity to reinforce their doctrinal unity against both pagan polytheism and legalistic misinterpretations of monotheism.</meta>

<header>THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ANTIOCHIANS. I. II. III.</header>

### BY THE SAME AUTHOR, THE EPISTLE TO THE ANTIOCHIANS.

Ignatius, who is also called <term>Theophoros: "God-bearer"</term>, to the church which has found mercy from God and has been chosen by Christ, dwelling in Syria—the first to receive the name of Christ <note>A reference to Acts 11:26, which states that the disciples were first called Christians in Antioch</note>—at Antioch; in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, greetings.

I. The Lord has made my bonds light and easy for me, because I have learned that you are at peace and are living in all harmony, both of the flesh and of the spirit. I, therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, exhort you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called, guarding yourselves against the heresies of the Evil One that have rushed in for the deception and destruction of those who are persuaded by him. Pay heed to the teaching of the Apostles, and believe the Law and the Prophets. Reject every Jewish and Greek error; neither introduce a multitude of gods, nor deny Christ under the pretext of maintaining the "one God."

II. For Moses, the faithful servant of God, when he said, "The Lord your God is one Lord," and preached the one and only God, immediately acknowledged our Lord as well, saying: "The Lord rained fire and brimstone upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord." And again: "God said, 'Let us make man according to our image'; and God made man, according to the image of God He made him." And further: "In the image of God He made man." And that He would become man, he says: "The Lord shall raise up for you a Prophet from among your brethren, like unto me." <note>Ignatius is using Old Testament passages (Genesis 19:24, Genesis 1:26, and Deuteronomy 18:15) to argue that the "one God" of Moses already includes the person of the Son.</note>

III. And the Prophets, when they speak as if from the person of God, saying, "I am the first God, and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God," they are speaking about the Father of all things. But regarding our Lord Jesus Christ, [the scripture] says: "A Son is given to us, whose government is upon His shoulder from above, and His name is called Messenger of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, Ruler." And concerning His incarnation: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb and bear a son, and they shall call His name Emmanuel." And concerning His passion: "He was led as a sheep to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent." And: "I was as an innocent lamb being led to be sacrificed."

<header>THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ANTIOCHIANS. I. II. III.</header>

# BY THE SAME AUTHOR, THE EPISTLE TO THE ANTIOCHIANS. WRITTEN FROM PHILIPPI.¹

Ignatius, who is also called <term>Theophorus</term> <note>Literally "God-bearer." It was a title Ignatius used to signify his close union with Christ.</note>, to the Church at Antioch which has obtained mercy from Christ, dwelling in Syria—which first received the name of Christ—located in Antioch; in God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ, greetings.

I. The Lord has made my bonds light and easy for me, since I have learned that you are at peace and that you live in all harmony, both of the flesh and of the spirit. I, therefore, a prisoner in the Lord, beseech you to walk worthily of the calling to which you were called, guarding yourselves from the malignant heresies that are entering in for the deception and destruction of those who consent to them. Instead, attend to the doctrine of the Apostles, and believe the Law and the Prophets; reject every Jewish and Pagan error; and neither admit a multitude of gods, nor deny Christ under the pretext of defending the "one God."

II. For Moses, the faithful servant of God, said to the people: "The Lord your God is one God." And while preaching the one and only God, he immediately confessed our Lord as well, saying: "The Lord rained fire and sulfur upon Sodom and Gomorrah from the Lord out of heaven." And again: "And God said: Let us make man in our image and likeness." And further: "And God made man; in the image of God He made him." And a little later: "In the image of God He made man." And because man was destined to be born [of woman], he says: "The Lord your God will raise up for you a Prophet from your brothers, like me."

III. For the Prophets also spoke in the person of God: "I am the first God, and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God." This they said regarding the Father of all. But regarding our Lord Jesus Christ, the Prophets again proclaimed, saying: "Behold, a child is born to us, and a son is given to us, whose beginning is from above: and his name shall be called Messenger of Great Counsel, Wonderful, Counselor, Mighty God, having power, Prince of Peace." For they also say of His incarnation from the Virgin: "Behold, a Virgin shall conceive in her womb, and shall bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel." And regarding His passion, they nonetheless added, saying: "As a sheep he was led to the slaughter, and as a lamb before its shearer is silent." And again, he says, referring to himself: "I, however, like an innocent lamb, was led to be sacrificed."

310 THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ANTIOCHIANS. VII. VIII. IX. X. XI. XII.

...let him be accursed. Become imitators of me. May I be a ransom for your soul <note>original: "antipsychon" — a term expressing the author's willingness to sacrifice his life for the spiritual benefit of others</note> when I attain to Jesus. Remember my chains.

VIII. You <term>presbyters</term> <note>From the Greek "presbyteroi," referring to the elders or priests of the church.</note>, shepherd the flock that is among you, until God reveals the one who is to rule over you; for I am already being poured out as a drink offering <note>original: "spendomai" — a sacrificial metaphor also used by the Apostle Paul to describe his approaching martyrdom</note>, so that I may gain Christ. Let the <term>deacons</term> <note>From "diakonoi," meaning servants or ministers who assisted the elders.</note> know of what dignity they are, and let them strive to be blameless, so that they may be imitators of Christ. Let the people be subject to the elders and the deacons. Let the virgins know to whom they have consecrated themselves.

IX. Let husbands love their spouses, remembering that one woman was given to one man, not many to one, at the time of creation. Let wives honor their husbands as their own flesh; let them not even dare to call them by their names <note>A traditional expression of deep respect and submission in the ancient world, where a wife would address her husband by a title of honor rather than his personal name.</note>; but let them be self-controlled, considering their spouses alone to be their husbands, to whom they were joined according to the will of God. Parents, train your children in holy instruction. Children, honor your parents, so that it may be well with you.

X. Masters, do not treat your servants with pride, imitating the patient Job, who said: *“If I have despised the cause of my manservant or my maidservant, when they contended with me; what then shall I do when the Lord makes an inquiry of me?”* and you know the rest of the passage. Servants, do not provoke your masters in anything, lest you become the cause of incurable evils for yourselves.

XI. Let no idle person eat, lest he become a wanderer and a fornicator. Let drunkenness, anger, envy, slander, clamor, and blasphemy not even be named among you. Let widows not live in luxury, lest they grow wanton against the Word. Be subject to Caesar in things where subjection is safe. Do not provoke rulers to wrath, lest you give an opportunity to those seeking an occasion against you. But concerning witchcraft, or <term>pederasty</term> <note>In the ancient context, this refers to the sexual exploitation of youths.</note>, or murder, it is unnecessary to write, since these things are forbidden even for the pagans to do. I do not command these things as an apostle, but as your fellow-servant I remind you.

XII. I salute the holy <term>presbytery</term> <note>The collective body of elders/priests.</note>. I salute the sacred deacons, and that name dear to me, whom I would see in my place in the Holy Spirit when I attain to Christ; for whom may I be a ransom. <meta>This page continues the Epistle to the Antiochians from the previous page. Having finished his warnings against heresy, the author—writing in the name of Ignatius—now provides a code of conduct for the various social and ecclesiastical ranks within the church at Antioch.</meta>

### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ANTIOCHIANS. VII. VIII. IX. X. XI. XII. 311

...let him be accursed. Be imitators of me$^8$. May I be a ransom for your souls <note>original: "Pro animabus vestris ego efficiar" — literally "I would be for your souls," a sacrificial expression indicating the author's devotion to the point of death</note> when I am worthy to attain to Christ. Remember my chains.$^4$

VIII. <term>Presbyters</term> <note>From the Greek "presbyteroi," referring to the elders or priests of the church.</note>, shepherd the flock which$^1$ is among you, until God reveals the one who is to be your future$^2$ leader. For I am now hurrying that I may gain Christ.$^3$ Let the <term>deacons</term> <note>From "diakonoi," meaning servants or ministers who assisted the elders.</note> recognize of what dignity they are, and let them strive to be blameless, so that they may be imitators of Christ. Let the people be subject to the Presbyters and Deacons. Let the virgins know to whom they have consecrated themselves.

IX. Let men love their spouses,$^1$ remembering that one woman was given to one man, and not many to one man,$^2$ as a possession at the beginning of creation. Let women honor their husbands as$^3$ their own flesh: and let them not dare to call them by their [personal] name. Let them know instead that only their husbands are their equals,$^4$ to whom they have been joined according to the ordinance of God. Parents,$^5$ educate your children with holy instruction. Children, honor your parents, that it may be well with you, and that you may live long upon the earth.

X. Masters, do not use your servants with pride, imitating the most patient Job when he said:$^1$ "If I have judged my manservant or my maidservant unjustly, let me be judged by them: for what shall I do if the Lord makes an inquiry$^2$ concerning me?" and the rest which follows, you know well. Servants, do not provoke your masters to anger in anything,$^3$ lest some evil happen to you, and you yourselves shall be responsible for your own harm.

XI. Let no one eat while idle,$^1$ lest he become a wanderer and a fornicator. Let drunkenness, anger, envy, evil-speaking, clamor, and blasphemy not be named among you.$^2$ Let widows not live in luxury, lest they cast off the word through wantonness. Be subject to Caesar in those things in which subjection itself is without danger [to the soul].$^3$ Do not provoke rulers, lest you give opportunities to those seeking them against you.$^4$ Regarding sorceries, poisonings, or murder, it is superfluous to write to you,$^5$ since even$^6$ among the Gentiles it is an abominable thing to do these things. However, I do not command these things as an Apostle, but as your fellow-servant, reminding you.

XII. I salute the holy Presbytery. I salute the sacred Deacons, and his name is dear to me,$^1$ whom I have reserved in my place in the Holy Spirit, when I shall be worthy to attain to Christ: for whose soul may I be a ransom. I salute the subdeacons, the readers, the singers, the doorkeepers,$^2$ the laborers, and the exorcists...

# THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ANTIOCHIANS. XII. XIII. XIV.

...<term>exorcists</term> <note>From the Greek "eporkistai"; those appointed to pray for the healing of the possessed.</note> and <term>confessors</term> <note>From "homologētai"; those who maintained their faith despite persecution but were not executed.</note>. I greet the female keepers of the holy gates, and the <term>female deacons</term> <note>From "diakonous"; women who held an official service role in the early church.</note> in Christ. I greet the **Christ-filled** <note>original: "christolēptous" — a poetic term suggesting being "seized" or "possessed" by Christ's spirit.</note> virgins, in whom I find joy in the Lord Jesus. I greet the people of the Lord, from the least to the greatest, and all my sisters in the Lord.

XIII. I greet Cassianus, his wife <note>original: "homozygon" — literally "yoke-mate" or partner.</note>, and his most beloved children. Polycarp, the worthy bishop, greets you; he cares for you, and I have entrusted you to him in the Lord. The entire church of the Smyrnaeans remembers you in their prayers in the Lord. Onesimus, the shepherd of the Ephesians, greets you. Demas, the bishop of Magnesia, greets you. Polybius, the bishop of Tralles, greets you. Philo and Agathopus, the deacons who are my fellow-travelers, greet you. **Greet one another with a holy kiss.**

XIV. I write these things to you from Philippi. May He who alone is **unbegotten**, through the One **begotten** before the ages, preserve you in spirit and flesh; and may I see you in the kingdom of Christ. I greet the man who is to lead you in my place; may I find joy in him in Christ. **Fare well** in God and Christ, being enlightened by the Holy Spirit.

# THE EPISTLE OF THE SAME AUTHOR¹ TO HERO, DEACON OF ANTIOCH.²

Ignatius, also called Theophoros <note>original: "Theophoros"; meaning "God-bearer."</note>, to the one honored by God and most beloved, most venerable,³ bearer of Christ, bearer of the Spirit, a true child in faith and love, Hero—deacon of Christ and servant of God: grace, mercy, and peace from God the Almighty, and Christ Jesus our Lord, His only-begotten Son, who gave Himself for our sins⁴ so that He might deliver us from this present evil age and save⁵ us into His heavenly kingdom.

I. I urge you in God to press on in your course and to defend your dignity. Care for the harmony with the holy ones; support the weak so that you may fulfill the law of⁶ Christ. Devote yourself to fasts and prayers, but not beyond measure, so that you do not exhaust yourself. Do not abstain entirely from wine and meat, for they are not abominable. For "you shall eat the good things of the earth," it says. And, "You shall eat meat like green herbs." And, "Wine gladdens the heart of man, oil makes his face shine, and bread strengthens him."⁷ But do these things with moderation and order, as God provides them. For who eats or who drinks apart from Him? Whatever is⁸ good is His, and if anything is excellent, it is His. Attend to reading, so that you may not only know⁹ the laws yourself but may also explain them to others as God's athlete. "No one serving as a soldier entangles himself in the affairs of life,"¹⁰ so that he may please the one who enlisted him; "and if anyone competes in the games, he is not crowned unless he competes according to the rules."¹¹ I, the prisoner, am a <term>ransom for your soul</term> <note>original: "Antipsuchon"; a favorite term of Ignatius meaning "I give my life for yours."</note>.

II. Anyone who speaks contrary to what has been commanded, even if he is trustworthy, even if he fasts, even if he lives in celibacy, even if he performs signs, or even if he prophesies—let him appear to you as a wolf in sheep’s clothing, working the destruction of the sheep. If anyone denies the cross and is ashamed of the passion, let him be to you as the Adversary himself, even if he gives away his possessions to the poor, moves mountains, or gives his body to be burned—let him be abominable to you. If anyone treats the Law or the Prophets with contempt, whom Christ fulfilled by His presence, let him be to you as the Antichrist.¹ If anyone says the Lord is a <term>mere man</term>,² <note>original: "psilon anthropon"; a reference to the heresy that Jesus was only human and not divine.</note> he is a Christ-killing Jew.

III. Honor widows, those who are truly widows; take care of orphans, for God is the father of orphans and the judge of widows. Do nothing without—

<header>THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO HERO. I. II. III.</header>

### BY THE SAME AUTHOR TO HERO, DEACON OF THE CHURCH OF ANTIOCH, WHOM THE LORD REVEALED TO HIM AS THE ONE WHO WOULD SIT UPON HIS OWN SEAT. WRITTEN FROM PHILIPPI.¹

Ignatius, also called Theophorus <note>original: "Theophorus"; meaning "God-bearer."</note>, to Hero—a man honored by God, desirable, modest, a bearer of Christ and a bearer of the Spirit, in faith and love—deacon² of Christ and servant of God: may there be grace, mercy, and peace from Almighty God, and Christ Jesus our Lord, His only-begotten Son, who³ gave Himself for our sins so that He might redeem us from this present evil age and save us into His heavenly kingdom.

I. I entreat you in the Lord to press on in your course and to defend your dignity: take care for the harmony that exists among the Saints. Support the weaker ones so that you may fulfill the law of Christ.⁴ Devote yourself to fasts⁵ and prayers, but not beyond measure, so that you do not exhaust yourself. Do not abstain entirely from wine and meat, for they are not abominable. "You shall eat the good things of the earth," says the scripture.⁶ And, "You shall eat meat like green herbs."⁷ Also,⁸ "Wine gladdens the heart of man, oil makes him cheerful, and bread strengthens him." But do these things with moderation and in an orderly way, as if God were granting them. For who eats, or who drinks, except by His permission? For whatever is good is His, and whatever is excellent belongs to Him. Attend to reading, so that you may not only know the laws yourself but may also explain them to others⁹ as an athlete of God. "No one serving as a soldier for Christ¹⁰ entangles himself in worldly affairs,¹¹ so that he may please the one to whom he has proven himself. Furthermore, a man¹² who is an athlete will not be crowned unless he competes according to the rules."¹³ For the sake of your soul, I am in chains.

II. Therefore, anyone who speaks anything beyond what has been handed down, even if¹ he is worthy of trust, even if he fasts, even if he preserves his virginity, even if he performs signs, or even if he prophesies,² let him appear³ to you as a wolf in the flock of sheep, working toward its corruption. If anyone denies the cross and is ashamed of the suffering, let him be to you as an adversary—even if⁴ he gives his substance to the poor, even if he moves mountains, even if he gives his body to be burned, let him be detestable and abominable to you. If anyone falsifies the Law and⁵ the Prophets, which Christ fulfilled by His presence, let him be to you as an Antichrist. If anyone says the Lord is merely a man, he is a Jew and a murderer of Christ.

III. Honor widows¹ who are truly widows. Protect orphans.² For God is the father of orphans and the judge of widows. Do nothing without the Bishops

->THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO HERO. III. IV. V. VI.<-

III. Do nothing without the bishops; for they are priests,¹ while you are a servant <note>original: "diakonos"; deacon</note> of the priests. They baptize, perform the sacred rites, ordain, and lay on hands;² but you are to serve them,³ just as the holy Stephen served James and the elders in Jerusalem. Do not neglect the church gatherings; seek out everyone by name. Let no one look down on your youth, but be an example to the faithful in word and in conduct.

IV. Do not be ashamed of servants; for we and they share a common¹ nature. Do not detest women; for they have given birth to you² and nourished you.³ It is necessary, therefore, to love those who are the causes of our birth—though only in the Lord. Without a woman, a man cannot father a child; one must therefore honor those who cooperate in giving life. Neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, except in the case of the first-formed parents;⁴ for Adam’s body was made from the four elements, and Eve's from the rib of Adam. Even the extraordinary birth of our Lord, from the Virgin alone, was not because lawful union is abominable, but because the birth was divinely fitting. For it was proper for the Creator not to use the common⁵ method of birth, but a miraculous and strange one, as befits the Creator.

V. Flee from pride;¹ for the Lord resists the proud.² Detest lying; for He says, "You shall destroy³ all those who speak lies." Guard yourself against envy; for its author⁴ is the devil, and his successor was Cain, who was begrudging toward his brother and committed murder out of envy. Exhort my sisters to love God, and to be content only with their own husbands; likewise, exhort my brothers to be content with their spouses. Guard the virgins as the treasures of Christ. Be patient, so that you may be rich in wisdom. Do not neglect the poor, as far as your means allow; for by almsgiving and faith, sins are purged⁵ away.

VI. Keep yourself pure, like a dwelling place of God; you are a temple of Christ and an instrument of the Spirit. You know how I have raised you; even if I am the least of men, become an imitator of me. Imitate my way of life; I do not boast in the world, but in the Lord. I exhort Hero, my child: "Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord." May I have joy of you, my beloved child, may the only unbegotten God and the Lord be your guardian.

->THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO HERO. III. IV. V. VI.<-

III. ...you should do.³ For they are priests; but you are a servant <note>original: "minister"; likely referring to the office of deacon</note> of the priests. For they baptize, perform the sacred rites, ordain, and lay on hands; but you minister to them,⁴ just as the holy Stephen served James and the elders in Jerusalem.⁵ Do not neglect the assembly: seek out everyone by name. Let no one despise your youth; but be an example to the faithful in word and in conduct.⁶

IV. Do not look down upon servants; for the same nature is common¹ to us and to them.² Do not detest women; for they give birth and provide nourishment. It is necessary, therefore, to love them³ for the sake of procreation—yet only in the Lord—because without a woman, a man cannot father a child at all. One must therefore honor them as coworkers in procreation, because⁴ neither is the man without the woman, nor the woman without the man, ever able to trace their origin,⁵ except in the case of those first-formed parents <note>original: "protoplastis"; referring to Adam and Eve</note>: for the body of Adam was made from the four elements,⁶ while Eve was made from⁷ the side of Adam. Truly the glorious dwelling place of the Lord was in⁸ the Virgin alone. Legitimate union does not⁹ seem detestable, but the ordering of procreation itself is fitting to God. For it was proper for the Creator <note>original: "Opificem"; the Craftsman or Maker</note>¹⁰ not to use the common¹¹ human method for his birth, but to be born in a glorious and new way, as befitted the Maker.

V. Flee from pride;¹ "For God resists the proud." Abhor lying. "For," He says,² "you shall destroy all those who speak lies." Guard yourself against envy. For its author³ is the Devil, and his successor was Cain, who was envious of his brother and committed murder out of that envy. Admonish my sisters to love God, and that they ought to be content with their husbands alone. Likewise, admonish my brothers that they ought to be content with their own wives.⁴ Guard the virgins as the sacred treasures <note>original: "sacramenta"</note> of Christ. # THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO HERO. VI. VII. VIII. IX.

Jesus Christ. Do not believe everyone, do not trust everyone—not even if someone speaks to you with flattery <note>original: ὑποκορίζηταί; to use endearing or flattering language to deceive</note>; for many are servants of Satan. And he who trusts too quickly is flighty in heart <note>A reference to the Book of Sirach (Ecclesiasticus) 19:4</note>.

VII. Remember God, and you will never sin. Do not be double-minded in your prayer; for blessed is he who does not doubt <note>A reference to the Epistle of James 1:6-8 regarding "double-mindedness"</note>. For I believe in the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, and in His only-begotten Son, that God will show me Hero sitting upon my throne <note>Ignatius is anticipating his martyrdom and expects Hero to succeed him as the Bishop of Antioch</note>; therefore, press on in your course. I charge you before the God of all things, and before Christ, in the presence also of the Holy Spirit and the ministering ranks <note>referring to the angelic hosts</note>: guard the deposit <term>deposit: (Greek: παραθήκην) the core teachings and traditions of the faith entrusted to a leader</term> which I and Christ have committed to you, and do not judge yourself unworthy of the things which were shown to God concerning you. I entrust to you the church of the Antiochians. I have commended you all to Polycarp <note>The famous Bishop of Smyrna and contemporary of Ignatius</note> in the Lord Jesus Christ.

VIII. The bishops Onesimus, Bitus, Damas, Polybius, and all those from Philippi in Christ greet you, from where I also have written to you. Greet the God-worthy presbytery <note>the council of elders or priests</note>. Greet your holy fellow-deacons, in whom may I have joy in Christ, both in flesh and spirit. Greet the people of the Lord, from the least to the greatest, by name, whom I entrust to you as Moses did to Joshua <note>original: "Jesus"; the Greek name for Joshua, son of Nun</note>, the leader after him. And let not what is said seem heavy to you; for even if we are not such as they were, yet at least we pray to become so, since we are also children of Abraham. Be strong, therefore, O Hero, heroically and manfully; for from now on you shall lead the people of the Lord in Antioch in and out, and the congregation of the Lord shall not be as sheep who have no shepherd.

IX. Greet Cassian my host, and his most venerable wife, and their dearest children; to whom may God grant to find mercy from the Lord on that day <note>the Day of Judgment</note> because of their service to us; whom I also entrust to you in Christ. Greet all the faithful in Laodicea, each by name, in Christ. Do not neglect those in Tarsus, but look after them more frequently, strengthening them in the Gospel. I greet Maris, the bishop in Neapolis near Anazarbus, in the Lord. Greet also the most honorable Mary, my daughter, a woman of great learning, and the church in her house; may my soul be as hers <note>original: ἀντίψυχον; a term of deep affection meaning "a ransom for her soul" or "devoted to her"</note>, for she is a model of godly women. Fare you well...

the unbegotten God and the Lord Jesus Christ. Do not believe everyone, nor trust in everyone, lest someone should sneak in upon you. For many are ministers of Satan; and he who believes quickly is fickle in heart.⁸ <note>original: "levis est corde"; a reference to the Book of Sirach 19:4, suggesting that a person who is too easily persuaded lacks spiritual depth.</note>

<meta>This page continues the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians.
