...he was not ashamed of my chain <note>original: "halysin"; Ignatius refers to his physical shackles as he is led to Rome</note>, just as the Father of Jesus Christ will also refresh him, together with Onesimus and Burrus and Euplus and Fronto, through whom I saw all of you in love. May I have joy in you always, if indeed I am worthy. It is fitting, therefore, that you should in every way glorify Jesus Christ, who has glorified you, so that you may be perfected in one subjection, being of the same mind and the same judgment, and that you may all speak the same thing about the same matter, so that being subject to the bishop and the presbytery <term>presbytery: the council of elders or priests</term> you may be sanctified in all things.

III. I do not issue commands to you as if I were someone of importance. For even if I am bound for the sake of the Name <note>The "Name" refers to the name of Christ, for which Ignatius is being martyred</note>, I have not yet been perfected in Jesus Christ. For now I am beginning to be a disciple, and I speak to you as fellow-servants. For I ought to have been reminded by you in faith, admonition, endurance, and long-suffering. But since love does not allow me to be silent concerning you, I have therefore taken it upon myself to exhort you, that you may run together in harmony with the mind of God. For Jesus Christ also does everything according to the mind of the Father, as He himself says somewhere: "I always do those things that are pleasing to Him." Therefore, it is necessary for us also to live according to the mind of God in Christ, and to be zealous as Paul was; for he says, "Become imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ."

IV. Therefore it is also fitting for you to run together in harmony with the mind of the bishop, who shepherds you according to God; which is exactly what you are doing, having been made wise by the Spirit. For the rightfully named presbytery, being worthy of God, is so harmoniously joined to the bishop as strings are to a lyre; thus being bound together in concord and symphonic love, of which Jesus Christ is the leader and guardian. And you, each of you individually, become a choir, so that being in harmony in concord, receiving the melody of God, you may become one in unity through the symphony with God the Father and His beloved Son Jesus Christ our Lord. For He says, "Holy Father, grant to them that as I and You are one, they also may be one in Us." It is useful, therefore, that you, being joined to God in blameless unity, should be imitators of Christ, whose members you are.

V. For if I, in a short time, have had such intimacy with your bishop—which was not merely human, but spiritual—how much...

# THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. II. III. IV. V.

...with Burrus and Euplus and Fronto, through whom the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ may refresh you <note>original: "refrigeret"; a term used in early Christianity to describe spiritual rest or divine comfort</note>, through whom I have held you all in love. I have gained you in all things, if indeed I may be worthy. For it is right for you to glorify Jesus Christ in every way, who has also glorified you, so that you may be perfected in one instruction <note>original: "praeceptione"; referring to a shared rule of life or teaching</note>, in the same mind and in the same knowledge, that you may all say the same thing about the same matter, so that being subject to the Bishop and the Presbytery <term>Presbytery: the council of elders or priests who advise the bishop</term>, you may be sanctified in all things.

III. I do not issue commands to you as if I were someone of importance. Even though I am a prisoner for the name of Jesus Christ, I have not yet reached perfection. For now I am only beginning my instruction, and I address you as fellow-servants. For I ought to have been encouraged by you in faith, in warning, in patience, and in long-suffering. Since love does not allow me to be silent about you, I have therefore taken it upon myself to ask you that you may run together in harmony with the mind <note>original: "dispositioni"; the divine arrangement or plan</note> of God. For Jesus Christ also does everything according to the mind of God the Father, just as he says in a certain place: "I always do those things that are pleasing to him." Therefore, we also ought to live according to the mind of God in Christ, and to be zealous as Paul was; for he says: "Be imitators of me, even as I also am of Christ."

IV. Wherefore it also becomes you to follow the mind of the Pastors, who shepherd you according to God—which is indeed what you are doing, being wisely instructed by the Holy Spirit. Truly, your famously named Presbytery, which is worthy of God, should be as closely fitted to the Bishop as strings are joined to a lyre. In this way, in your concord and harmonious love, Jesus Christ is sung. And let each of you individually become a choir, so that being harmonious in unanimity, taking up the melody of God in unity, you may sing with one voice through Jesus Christ to the Father, so that He may both hear you and recognize you, through your good deeds, as members of His Son. It is profitable for you, therefore, to live in blameless unity, so that you may always participate in God.

V. For if I, in a short time, had such fellowship with your Bishop—which was not merely human but spiritual—how much [more]...

<meta>This page continues the Epistle of Ignatius to the Ephesians, moving from Chapter V to Chapter VI. Having previously discussed the importance of harmony and submission to the church leadership, Ignatius now elaborates on the spiritual benefits of this unity and the role of the bishop as God's representative.</meta>

### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. V. VI.

I account you even more blessed, you who are joined <note>original: "ἀνακρεμαμένους" (anakremamenous); literally "hanging upon" or "clinging to"</note> to him, as the church is to the Lord Jesus, and the Lord to God his Father, so that all things may be harmonious in unity. Let no one be deceived: if anyone is not within the sanctuary <note>original: "θυσιαστηρίου" (thusiastēriou); literally 'altar,' but here referring to the gathered community of the church</note>, he is deprived of the bread of God. For if the prayer of one or two has such strength that Christ stands among them, how much more shall the harmonious prayer of the bishop and the entire church, ascending to God in faith, persuade Him to grant them all their requests in Christ. Therefore, he who separates himself from such people and does not come together in the council of sacrifices and the church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven, is a wolf in sheep’s clothing, showing a gentle appearance.

Strive, beloved, to be subject to the bishop, the presbyters, and the deacons; for he who is subject to these obeys Christ, who appointed them. But he who is disobedient to them is disobedient to Christ Jesus; and "he who is disobedient to the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." For such a person is self-willed and quarrelsome, and proud, not obeying those who are better than him. "God opposes the proud," it says, "but gives grace to the humble"; and, "The proud acted most lawlessly." Moreover, the Lord says to the priests: "He who hears you, hears me; and he who hears me, does not hear me [alone], but the Father who sent me. He who rejects you, rejects me; and he who rejects me, rejects Him who sent me."

VI. Therefore, the more you see the bishop keeping silence, the more you should revere him. For everyone whom the Master of the house sends for His own stewardship, we ought to receive him as the one who sent him. It is clear, then, that we must look upon the bishop as the Lord Himself, standing before the Lord. "A man who is discerning and quick in his work should stand before kings, and not stand before sluggish men." <note>A reference to Proverbs 22:29</note> Indeed, Onesimus <note>The Bishop of Ephesus at the time, possibly the same Onesimus mentioned by the Apostle Paul in the Bible</note> himself highly praises your good order in God, because you all live according to the truth, and no heresy dwells among you; nor do you listen to anyone except Jesus Christ alone, the true Shepherd and Teacher. You are, as Paul wrote to you, "one body and one spirit," because you were also called in the one hope of your faith; since there is "one Lord, one faith, one baptism, one God and Father of all, who is over all..."

### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. V. VI.

I bless you all the more, you who cling to him, just as the Church clings to the Lord Jesus, and the Lord himself to his Lord <note>original: "Dominum suum"; some manuscripts vary here, but it refers to the Father</note> and Father, so that all things may be in harmony through unity. Let no one be deceived. If anyone is not within the sanctuary <note>original: "intra altare" (within the altar); used here to denote the gathered community of the church</note>, he will be deprived of the bread of God. For if the prayer of one or two has such power that Christ stands among them, how much more does the prayer of the blameless priest <note>A title for the Bishop</note> and the holy people, rising together to God, persuade Him to grant all their requests in Christ. 

Therefore, he who separates himself from such people and does not come together in the congregation of sacrifices—the Church of the firstborn who are enrolled in heaven—is a wolf in the flock of sheep, though he displays a gentle appearance. Strive therefore, most beloved, to be subject to the Bishop, the Presbyters <note>The elders or priests</note>, and the Deacons. For whoever is subject to these obeys Christ, who granted them this authority. But whoever does not agree with them does not agree with Jesus Christ. And "whoever does not agree with the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains upon him." Such a person is reckless, terrible, and proud, for he is not subject to those who are greater than him. "For God," it says, "resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble." And again: "The proud acted most lawlessly." The Lord also says to the priests: "Whoever hears you, hears me; and whoever hears me, hears him who sent me; and whoever rejects you, rejects me; and whoever rejects me, rejects him who sent me."

VI. Therefore, when you see a Bishop keeping silent, fear him all the more. For we must receive everyone whom the master of the house sends for his stewardship just as we would receive the one who sent him. It is necessary, then, to look upon the Bishop as the Lord himself, as he stands before the Lord. For it is fitting for kings to be assisted by a man who is a true and sharp-sighted observer <note>original: "Prospectorem"; the Greek original "οἰκονόμον" implies a steward or manager</note> of his own works, rather than by weak men. 

Onesimus <note>The Bishop of Ephesus mentioned in the New Testament (Philemon 1:10)</note> himself praises your excellent stewardship in God, because you all live according to the truth, and because no heresy dwells among you. Indeed, you do not listen to anyone except Jesus Christ alone, the true Shepherd and Teacher; and you are, just as Paul wrote to you, "one body and one spirit," since you are joined together in one hope of faith. ### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. VI. VII. VIII. IX.

...and through all and in all. <note>original: "καὶ διὰ πάντων καὶ ἐν πᾶσιν"; a reference to God's omnipresence</note> You, then, are such people, having been established in the basic principles by such instructors: Paul the "Christ-bearer" <note>original: "Christophoros"; a title Ignatius often applied to himself and other holy leaders, meaning one who carries Christ within</note> and Timothy the most faithful.

VII. But some most wicked men are accustomed to carry around the Name <note>The name of Christ</note> with evil deceit, while practicing other things unworthy of God and holding opinions contrary to the teaching of Christ, to their own destruction and the destruction of those who believe them. You must avoid these men as you would wild beasts. "For a righteous man, by turning away, is saved forever; but the destruction of the ungodly is ready at hand and a cause for mockery." For they are "silent dogs" <note>original: "κύνες ἐνεοὶ"; a reference to Isaiah 56:10, describing leaders who fail to warn the people of danger</note> who are unable to bark; they are rabid, biting in secret, and you must be on your guard against them, for they suffer from an incurable disease. But our Physician is the only true God, the unbegotten <term>unbegotten: meaning he was not created and has no beginning</term> and unapproachable, the Lord of all things, and the Father and Begetter of the Only-begotten Son. We also have as a physician our Lord God, Jesus the Christ, the Only-begotten Son and Word before the ages began, but who later also became man from Mary the Virgin; for "the Word became flesh." He who is bodiless was in a body; the impassible <term>impassible: not subject to suffering or change</term> was in a passible body; the immortal was in a mortal body; Life was in the midst of corruption, so that He might set our souls free from death and corruption and heal them, curing them of the disease of ungodliness and evil desires.

VIII. Therefore, let no one deceive you, just as you are indeed not deceived; for you belong entirely to God. For when no desire exists within you that is able to defile you or bring you into torment, then you are truly living according to God and you belong to Christ. I am the "offscouring" <note>original: "Peripsēma"; a term of extreme humility, literally meaning the scrapings or refuse of a sacrifice offered on behalf of others</note> of you and of the most holy church of the Ephesians, which is famous and celebrated throughout the ages. Those who are carnal <note>living by the lower, physical nature</note> cannot do spiritual things, nor can those who are spiritual do carnal things; just as faith cannot do the works of unbelief, nor can unbelief do the works of faith. But you, being full of the Holy Spirit, do nothing according to the flesh, but perform all things spiritually. You are being made perfect in Christ Jesus, who is the Savior of all men, especially of those who believe.

IX. I have known of some who passed through your way, carrying evil doctrine from an alien and wicked spirit. You did not allow them to sow their weeds <note>referring to the Parable of the Tares/Weeds in Matthew 13</note> among you, but stopped up your ears so as not to receive the things sown by...

This page contrasts the "people-deceiving spirit" of those heretics with the true Holy Spirit, and describes the spiritual architecture of the Ephesian church.</meta>

### THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. IX. X.

...the error announced by them¹ <note>original: "πλάνην" (planēn); referring to the false teachers previously mentioned</note>, being persuaded that the people-deceiving² spirit speaks not the things of Christ, but its own; for it is a liar.³ But the Holy Spirit speaks not its own things, but the things of Christ; and not from itself, but from⁴ the Lord, just as the Lord also announced⁵ the things from the Father to us.⁶ For the word, He says, which you hear is not mine, but the Father’s who sent me. And concerning the Holy Spirit: He will not speak,⁷ He says, of himself, but whatever he shall hear from me. And concerning Himself He says to the Father: I, He says, have glorified thee upon the earth; the work which thou gavest me, I have finished; I have manifested thy name to men. And concerning the Holy Spirit: He shall glorify me, because he takes from what is mine. 

But the deceiving spirit preaches itself⁸ and speaks its own things, for it is self-pleasing; it glorifies itself,⁹ for it is full of conceit;¹⁰ it is a liar, a cheat, a flatterer, a fawner,¹¹ treacherous, a weaver of fables, a babbler,¹² discordant, long-winded, greedy, and cowardly. From its influence¹³ Jesus Christ will rescue you,¹⁴ who has established you¹⁶ upon the Rock as chosen stones, well-fitted for a divine building¹⁷ of the Father, being carried up¹⁸ to the heights¹⁹ through Christ who was crucified for us, using the Holy Spirit as a rope <note>The author uses the metaphor of a crane or hoist, where the Cross of Christ is the machine and the Holy Spirit is the rope</note>; being raised up²⁰ by faith, and lifted by love from earth to heaven, walking²¹ together with the blameless. For "Blessed," He says, "are the blameless in the way, who walk in²² the law of the Lord." And the way is without error, Jesus Christ;²³ for "I am," He says, "the way and the life." And the way leads to the Father; for "no one," He says,²⁴ "comes to the Father, except through me." 

Therefore, you are blessed, you who are God-bearers, Spirit-bearers, Temple-bearers, and Bearers-of-holy-things,²⁵ <term>theophoroi: a title Ignatius often applied to himself and his readers, meaning those who carry God within them</term> adorned in all things with the commandments of Jesus Christ, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for His possession. For your sake I rejoice and have been counted worthy, through these things which I write, to converse with the saints who are in Ephesus, the faithful in Christ Jesus. I rejoice therefore over you, because you do not attend to vanity, and you do not love according to the flesh, but according to God.

X. And pray without ceasing for other men; for there is in them a hope of repentance, that they may find God.¹ For does he who falls not rise again? Or does he who turns away not return? Turn back, therefore...

**Notes on Chapter IX:** 
1) *concerning* them: found in Manuscript B. 
2) *people-deceiving*: found in Manuscript R. 
3) *liar*: found in Manuscripts F and O. 
4) *but*: according to Manuscript R; others (B, F, O, V) use a slightly different conjunction. 
5) *the*: omitted in Manuscripts F, O, V. 
6) *they announced*: found in Manuscript R. 
7) *will speak*: written with a spelling error in Manuscript V. 
8) *himself*: found in Manuscripts O and V, corrected in the margin of V. 
9) *himself*: corrected from masculine to neuter in Manuscripts O and R. The handwriting in Codex V is ambiguous. 
10) The phrase "for it is full of conceit" is likely an addition and should be omitted according to Manuscript R and the old Latin Translation. 
11) The word "fawner" ends the sentence in Manuscripts F, O, V. 
12) A variant spelling of "babbler" appears in O and V. 
13) *influence*: variant spelling in Manuscript F. 
14) *us*: used instead of "you" in Manuscripts F, O, R, V, and the old Latin Translation. 
15) *the*: added from Manuscript R.

<column-break/>

16) *us*: used in Manuscript F and the old Translation. 
17) *of God*: used in Manuscript F. 
18) *being carried up*: variant accenting in O and V; standard in F and R. 
19) *height*: singular variant in V. 
20) *being raised up*: variant grammatical forms (participle vs. subjunctive) across R, F, V, and O. 
21) *walking together*: Manuscript B uses one form; F, O, R, and V use another; the Voss manuscript uses a different verb meaning "traveling." 
22) *in*: omitted in the Voss manuscript. 
23) *the*: omitted in F, O, V. 
24) *He says*: omitted in B, F, O, R, and V. 
25) The terms *Spirit-bearers, Temple-bearers, Bearers-of-holy-things* are missing in R and considered redundant; *Temple-bearers* is omitted in F, O, V.

**Notes on Chapter X:** 
1) *they may find*: variant spelling between O, V and B, F, R.

<meta>This page continues the "Long Recension" of Ignatius’s Letter to the Ephesians. # THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. X. XI.

...to those <note>The text refers to unbelievers who might be "discipled" or taught by the behavior of the Christians.</note> who are being discipled by you. Therefore, become ministers of God and the mouth of Christ. For the Lord says: "If you bring forth the precious from the worthless, you shall be as my mouth." <note>A reference to Jeremiah 15:19.</note> In the face of their anger, be humble; against their blasphemies, set your earnest prayers; while they are wandering in error, stand firm and steadfast in the faith; conquer their wild character with mildness, and their wrath with gentleness. For "Blessed are the meek"; <note>Matthew 5:5.</note> and Moses was "meek beyond all men," and David was "exceedingly meek." For this reason Paul also exhorts us, saying: "The servant of the Lord must not fight, but must be kind to all, able to teach, patient, in gentleness correcting those who are in opposition." <note>2 Timothy 2:24-25.</note> Do not be eager to take revenge on those who wrong you. For he says: "If I have returned evil to those who returned evil to me..." <note>Psalm 7:4.</note> Let us make them our brothers by our kindness; for you should say to those who hate you: "You are our brothers," so that the name of the Lord may be glorified. And let us imitate the Lord, who, "when He was reviled, did not revile in return," <note>1 Peter 2:23.</note> when He was crucified, He did not resist, and when He suffered, He did not threaten, but prayed for His enemies: "Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do." <note>Luke 23:34.</note> If anyone is wronged more, let him endure more; if anyone is defrauded, if anyone is despised for the sake of the name of the Lord, he is truly Christ’s. See to it that no "weed of the Devil" <note>An image of false teaching or sin growing within the community, likely referencing the Parable of the Tares.</note> is found among you; for such a thing is bitter and salty. Be sober and self-controlled in Christ Jesus.

XI. These are the last times. Therefore, let us be ashamed and fear the long-suffering of God; let us not despise the riches of His goodness and forbearance. For we should either fear the coming wrath or love the present joy in this life; and let this present joy be the true joy: merely to be found in Christ Jesus, so as to truly live. Apart from Him, may you never even choose to draw breath. For He is my hope, He is my boast, He is my never-failing wealth. In Him I carry around these chains from Syria even to Rome—spiritual pearls, in which I pray that I may be perfected by your supplication, becoming a partaker of the sufferings of Christ, and a sharer in His death, and in the resurrection from the dead, and in the life that never fails. May it be my lot to attain this, so that I may be found in the portion of the Ephesian Christians, who also...

Hasten, therefore, to meet frequently for the Eucharist <note>The word "eucharistiam" here refers both to the act of thanksgiving and the communal meal of the early Church.</note> and <gloss>1</gloss> the glory of God. For when this is done assiduously, the powers of Satan are driven away, and his deeds <gloss>2</gloss> are turned into fiery arrows <gloss>3</gloss> leading to sin. Your concord and harmonious faith is his destruction and a torment to his companions. For nothing is better than to have peace in Christ, in which every weapon <gloss>4</gloss> of aerial <gloss>5</gloss> and earthly spirits <gloss>6</gloss> is neutralized. "For we do not <gloss>7</gloss> struggle against flesh and blood, but against principalities and powers, and against the world-rulers of this darkness, against spiritual wickedness in the heavens." <note>Ignatius is quoting the New Testament book of Ephesians 6:12.</note>

XIV. Therefore, do not wound yourselves with any contagion <gloss>2</gloss> of the Devil, just as Paul says, but have faith and love in Christ <gloss>3</gloss>, which <gloss>4</gloss> is the beginning and end of life. The beginning of life is faith, and its end is love; both joined together <gloss>5</gloss> in unity <gloss>6</gloss> make the person of God perfect. All other things that follow in benevolence complete the character. No one proclaiming faith should sin, nor should one possessing love hate his brother. For He who said: "You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart," also said: "And your neighbor as yourself." Those who proclaim themselves to be Christ's are recognized not only by what they say, but by what they do. "For the tree is known by its fruit." <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 12:33.</note>

### XV.
It is better<gloss>1</gloss> to keep silence and *be*, than to speak and *not be*. The kingdom of God is not in word, but in<gloss>2</gloss> power. With the heart one believes, and with the mouth one confesses: the former leads to righteousness, the latter to salvation. It is good to teach, if the one who speaks<gloss>3</gloss> also acts. For whoever acts<gloss>4</gloss> and teaches,<gloss>5</gloss> this person shall be great in the kingdom. -># THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. XV. XVI. XVII.<-

### XV.
It is therefore better to keep silence and to *be*, than to speak and *not* to be, because the kingdom of God is not in word, but in power. <note>original: "virtute" — translating the Greek 'dynamis'. Reference to 1 Corinthians 4:20.</note> "For with the heart one believes unto righteousness, but with the mouth confession is made unto salvation." <note>Romans 10:10.</note> It is good to teach, but only if one does what they say. "For whoever teaches and acts, this person shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven." <note>Matthew 5:19.</note> Now our Lord and God, Jesus Christ, who is the Son of the living God, first acted and then taught, as Luke witnesses, "whose praise is in the Gospel throughout all the Churches." <note>2 Corinthians 8:18; early traditions often identified this "brother whose praise is in the Gospel" as Luke the Evangelist.</note> For nothing is hidden from the Lord, but even our secrets are present before Him. Let us therefore do all things as if He were dwelling within us, so that we may be His temples, and He may dwell in us. Thus let Christ the Lord speak in us, just as He did in Paul; and let the Holy Spirit teach us to respond with the things of Christ, being joined to Him.

### XVI.
Do not be led astray, my brothers: do not be those who lie with men, for such people shall not possess the kingdom of God. <note>1 Corinthians 6:9-10.</note> For if those who corrupt human dwellings are condemned to death, how much more shall those who attempt to corrupt the doctrine of Christ receive eternal damnation? This is because of the cross and death which the Lord Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, endured. Whoever depraves His doctrine shall be cast out, polluted, into Gehenna. <note><term>Gehenna</term>: a term used in the New Testament for a place of fiery judgment/hell.</note> Likewise, every person who despises what they have received from God shall be condemned. He who follows an unskilled shepherd and accepts false glory as if it were true cannot be a partaker of Christ. "For what fellowship has light with darkness? Or Christ with Belial?" <note><term>Belial</term>: a biblical name for the devil or a personification of worthlessness and wickedness.</note> Or what part has the faithful with the unfaithful? Or the temple of God with idols? <note>2 Corinthians 6:14-16.</note> And I also say: what communication has truth with a lie? Or what fellowship has righteousness with unrighteousness? Or true glory with false glory?

-># THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. XVII. XVIII. XIX. XX.<-

...why do we not all become wise? Why, having received the innate power of judgment concerning God from Christ, do we fall into ignorance? And why, through our own negligence, remaining ignorant of the gift which we have received, do we perish in our foolishness?

### XVIII.
The cross of Christ is a stumbling block <note>original: "skandalon"</note> to those who do not believe, but to those who believe, it is salvation and eternal life. "Where is the wise man? Where is the debater? Where is the boasting of those called powerful?" <note>A paraphrase of 1 Corinthians 1:20.</note> For the Son of God, who was begotten before the ages and established all things by the will of the Father, was carried in the womb of Mary according to the <term>economy of God</term> <note>original: "oikonomia" — referring to God’s divine plan or management of human salvation.</note>, truly being of the seed of David, but by the Holy Spirit. For it says: "Behold, the virgin shall conceive in her womb, and shall bear a son, and he shall be called Emmanuel." <note>Isaiah 7:14; Matthew 1:23.</note> He was born and was baptized by John, so that He might confirm the order of things <note>original: "diataxin"</note> entrusted to the Prophet.

### XIX.
Now, the virginity of Mary and her giving birth were hidden from the prince of this age <note>A common early Christian title for the Devil or Satan.</note>, as was the death of the Lord. These are three mysteries to be proclaimed aloud, yet they were wrought in the silence of God, though they have now been revealed to us. A star shone in heaven, brighter than all the stars that came before it; its light was beyond words, and its novelty caused amazement to those who saw it. All the other stars, together with the sun and moon, formed a chorus around this star, yet it exceeded them all in its brilliance. There was trouble and confusion as to where this new thing appearing among them had come from. Because of this, worldly wisdom was made foolish, and the depths of sorcery were exposed as vanity; the magic of the pagans became a laughingstock. Every law of wickedness vanished, the darkness of ignorance was scattered, and tyrannical rule was pulled down, for God appeared as a man, and man acted as God. However, the former was not a mere display of glory, nor was the latter a mere simplicity of nature; rather, the one was truth and the other was the divine <term>economy</term>. Now that which had been perfected by God was taking its beginning; hence, all things were moved and shaken because the destruction of death was being prepared.

### XX.
Stand firm, brothers, settled in the faith of Jesus Christ and in His love, in His suffering and His resurrection. Gather together in grace, every one of you, in a common assembly, in the one faith of God the Father and of Jesus Christ, His only-begotten Son, and the firstborn of all...

-># THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. XVII. XVIII. XIX. XX.<-

...[Why] are we not made wise, we who are endowed with reason?⁸ Why do we not guard the planting which we received from God through Christ, but instead fall into judgment through ignorance out of negligence, not knowing the grace we have received, and perishing unknowingly⁹?

### XVIII.
Because the cross of Christ¹ is indeed a stumbling block to the unfaithful, but to the faithful it is salvation and eternal life.² Where is the wise man? Where is the scribe? Where is the seeker? Where is the boasting of words? For the Son of God, who was begotten before the ages³ and established all things by the Father’s arrangement, was Himself carried in the womb by Mary, according to God’s⁴ arrangement <note>original: "dispositionem" — often used to translate the Greek "oikonomia," referring to God's plan for salvation.</note>, from the seed of David and the Holy Spirit. "For behold," it says, "a Virgin⁵ shall conceive in her womb and bear a son: and his name shall be called Emmanuel." He Himself was baptized by John, so that he might make the ordinance⁶ faithful, which was handed down to the Prophets by God.

### XIX.
And the virginity of Mary and her giving birth were hidden from the prince of this world;¹ similarly also the death of the Lord. These are three² mysteries to be cried out in silence. For the works of God have been manifested to us.³ A star shone forth in the heaven⁴ above all those that were before it: and its light was inestimable and new, and its strangeness⁵ appeared to those seeing it. But the other⁶ stars, together with the sun and moon, became a choir for that star; but it exceeded all in its own brilliance: and there was a disturbance as to whence⁷ this novelty had come, which had appeared. From this the wisdom of this world was dulled, sorceries were nullified, magic was mocked,⁸ iniquity and malice were banished, darkness and ignorance were scattered, and the principalities of tyrants were abolished,⁹ God appearing as man,¹⁰ and man working as God. But there was neither glory in the first, nor purity in the second: but that truth and that¹¹ way of life received the primacy from God. All things were established perfectly in him;¹² because of which he meditated on the dissolution of death.

### XX.
Stand firm, therefore, brothers, in the faith of Jesus Christ and in¹ His love and resurrection. All of you in every place, in² grace, and in His name, gather together in common; in the one faith of God the Father, and of Christ Jesus, His only-begotten Son, and the firstborn of all creation,³ according to the flesh...

### XX.
...of creation, but according to the flesh from the lineage of David, being guided <note>original: ἐφοδηγούμενοι (ephodēgoumenoi). The footnote indicates a variant reading in manuscripts B and F: ἐποδηγούμενοι (epodēgoumenoi), meaning "being led."</note> by the Comforter <note>The Paraclete or Holy Spirit.</note>; obeying the bishop and the presbytery <note>The council of elders or priests.</note> with an undisturbed mind; breaking one bread, which is the **medicine of immortality** <note>original: φάρμακον ἀθανασίας (pharmakon athanasias). This is one of Ignatius's most famous descriptions of the Eucharist, viewed as a spiritual remedy.</note>, an antidote so that we do not die but live forever in God through Jesus Christ, a cleansing power that wards off evil.

### XXI.
May my soul be a ransom for yours <note>original: ἀντίψυχον (antipsychon). A term of deep devotion, implying Ignatius offers his life for the benefit of the Ephesian church.</note>, and for those whom you sent for the honor of God to Smyrna, from where I also write to you, giving thanks to the Lord, and loving Polycarp <note>The famous Bishop of Smyrna and martyr.</note> as I also love you. ### THE LETTER OF IGNATIUS TO THE EPHESIANS. CHAPTERS XX. XXI.

<header>THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ROMANS. I. II.</header>

### THE EPISTLE OF THE SAME AUTHOR TO THE ROMANS.¹

Ignatius, also called **Theophorus** <note>original: *Theophoros*. Literally "God-bearer," a title Ignatius used to describe his intimacy with the Divine.</note>, to the church which has found mercy in the majesty of the Most High God the Father and Jesus Christ, His only-begotten Son; to the church beloved³ and enlightened by the will⁴ of God, who created all things that exist,⁵ according to the faith and love of Jesus Christ, our God and⁶ Savior; which also presides in the place of the Roman region, worthy of God,⁷ worthy of honor, worthy of blessing, worthy of praise, worthy of success,⁸ worthy in purity, and presiding in love, bearing the name of Christ,⁹ bearing the name of the Father, and bearing the Spirit. I greet you in the name of God the Almighty and of Jesus Christ His Son; to those who are united in flesh and spirit¹⁰ to His every commandment, filled with the grace of God without wavering, and filtered pure from every foreign stain, I wish you the greatest joy without blame¹¹ in God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

### I.
Since, by praying¹² to God, I have attained my request to see your God-worthy¹³ faces—which I have longed for even more than I asked—for being bound in Christ Jesus, I hope to greet you, if indeed it be the [Divine] will that I be deemed worthy to reach the end.¹⁵ For the beginning¹⁶ is well-ordered, if only I may attain grace to receive my lot at the end without hindrance. For I fear your love, lest it do me harm;¹⁷ for it is easy for you to do what you wish, but for me, it is difficult to attain God¹⁸ unless you¹⁹ spare me from the excuse of worldly friendship.²⁰ <note>Ignatius is famously concerned that the influential Roman Christians might use their status to secure a pardon for him, thereby "robbing" him of the crown of martyrdom.</note>

### II.
For I do not wish you to be "men-pleasers," but to please God, just as¹ you indeed do please Him. For I shall never² have such an opportunity³ to attain God, nor will you, if you remain silent,⁴ have a better work to be credited to your name.⁵ For if you remain silent and leave me alone, I shall become a word of God; but if you love my flesh [too much], I shall again be a mere voice <note>original: *trechōn*. Some manuscripts suggest "a runner" or "a fleeting sound," implying he would lose his spiritual significance if he escapes death.</note>. Grant me nothing more than to be poured out as a drink-offering to God while the altar is still ready, so that you, becoming a choir in love, may sing to the Father in Christ Jesus—

### TO THE ROMANS. WRITTEN FROM SMYRNA BY WAY OF THE EPHESIANS.¹

Ignatius, also known as **Theophorus** <note>original: *Theophoros*, meaning "God-bearer."</note>, to the church that has found mercy in the majesty of the Most High Father and Jesus Christ, His only-begotten Son; to the church sanctified and enlightened by the will of God, who created all things that exist, according to the faith and love of Jesus Christ, our God and Savior. This is the church which presides in the region of the Romans; worthy of God, worthy of honor, worthy of blessing, worthy of praise, worthy of success, worthy in purity, and presiding in love, bearing the name of Christ and the name of the Father, and bearing the Spirit. I greet you in the name of God the Almighty and of Jesus Christ His Son. To those who are united in His commandment, both in flesh and spirit, filled with the grace of God inseparably, and washed clean of every foreign color and stain, I wish you abundant and pure greeting in God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ.

### I.
By praying to God, I have finally earned the right to see your worthy faces, just as I have greatly desired to do. For as a prisoner in Christ Jesus, I hope to greet you, if indeed it be His will that I am deemed worthy to complete my purpose to the very end. The beginnings are indeed promising, if only I may obtain the grace to receive my lot at the end without hindrance. For I fear your love, lest it should do me harm. <note>Ignatius fears the Roman Christians might use their influence to save him from execution, which he views as "harming" his chance to be a martyr.</note> For it is easy for you to do what you wish; but for me, it is difficult to attain to God, unless you spare me <margin>on the pretext of fleshly friendship</margin>.

### II.
Therefore, I do not want you to please men, but to please God, as indeed you do. For I shall never again have such an opportunity to attain to God. If you remain silent, you will be credited with a better work. But if you speak up out of love for my flesh <note>meaning, to save his physical life</note>, I shall again be merely a runner <note>The original Latin *currens* suggests one who is still running the race and has not yet reached the goal of heaven.</note>. You can offer me no greater favor than to let me be poured out as a sacrifice to God while the altar is already prepared. Then, having formed a chorus in love, you may sing

<header>THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ROMANS. II. III. IV.</header>

...of you, because God has deemed it worthy that the bishop of Syria be found, having summoned him from the east to the west, calling him to be a witness <note>original: *martyra*, meaning both a witness and a martyr</note> of His own sufferings, that he might pass from the world to God, so that I may rise in Him.

### III.
You have never envied anyone; you have taught others. But I desire that those instructions you give while teaching others may remain firm. Only pray for strength for me, both within and without, so that I may not only speak, but truly desire; so that I may not only be called a Christian, but truly be found to be one. For if I am found to be one, I can also be called one, and then be faithful even when I am no longer visible to the world. Nothing that is visible is eternal. For "the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal" <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:18</note>. This is not a work of mere persuasion, but of greatness. A Christian is hated by the world, but loved by God. For He says, "If you were of this world, the world would love its own; but now you are not of this world, but I have chosen you; abide in me" <note>A paraphrase combining John 15:19 and 15:4</note>.

### IV.
I am writing to all the churches, and I declare to all that I die willingly for God, provided that you do not hinder me. I entreat you, do not show me an "untimely kindness." <note>Ignatius is concerned that the influential Roman Christians might attempt to use legal or political means to stop his execution, which he views as his final spiritual trial.</note> Let me be food for the wild beasts, for through them I can reach God. I am God's wheat, and I am being ground by the teeth of wild beasts so that I may be found to be the pure bread of God. Rather, coax the wild beasts to become my tomb, and to leave nothing of my body behind, so that once I have fallen asleep, I will not be a burden to anyone. Then I shall truly be a disciple of Jesus Christ, when the world will not even see my body. Beseech the Lord for me, that through these instruments <note>referring to the wild beasts in the arena</note> I may be found a sacrifice to God. I do not command you as Peter and Paul did. They were Apostles of Jesus Christ, but I am the least of men. They were free, as servants <note>original: *douloi*</note> of God, but I am a slave even until now. Yet if I suffer, I shall become a freedman of Jesus Christ, and I shall rise again in Him as a free man. Now, in my bonds, I am learning to desire nothing worldly or vain.

...to God the Father in Christ Jesus, because God has seen fit for the bishop of Syria to be found in the West, having summoned him from the East to his own passion, as a good witness <note>original: *martyrem*, meaning both witness and martyr</note>, departing from the world to God, so that I may rise in Him.<note>4</note>

# THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ROMANS. V. VI. VII.

### V.
From Syria all the way to Rome, I fight with wild beasts <note>original: θηριομαχῶ (theriomachō); likely a metaphor for the cruelty of his guards, though he expects literal beasts in Rome.</note>, by land and sea, by night and day, bound to ten "leopards" <note>original: λεοπάρδοις; this is one of the earliest recorded uses of this word in Greek literature.</note>, which is a company of soldiers; even when they are treated well, they only become worse. But by their mistreatment I become more of a disciple; "yet I am not thereby justified." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 4:4.</note> May I enjoy the wild beasts that are prepared for me, which I pray may be found ready for me. I will even coax them to devour me quickly, not like some whom they were too timid to touch. And even if they are unwilling, I will compel them. Bear with me; I know what is to my advantage. Now I begin to be a disciple. Let nothing, whether visible or invisible, envy me <note>In the sense of "trying to keep me from my goal."</note>, so that I may attain to Jesus Christ. Let fire and cross, packs of wild beasts, cuttings and tearings, the scattering of bones, the crushing of limbs, the grinding <note>original: ἀλυσμοὶ (alysmoi), though some manuscripts suggest ἀλεσμοὶ (alesmoi), "grinding" or "milling."</note> of the whole body, and the cruel tortures of the devil come upon me, only let me attain to Jesus Christ!

### VI.
The ends of the world <note>original: τὰ πέρατα τοῦ κόσμου</note> will profit me nothing, nor will the kingdoms of this age. It is better for me to die for the sake of Jesus Christ than to reign over the ends of the earth. "For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but loses his own soul?" <note>Matthew 16:26.</note> I long for the Lord, the Son of the true God and Father, Jesus Christ. I seek Him who died and rose again for us. Forgive me, brothers; do not hinder me from coming to life <note>Ignatius views his death as the true beginning of his life with God.</note>. Jesus is the life of the faithful; do not wish for me to die. Since I desire to belong to God, do not give me over to the world. Let me receive the pure light; when I arrive there, I will be a man of God. Permit me to be an imitator of the passion of my God. If anyone has Him within himself, let him understand what I desire, and let him sympathize with me, knowing the things that constrain me.

### VII.
The ruler of this age <note>A reference to Satan or the demonic forces driving the world system.</note> wants to snatch me away and corrupt my mind which is set toward my God. Therefore, let none of you who are present help him. Rather, be on my side—that is, on the side of God. Do not speak of Jesus Christ while you prefer the world. Let no envy dwell among you. Even if I should exhort you otherwise when I arrive, do not be persuaded; rather, believe these things which I write to you now. For I write to you while living, yet longing to die for Christ. My earthly desire <note>original: ἔρως (eros); often interpreted here as his "earthly passions" or as "Christ, my Love."</note> has been cruci-

->**THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO THE ROMANS. V. VI. VII.**<-

**V.** From Syria all the way to Rome, I fight with wild beasts, by land and sea, by night and day, bound to ten leopards <note>original: "leopardis"; Ignatius uses this term to describe the soldiers guarding him. This is one of the earliest known uses of the word "leopard" in literature.</note>, that is, a company of soldiers, who only become worse when they are treated with kindness. Yet by their mistreatment I am more fully instructed; but "not by this am I justified." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 4:4.</note> May I enjoy the wild beasts that are prepared for me, and I pray that they may be found ready for me; I will even coax them to devour me quickly, unlike those whom they have been afraid to touch. And if they are unwilling, I will compel them. Forgive me: I know what is to my advantage. Now I begin to be a disciple. Let nothing, visible or invisible, envy me <note>In the sense of "begrudge" or "prevent."</note> the chance to attain Jesus Christ. Let fire and cross, and the persistent onslaught of wild beasts, the cutting, the tearing, the shattering of bones, the mangling of limbs, the destruction of the whole body, and the damnation of the Devil <note>Referring to the tortures orchestrated by the enemy.</note> come upon me, provided only that I attain to Jesus Christ.

**VI.** The things of this world and the kingdoms of this age will profit me nothing. It is better for me to die <note>original: "mori"</note> in Jesus Christ than to reign over the ends of the earth. "For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world, but loses his own soul?" <note>Matthew 16:26 and Luke 9:25.</note> I seek Him who died for us; I desire Him who rose again for our sake. Forgive me, brothers; do not hinder me from living; for Jesus is the life of the faithful. Do not wish for me to die; for a life without Christ is truly death. Since I long to belong to God, do not give me back to the world. Let me receive the pure light. When I arrive there, I shall be a man of God. Allow me to be an imitator of the passion of Christ, my God. If anyone has Him within himself, let him understand what I desire, and let him have sympathy for me, knowing the things that constrain me.

**VII.** The Prince of this world <note>A traditional term for the Devil or Satan.</note> wishes to seize me and to corrupt my mind directed toward God. Therefore, let none of you who are present help him; instead, be on my side, that is, on the side of God. Do not speak of Jesus Christ while you still love the world. Let no envy dwell among you; even if I should urge you otherwise when I arrive, do not obey me. Rather, believe these things that I write to you now. I write to you while living, yet longing to die for Christ. My earthly desire <note>original: "amor"; often translated here as "eros" or "longing."</note> has been crucified, and there is no fire in me for earthly things; but there is a living water <note>original: "aqua"</note>...

### IGNATIUS’S EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS. VII. VIII. IX. X. ###

...but another living <note>original: "viva"</note> water remains within me, saying to me from inside: "Come to the Father." I do not eat the food of corruption <note>Referring to physical food that sustains the decaying mortal body.</note>, nor do I desire the pleasures of this life. I want the Bread of God, the heavenly bread, the bread of life, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ the Son of God, who was born in the end of times from the seed of David and Abraham; and I want as a drink His blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.

**VIII.** I no longer wish to live according to human standards; and this shall be so, if you desire it. I am crucified with Christ; it is no longer I who live, for Christ lives in me. Through these brief writings I beseech you: do not oppose me. Believe me, that I love Jesus, for He Himself loved me and gave Himself up for me. "What shall I render to the Lord for all the things He has rendered to me?" <note>A quotation from Psalm 116:12 (numbered 115 in the Latin Vulgate).</note> God the Father Himself and the Lord Jesus Christ will make all these things manifest to you, that I speak the truth. And pray together with me, that I may achieve my labor in the Holy Spirit. I have not written to you according to the flesh, but according to the plan <note>original: "dispositionem," referring to God's divine arrangement or will.</note> of God. If I suffer, it was because you loved me; but if I am rejected, it was because you hated me <note>Ignatius suggests that if the Romans successfully intervene to save his life, it would actually be an act of "hatred" toward his spiritual goal of martyrdom.</note>.

**IX.** Remember in your prayers that man <note>referring to Jesus Christ or a successor</note> who is to govern the Church in Syria in my place. Trust the Lord who said: "I am the good shepherd"; He alone will watch over it, along with your love for Him. But as for me, I am ashamed to be counted among them. For I am not worthy, being the very last of them, or like a piece of refuse <note>original: "purgamentum," meaning the scrapings or offscourings of a thing; a term of extreme humility.</note>; but I am a man of misery now, until I deserve to attain God. My spirit salutes you, as does the love of the churches which received me in the name of Jesus Christ. For they did not treat me as a mere traveler, but looked upon my journey and escorted me through every city.

**X.** I write these things to you from Smyrna by way of the Ephesians, who are worthy of all blessing. Crocus is here with me, a name very dear to me, along with others. Regarding those who have already gone from Syria to Rome for the glory of God, I believe you have recognized them, as I instructed you when I was nearby.

->[**B. THE EPISTLE OF IGNATIUS TO ST. JOHN,**<-
->**APOSTOLOR AND EVANGELIST.**<-

**TO HOLY JOHN THE ELDER, IGNATIUS, AND THE BROTHERS WHO ARE WITH HIM.**

We grieve heavily over your delay, as we are in need of being strengthened by your speeches and consolations. If your absence is prolonged, it will leave many of ours destitute. Hasten, therefore, to come: because we believe it is necessary. There are also many of our women here, desiring to see Mary, the mother of Jesus, and wanting daily to run from us to you: so that they might touch her, and handle those breasts which nourished the Lord Jesus, and inquire of her concerning certain more secret matters. 

But also Salome, whom you love, the daughter of Anna, who stayed with her in Jerusalem for five months, and certain other acquaintances report that she is full of all graces and all virtues, fruitful in the manner of a virgin of virtue and grace. And, as they say, she is cheerful in persecutions and afflictions; not complaining in poverty and want: grateful to those who injure her, and she rejoices in the midst of troubles. She suffers with the miserable and the afflicted, and does not shrink from helping them. 

Against the pestilent conflicts of vices, she shines forth, contending in the battle of faith. She is the teacher of our new religion and of penitence, and among the faithful, she is a minister of all works of piety. She is indeed devoted to the humble, and humbles herself more devotedly to the devoted: and she is wonderfully magnified by all, even while she is disparaged by the Scribes and Pharisees. 

Furthermore, many report many other things about her: however, we do not dare to grant faith to all things in every way, nor to report them to you. But, as is told to us by those worthy of faith, in Mary the mother of Jesus, the nature of holiness is joined with human nature like that of an angel. And these such things have stirred our inner hearts: and they compel us to greatly desire the sight of this (if it is right to say) heavenly miracle <note>original: "prodigii"</note> and most sacred wonder <note>original: "monstri" - in this context, the word signifies a divine omen or a miraculous sign rather than something terrifying.</note>. You, however, dispose of this in a diligent manner according to our desire; and fare well. Amen.]

### [ANOTHER LETTER TO THE SAME. <note>original: "Ad eundem, altera" — referring to the Apostle John mentioned in the previous letter.</note>
#### TO THE HOLY ELDER JOHN, HIS OWN IGNATIUS.

If it is permitted for me in your presence, I wish to travel <note>original: "adscendere" — literally "to go up," a common biblical expression for traveling to Jerusalem due to its higher elevation compared to the surrounding areas.</note> to the regions of Jerusalem and see the faithful Saints who are there: especially Mary, the mother of Jesus, whom they say is worthy of admiration by all and desired by everyone. For who would it not delight to see her and speak with her—she who gave birth to the true God from herself—if they are a friend of our faith and religion?

Similarly, I wish to see that venerable James, who is surnamed the Just: whom they report is most like Christ Jesus in face, life, and manner of conduct, as if he were a twin brother from the same womb. If I see him, they say, I see Jesus himself according to all the features of his body. Furthermore, I wish to see the other holy men and women. Alas, why do I delay? Why am I held back? Good teacher, bid me to hasten, and fare well. Amen.]

<meta>Following the previous page's collection of likely apocryphal correspondence with the Virgin Mary and St. John, this page transitions to the "Martyrium," a narrative account of the trial and death of Saint Ignatius. While the letters were personal, this text is a formal hagiography intended for the church community.</meta>

->THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. I. II. III.<-

### THE MARTYRDOM OF THE HOLY AND GLORIOUS¹ PRIEST-MARTYR <term>Hieromartyr: A term for a martyr who was also an ordained priest or bishop.</term> IGNATIUS THE GOD-BEARER <note>original: "Theophoros"</note>.

I. Just as Trajan had taken up the scepters of the Roman Empire, Ignatius—who was "God-bearer" both by name and in reality—was the bishop of the church of the Antiochians. For Evodius succeeded the great Peter, and Ignatius succeeded Evodius; Ignatius became an imitator of his character and virtue. Regarding this "God-bearer," they say that when he was a very small child, while Christ was still spending His time in the world, He placed His pure hands upon him, and looking toward the crowd, He said: "Unless someone humbles himself like this child, he shall by no means enter into the kingdom of heaven; and whoever receives one such child in my name, receives me." <note>This is a reference to the Gospel of Matthew 18:3–5. Tradition held that Ignatius was the actual child held by Jesus.</note> Ignatius would be the sort of person who, as he advanced in age, made manifest from that point forward his apostolic teaching, which he wisely revealed.

II. This divine Ignatius, therefore, along with Polycarp (who was the leader of the church in Smyrna), became a disciple of John the Evangelist. Having studied with him alone and having industriously practiced every form of virtue—especially those becoming of a priest—he was then ordained a priest by the common vote of all the apostles together, and was appointed as the bishop of the Antiochians. Having taken charge of the church and having sown the preaching of piety within it through frequent sweat¹ and labor, he displayed an apostolic life in all things. Having already appeared as a perfect minister of the mysteries of Christ, he later became a martyr, being delivered to wild beasts for His sake, as the account, taking up the story from a little further back, will show.

III. For when Trajan, the Emperor of the Romans, was exalted by his victory against the Scythians, he did not allow his good fortune to stop there. Instead, wishing to advance his prosperity further and to bring many others under the Roman rule, he considered—before all other things—that the war against the Christians (that is to say, against piety) was most excellent and advantageous for him. He thought that in that way he would not only benefit the state, but would also serve his own gods and bring them in as allies against his enemies. Naturally, he brought a harsh persecution against the pious faith and issued decrees throughout all his subjects, so that either everyone should be a partner in his impiety, or those remaining as Christians should be given over to various punishments and cruel deaths. It happened at that time that Trajan was staying in the city of the Antiochians, as he was about to go on an expedition against the Persians and was preparing for war there. There, indeed, the facts regarding the God-bearer Ignatius were reported to him: that he was an ambassador for the Christian way of life and was persuading men to honor Christ as equal to the gods²—and this despite His being condemned by Pilate to the cross and death, as the memoirs <note>original: "hypomnemata" — referring to the Gospels or official records.</note> about Him teach. He also legislates virginity and...

<meta>Following the previous page's collection of likely apocryphal correspondence with the Virgin Mary and St. John, this page transitions to the "Martyrium," a narrative account of the trial and death of Saint Ignatius. While the letters were personal, this text is a formal hagiography intended for the church community. The narrative picks up with Ignatius's background before moving into the Roman persecutions under Emperor Trajan.</meta>

->THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. I. II. III.<-

### THE MARTYRDOM OF THE HOLY AND GLORIOUS PRIEST-MARTYR <term>Hieromartyr: A title for a martyr who was also an ordained priest or bishop.</term> IGNATIUS THE GOD-BEARER <note>original Latin: "Theophorus"</note>.

I. When Trajan took up the scepters of the Roman Empire, Ignatius—who was called "God-bearer" both in name and in reality—was the Bishop of the church of Antioch. For Evodius succeeded the great Peter, and Ignatius succeeded Evodius, becoming an imitator of his character and virtue. Regarding this "God-bearer," they say that when he was a mere boy, while Christ was still dwelling in the world, He placed His pure hands upon him, and looking toward the people, He said:

> “Unless someone humbles himself like this child, he shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven; and whoever receives one such child in my name, receives me;” <note>Referencing Matthew 18:3–5. Ancient tradition suggested Ignatius was the child Jesus held to teach humility.</note>

thus showing what kind of man Ignatius would become as he grew in age, and clearly indicating his future apostolic teaching.

II. This divine Ignatius, therefore, along with Polycarp (who presided over the church at Smyrna), became a disciple of John the Evangelist. When he had come to him alone and had diligently practiced every form of virtue—and especially that which befits a priest—he was afterward chosen as a priest by the common consensus of all the Apostles together, and was created Bishop of Antioch. When he had taken charge of the church, and with much sweat and labor had sown the proclamation of piety <note>original: "praeconium pietatis"</note> within it, and had shown apostolic zeal and doctrine through all things, and had stood out as a perfect minister of the mysteries of Christ, he also later became a martyr, delivered to the beasts for His sake, as the following account will explain in greater detail.

III. For to the Roman Emperor Trajan, who was puffed up by the victory he had gained over the Scythians <note>The Scythians were nomadic people from the region of modern-day Ukraine and southern Russia; Trajan’s victory here solidified his military reputation.</note>, it did not seem enough to let his good fortune rest there. Instead, wishing to extend it further and subject many other nations to the Roman Empire, a war against the Christians—or rather, against piety itself—seemed to him above all else to be the best and most expedient course. For in that way he thought he might benefit the Republic; and also that by worshiping his own gods, he might induce them to bring aid against his enemies. Therefore, he brought a heavy and difficult persecution against the pious faith, and published edicts throughout the entire land that obeyed his empire, commanding that either all should be sharers in his impiety, or those remaining as Christians should be afflicted with various punishments and bitter deaths. It happened that Trajan was then staying in Antioch, as he was about to undertake an expedition against the Persians and was preparing for war there. It was here that he was informed about Ignatius the God-bearer: that he held to the Christian religion and persuaded men to honor Christ as God—even though He had been condemned to the cross and death by Pilate, as his *Acts* <note>Referring to the formal records of the trial or the Gospels.</note> teach—and that he brought a law regarding the preservation of...

# THE MARTYDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. III. IV. V. VI.

...to look down upon wealth and luxury and the other delights of life; and what is most difficult of all, neither to believe in the gods, nor to take any account of the emperors.

IV. When Trajan heard these things, he immediately summoned the holy man, while the Senate was also present with him. "Are you," he said, "the one called the 'God-bearer' <note>original Greek: "Theophoros"</note> who mocks <gloss>1</gloss> our decrees and turns all of Antioch upside down <gloss>2</gloss>, leading everyone away after the Christ you preach, and not even considering the gods worthy of a mere name?" And the divine Ignatius said, "I am." Then the Emperor <gloss>3</gloss> inquired, "And what is a 'God-bearer'?" To which the martyr replied, "He who carries Christ in his soul." <gloss>4</gloss> And the King said, "Are you then the one who carries Christ within himself?" <gloss>5</gloss> "Yes," <gloss>6</gloss> he said, "for it is written: 'I will dwell in them and walk among them.'" <gloss>7</gloss> "But what about us?" <gloss>8</gloss> the Emperor replied. "Do we not seem to you to remember the gods continually and to carry them always in our souls, <gloss>9</gloss> bringing them in as allies against our enemies and doing everything according to their will?" And the divine Ignatius replied, "Alas, King, that you call the idols of the nations 'gods.' For there is one true God, who is the creator of heaven and earth and the sea and all things in them; and there is one Christ Jesus, <gloss>10</gloss> the only-begotten Son of God, whose kingdom shall have no <gloss>11</gloss> end. If you <gloss>12</gloss> yourself would recognize Him, O <gloss>13</gloss> King, your purple robe, your crown, and your royal throne would be far more secure." <gloss>14</gloss>

V. And the King said, "Let us leave most of these words aside. But if you wish," <gloss>1</gloss> he said, "Ignatius, to grant a great favor to my power and to be ranked among my friends from now on, change your mind and sacrifice with us to the gods. And immediately—let everyone here know it—I will appoint you High Priest of the great Jupiter <note>original: "Dios" (Zeus), here identified with the Roman Jupiter</note> and I will name you 'Father of the Senate' <note>A prestigious honorary title, "Pater Senatus," usually reserved for the most respected statesmen.</note>." To these things the God-bearer replied, "To grant favors, O King, is beautiful for everyone, and especially for kings, insofar as they are able to grant greater things in return. <gloss>2</gloss> But these favors should be entirely profitable and helpful to both parties. Those that are able to cause harm, and especially to the soul, lighting the hell-fire that is more intense <gloss>3</gloss> than physical fire, make not only the giver but also the asker himself most wretched. Your promise, O King, is wonderful and generous. But what is it to me to be appointed High Priest of your <gloss>4</gloss> 'great' Jupiter and to be called 'Father of the Senate,' when I am already a priest of Christ and sacrifice to Him a daily offering of praise? Indeed, I am even now hurrying to offer myself entirely as a sacrifice <gloss>5</gloss> and to be planted together with Him in the likeness of His death."

VI. And the King asked, "To whom are you hurrying to sacrifice yourself? To the one crucified under Pontius Pilate?" "Yes," said the great Ignatius, "to the one who crucified sin and cast down the devil, its inventor, and through the cross destroyed all of his power." Again...

# THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. III. IV. V. VI.

...regarding virginity, and the scorning of riches and luxuries and other things which are pleasant in life; and what is the most serious charge of all: that one must not believe there are Gods, and that no regard should be paid to the Emperors.

IV. After Trajan heard these things, he immediately summoned the Saint, while the Senate was also present with him. "Are you," he said, "the one called *Theophorus* <note>Theophorus literally means 'God-bearer' in Greek</note>, who mocks our commands, subverts all of Antioch, and makes everyone followers of the Christ you preach, not even deigning to call the Gods by their names?" But the divine Ignatius said, "I am." The Emperor then inquired, "And what does that name *Theophorus* mean?" The martyr replied, "He who carries Christ in his soul." The Emperor said, "Do you then carry Christ within yourself?" "Certainly," he replied. "For it is written:
> 'I will dwell in them and walk among them.'" <note>Original Latin quoting 2 Corinthians 6:16</note>
"But what of us?" said the Emperor. "Do we not seem to you to remember the Gods constantly, and to carry them always in our soul, and to bring them in to bring help against our enemies, and through them to do everything according to our heart's desire?" The divine Ignatius answered, "Woe is me! Do you, O Emperor, call the idols of the nations 'Gods'? For there is one true God, who is the creator of heaven, earth, the sea, and all that is in them. There is one Christ Jesus, the only-begotten Son of God, whose kingdom shall have no end. If you would acknowledge Him, O Emperor, your purple robe, your crown, and your royal throne would be more secure and far more stable for you."

V. But the Emperor said: "Let us put these many words aside. If you wish, Ignatius, to do something most pleasing to my power, and henceforth be numbered among my friends, change your mind and sacrifice to the Gods with us. I will immediately (let all these men know!) appoint you High Priest of Great Jupiter <note>Latin: *Iovis*</note> and name you 'Father of the Senate.'" To this *Theophorus* replied: "To offer thanks, O Emperor, is a beautiful thing for everyone, but especially for Emperors, because they themselves are able to grant even greater favors in return—but only those favors which are altogether useful and beneficial to both parties. But if they are of such a kind that they can harm, and especially the soul, and kindle a hell <note>original: *gehennam*</note> more vehement than fire, then not only the giver, but also the seeker, becomes most miserable. Your promise, O Emperor, is admirable and generous. But what does it matter to me if I am appointed High Priest of your 'Great Jupiter' and called 'Father of the Senate,' I who am a priest of Christ and sacrifice to Him daily the 'sacrifice of praise,' and even now hasten to sacrifice my whole self and be made like unto the likeness of His death?"

VI. The Emperor then said: "To whom do you hasten to sacrifice yourself? To the one who was driven to the cross by Pontius Pilate?" "Indeed," said the great Ignatius, "to Him who crucified sin, and destroyed the devil, the inventor of sin, and abolished all his power through the cross." Again the Emperor...

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. VI. VII. VIII.

**VI.** The king, therefore, said, "Ignatius, you seem to me to be entirely devoid of right judgment and a sound mind¹ <note>original Greek: φρενὸς (phrenos), referring to the seat of intellect</note>. For you would not have been so clearly deceived by the writings of the Christians, but would have known how great a good² it is to obey royal decrees and to offer sacrifices to the gods along with everyone else." In response to this, the saint, using even greater boldness <note>The Greek term *parrhesia* implies the courageous public speaking of a subordinate to a superior</note>, said: "Even if you consume me with wild beasts, even if you condemn me to the cross, even if you hand me over to the sword³ and fire—things which are within your power—I would never endure offering sacrifice to demons. For I neither fear death, nor do I desire the present things whose enjoyments you, as lords, provide; rather, I long for future things alone, and all my zeal is to pass over to Christ, who died for me."

**VII.** At this, the Senate, wishing to catch the martyr out of their supposed cleverness,¹ said: "Why do you yourself also confess that your God died? And how will this one,² having undergone death—and an accursed death at that—be able to help others? For the gods are immortal and are called so by us." Taking this as a starting point,³ the divine Ignatius—so that he might simultaneously mock their gods and open for them the door to the mystery of the <term>Economy</term> <note>The "Economy" (oikonomia) refers to God's plan for the salvation of humanity through the Incarnation of Christ</note>, and thus lead them by the hand to the faith of the knowledge of Christ—composed his words thus: "My Lord and God, Jesus Christ, first became man for our sake and for our salvation, and he accepted a voluntary cross, death, and burial. However, he rose again on the third day, casting down the power of the enemy, and ascended into the heavens from whence he had come,⁴ raising us up with him from the fall of sin and leading us back into Paradise, from which we had been wickedly cast out, and gifting us with goods⁶ greater than the former ones. But as for whether any of those considered gods among you has displayed such a thing,⁷ no one at all could assert it. For these were merely men, utterly villainous and corrupters, who performed many deeds for the harm and corruption of our life and state. They provided a small bit of the glory and appearance of gods to the more irrational of men in a most irrational way; later, when the veils of deception were drawn back and the stage was removed, they were exposed for what they were. They left this life shamefully and were handed over to an eternal death because of the destruction they brought upon the many. Indeed, Zeus—the first and greatest of your gods⁸—is buried in Crete; Asclepius was struck by a lightning bolt; the tomb of Aphrodite⁹ is shown in Paphos; and Hercules was consumed by fire. Truly, the worth of their deeds is of such a kind, or rather, much worse.¹⁰"

**VIII.** When these words had been spoken by Ignatius, the king, together with the Senate, feared lest, if the discussion¹ were extended further, the religion of the Greeks might be shaken and look toward disbelief² or even mockery, while the cause of piety would bloom and the cloud of error that darkened it would be removed.⁴ They [ordered] him to be put under bonds and guard...

<meta>This page continues the trial of Ignatius of Antioch before the Roman Emperor Trajan. ### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. VI. VII. VIII.

The Emperor said: "Ignatius, you seem to me to be entirely lacking in right judgment and a sound mind. For you would not have been so clearly deceived by the writings of the Christians if you had fully understood how great a benefit it is to obey the Imperial Edicts and to offer sacrifices to the gods along with everyone else." At this, the Saint, using even greater freedom of speech <note>original: *libertate dicendi*, often translating the Greek *parrhesia*, a bold and frank style of speech used before authorities</note>, replied: "Even if you consume me with wild beasts, even if you condemn me to the cross, though you hand me over to the sword and fire—things which are within your power—I will never endure offering a sacrifice to demons. For I neither fear death nor do I desire the present things which are in your power to provide for enjoyment; instead, I long only for the things of the future, and I apply all my effort to pass over to Christ, who died for me."

**VII.** Because of these words, the Senate, wishing to challenge the martyr out of their own cleverness, said: "Why do you also confess that your God is dead? How indeed can one who underwent death—and an accursed death at that—be able to help others? Our gods, however, are both immortal and are called so by us." Taking this as an opportunity both to mock their gods and to open for them the door to the mystery of the <term>Economy</term> <note>original: *dispensatione*, translating the Greek *oikonomia*, referring to God’s plan for the Incarnation and salvation of humanity</note> concerning the flesh he assumed, and thus to lead them to the knowledge of the faith of Christ, the divine Ignatius spoke these words: "My Lord and God Jesus Christ first became man for our sake and for our salvation; he voluntarily underwent the cross, death, and burial. But then he rose again on the third day, having cast down and prostrated the power of the enemy, and ascended into the heavens from whence he had come. He causes us to rise at the same time from the fall of sin and leads us again into paradise, from which we had been wickedly cast out, granting us greater blessings than those that came before. No man could ever assert that any of those whom you count as gods has done such a thing. For since those 'gods' were wicked and destructive men who did much to damage and corrupt our life and state, they offered a very base opinion and appearance of gods to men who are somewhat lacking in reason. Later, when the veils of deception were drawn back and the stage-play was removed, those who they really were were found out—namely, men who departed from life disgracefully and were handed over to an 'immortal death' because of the destruction of so many people. Certainly Jupiter, who is your first and greatest of gods, is buried in Crete; Aesculapius <note>The god of medicine</note> was struck by a lightning bolt. The tomb of Venus is shown at Paphos, and Hercules was consumed by fire. For their affairs and their lives truly deserved such ends, or indeed, much worse."

**VIII.** When these things had been said by Ignatius, the Emperor, together with the Senate, feared that if his speech became any longer, the affairs of the pagans would be undermined—either by no longer being believed or by being held up to ridicule—while the true religion would flourish and the cloud of error that pours darkness upon it would be removed. He therefore threw Ignatius into chains and placed him in the most secure custody.
