<meta>This page continues the narrative of the trial of Ignatius of Antioch before Emperor Trajan. Following his bold confession of faith, the Emperor now deliberates on the manner of his execution, deciding to send him to Rome to face the wild beasts in the arena, a journey that begins with a significant meeting in Smyrna.</meta>

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. VIII. IX. X.

The Emperor established his decision with the utmost certainty. He himself spent the entire night considering how he might worthily punish Ignatius, and by what means he might remove him from the present life. He decided to hand him over as food for wild beasts <note>original: *θηρίοις ἔγνω παραδοῦναι βοράν*</note>, so that the saint might perish by being torn apart by them. Indeed, this most heavy form of death was the one decided upon by the King. In the morning, he shared this plan with the Senate, and they themselves praised his judgment. However, they advised that the execution should not take place in Antioch, "lest," they said, "we make Ignatius even more beloved and more famous among his fellow citizens if he should end his life in such a martyr’s death." Therefore, they argued that it was fitting for him to be led away as a prisoner to Rome and there be handed over to the beasts. For in this way, he would suffer a more difficult punishment due to the length of the journey, and at the same time, being unknown to the Romans, he would appear to be killed as just one of the common criminals, and would not be considered worthy of even a brief memory among them afterwards.

**IX.** This plan was therefore pleasing, and the sentence against him was immediately carried out. The King summoned him from the prison and once more applied this final test to him. At first, he was full of many promises of good things, trying to coax and stroke the athlete of Christ; but afterwards, he tried to terrify him even more with threats. But when he saw that Ignatius neither yielded to the promises nor cowered at the threats, he completely despaired of changing his mind and began to carry out what he had announced. He ordered heavier chains than before to be placed upon him and handed him over to a military squad. He sent him off to Rome, giving instructions that when the day of the public festival arrived for the citizens, he should be handed over to the beasts for the common entertainment of the theater—so that, according to the divine Paul, he might become "a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men" <note>This is a reference to 1 Corinthians 4:9</note>.

**X.** The martyr, having received that final sentence, thanked God with a great cry as was fitting, and with as much pleasure and brightness as possible, he put on his chains. Then the King set out against the Persians with the army under him. But the <term>God-bearer</term> <note>original: *theophoros*, a title Ignatius used for himself, meaning one who carries God within</note>, having first prayed for the church and entrusted his flock with tears to God, followed the soldiers as a prisoner. From there, without delay, without losing heart, and without showing any sign of a gloomy countenance at his suffering, but with a ready step, he reached Seleucia and was placed on a ship by the soldiers, and with them he put in at Smyrna. There he embraced the divine Polycarp, the companion of the Apostles, who presided over the church in Smyrna; the account mentioned earlier showed that Polycarp had been a fellow-disciple with Ignatius. He embraced him, taking pride and rejoicing in his chains. For what else could make him more proud than to be seen suffering for a Master who had loved him so much? Then, after giving the proper greetings to the other bishops, priests, and deacons—since many had gathered from the churches of Asia—

<meta>This page continues the narrative of the trial of Ignatius of Antioch before Emperor Trajan. Having failed to persuade Ignatius to renounce his faith, the Emperor and the Senate now finalize the plan for his execution, intending to minimize his influence by sending him to the heart of the Empire.</meta>

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. VIII. IX. X.

He himself, however, having thought throughout the entire night how he might punish him as he deserved and by what means he might remove him from this present life, decided to hand him over to be devoured by wild beasts, so that the Saint might perish by being torn apart by them. For this mode of death seemed to the Emperor to be by far the most severe. When he had communicated this matter to the Senate in the morning, they also praised his decision; but they advised that this throwing to the beasts should not take place in Antioch. "Lest," they said, "we make Ignatius even more beloved and glorious among his own citizens if he departs from life through the end of martyrdom <note>The Senate feared that a local execution would create a "cult of the martyr" and inspire the local Christian community.</note>." For this reason, they said it was necessary for him to be led away to Rome in chains and there be handed over to the beasts. For in this way, he would undergo a more grievous punishment due to the length of the journey, and at the same time, since the Romans would not know who he was, he would appear to have been killed as just one of the common criminals, and there would not be even the slightest memory of him among them afterwards.

**IX.** When this plan had been agreed upon and the sentence against him had been passed immediately, the Emperor brought him out of custody again, making this his final test. And at first, indeed, he tried to soften and soothe the <term>athlete</term> <note>Early Christian writers often used the term "athlete" to describe martyrs, viewing their suffering as a spiritual contest or "agon."</note> with many promises of good things; then again, he tried to terrify him further with threats. But after he saw that he neither yielded to promises nor feared threats, despairing entirely that he would change, he carried out the things that had been decreed. And when he had ordered heavier chains than before to be placed on him, he handed him over to a military cohort and sent him to Rome, commanding that when the festival day of public celebration and solemn games arrived for the citizens, he should be handed over to the beasts for the common entertainment of the theater, so that, fittingly to what the divine Paul said, he too might become "a spectacle to the world, and to angels, and to men." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 4:9.</note>

**X.** Therefore, when the Martyr had received that final sentence and had given thanks to God with a great shout, as was fitting, he placed the chains upon himself with great pleasure and joy. And the Emperor indeed set out against the Persians with his army. But the <term>Theophorus</term> <note>Theophorus (Greek: Θεοφόρος) means "God-bearer." This was Ignatius's chosen title.</note>, after he had first prayed well for the church and commended his flock to God with tears, followed the soldiers in his bonds. Then, not hesitating, not losing heart, and not showing that he was suffering anything difficult at all, he came with swift feet to Seleucia and was put on a ship by the soldiers and arrived with them at Smyrna. Here he greeted the divine apostle Polycarp, who we have already said and declared above had presided over the church of Smyrna, since he had been a fellow-disciple of Ignatius. He greeted him, therefore, boasting and rejoicing in his chains. For what could be a greater ornament to him than to be seen suffering for the Lord, who had so loved him? Then, after he had returned the proper greetings to the remaining Bishops, Presbyters, and Deacons (since many were hurrying together from the churches and cities of Asia...)

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. X. XI. XII. XIII. XIV.

...of the churches and the<gloss>9</gloss> cities, both to see that sight and to enjoy the beautiful stream flowing from his tongue. He himself, exhorting them with fitting words, requested them all to pray for him, so that by means of the wild beasts he might sooner depart <note>original: *analysai*, a term often used for death as a release or a departure on a journey</note> toward the One he desired and appear before His divine face.

XI. But seeing them in such a state of great distress, hanging as it were upon his very soul and considering his departure and death an unbearable loss, and fearing also for the believers in Rome—lest they, being similarly disposed, would not endure to see him given over to the beasts, but might lay hands on those entrusted with his delivery to oppose them, and thus close the door of martyrdom that had been opened to him—he decided to write to them. He did this so that they too might pray for him, that his course of struggle <gloss>1</gloss> <note>The Greek *athlēsis* refers to the contest of an athlete, a favorite metaphor for the suffering of martyrs</note> might not be hindered, but that through the beasts, as has been said, he might sooner depart to his beloved Lord. It is worthwhile to record that very letter, which reads word for word as follows:

XII. Ignatius, also called <term>Theophorus</term> <note>Meaning "God-bearer." It was a title Ignatius used to signify his close union with Christ</note>, bishop of the holy church of God in Antioch: To the church that has found mercy<gloss>1</gloss> in the majesty of the Most High Father and the Lord<gloss>2</gloss> Jesus Christ His only Son; the church beloved and enlightened by the<gloss>3</gloss> will of Him who willed all things that exist according to the love of Jesus Christ our God; which also presides in the place of the region of the Romans; which I also greet in the name of Jesus Christ, joined to His every commandment in both flesh and spirit, filled with the grace of God: Greeting in Christ Jesus our God.

Since, through prayer to God, I have succeeded in seeing your faces—which I so longed to behold—now, as a prisoner in Christ Jesus, I hope to greet you,<gloss>4</gloss> if indeed it be the will of God that I be deemed worthy to continue so to the end. For the beginning is well-ordered, if only I may obtain grace to receive my lot without hindrance. For I fear your love, lest it should do me wrong. For it is easy for you to do what you will; but for me, it is difficult to attain to God, if you should spare me.

XIII. For I do not wish you to be men-pleasers, but to please God, as indeed you do please Him. For I shall never again have such an opportunity to attain to God, nor shall you [have a better work to do]. If therefore<gloss>1</gloss> you remain silent regarding me, I shall belong to God; but if you love my flesh, I shall again be running <note>The martyr views his life as a race; to be saved from death would mean he has to continue "running" in the physical world rather than reaching the finish line of God’s presence</note>. Rather, grant me nothing more than to be poured out as a libation to God while an altar is still prepared, so that, becoming a choir in love, you may sing to the Father in Christ Jesus, because God has deemed the bishop of Syria worthy to be found in the West, having summoned him from the East. It is good to set from the world unto God, that I may rise<gloss>3</gloss> in Him.

XIV. You have never envied anyone; you have taught others. And I desire that those things which you enjoin in your teaching may be firm. Only [pray] for me

<meta>This page continues the text of the letter from Ignatius to the Roman Christians. Having previously greeted them, he now moves into the core of his plea: that they should not interfere with his impending execution, which he views as his final transition into true discipleship and union with Christ.</meta>

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. 14. 15. 16. 17.

...ask that power be given to me from God, so that I may not only be called a Christian, but also be found to be one and be able to be so named. For then I shall be seen to be faithful, when I am no longer visible to the world. <note>original: κόσμῳ (kosmō). Ignatius suggests that his true "visibility" as a believer begins when he is removed from the physical world.</note> For nothing that is visible is eternal; for the things that are seen are temporary, but the things that are not seen are eternal. <note>A reference to 2 Corinthians 4:18.</note>

XV. I am writing to all the churches and I charge everyone that I die willingly for God, provided that you do not hinder me. I beseech you, do not become an "untimely kindness" to me. <note>He fears their legal or social influence might get his death sentence overturned.</note> Allow me to be food for the wild beasts, through whom it is possible to attain God. I am God's wheat, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found to be the pure bread of Christ. Rather, coax the wild beasts so that they may become my tomb, and leave nothing of my body behind, so that once I have fallen asleep, I may not be a burden to anyone. Then I shall be a true disciple of Christ, when the world no longer even sees my body. Entreat Christ for me, that through these instruments <note>the beasts</note> I may be found a pure sacrifice. I do not command you as Peter and Paul did. They were apostles; I am a condemned man. They were free; but I am a slave until now. But if I suffer, I shall be a freedman of Jesus Christ, and I shall rise again free in Him. Now, in my bonds, I am learning to desire nothing worldly or vain.

XVI. From Syria even unto Rome, I fight with wild beasts <note>original: θηριομαχῶν (thēriomachōn). A term for gladiatorial combat with animals, used here metaphorically for his journey under guard.</note> by land and sea, by night and day, bound to ten leopards—that is, a company of soldiers—who grow worse even when they are treated well. But in their mistreatment, I am more fully becoming a disciple. May I enjoy the wild beasts prepared for me; and I pray that they may be found ready for me. I will even coax them to devour me quickly, unlike some whom they were too afraid to touch. And even if they are unwilling, I will compel them. Forgive me; I know what is best for me. Now I begin to be a disciple, that I may attain Jesus Christ. Let fire and cross, packs of wild beasts, cuttings, tearings, scatterings of bones, mangling of limbs, grinding of the whole body, and the evil punishments of the devil come upon me, only let me attain Jesus Christ.

XVII. Nothing of the pleasures of the world nor the kingdoms of this age shall benefit me. It is better for me to die in Christ Jesus than to reign over the ends of the earth. For what does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but loses his soul? <note>A reference to Matthew 16:26.</note> I seek Him who died for us. Forgive me, brothers; do not hinder me from living; <note>Ignatius views his physical death as the beginning of "living" in the true sense.</note> do not wish for me to die. Let me receive the pure light. When I have arrived there, I shall be a man of God. Allow me to be an imitator of the passion of my God. If anyone has Him within himself, let him understand what I desire, and let him sympathize with me, knowing what constrains me.

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. XVIII. XIX. XX. XXI. XXII.

**XVIII.** The ruler of this age <note>The "ruler" (archon) refers to Satan or the demonic forces Ignatius believes are trying to prevent his martyrdom.</note> wants to seize me and corrupt my mind which is set toward my God. Let no one, therefore, who is present there help him; rather, be on my side—that is, on the side of God. Do not speak of Jesus Christ while you still desire the world. Let no envy dwell among you; even if I myself, when I arrive, should plead with you, do not be persuaded by me. Instead, be persuaded by these things I am writing to you now. For I write to you while living, yet longing to die. My Love has been crucified, <note>original: "ho emos eros estaurōtai." This famous phrase could mean his earthly passions are dead, or it could be a title for Christ himself: "My Beloved is crucified."</note> and there is no fire of material longing within me; rather, there is "living water" <note>A reference to the Gospel of John 4:10.</note> speaking within me, saying from deep inside: "Come to the Father." I find no pleasure in the food of corruption, nor in the pleasures of this life. I desire the Bread of God, the heavenly bread, the bread of life, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who was born in later times of the seed of David and Abraham; and I desire the drink of God, his blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.

**XIX.** I no longer desire to live according to human standards; and this shall be so, if you desire it. Desire it, therefore, so that you yourselves may be desired by God. I ask you with these few words: believe me. Jesus Christ will make these things clear to you—He is the mouth that cannot lie, through whom the Father has spoken truly. Pray for me, that I may succeed. I have written to you not according to the flesh, but according to the mind of God, regarding what I must suffer.

**XX.** Remember in your prayer the church in Syria, which now has God for its shepherd in my place. Jesus Christ alone shall be its overseer, <note>original: "episkopēsei" (act as bishop/overseer).</note> along with your love. My spirit greets you, as does the love of the churches that received me in the name of Jesus Christ, and not merely as a traveler. For even those churches that did not lie on my physical route went before me from city to city to meet me.

**XXI.** I am writing these things to you from Smyrna by the hand of the Ephesians, who are most worthy of blessing. Crocus—a name very dear to me—is also here with me, along with many others who came with me from Syria for the glory of God. I have written this to you on the ninth day before the Kalends of September. <note>August 24th.</note> Farewell until the end, beloved ones, in the patient endurance of Jesus Christ. Amen.

**XXII.** These then were the contents of the letter. But shortly thereafter, he was led away from Smyrna by the soldiers and, having reached Troas and Neapolis, he passed through Philippi and Macedonia on foot, visiting the churches along the way, teaching in them, exhorting them, and conversing with them. He strengthened the simpler brothers and prepared everyone to be watchful and sober. Having reached Epirus at Epidamnus, and having sailed across the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian seas, he landed at Puteoli <note>Modern-day Pozzuoli, near Naples.</note> in Rome. After being hosted by the faithful there together with the soldiers, and sharing the greeting in the Lord with them, he reached Rome and appeared before the prefect of the city. He, upon seeing the "God-bearer" <note>original: "theophoron," a title Ignatius used for himself.</note> and receiving the imperial orders—

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. XVIII. XIX. XX. XXI. XXII.

**XVIII.** The Prince of this world <note>The "Prince" or "Ruler" (archon) refers to Satan, whom Ignatius believes is trying to distract him from his goal of martyrdom.</note> wants to snatch me away and corrupt my resolve toward God. Let no one, therefore, among those present there, offer him help; rather, be on my side—that is, on the side of God. Do not speak of Jesus Christ while you still desire the world. Let no envy dwell among you; even if I myself, when I arrive, should plead with you, do not obey me; instead, obey these things I am writing to you now. For I write to you while living, yet longing to die. My Love has been crucified, <note>Latin: "Meus amor est cruci affixus." This famous phrase likely refers to Christ as his "Love" or "Beloved," though some interpret it as his earthly passions being dead.</note> and there is no fire of material longing within me; rather, there is "living water" <note>A reference to the Gospel of John, symbolizing the Holy Spirit.</note> speaking within me, saying from deep inside: "Come to the Father." I find no pleasure in the food of corruption, nor in the delights of this life. I desire the Bread of God, the heavenly bread, the bread of life, which is the flesh of Jesus Christ, the Son of God—who was born in later times of the seed of David and Abraham; and I desire the drink of God, his blood, which is incorruptible love and eternal life.

**XIX.** I no longer wish to live according to human standards; and this shall be so, if you desire it. Therefore, desire it, so that God may also desire you. I ask this of you in these few words; believe me. Jesus Christ will reveal these things to you—He is the mouth that cannot lie, through which I speak the truth. Pray for me, that I may attain my goal. I have written to you not according to human desires, but according to the mind of God, regarding whether I shall suffer.

**XX.** Remember in your prayers the church in Syria, which now has God as its shepherd instead of me. Jesus Christ alone will watch over it, acting as its Bishop, along with your love. My spirit greets you, as does the love of the churches that received me in the name of Jesus Christ, and not merely as a traveler. For even those churches that did not lie on my physical path met me from city to city to escort me.

**XXI.** I have written these things to you from Smyrna by the hand of the Ephesians, who are worthily blessed. Also with me, among many others, is Crocus—a name very dear to me—and those who came with me from Syria for the glory of God. I wrote this to you on the ninth day before the Kalends of September <note>August 24th.</note>. Farewell forever, beloved, in the endurance of Jesus Christ. Amen.

**XXII.** So ends the letter. A short time later, he was taken from Smyrna by the soldiers. When he had reached Troas and Neapolis, he crossed on foot through Philippi and Macedonia, visiting the churches along the way, teaching in them, exhorting them, and holding discussions. He strengthened the simpler and weaker brothers and ensured that everyone remained watchful and sober. When he had reached Epidamnus in Epirus and crossed the Adriatic and Tyrrhenian seas, he landed at Puteoli <note>A major Roman port near modern-day Naples.</note> in Italy. There he was welcomed as a guest, along with the soldiers, by the faithful who lived there. After delivering greetings in the Lord there as well, he came to Rome and was presented before the Prefect of the City. The Prefect, looking upon "Theophorus" <note>Ignatius's second name, meaning "God-bearer."</note> and having received the Emperor's letters, when—

### THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. XXII. XXIII. XXIV. XXV. XXVI.

...when the opportune day arrived, as it was a feast day and a grand celebration for the Roman people, he <note>The Roman official in charge.</note> led him into the middle of the theater, just as that wicked Edict of the Emperor <note>Referring to Emperor Trajan.</note> commanded.

XXIII. When the entire city was seated in the theater with burning spirits and eyes longing for the spectacle—since rumor had already announced everywhere that the Bishop of Syria was to fight with wild beasts on this day—he turned to the people with a clearly noble and intrepid soul, as one who boasted and took great pleasure in this apparent shame for Christ's sake:

> "Men of Rome," he said, "and spectators of this present contest, these things are not happening to me because of any crime, nor to pay the penalty for wicked deeds, but so that I may attain to God, by whose desire I am held and whom I insatiably long for. For I am His wheat and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may become pure bread for Him."

He said these things, and the lions, having been let loose, immediately tore him apart and devoured him, refraining only from his harder bones. Thus, the man's prayers were truly fulfilled, so that the beasts became a tomb for him and nothing of his body remained; for God valued the fulfillment of His servant's prayers and love more than ensuring he was not touched by the lions, so that He might give glory to His own name.

XXIV. After these things occurred and reached their end, the faithful who were in Rome—to whom Ignatius the <term>Theophorus</term> <note>God-bearer; a title Ignatius used to signify one who carries God within.</note> had written while still alive—gathered when the theater was dismissed. They took up the bones with eager hands and, having arranged them honorably and reverently, they laid them in a prominent place outside the City, it being then the twentieth day of the month of December. These were later carried back to the martyr's homeland, Antioch; and the cities located between the two great cities received a double blessing: first when the martyr was led bound from Antioch to Rome, and now when he was brought back from there with such noble trophies, like bees flying around a honeycomb.

XXV. And it is said that after the man’s completion through martyrdom, while the faithful in Rome were mourning their loss and receiving no consolation for their grief, and while they were occupied with funeral hymns and vigils, he appeared to them in dreams. He seemed to embrace them—those who had previously shown themselves worthy of his company—and this made their mourning easier and lighter, calming the intensity of their sorrow. Others, again, said they saw him dripping with sweat, as if he had just caught his breath after the labors of his great struggle, and that he was praying for the safety of the city and all the faithful.

XXVI. This was the end of the <term>Theophorus</term>; these were his struggles; these were his conspicuous loves for Christ. And Irenaeus of Lyons <note>A prominent early Church Father and theologian.</note> bears witness—

-># THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. XXVI, XXVII.<-

And Irenaeus, the Bishop of Lyons <note>original: "Λουγδάνων". Irenaeus (c. 130–202 AD) was a prominent early Christian theologian and bishop.</note>, a man worthy of mention, held the memory of the <term>Theophorus</term> <note>God-bearer; Ignatius's title.</note> in high regard. Furthermore, Polycarp, who presided over the church at Smyrna <note>A city in modern-day Turkey.</note> and who had been a fellow disciple with him under John the Evangelist and the Theologian <note>John the Apostle; "Theologian" is a traditional title for him in the Eastern tradition.</note>, also greeted him while he was being led as a prisoner from Antioch to Rome, as we have already learned. Polycarp wrote something like this in his own letters: "I urge you, brothers, to be obedient and to practice all endurance, which you saw with your own eyes, not only in the blessed Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus, but also in many others from among you, and in Paul himself and the other apostles. For all these did not run in vain, nor did they labor in vain, but in faith and righteousness in Christ Jesus; therefore, they are now in their deserved place with the Lord, with whom they also suffered. For they did not love this present world, but rather Christ, who died and rose again for us." Thus did the divine Ignatius dwell in those holy souls; and though he desired the bellies of wild beasts to be his tomb, he lives even more in the souls of God-loving men.

---

### XXVII.

Later, when Emperor Trajan learned the details concerning this <term>Theophorus</term> Ignatius—how nobly he had completed the struggle of martyrdom and how, according to his own wish, he had become the food of wild beasts—and having heard many things about the Christians throughout the region, he realized they did nothing illegal or unholy against the laws. Instead, they rose at dawn to worship Christ as the Son of God, and they practiced all self-control in their food and drink, touching nothing that the law forbids. Upon hearing these things, it is said that he felt a sense of regret for what had already occurred and issued a decree. This decree stated that the Christian people should be sought out and made known everywhere, but once found, they should not be put to death, though they were not to be entrusted with public offices or the administration of public affairs. Thus, not only the life of Ignatius, but now even his death, became the source of many good things: a boast of faith in Christ, an increase in piety, an encouragement toward labors for God's sake, a contempt for this temporary life, self-control against harmful things, and a care for purity of life—through the grace and love for mankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father and the holy and life-giving Spirit, now and forever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen.

-># THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. IGNATIUS. XXVI. XXVII.<-

...Bishop of Lyons <note>The text reads "dunensis," a shorthand for Lugdunensis (Lyons, France).</note>, a man of great importance, who makes frequent mention of the **Theophorus** <note>The "God-bearer," Ignatius’s title.</note>. Furthermore, Polycarp, the Overseer of the church of Smyrna, who frequently visited John the Evangelist and Theologian alongside Ignatius, and who—as we have already seen—greeted him while he was being led as a prisoner from Antioch to Rome, writes these words somewhere in his epistles:

> "I urge you, brothers, to obey and to practice all endurance, which you saw with your own eyes not only in the blessed Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus, but also in many others from among you, and in Paul himself and those who believed with him. For all these did not run in vain, nor did they labor in vain, but in faith and righteousness, which is in Christ Jesus. For this reason, they are now in the place that is due to them alongside the Lord, with whom they also suffered. For they did not love this present age, but Christ, who died and rose again for us."

Thus the divine Ignatius was established in their holy souls; and though he had desired to make the bellies of wild beasts his tomb, he dwells even more in the souls of pious men.

### XXVII.

When the Emperor Trajan later learned about the deeds of this **Theophorus** Ignatius, and how bravely he had endured the struggle of martyrdom—and that he had been devoured by beasts just as the Emperor himself had decreed—and when he also heard many things about the Christians throughout the regions, specifically that they did nothing against the laws and committed no impious acts, but rather rose at dawn to worship Christ as the Son of God, and practiced total abstinence in their food and drink, touching nothing forbidden by the law; when, I say, he heard these things, he was moved by regret for what had been done. He is then said to have issued a Decree: that the Christian people should indeed be sought out and made known to all, but those who were found should not be put to death; however, they were not to hold magistracies nor undertake any administration of the Republic. Thus, not only the life of Ignatius, but now his death as well, became a reconciler of many good things, a glorification of the faith which is in Christ, a proof of piety, an exhortation to divine labors, and a contempt for this temporary life, as well as a source of restraint from harmful things and a zeal for a life of purity, by the grace and kindness of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom be glory to the Father and to the holy and life-giving Spirit, now and forever, and for ages of ages. Amen.

<meta>This page begins a new account of the martyrdom of Ignatius of Antioch, labeled as an "unpublished" (ined.) version. While the previous page concluded a narrative involving the testimony of Polycarp and Irenaeus, this section restarts the history from the beginning of Ignatius's journey under the reign of the Emperor Trajan.</meta>

<header>THE MARTYRDOM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. I. II.</header>

# THE MARTYRIUM OF THE HOLY IGNATIUS, BISHOP OF ANTIOCH.

I. In the fifth year of the reign of Trajan Caesar, and in the second year of the consulship of Atticus, Suburanus, and Marcellus <note>This dating traditionally places the events around 107–108 AD.</note>, Ignatius—the second bishop of the Church of God in Antioch after the Apostles, having succeeded Evodius—was sent from Syria to the city of the Romans to bear witness to Christ, under a most diligent guard-watch. Those guarding him were ten of Trajan’s "protectors" <note>original: "προτίκτορες" (protectores); these were elite imperial guards.</note>, men who were savage and beastly in their character. They led the blessed man as a prisoner through Asia; from there, they pressed the holy man on toward Thrace and Rhegium by land and sea, day and night. This was despite the fact that in every city he was treated with kindness by the brothers <note>The local Christian communities.</note>; yet nothing could soften the rages of these savage men. Instead, they tormented the saint with disorderly and shameless eyes, just as he himself writes somewhere in a letter: "From Syria even unto Rome I fight with wild beasts <note>original: "θηριομαχῶ"</note> by land and sea, being led bound to ten leopards, which is a company of soldiers; and these, even when treated well, only become worse." <note>This is a famous quote from Ignatius’s *Epistle to the Romans*, chapter 5.</note> Having set out from Rhegium, they arrived in Rome.

II. And they announced his arrival to the Emperor Trajan. The Emperor ordered him to be brought in while the Senate was also present. And he said to him: "Are you that Ignatius who has turned the city of the Antiochians upside down? For it has reached my ears that you have converted all of Syria from Hellenism <note>The traditional Greek polytheistic religion.</note> to Christianity." Ignatius said: "O King, I wish I were able to convert even you from the worship of idols and bring you to the God of all things, to establish you as a friend of Christ and make your empire even stronger." Trajan said: "If you wish to do me a favor and be numbered among my friends, change your mind and sacrifice to the gods; then you shall be the High Priest of the Great Zeus, and you shall reign with me." Ignatius said: "One must grant favors, O King, that do not harm the soul, not those that lead away into eternal punishment. As for the promises you have pledged to give me, I judge them to be worth nothing; for I do not worship gods whom I do not know, nor do I understand who this 'Zeus' is, nor do I desire a worldly kingdom. For what benefit will I gain, if I win the whole world but lose my own soul?" <note>A reference to Matthew 16:26.</note> Trajan said: "You seem to me to be lacking in sensible judgment; that is why you treat my promises with such contempt. Therefore, if you provoke me to anger, I will punish you with every kind of torture, not only as a disobedient man but as one who is ungrateful, who does not obey the sacred Senate and does not sacrifice." Ignatius said: "Do what seems good to you, O King, for I will not sacrifice. For neither fire, nor the cross, nor the fury of wild beasts, nor the cutting off of limbs shall make me depart from the living God. For I do not love this present age, but rather Christ, who died and rose again for me." The Senate said: "We know that the gods are immortal; how then did you say, Ignatius, that Christ died?"

<meta>This page continues the "unpublished" account of the martyrdom of St. Ignatius of Antioch. In the previous section, Ignatius was brought to Rome under heavy guard and presented before the Emperor Trajan. This page captures their high-stakes theological debate and the beginning of Ignatius's physical torments.</meta>

<header>MARTYRIUM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. II.</header>

<columns>2</columns>

Ignatius said: "Even if my Lord died, He died by a divine plan <note>original: "δι’ οἰκονομίαν" (di’ oikonomian); this refers to the 'economy' or strategic plan of salvation.</note>, yet after three days He rose again. But your gods died as mortals and did not rise as gods. For instance, Zeus is buried in Crete; Asclepius was struck by a thunderbolt and lies in Cythēne <note>The manuscript reads "Cythēne," but likely refers to Mt. Cithaeron.</note>; Aphrodite is buried in Paphos with Cinyras; and Heracles was consumed by fire. Your gods were deserving of such punishments because they were undisciplined and evildoers, the corrupters of humanity. But our Lord was put to death in the flesh by wicked men who could not endure His rebukes, even though He offered every kind of blessing and was met with ingratitude by those without faith."

Trajan said: "I advise you to turn away from death and run toward life."

Ignatius said: "Your advice is good, O King; for I flee from eternal death and take refuge in eternal life."

Trajan said: "And how many deaths are there?"

Ignatius said: "Two: one is temporary, the other is eternal. Likewise, there are two lives: one is short-lived, the other is eternal."

Trajan said: "Sacrifice to the gods and escape these punishments; for you are surely not better than the Senate."

Ignatius said: "To which gods do you wish me to sacrifice? To the one who was imprisoned in a jar for thirteen months because of his adultery? <note>This likely refers to a myth involving Ares, though Ignatius attributes such scandals to the pagan pantheon generally.</note> Or to the one whose feet were bound in bronze? Or to the one who failed at prophecy and was defeated by a woman? Or to the androgynous one torn apart by Titans? Or to those who built the walls for the Sun but were cheated of their wages? Or to those goddesses who imitate the deeds of men and forget the works of women? I am ashamed even to speak of gods who are sorcerers, corrupters of children, and adulterers who—as you say—transform themselves into eagles, bulls, gold, swans, and dragons. They do this not for any good purpose, but to destroy the marriages of others. Such beings should be loathed, not worshipped! And yet your wives pray to these gods to protect their own chastity!"

Trajan said: "I am the one to blame for your blasphemy against the gods, because I have not yet tortured you."

Ignatius said: "I told you long ago that I am ready for every torture and every kind of death, because I hasten toward the immortal God."

Trajan said: "If you do not sacrifice, you will regret it. Therefore, spare yourself before you suffer."

Ignatius said: "If I were not sparing myself <note>Ignatius implies that "sparing himself" means saving his soul for eternity rather than saving his body for a moment.</note>, I would be doing exactly what you command."

Trajan said: "Torture his back with lead-tipped whips <note>original: "μολυβδίσιν" (molybdīsin); these were whips weighted with lead balls to increase the impact.</note>."

Ignatius said: "O King, you have only increased my longing for God."

Trajan said: "Lacerate his sides with iron claws and rub them with salt."

Ignatius said: "My whole mind is stretched upward toward God, and I take no account of what I suffer."

Trajan said: "Sacrifice to the gods!"

Ignatius said: "Perhaps you are commanding me to sacrifice to the gods of the Egyptians—to an ox, to the pride of a goat <note>Possibly a reference to the cult of Mendes.</note>, to an ape, to a venomous asp, to a dog-headed lion, or a crocodile? Or to the Persian fire, or the water of the sea, or to Pluto who dwells beneath the earth, or to Hermes the thief?"

Trajan said: "I told you: sacrifice! Speaking these things will benefit you nothing."

Ignatius said: "I told you: I will not sacrifice, nor do I depart from the one and only God, who made the heaven and the earth and the sea and all things in them..."

<meta>This page continues the "unpublished" account of the martyrdom of St. Ignatius of Antioch. Previously, Ignatius stood before the Emperor Trajan and argued that the pagan gods were mere mortals or evildoers. This page transitions from a verbal debate into physical torture, illustrating the common hagiographic trope where the martyr remains defiant despite increasing agony.</meta>

<page-num>370</page-num>
<header>MARTYRIUM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. II. III.</header>

among them, [the power] of the God of spirits, <note original: "τοῦ θεοῦ τῶν πνευμάτων">A biblical title for God, emphasizing His sovereignty over both the physical and spiritual realms.</note> the King of all things sensible and intelligible, who has authority over all flesh.

Trajan said: "What prevents you from worshipping him—if indeed he exists as a god—and also these gods whom we all commonly acknowledge?"

Ignatius said: "Natural discernment, when it is pure, does not compare falsehood with truth, darkness with light, or bitter with sweet. For a 'woe' hangs over those who do not distinguish these things. For what agreement has Christ with Belial? <note original: "Βελίαρ">A Hebrew name for the devil or a personification of worthlessness, used here in a quote from 2 Corinthians 6:14-16.</note> Or what part has a believer with unbelievers? And what agreement has the temple of God with idols?"

Trajan said: "Spread out his hands and fill them with fire."

Ignatius said: "Neither burning fire, nor the teeth of beasts, nor the scattering of bones, nor the mangling of limbs, nor the grinding of the whole body, nor the punishments of the devil shall move me from the love of God." <note>This specific list of tortures is famous in the history of the early church; it appears in the genuine letters written by Ignatius while he was traveling to his death.</note>

Trajan said: "Dip papyrus in oil, light it, and burn his sides."

Ignatius said: "You seem to me, O King, to be ignorant that God is within me, who supplies me with power and makes my soul firm; for otherwise I would not be able to bear your tortures."

Trajan said: "Perhaps you are made of iron and have become hardened; for surely you would have yielded by now, being pained by the bruises, to sacrifice to the gods."

Ignatius said: "It is not because I do not feel the tortures, O King, that I bear and endure these things, but because my devotion to God, through the hope of good things, lightens my pains; for neither burning fire nor flooding water will ever be able to quench the love for God."

Trajan said: "Bring fire and spread the coals on the ground, and stand Ignatius upon them, so that he may be persuaded to yield and sacrifice to the gods."

Ignatius said: "The burning quality of your fire—though it is only temporary—brings me to a remembrance of that fire which is eternal and unquenchable."

Trajan said: "I think it is a matter of sorcery <note original: "γοητείας">The Romans often explained the unusual endurance of Christian martyrs by accusing them of using magic or "curious arts."</note> to despise tortures; for surely you would have yielded to us after being so abused by our hands."

Ignatius said: "Tell me, how could those who turn away from demons as rebels against God and who loathe idols be sorcerers? For you who worship these things are more subject to such nonsensical talk. We have been commanded by law not to let sorcerers live, nor chanters, nor omen-seekers; instead, we are even accustomed to burning the books of those who practice curious arts as forbidden things. Therefore, I am no sorcerer; rather, it is you who are bowing down to demons."

Trajan said: "By the gods, Ignatius, I am weary of you, and I am at a loss as to what tortures I should use to persuade you to yield to my commands."

Ignatius said: "Do not grow weary, O King, but either hand me over to the fire, or cut me with the sword, or cast me into the depths, or give me up to the beasts, so that you may be convinced that none of these things is terrifying to us because of our love for God."

### III.

Trajan said: "What hope do you expect, Ignatius, by dying in these things which you suffer and endure? I cannot say."

Ignatius said: "Those who are ignorant of God are also ignorant of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Master over all, and the good things prepared [for us]. Thus, they think their existence is only here, just like that of irrational animals; they imagine nothing more after their departure from here. But we who know..."

Ignatius remains defiant, refuting charges of sorcery and contrasting his temporary pain with the promise of eternal life.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "unpublished" account of the martyrdom of Saint Ignatius of Antioch. In the previous section, Ignatius was being subjected to fire and physical torture by Emperor Trajan while maintaining his defiance through faith. On this page, the dialogue shifts from the nature of suffering to a historical and theological defense of Christianity as a force for peace within the Roman Empire.</meta>

<page-num>371</page-num>
<header>MARTYRIUM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. III.</header>

...piety, we know that after our departure from here, having risen, we shall have eternal life in Christ, unfailing and without succession, from which pain, grief, and sighing have fled. <note>This phrase reflects the language of the Eastern Orthodox funeral liturgy and Isaiah 35:10, describing the joy of the afterlife.</note> Trajan said: "By destroying your heresy, I will teach you to be sober-minded and not to fight against the decrees of the Romans." Ignatius said: "And who can, O King, destroy a building of God? For even if one attempts it, nothing more remains for him than to be a fighter against God. For Christianity will not only not be destroyed by men, but daily, by the power of Christ, it will increase in growth and magnitude according to these same principles;¹ and likewise possessing a progress of brilliance and dignity alike, it will flash forth² like rays of light. For the whole earth shall be filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as much water covers the seas. <note>A reference to Isaiah 11:9.</note> For you do not do well, O King, to call Christianity a 'heresy' <note original: "αἵρεσιν">The word *hairesis* originally meant a 'choice' or a 'sect,' but Trajan uses it here as a pejorative term for a rebellious faction.</note>; for Christianity is far removed from being a heresy. For Christianity is the knowledge of the truly existing³ God, and of His only-begotten Son, and of His coming in the flesh, following the way of Moses and the beautiful things of the state with unerring religion;⁴ what rebellion or war have you known us to love? Do we not rather submit to rulers, to whom submission is without danger? We are of one mind⁵ peacefully among the guards, paying our debts to all: tax to whom tax is due, fear to whom fear, custom to whom custom, honor to whom honor, striving to owe no one anything except to love one another. <note>Ignatius is quoting the Apostle Paul’s Letter to the Romans (13:7-8), arguing that Christians are the Empire's most law-abiding citizens.</note> For we have been taught by our Lord Jesus Christ not only to love our neighbor, but also to do good to our enemy,⁶ and to benefit those who hate us, and to pray for those who insult and persecute us. In what way has the preaching of Christianity offended you since it began? Tell me: has any uprising happened against the Roman rule because of it? On the contrary, did not the rule of many <note original: "πολυαρχία">polyarchy</note> fall into a monarchy, and your ancestor Augustus—under whom our Savior was born of a virgin and the Word, who was formerly God, became man for our sake—did he not alone⁷ rule for a whole age, for fifty-seven years and seven months, holding the Roman Empire and ruling as a monarch like no other before him? Was not every tribe subjected to him? And the former lack of communication between nations and their mutual hatred was dissolved by the arrival of our Savior." The Senate said: "Yes, these things are as you have said, Ignatius. But this is what we are indignant about: that he has destroyed the worship of the gods." Ignatius said: "O Luminous Senate, just as he subjected the more irrational of the nations to the Roman Empire—which our scriptures call an 'iron rod'—so also has he driven out the evil spirits from men, proclaiming the one and only God over all. And not only this, but he also delivered them from their bitter slavery, for they were bloodthirsty and pitiless. Did they not revel⁸ in the death of your dearest ones? Did they not defile you with civil wars? Did they not force you to behave shamefully, putting you on display naked, and parading your women naked as if in captivity?"⁹

--- Page 478 ---
<meta>This page continues the dialogue between the Bishop Ignatius of Antioch and the Emperor Trajan. Having previously discussed the survival of Christianity despite persecution, the debate now turns to a philosophical critique of Roman polytheism and the nature of the physical universe as a created work rather than a collection of deities.</meta>

<page-num>372</page-num>
<header>MARTYRIUM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. III.</header>

...staining the earth with blood and clouding the pure air with impurities. Ask the Scythians if they do not sacrifice humans to Artemis; for surely you deny it out of shame, the virgin slaughtered to Cronus. <note>Ignatius refers to the ancient and often debated practice of human sacrifice in "barbarian" cultures, using it to shame the Romans who viewed themselves as civilized yet maintained similar myths.</note> And the Greeks boast of such human sacrifices, having received such evil from the barbarians.

Trajan said: "By the gods, I am amazed at you, Ignatius, for your wide learning, even if I do not praise your religion."

Ignatius said: "And what do you condemn in our divine religion?"

Trajan said: "That you do not worship our master the Sun, nor the Heavens, nor the sacred Moon, the nourisher of all."

Ignatius said: "And who would choose, O King, to worship the Sun, which exists in a fixed form, which is perceived by our senses, and which loses and then regains its heat from fire? One that does not even remain constant during an eclipse, <note original: "τὸν [ἐν] ἐκλείψει οὔπω μενόντα">The manuscript notes a variation in the Vatican codex here; Ignatius argues that a god should not be subject to physical phenomena like eclipses.</note> and can never change its own order against the will of the One who commanded it to complete its course? 

And how is the sky worshipful, which is covered by clouds, which the Creator stretched out like a skin <note>This echoes Psalm 104:2, comparing the heavens to a tent or a curtain.</note> and fixed like a vaulted chamber and established like a cube? Or the moon that increases and decreases and is subject to changes? Simply because they possess a brilliant light, they should be worshipped? This reasoning is not entirely true. They were given for the illumination of men, but not for worship; they were commanded to ripen and warm the fruits, to brighten the day and light the night. 

And the stars of heaven were appointed for signs and seasons and cycles, and for the comfort of those sailing the sea; but none of these is worshipful—not water, which you call Poseidon; not fire, which you call Hephaestus; not air, which you name Hera; not earth, which you call Demeter; nor the crops. <note>Ignatius is dismantling "natural theology," where the four elements were personified as gods.</note> For even if all these things exist for our sustenance, they are nonetheless perishable and soulless."

Trajan said: "Was I not right to say at the beginning that you are the one who has turned the East upside down, teaching men not to revere the gods?"

Ignatius said: "And are you indignant, O King, because we advise men not to revere things that are not worthy of worship, but rather the true God, the living one, the maker of heaven and earth, His only-begotten Son, and His Holy Spirit? For this alone is the true religion, prevailing and confessed, priding itself on divine and spiritual doctrines. 

But your teaching of Hellenism is godless <note original: "ἄθεος">While Trajan calls Christians "atheists" for rejecting his gods, Ignatius reverses the term, calling paganism "atheos" because it lacks the true God.</note>, an easily overturned polytheism that wanders unsteadily, standing upon no firm foundation; for an unexamined education <note original: "ἀνεξέλεγκτος παιδεία">The Vatican manuscript uses a slightly different spelling here, but the meaning remains: a tradition that has not been tested by truth.</note> goes astray. For how is it not wandering among all kinds of false words, saying at one time that there are twelve universal gods of the world, and then again assuming there are many more?"

Trajan said: "I can no longer bear your arrogance; for you mock us terribly, wishing to defeat us with your glibness of words. Therefore, sacrifice! For enough of your rhetoric against us. If not, I will torture you again and later hand you over to the wild beasts."

Ignatius said: "How long will you threaten and not do what you promise? For I am a Christian and I do not sacrifice to evil demons, but I worship the true God, the Father of the Lord Jesus Christ, who has enlightened me with the light of knowledge, who has opened my eyes to the understanding of His wonders; for Him I honor and revere; for He is God and Lord and King..."

<summary>Ignatius engages in a philosophical debate with Emperor Trajan, systematically deconstructing the divinity of the celestial bodies and the elements, and asserting that only the Triune God is worthy of worship. Frustrated by Ignatius’s refusal to sacrifice and his "loquacity," Trajan threatens him with further torture and death by wild beasts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the trial of Ignatius of Antioch before the Emperor Trajan. Having dismissed the Roman gods as mere physical elements in the previous section, Ignatius now faces direct threats of torture and execution as the legal proceedings move toward a final sentence.</meta>

<page-num>373</page-num>
<header>MARTYRIUM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. III. IV.</header>

...King, the blessed and only Sovereign. Trajan said: "I will destroy you with burning beds <note>The Greek term *krabatopyriais* refers to a form of torture involving a heated iron bed or gridiron.</note> if you do not repent." Ignatius said: "Repentance from evil is good, O King, but repentance from good deeds is a crime; for we ought to run toward better things, not toward worse." Trajan said: "Scrape his back with iron claws and tell him: Obey the Emperor and sacrifice to the gods according to the decree of the Senate." Ignatius said: "I fear the decree of God which says: *You shall have no other gods before me,* and *He who sacrifices to other gods shall be utterly destroyed.* <note>Ignatius is quoting Exodus 20:3 and 22:20.</note> When the Senate and the King command me to break the law, I will not listen; for 'you shall not show partiality to the person of the powerful,' as the divine laws declare, 'and you shall not follow a multitude to do evil.'" <note original: "οὐ λήψῃ^12 γὰρ πρόσωπον δυνάστου... οὐκ ἔσῃ μετὰ πολλῶν ἐπὶ κακίᾳ">These quotes are from Leviticus 19:15 and Exodus 23:2. Footnote 12 notes that the Vatican manuscript uses a slightly different verb form for "receiving" or "accepting."</note>

Trajan said: "Pour vinegar and salt into his wounds." Ignatius said: "Know that all these things happening to me for the sake of confessing God are the means of winning rewards. For the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the glory that is to be revealed." <note>A direct reference to Romans 8:18.</note> Trajan said: "Spare yourself at last, man, and yield to what is commanded of you, since I will use worse tortures against you." Ignatius said: "Who shall separate us from the love of Christ? Shall tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword? For I am persuaded that neither life nor death shall be able to turn me away from my devotion, as I take courage in the power of Christ." <note>A paraphrase of Romans 8:35-39.</note>

Trajan said: "Do you think you can defeat me with your endurance? For man is a victory-loving animal." Ignatius said: "I do not merely think so, but I trust in God that I have conquered and will conquer, so that you may be convinced of how great a gap lies between piety and impiety." Trajan said: "Take him and put irons around him, and having secured his feet in the stocks, <term>the stocks (ξύλον)</term> <note>The *xylos* was a wooden instrument of confinement, often keeping the legs painfully spread.</note> throw^2 him into the inner prison. Let no one at all see him in the dungeon; and for three days and three nights let him eat no bread, so that after the three days he may be thrown to the wild beasts and so depart from this life." The Senate said: "We also cast our vote for the sentence against him; for he has insulted all of us along with the Emperor, by not yielding to sacrifice to the gods, but insisting that he is a Christian." Ignatius said: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who in His great goodness has deemed me worthy to become a partaker in the sufferings of His Christ and a true and faithful witness of His divinity."

IV. On the third day, Trajan, having summoned the Senate and the Prefect, proceeded to the amphitheater, and the Roman people also ran together; for they heard that the Bishop of Syria was about to fight the wild beasts. Then the Emperor ordered him to be brought in. When he saw him, he said to him: "I marvel that you are still alive after such outrages and such hunger. Now, obey me so that you may be delivered from the evils set before you; and we shall have you as a friend from now on." Ignatius said: "You seem to me to have the form of a man, but the ways of a fox—wagging your tail but plotting in your mind, fashioning words of kindness while planning nothing healthy. Hear me then with <term>boldness (παῤῥησίας)</term> <note>The term *parrhesia* implies the frank, fearless speech of a free citizen or a martyr before a tyrant.</note>, for I shall have no regard^1 for this mortal and fleeting life..."

After the previous page's defiance of the Emperor Trajan, the narrative shifts from the imperial tribunal to the arena, followed by the historical aftermath involving Pliny the Younger’s correspondence.</meta>

<page-num>374</page-num>
<header>MARTYRIUM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. IV.</header>

...because of this Jesus, for whom I long as I depart to be with him; for he is the wheat of immortality and the drink of eternal life. I am entirely his, and I have stretched out my mind toward him; I look down upon your tortures, and I spit upon your glory." Trajan said: "Since he is arrogant and defiant, let two lions loose upon him, so that not even a relic of him may be left behind." When the beasts were seen, the blessed man, beholding them, said to the people: "Men of Rome, spectators of this contest, I do not suffer these things because of any wicked crime, but for the sake of piety; for I am the wheat of God, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may become pure bread." <note>This is Ignatius’s most famous quote, often interpreted as eucharistic imagery where his death is an offering to God.</note> Hearing these things, Trajan was greatly amazed, saying: "Great is the endurance of the Christians! For who among the Greeks or barbarians would endure to suffer such things for the sake of his own god as this man suffers for the one in whom he has believed?" Ignatius said: "It is not within human power to cherish such things, but results from readiness of heart alone and faith that draws Christ to its aid."

And as he said these things, the lions ran toward him, and falling upon him from both sides, they only suffocated him; they did not touch his flesh, so that his remains might be a <term>phylactery</term> <note>A term usually meaning an amulet or safeguard; here it implies the martyr’s body serves as a spiritual protection for the city.</note> for the city of the Romans, in which Peter also was crucified, Paul was beheaded, and Onesimus was perfected in the glory of Christ.

Then Trajan, having risen, was seized with wonder. Letters also came to him from Pliny Secundus <note>Better known as Pliny the Younger, the governor of Bithynia-Pontus.</note> the governor, who was moved by the multitude of those becoming martyrs and being killed for the faith without flinching. At the same time, the letters reported that they did nothing unholy or contrary to the laws, except that they rose at dawn to worship Christ as God and to undergo judgment for his sake. They also forbade adultery, murder, and similar unlawful offenses among themselves, doing all things in an orderly manner;² these things [were written] to Trajan, who took into consideration what had happened regarding the blessed and holy Ignatius—for he had been a champion for the rest of the martyrs—and he issued a decree that the race of Christians should indeed be sought out, but if found, they should not be executed.³ <note>This manuscript's version of the decree differs slightly from the historical record in Pliny's letters, which suggested they should not be sought out, but punished if they refused to recant.</note> He ordered that those who wished to take the remains of the blessed Ignatius for burial should be allowed to do so without hindrance. The brothers in Rome, to whom he had also written so that they would not deprive him of his longed-for martyrdom by pleading for him,⁴ took his body and laid it in a place where it was possible for them to gather and praise God and our Lord Jesus Christ and the Holy Spirit upon the perfecting of the holy and blessed bishop and martyr Ignatius; for "the memory of the righteous is accompanied by praise."

Irenaeus, the bishop of Lyons, also knows of his martyrdom and mentions his letters, saying: "As one of our people said when condemned to the wild beasts for his testimony toward God: 'I am the wheat of my God, and I am ground by the teeth of wild beasts, so that I may be found to be pure bread.'"⁶ And Polycarp, the bishop of Smyrna...

<meta>This page concludes the account of the martyrdom of Saint Ignatius of Antioch. Following the description of his death in the Roman arena on the previous page, the text now provides historical corroboration by quoting the Epistle of Polycarp to the Philippians and concludes with the liturgical feast day and the succession of the church leadership in Antioch.</meta>

<page-num>375</page-num>
<header>MARTYRIUM (UNPUBLISHED) OF ST. IGNATIUS. IV.</header>

[Polycarp] mentions their <term>communities</term> <note>Original: "παροικίας" (paroikias), referring to the local church groups or "sojournings" of the Christians in a foreign land.</note> saying: "I exhort you, brothers, to be obedient and to practice all endurance, which you saw with your own eyes, not only in the blessed Ignatius, Rufus, and Zosimus, but also in many others from among us, and in Paul himself and the others who believed with him. For all these did not run in vain, nor did they labor in vain, but in faith and righteousness; and they are now in the place deservedly theirs beside the Lord, with whom they also suffered. For they did not love this present age, but they longed for Christ, who died for us and rose again."⁷ And shortly thereafter: "The letters of Ignatius sent to us by him, and any other letters we had with us, I have sent to you, just as you commanded; these are attached to this letter. You will benefit greatly from them, for they contain faith and endurance toward our Lord Jesus Christ."⁸

For such was the martyrdom of Ignatius; and Heron succeeded him in the <term>episcopacy</term> <note>The office or jurisdiction of a bishop.</note> of Antioch. The memory of the most God-beloved and noble martyr Ignatius is celebrated on the 20th of the month of December, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory forever and ever. Amen.

# OF THE HOLY POLYCARP,
## BISHOP OF SMYRNA AND HOLY MARTYR,
### TO THE
## PHILIPPIANS, AN EPISTLE.¹

*Polycarp and the elders who are with him, to the church of God dwelling as a pilgrim <note>original: "παροικούσῃ" (paroikousē), implying a community living in a temporary home on earth while their true citizenship is in heaven.</note> at Philippi:² may mercy to you³ and peace from God the Almighty and the Lord⁴ Jesus Christ our Savior be multiplied.*

---

1) This title is found in Codices B, C, F, O, and V. To the version by Cotelerius, a correction was added from the complete old Latin interpretation, which I have emended with the help of two manuscripts from the Vatican Library, the "Royal" and the "Palatine." The subject matter of the entire Epistle is clearly indicated by the title in those Codices.
2) *Philippous* was restored by Jacobson from manuscript V, which I also find in manuscript O; *Philippois* appears in B, C, L, P and in books printed before Routh. In the latter case, the preposition *en* [in] was necessary. Both forms of expression occur in the Inscription of the Circular Epistle of the Smyrnaeans regarding Polycarp’s Martyrdom. However, the scribe who wrote the Vatican manuscript frequently confused the letter *iota* (ι) with *upsilon* (υ) by adding a light stroke: a fact you will understand more than sufficiently from the variant readings I have cited for the Epistles of Barnabas and the Interpolated Ignatius. For this reason, in similar cases, the authority of a single manuscript (V) is not always to be preferred over the others. Gallicciolli is correct: "who stays in Philippi," implying a pilgrim status. Compare the inscription of Clement of Rome’s First Epistle to the Corinthians.
3) "to us" in manuscript C.
4) "Lord" is omitted in manuscripts F, O, P, V, and the old Latin Translation.

# THE EPISTLE OF SAINT POLYCARP TO THE PHILIPPIANS. I.

### I. Praise for their kindness toward the imprisoned brothers and for their firm faith.

I rejoiced with you greatly in our Lord Jesus Christ, because you welcomed the representations of true love and, as was fitting for you, escorted those who were entangled in holy bonds <note>original: "ἁγιοπρεπέσι δεσμοῖς" (hagioprepessi desmois). These "holy bonds" refer to the chains of Christian prisoners—likely Ignatius and his companions—who were being transported to Rome for execution.</note>; these bonds are the diadems <term>diadems: "διαδήματα" (diadēmata), royal crowns or headbands signifying victory, here used to describe the honor of suffering for Christ</term> of those who have been truly chosen by God and our Lord. I rejoice also because the firm root of your faith, which has been famous from ancient times <note>A reference to the church at Philippi being one of the first established by the Apostle Paul in Europe.</note>, remains until now and bears fruit unto our Lord Jesus Christ. He endured even to face death for our sins, "whom God raised, having loosed the pangs of Hades." <note>A quotation from Acts 2:24.</note> "In whom, though you do not see Him, you believe; and believing, you rejoice with joy unspeakable and full of glory" <note>A quotation from 1 Peter 1:8.</note>—into which joy many desire to enter, knowing that "by grace you are saved, not of works," <note>A quotation from Ephesians 2:8-9.</note> but by the will of God through Jesus Christ.

<column-break/>

I have greatly rejoiced with you in our Lord Jesus Christ, because you received the images of true charity, and because, as became you, you accompanied those who were bound in chains—which are fitting for the saints and which are the crowns of those who are truly chosen by God and our Lord. And I rejoice because the firm root of your faith, announced from ancient times, remains until now and brings forth fruit in our Lord Jesus Christ, who for our sins sustained even the coming unto death; "whom God raised, having loosed the pains of hell." "In whom, not seeing, you believe; but believing you exult with joy unspeakable and glorified;" into which many desire to enter, knowing that "by grace you are saved, not of works," but by the will of God through Jesus Christ.

* I. I have congratulated <note>original: "Congratulatus sum." This section represents a different Latin manuscript tradition, often called the "Old Latin" version, which sometimes preserves different nuances than the Greek.</note> you magnificently in our Lord Jesus Christ, looking upon the imitable words of love which you showed in those who were sent ahead—holy men, bound in beautiful chains—which are the chosen crowns for God and for His true kingdom, through our Lord Jesus Christ. And I rejoice because the firmness of your faith remains from the beginning until now and is fruitful in our Lord Jesus Christ, who endured for our sins even unto death: "whom God raised, dissolving the pains of hell. Whom, although you have not seen, you now love; in whom, though you do not now look upon Him, you believe: and believing, you shall rejoice with joy unspeakable and glorified:" into which many desire to enter, knowing that "by grace you have been saved, not of works," but in the will of God, through Jesus Christ.

## II. An exhortation to virtue.

“Wherefore, girding up your loins,” <note>original: "Διὸ ἀναζωσάμενοι τὰς ὀσφύας ὑμῶν". A reference to 1 Peter 1:13 and Ephesians 6:14, using the metaphor of tucking in long robes to prepare for physical labor or a journey—here meaning mental and spiritual readiness.</note> serve God in fear and truth, leaving behind empty vanity and the error of the many, “having believed in him who raised our Lord Jesus Christ” from the dead, and gave him glory and a throne at his right hand; to whom all things in heaven and on earth were subjected; whom every living breath serves; who comes as judge of the living and the dead; whose blood God will require from those who disobey him. But he who raised him from the dead will also raise us, if we do his will, and walk in his commandments, and love what he loved, refraining from all unrighteousness, greed, love of money, slander, and false witness; “not returning evil for evil, or”

<column-break/>

“Wherefore, having girded your loins, serve God in fear” and truth, abandoning empty idle-talk and the error of the common crowd, “believing in him, who raised our Lord Jesus Christ from the dead, and gave him glory” and a seat at his right hand; to whom all things heavenly and earthly are subject; whom every spirit serves; who comes as the judge of the living and the dead; whose blood God will demand from those who do not believe in him. He, truly, who raised him from the dead, will also raise us, if we have done his will and walked in his commands, and have loved those things which he himself loved, abstaining from all injustice, fraud, avarice, detraction, and false testimony; “not rendering evil for evil, nor [insult for insult]...”

### VII. Flee the Docetists, and persevere in fasts and prayer.

“For everyone who does not confess¹ that Jesus Christ has come in the flesh is antichrist;² and whoever does not confess the testimony of the cross is of the devil;³ and whoever⁴ perverts the words of the Lord to his own desires, and says⁵ there is neither resurrection nor judgment,⁶ this one is the firstborn of Satan. # SAINT POLYCARP’S EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS. IX.
### 25 *

...which you also saw before your own eyes, not only in the blessed **IGNATIUS**, **ZOSIMUS**, and **RUFO**, but also in others from among us, and in **PAUL** himself and the rest of the Apostles; being persuaded that all of these did not run in vain, but in faith and righteousness; and that they are now in the place due to them in the presence of the Lord, with whom they also suffered. For they did not love this present <term>age<note>original: αἰῶνα (aiona); often translated as "world" or "world-system," referring to the current fallen state of human affairs.</note></term>, but him who died for our sake, and for our sake was [raised up by God].

<column-break/>

...exercise [patience], which you also have before your eyes, not only in the blessed **IGNATIUS**, **ZOSIMUS**, and **RUFO**, but also in others who are from among us, and in **PAUL** himself and the rest of the Apostles; as those who are persuaded that all these have not run in vain, but in faith and justice; and that they are in the place deserved by them with the **LORD**, with whom they also suffered. For they did not love the present world, but him who died for us, and was raised by **GOD** for our sake.

...which³ you also saw with <term>eyewitness faith<note>original: oculata fide; a legalistic or certain type of witnessing based on having seen the events oneself.</note></term>,⁴ not only in those most blessed men,⁵ namely⁶ **IGNATIUS**, **ZOSIMUS**, and **RUFO**, but also in others who are from among you, and⁷ in **PAUL** himself, and the rest of the Apostles, trusting that all these⁸ did not run in⁹ vain, but in faith and justice; and they have gone to the place due to them from¹⁰ the **LORD**, with whom they also suffered, because they did not love this present¹¹ world, but him who¹² died for them and for us, and was raised by **GOD**.

3) The Roman Martyrology indicates that the <term>birthday<note>original: diem natalem; in early Christian context, this refers to the date of a martyr's death—their "birth" into eternal life.</note></term> of the martyrs Rufus and Zosimus is celebrated at Philippi in Macedonia on December 18.
4) I have given "of us" (ἡμῶν) from manuscript C and Eusebius; manuscripts B, F, O, V, the ancient Interpreter, and the Vulgate read "of you" (ὑμῶν). Subsequently, there is a mark in O¹; in the margin "himself." The preposition "in" (ἐν) is missing before "himself" in manuscript B.
5) "Others" in V and O, to whose margin "the rest" is added.
6) I have restored "of those being persuaded" (πεπεισμένων) from manuscript C, which reading I think is uniquely genuine; O, V, and the Vulgate have "those being persuaded" (πεπεισμένους), while B has "to those being persuaded" (πεπεισμένοις). The genitive "of us" is to be joined; the fourth case (accusative) depends on "I exhort," the third (dative) refers to "the rest."
7) Compare Philippians 2:16 and Galatians 2:2.
8) Compare Clement of Rome, 1st Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter 5.

10) Thus all our manuscripts, Cotelerius, and the 1698 edition of Le Clerc; the 1724 edition of the same has "who died for you."
11) Ussher supplied the words in brackets from Eusebius and Nicephorus. In manuscript O, this fragment of Polycarp's Epistle is found joined with the Epistle of Barnabas thus: "having died. And for us under the empty people." In the margin, a second hand, following Eusebius, has "and for us raised by God," which reading agrees with

# ST. POLYCARP’S EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS. X. XI.
### 388

->An exhortation to virtues.<-

*X. Stand fast, therefore, in these things, and follow the example of the Lord, being firm in faith and unchangeable, lovers of the brotherhood^1, loving one another, joined together in the truth, showing the gentleness of the Lord^2 to one another, despising no one. When you are able^3 to do good, do not put it off, because "almsgiving^4 delivers from death." Be all of you subject to one another, "having your conduct^5 irreproachable among the Gentiles," so that from your good works both you may receive praise, and the Lord may not be blasphemed because of you. But woe^6 to him through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed. Therefore, teach sobriety to all, in which you also live.

->I am saddened for Valens. Beware of greed.<-

*XI. I am greatly saddened for Valens, who was once made a presbyter^1 <note>original: presbyter; an elder or priest in the early church hierarchy.</note> among you; that he so ignores the place that was given to him. I warn you, therefore, that you abstain from greed,^4 and that you be chaste and^5 truthful. Abstain from every evil. But he who cannot govern himself^6 in these things, how does he preach it to another?^7 If anyone does not abstain from greed, he shall be defiled by idolatry,^9 and shall be judged as if among the Gentiles. But who^10 is ignorant of the judgment of the Lord? "Or^11 do we not know that the saints shall judge the world?" as^12 Paul teaches. But I^13 have neither perceived nor heard any such thing in you, among whom the blessed Paul labored, you who are praised^14 in the beginning of his epistle. For he boasts of you in all the churches which alone then knew God;^16 but we^17 did not yet know Him.

---

# THE EPISTLE OF ST. POLYCARP TO THE PHILIPPIANS. XI. XII. XIII.

Therefore, brothers, I am deeply grieved for him <note>Referring to Valens, the disgraced presbyter mentioned on the previous page.</note> and for his wife; may the Lord grant them true repentance. Therefore, be sober yourselves in this matter, and do not consider such people as enemies, but recall them as suffering and straying members, so that you may save the whole body of your community. For by doing this, you build yourselves up.

->*Forgive him. May God grant you virtues. Pray for all, even for enemies.*<-

\* **XII.** For I am confident that you are well-trained in the Sacred Scriptures, and nothing is hidden from you; but to me, this has not been granted. Only, as it is said in these scriptures, “Be angry and do not sin,” <note>original: irascimini et nolite peccare; citing Psalm 4:5</note> and “let not the sun go down upon your anger.” <note>citing Ephesians 4:26</note> Blessed is he who remembers this; which I believe is true of you. Now may God and the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the eternal High Priest <term>High Priest <note>original: pontifex; Polycarp uses this term for Christ, emphasizing his role as the ultimate mediator.</note></term> himself, the Son of God, Jesus Christ, build you up in faith and truth, and in all gentleness, and without anger, and in patience, long-suffering, endurance, and chastity; and may he grant you a lot and a part among his saints, and to us along with you, and to all those under heaven who shall believe in our Lord Jesus Christ and in his Father, who “raised him from the dead.” <note>citing Galatians 1:1</note> Pray for all the saints. Pray also for kings and powers and princes, and for those who persecute and hate you, and for the enemies of the cross; so that your fruit may be manifest in all, that you may be perfect in him.

### *XIV. I have written these things to you by Crescens, whom I commended to you in the past^1 and now commend again. For he has conducted himself blamelessly among us, and I believe he will do^2 the same with you. You shall also have his sister as one commended to you when she comes to you. Be kept safe in the Lord Jesus Christ. His grace^3 be with you all. Amen.

5) That is, to Antioch. Ignatius (Chapter 7) had commanded Polycarp to send a messenger to the church at Antioch because peace had been restored there, and (Chapter 8) to hand over congratulatory letters from other churches to this messenger. In addition to this command from Ignatius, the Philippians themselves had approached Polycarp with requests that he give their letter to his messenger to be carried to the Antiochians. Polycarp promises that he will fulfill these wishes. *Hefele.*
