<meta>This page transitions from the personal letters of Polycarp to the Philippians to the "Martyrdom of Polycarp," a famous account written by the church in Smyrna shortly after his death. This marks the beginning of one of the earliest "Acts of the Martyrs," shifting from the bishop's own voice to his community's testimony of his final days.</meta>

# THE CHURCH AT SMYRNA

## CONCERNING

## THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT POLYCARP

### AN ENCYCLICAL LETTER.<sup>1</sup>

The Church of God, which sojourns <note>original: *paroikousa*; this term suggests Christians living as "resident aliens" or temporary residents in a worldly city</note> at Smyrna, to the Church of God sojourning at Philomelium, and to all the parishes <term>parish: originally meaning a community of Christians in a specific area</term> of the holy and catholic church in every place: may mercy, peace, and love from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ be multiplied.

---

-># THE CHURCH AT SMYRNA<-

->## CONCERNING<-

->## THE MARTYRDOM OF SAINT POLYCARP<-

->### AN ENCYCLICAL LETTER.<-

The Church of God, which dwells as a stranger at Smyrna, to the Church of God which dwells as a stranger at Philomelium, and to all the parishes of the holy and universal church throughout the world: may mercy, peace, and love from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ be increased.

---

Since I did not happen to find new supporting materials in the Vatican library for the purpose of correcting the text of this little work, I have mostly followed the critical work of Jacobson, who corrected many of its passages from the Vienna, Paris, and Baroccian <note>A collection held at the Bodleian Library, Oxford</note> Codices. However, it seems to me that an ascetic Interpolator <note>A later editor who adds or alters text to suit a specific theological or moral agenda</note> has exerted more influence on the narrative of the events than is appropriate. — **1)** Eusebius, after he spoke concerning the martyrdom of Polycarp (*Ecclesiastical History* IV, 15), continues thus: <note>original Greek: "The writing is from the perspective of the church which he himself led, signaling the things concerning him to the parishes in Pontus through these words."</note> See also Neander, *Church History*, Volume I, page 107 and following.

**2)** Compare Clement of Rome’s *First Epistle to the Corinthians*, chapter 1; the inscription of Polycarp's *Epistle to the Philippians*; and the *Epistle to Diognetus*, chapter 5.

<column-break/>

**3)** This should be read thus according to the Vienna Codex, along with the ancient Interpreter and Eusebius (*Ecclesiastical History* IV, 15). The remaining Codices read "Philadelphia." Philomelium is a town in Greater Phrygia, mentioned by Cicero in his *Letters to Friends* (3.8 and 3.15) and his speeches *Against Verres* (85). It is now called Ilgun.

**4)** The word "and" <note>original: *kai*</note> is omitted in the Vienna manuscript. Compare Ignatius’s *Letter to the Smyrnaeans*, chapter 8.

**5)** The term "parish" <note>original: *paroecia*</note> is taken either *broadly* for an entire diocese, as seen in Augustine's *Epistle 261*, and in this sense among Christians of a later age it denoted the *territory and region of a Bishop*... or it is taken *strictly* for the district of any particular churches. This latter meaning became common at the time after the name "diocese" began to be assigned to the regions designated for Bishops. See Boehmer, *Parochial Law*, III. 3. 2.

<meta>This page continues the introductory section of the "Martyrdom of Polycarp," shifting from the salutation provided by the Church of Smyrna into the narrative account of the events. It focuses on the theological significance of martyrdom and the specific bravery of the victims under Roman torture.</meta>

# THE MARTYDOM OF SAINT POLYCARP. I. II. III.

### I. *We write concerning the martyrdom of Polycarp and his companions.*

We have written to you, brothers, the account of those who suffered martyrdom, <note>original: "tous martyrēsantas" — those who bore witness unto death</note> and especially concerning the blessed Polycarp, who, by his martyrdom, acted as a seal <note>Polycarp’s death is viewed as the "final stamp" that brought this specific wave of persecution to a close</note> and put an end to the persecution. For nearly all the events leading up to it happened so that the Lord might show us from above a martyrdom modeled after the Gospel. For he waited to be betrayed, just as the Lord did, so that we too might become his imitators, looking not only to our own interests but also to the interests of our neighbors. For it is the mark of true and steadfast love to desire not only that oneself be saved, but also all the brothers.

### II. *The wonderful constancy of the martyrs.*

All the martyrdoms, then, were blessed and noble, having taken place according to the will of God. For we must be very reverent <note>original: "eulabesterous" — more cautious or devout</note> in attributing the ultimate authority over all things to God. For who would not admire their nobility, their endurance, and their love for their Master? For though they were torn by whips until the internal structure <term>structure: the original Greek "oikonomian" here refers to the physical arrangement or anatomy of the body</term> of their flesh was visible, even down to the inner veins and arteries, they endured it so that even the bystanders felt pity and lamented. Some reached such a level of nobility that none of them would cry out or groan, demonstrating to all of us that in that hour of torture, the martyrs of Christ were traveling away from the flesh—or rather, that the Lord stood by them and communed with them. And by fixing their gaze on the grace of Christ, they despised the tortures of this world, purchasing eternal life at the price of a single hour. To them, the fire of their cruel torturers felt cold. For they kept before their eyes the goal of escaping the eternal and unquenchable fire, and with the eyes of their hearts, they looked up to the good things reserved for those who endure—things "which no ear has heard, nor eye has seen, nor has entered into the heart of man." <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9</note> These things were shown to them by the Lord, for they were no longer merely men, but were already angels. In a similar way, those condemned to the wild beasts endured terrible punishments, being forced to lie on sharp shells <note>original: "kērykas" — likely murex shells or similar jagged objects used as a bed of torture</note> and being buffeted by various other forms of torment, so that, if it were possible, the tyrant might turn them to denial through continuous punishment.

For the most noble Germanicus <note>A young Christian of Smyrna who suffered alongside Polycarp</note> strengthened their timidity through the endurance shown in his own person; he even fought remarkably against the wild beasts. <meta>This page continues the introductory section of the "Martyrdom of Polycarp," shifting from the salutation provided by the Church of Smyrna into the narrative account of the events. # THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. I. II. III.

### I. We write concerning the martyrdom of Polycarp and his companions.

We have written to you, brothers, regarding the martyrs and the blessed Polycarp, who, by his martyrdom, acted as a seal <note>original: "signaculo" — a wax seal used to finalize a document; here, Polycarp’s death is seen as the final act that ended the persecution</note> and put an end to the persecution. For nearly everything that preceded it happened so that the Lord might show us from above a martyrdom in harmony with the Gospel. For he waited to be betrayed, just as the Lord did, so that we too might become his imitators, looking not only to our own interests, but also to those of our neighbors. For it is the mark of true and solid love to desire not only that one’s self be saved, but also all the brothers.

### II. The wonderful constancy of the martyrs.

All the martyrdoms were blessed and noble, occurring according to the will of God. For as we are people of great piety, we must ascribe the power over all things to God. For who would not admire their nobility, their patience, and their love for the Lord? They were so torn by whips that the very structure of their bodies was visible, even to the innermost veins and arteries; yet they endured it. Even the bystanders felt pity and lamented, yet the martyrs reached such a height of courage that not one of them uttered a moan or a groan. They showed us all that in that hour when they were being tortured, the martyrs of Christ were absent from the body, or rather, that the Lord stood by them and communed with them. And looking toward the grace of Christ, they despised the torments of this world, redeeming themselves from eternal punishment through a single hour of pain. Even the fire of their cruel executioners seemed cold to them. For they kept before their eyes the escape from that fire which is eternal and never extinguished, and with the eyes of the heart, they looked up to those good things reserved for those who endure—‘which no ear has heard, nor eye seen, nor has it entered into the heart of man’ <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 2:9</note>—things which were shown by the Lord to them, for they were no longer merely men, but already angels. Similarly, those condemned to the wild beasts endured terrible torments, being stretched out upon sharp shards <term>sharp shards: "murices" were spiked shells or jagged objects used to increase the agony of those lying on them</term> and tortured with various other agonies, so that, if it were possible, the tyrant might bring them to deny Christ through the relentless nature of the punishment.

### III. The constancy of Germanicus. The death of Polycarp is demanded.

For the devil devised many schemes against them. But thanks be to God; for he could conquer no one. For the most brave Germanicus strengthened their fearfulness by his own constancy; indeed, he fought magnificently against the wild beasts. For when the Proconsul <note>original: "proconsul" — the Roman governor of the province</note> wished to sway him and said,

# THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. III. IV. V. VI. VII.

...urging him <note>Referring to Germanicus, a young martyr mentioned in the preceding text who provoked a wild beast to hasten his death</note>, and saying that he should have pity on his youth, he dragged the wild beast toward himself by force, wishing to be released more quickly from their unjust and lawless life. From this, then, the whole multitude, marvelling at the nobility of the God-loving and God-fearing race of the Christians, shouted: "Away with the atheists! <note>original: "αἶρε τοὺς ἀθέους" — In this context, 'atheists' was a Roman slur for Christians because they refused to worship the traditional Roman gods.</note> Let Polycarp be sought!"

### IV. Quintus the apostate.

But one, named Quintus, a Phrygian, who had recently come from Phrygia, grew afraid when he saw the wild beasts. This was the same man who had forced himself and some others to come forward voluntarily for trial. The proconsul, after much entreaty, persuaded this man to swear the oath <note>An oath to the "Genius" or spirit of the Emperor</note> and to offer sacrifice to the gods. For this reason, then, brothers, we do not praise those who give themselves up; since the Gospel does not teach us to do so. <note>original footnote 3: "For the Gospel rather commands to flee to another city (Matthew 10:23); yet in such a way that, if it is not permitted to flee, death may be borne with constancy." — Commentary by the scholar Clericus.</note>

### V. Polycarp’s retreat and vision.

But the most admirable Polycarp, when he first heard the news, was not disturbed, but wished to remain in the city; however, the majority persuaded him to withdraw. And he withdrew to a small farm, not far distant from the city; and he stayed with a few companions, night and day doing nothing else but praying for all people and for the churches throughout the world; as was his custom. And while praying, he had a vision three days before he was seized; he saw his pillow being consumed by fire. And turning, he said prophetically to those with him: "I must be burned alive."

### VI. Polycarp is betrayed by a servant. Herod the police captain.

And as those seeking him persisted, he moved to another farm; and immediately the searchers arrived. When they did not find him, they seized two young servants, one of whom confessed under torture. For it was indeed impossible for him to remain hidden, since even those betraying him were of his own household. And the police captain <term>irenarch</term> <note>original: "εἰρήναρχος" — a magistrate responsible for maintaining public order and peace</note>, who happened to have the same name as the biblical king, being called Herod, hastened to lead him into the stadium; so that Polycarp might fulfill his own appointed lot by becoming a sharer with Christ, while those who betrayed him should suffer the punishment of Judas himself.

## VIII. *Polycarp is led into the city.*

When he had finished his prayer—in which he had made mention of all who had ever met him, small and great, famous and obscure, and of the whole universal church <note>original: "catholicae ecclesiae"</note> throughout the world—and when the hour for departure had come, they set him on a donkey and led him into the city on the day of the Great Sabbath. <note>The "Great Sabbath" usually refers to the Saturday before Easter, or a high festival in the Jewish calendar.</note> He was met by Herod the <term>irenarch: a local magistrate in charge of maintaining public order and policing</term> and his father Nicetas, riding in a carriage; they transferred him into their own carriage, and sitting beside him, they tried to persuade him, saying: "What harm is there in saying 'Caesar is Lord' <note>original: "dominus Caesar"</note> and offering sacrifice to save yourself?" Then they, frustrated in their hope of swaying him, spoke insulting words to him and threw him out of the carriage with such force that, as he fell from the vehicle, he scraped his shin. But he, not at all disturbed and as if he had suffered no harm, proceeded eagerly and quickly, being led to the stadium. There was such a great uproar in the stadium that no one could be heard.

# MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. IX. X. XI. XII.

<note>original: "MARTYRIUM S. POLYCARPI"</note>

...it is their custom to say: <gloss>2</gloss> <note>Manuscript variants from Vienna and Paris differ slightly in the phrasing of this introductory formula.</note> "Swear by the fortune of Caesar; repent; say, 'Away with the atheists!'" <gloss>3</gloss> <note>In the Roman Empire, Christians were often called "atheists" because they refused to worship the traditional Roman gods or the Emperor.</note> But Polycarp, with a solemn face, looked upon the whole crowd of lawless heathens in the stadium and waved his hand at them; then, groaning and looking up to heaven, he said: "Away with the atheists!" <gloss>4</gloss> <note>Polycarp uses the crowd's own phrase against them, implying that the true "godless" ones are those who do not know the one true God.</note> As the proconsul pressed him and said, "Swear, and I will release you; revile the Christ," Polycarp replied: "Eighty and six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King and Savior?"

### *X. Polycarp professes he is a Christian and wishes to speak of Christ.*

When the official persisted again, saying, "Swear by the fortune of Caesar," Polycarp answered: "If you vainly imagine <gloss>1</gloss> <note>Textual variants exist here between the Baroccianus and Parisian manuscripts regarding the verb "to pretend."</note> that I will swear by the fortune of Caesar, as you say, and pretend you do not know who I am, hear me plainly: I am a Christian. If you wish to learn the teachings of Christianity, set a day and listen." The proconsul said: "Persuade <gloss>2</gloss> the people." But Polycarp replied: "I have deemed you worthy of an explanation; for we have been taught to give fitting honor to the rulers <gloss>3</gloss> and authorities appointed by God, provided it does not harm us. But as for these people, I do not consider them worthy that I should defend myself before them."

### *XI. Neither the threat of beasts nor fire terrifies Polycarp.*

The proconsul said to him: "I have wild beasts; I will throw you to them if you do not repent." But he said: "Call them! For us, repentance from better things to worse is impossible; but it is a good thing to change from what is evil to what is righteous." Then the proconsul said again: "I will cause you to be consumed by fire, since you despise the wild beasts, if you do not repent." But Polycarp <gloss>1</gloss> said: "You threaten a fire that burns for an hour and is quenched shortly after; for you are ignorant of the fire of the coming judgment and eternal punishment reserved for the ungodly. But why do you delay? Bring what you will." <gloss>2</gloss>

### *XII. Polycarp is condemned to the pyre.*

While saying these things and many more, he was filled with courage and joy, and his face was so filled with grace that it did not drop in confusion <gloss>1</gloss> at what was being said to him. On the contrary, the proconsul was astonished and sent his own herald to proclaim three times in the midst of the stadium: "Polycarp has confessed himself to be a Christian!" When this was announced by the herald, the whole multitude of heathens and Jews living in Smyrna cried out with uncontrollable wrath and a loud voice: "This is the teacher of impiety, <gloss>2</gloss> <note>The Greek term implies a teacher of "atheism" or "lawlessness" in the eyes of the Roman religious system.</note> the father of the Christians, the destroyer of our gods, who teaches many not to sacrifice or worship the gods!" -># MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. IX. X. XI. XII.<-

...it is their custom to say: "Swear by the fortune <term>Fortuna: the protective spirit or 'luck' of the Emperor, which Romans were required to honor as a sign of political loyalty</term> of Caesar; repent; say, 'Away with the atheists!'" Then Polycarp, looking with a heavy and solemn face upon the whole crowd of lawless heathens <note>original: "gentilium"</note> in the stadium, gestured toward them with his hand, groaned, and looking up to heaven, said: "Away with the atheists!" <note>Polycarp ironically turns the crowd's own accusation of "atheism"—used against Christians for not worshiping the Roman gods—back upon the pagans themselves.</note> As the proconsul pressed him further, saying, "Swear, and I will release you; revile the Christ," Polycarp replied: "Eighty and six years I have served him, and he has done me no wrong. How then can I blaspheme my King and Savior?"

### X. Polycarp professes he is a Christian and wishes to speak of Christ.

When the official persisted again, saying, "Swear by the fortune of Caesar," Polycarp answered: "If you vainly seek glory from this <gloss>1</gloss> <note>original: "ὃ βούλει" (whatever you want). Textual variants here discuss the verb for "pretending."</note>—that I should swear by the fortune of Caesar, as you say—and you pretend not to know who I am, hear me plainly: I am a Christian. If you wish to learn the reason for Christian doctrine, grant me a day's time and listen." The proconsul said: "Persuade the people." <gloss>2</gloss> <note>The scholar Neander suggests the proconsul may have actually wanted to save Polycarp by shifting the responsibility to the crowd.</note> Polycarp replied: "I have deemed you worthy of an explanation; for we have been taught <gloss>3</gloss> <note>A reference to New Testament teachings in Romans 13 and Titus 3 regarding respect for civil authority.</note> to give to the princes and powers ordained by God such honor as is fitting and does us no harm; but as for these people, I do not consider them worthy that I should offer a defense to them."

### XI. Neither the threats of beasts nor fire terrify Polycarp.

But the proconsul said to him: "I have wild beasts; I will throw you to them unless you change your mind." But he replied: "Call them! For us, it is impossible to change from what is better to what is worse; but it is a good thing for me to pass from suffering to what is righteous." Again the official said to Polycarp: "Since you despise the beasts, I will have you consumed by fire unless you change your purpose." Polycarp answered: "You threaten a fire that burns for the space of an hour and is extinguished shortly after; for you are ignorant of the fire of the coming judgment and of the eternal punishment which is reserved for the ungodly. But why do you delay? Bring forth whatever you will." <gloss>1</gloss> <note>In some versions, this is phrased "Holy Polycarp says..."</note>

### XII. Polycarp is condemned to the pyre.

As he said these and many other things, he was filled with confidence and joy, and his face was so full of grace that he not only remained unshaken by the things said to him, but on the contrary, the proconsul was astonished. The proconsul then sent his herald <gloss>1</gloss> <note>The Baroccianus and Eusebius manuscripts support this reading; others suggest the proconsul was "disturbed."</note> to proclaim three times in the middle of the stadium: "Polycarp has confessed that he is a Christian!" When the herald had announced this, the entire multitude of heathens and Jews who lived in Smyrna cried out with ungovernable rage and a loud voice: "This is the teacher of Asia, <gloss>2</gloss> <note>While some texts say "teacher of impiety," the scholar Usher notes that "Teacher of Asia" is better supported by Eusebius and Rufinus.</note> the father of the Christians, the destroyer of our gods, who teaches many not to sacrifice and not to worship the gods!" Saying these things, they began shouting and asking—

-># MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. XII. XIII. XIV.<-

...shouting, they cried out and asked Philip the Asiarch <gloss>3</gloss> to let loose a lion upon Polycarp. But Philip said it was not legal for him to do so, since he had already completed the hunting games <term>hunting games: known as "venationes," these were staged hunts and battles with wild beasts in the Roman arena</term>. Then it seemed best to them to shout out with one voice that Polycarp should be burned alive. For it was necessary that the vision shown to him regarding his pillow be fulfilled—the one he saw while praying, when he saw it burning and said prophetically, turning to the faithful who were with him: "I must be burned alive."

### XIII. The pyre is prepared.

These things then happened with such great speed, faster than can be told, with the crowds immediately gathering wood and brushwood from the workshops and baths; the Jews especially assisted in this with zeal, as is their custom. When the pyre was ready, Polycarp laid aside all his garments and loosed his belt, and also tried to take off his own shoes. He had not done this before because each of the faithful was always eager to be the first to touch his skin; for he had been adorned with every good thing because of his noble conduct, even before his martyrdom. Immediately, the instruments prepared for the fire were placed around him. As they were about to nail <gloss>2</gloss> him as well, he said: "Leave me as I am; for He who grants me to endure the fire will also grant me to remain at the pyre unshaken, even without the security you provide with nails."

### XIV. Polycarp’s prayer.

So they did not nail him, but they bound him. Putting his hands behind him and being bound, like a noble ram <gloss>1</gloss> from a great flock prepared for an offering, a burnt sacrifice <term>burnt sacrifice: "holocaust," referring to an offering entirely consumed by fire</term> acceptable to God, he looked up to heaven and said: "Lord God, the Almighty, the Father of your beloved and blessed Son Jesus Christ, through whom we have received knowledge of you, the God of angels and powers, and of all creation, and of the whole race of the righteous who live in your presence: I bless you that you have deemed me worthy of this day and hour, to receive a portion among the number of your martyrs, in the cup <gloss>3</gloss> of your Christ, unto the resurrection of eternal life, both of soul and body, in the incorruptibility of the Holy Spirit. Among these may I be received before you today as a rich and acceptable sacrifice, just as you have prepared and revealed beforehand and have now fulfilled, <gloss>4</gloss> O faithful and true God. For this reason and for all things I praise you, I bless you, I glorify you, through the eternal and heavenly High Priest, Jesus Christ, your beloved Son; through whom be glory to you, with him and the Holy Spirit, both now and for the ages to come. Amen."

***

3) Asiarchs were those who managed the sacred games in honor of the Gods for the safety of their province at stated times. Because the spectacles they gave were sacred, they were called priests. (Mader). This priesthood was very burdensome, and for that reason only the more wealthy were chosen to hold it. Hence it is that Strabo observes the Asiarchs were mostly chosen from the citizens of Tralles,

<column-break/>

because the citizens of that city were the wealthiest in all of Asia. (Valesius). This same Philip is called the High Priest of Tralles below in chapter 21. (Jacobson).
4) Thus the manuscripts, as Jacobson notes, omitting the past-tense prefix (augment) of the verb, which Winer's Grammar notes often happens. (H.).
5) From the Vienna and Paris manuscripts I have restored the word "living" (original: <note>ζῶντα</note>), a word also found in the writings of Eusebius, Rufinus, and the Ancient Interpreter.

-># MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. XII. XIII. XIV.<-

...and asked Philip the Asiarch <note>original: "Philippum Asiarcham"; the Asiarch was a high-ranking provincial official responsible for overseeing religious festivals and public games</note> to release a lion against Polycarp. ### XIII. The pyre is built.

These things were carried out even more quickly than they were spoken, with the entire crowd immediately gathering wood and brushwood from the workshops and baths; the Jews especially assisted in this with a ready spirit, as is their custom <note>The author of the text reflects the historical tensions between the early Christian and Jewish communities in Smyrna</note>. ### XIV. Polycarp’s prayer.

Therefore, they did not indeed fix him with nails, but they bound him. He, with his hands placed behind his back and bound, like a noble ram chosen from a great flock for an offering, a sacrifice acceptable to God, looked up to heaven and said: "Lord God Almighty, Father of your beloved and blessed son Jesus Christ, through whom we have received knowledge of you, God of angels and powers, and of every creature, and of the whole race of the righteous who live in your sight: I bless you, because you have deemed me worthy of this day and this hour, that I might receive a portion among the number of your martyrs, in the cup of your Christ <note>original: "in calice Christi tui"; a reference to the "cup of suffering" mentioned in the Gospels</note>, unto the resurrection of eternal life, of both soul and body, in the incorruption of the Holy Spirit. For this reason, I praise you for all things, I bless you, I glorify you, along with the eternal and heavenly Jesus Christ, your beloved son, with whom to you and the Holy Spirit be glory, both now and for the ages to come. Amen."

-># MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. XV. XVI. XVII.<-
ae

### XV. Polycarp is not harmed by the fire.

When he had sent up his "Amen" and finished the prayer, the men in charge of the fire lit the flame. As a great flame blazed out, we saw a great wonder—those of us to whom it was given to see, and who were preserved to report what happened to the rest. For the fire, taking the shape of a vaulted chamber <note>original: "καμάρας εἶδος" (kamaras eidos)</note>, like the sail of a ship filled by the wind, surrounded the body of the martyr like a wall. He was there in the center, not like burning flesh, but like bread being baked, or like gold and silver glowing in a furnace. For we also perceived such a sweet fragrance <note>The author uses sensory details—sight and smell—to emphasize the divine nature of the event</note>, as if incense were breathing out its scent, or some other precious spice.

### XVI. Polycarp is pierced with a dagger.

Finally, when these lawless men saw that his body could not be consumed by the fire, they ordered a finisher <term>finisher: known as a "confector," this was a Roman official or gladiator tasked with delivering the final blow to wounded animals or condemned people in the arena</term> <note>original: "κομφέκτορα" (komphektora)</note> to go up to him and plunge in a dagger. When he did this, there came out a dove <note>original: "περιστερὰ" (peristera)</note> and a great quantity of blood, so much that it extinguished the fire; and the entire crowd marveled that there was such a difference between the unbelievers and the elect. Among these elect was the most admirable martyr Polycarp, who in our own times was an apostolic and prophetic teacher and bishop of the catholic <note>In this early context, "catholic" means "universal" or "whole," referring to the unity of the Christian church</note> church in Smyrna. For every word that he uttered from his mouth has been fulfilled and will be fulfilled.

-># THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. XVII. XVIII. XIX. XX.<-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, continuing from the previous page's description of the Christians attempting to recover Polycarp's body.</note> ...as we were about to take him from the fire. For they <note>Referring to the "envious and wicked" adversaries mentioned previously</note> did not know that we can never leave Christ—who suffered for the salvation of the whole world of those who are being saved [the blameless for the sinners], <note>original: "ἄμωμον ὑπὲρ ἁμαρτωλῶν" (amomon hyper hamartolon). ### XVIII. Polycarp’s body is burned. The Remains.

When the centurion saw the strife caused by the Jews, he placed the body in the middle of the fire and burned it, as was their custom. And so we, later on, took up his bones—more precious than costly stones and more excellent than gold—and laid them to rest in a fitting place. There, as far as it is possible for us to assemble in gladness and joy, the Lord will grant us to celebrate the "birthday" <term>birthday: "γενέθλιον" (genethlion). In early Christian tradition, the day of a martyr's death was called their "birthday" into eternal life.</term> of his martyrdom, both in memory of those who have already competed in the contest, and for the training and preparation of those yet to come.

### XIX. Praise of Polycarp the martyr.

Such is the account of the blessed Polycarp, who, together with those from Philadelphia, was the twelfth to suffer martyrdom in Smyrna. Yet he alone is remembered by everyone, so that he is talked about even by the pagans in every place. He proved himself not only a famous teacher but also an outstanding martyr, whose martyrdom everyone desires to imitate, as it happened according to the Gospel of Christ. For having overcome the unjust ruler through his endurance, and having thus received the crown of immortality, he now rejoices with the apostles and all the righteous, glorifying God the Father and blessing our Lord Jesus Christ, the savior of our souls, the governor of our bodies, and the shepherd of the universal <term>universal: "καθολικῆς" (katholikēs). Referring to the "catholic" or whole church throughout the world.</term> church.

### XX. Send this letter to the brothers.

Now, you indeed requested that the events be explained to you in greater detail; however, for the present, we have provided this summary through our brother Marc. Once you have learned these things, send the letter to the brothers further away, so that they too may glorify the Lord, who makes his choices from among his own servants. To Him who is able to bring us all by His grace and gift into His eternal kingdom, through His only-begotten Son, Jesus Christ: to Him be glory, honor, power, and majesty forever. Amen. Greet all the saints. Those who are with us greet you, as does Evarestus, who wrote the letter, with his whole household.

<header>THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. XVII. XVIII. XIX. XX.</header>
<columns>2</columns>

...as we were about to take him from the fire; they being ignorant that we shall never be able to desert Christ—who suffered for the salvation of the whole world of those who are being saved, [the blameless for the sinners] <note>original: "inculpatus pro peccatoribus"</note>—nor worship any other. For Him, as the Son of God, we adore; but the martyrs, as disciples and imitators of the Lord, we love as they deserve, because of their unsurpassable loyalty to their own King and Teacher. May it be granted to us also to become their companions and fellow-disciples.

### XVIII. *Polycarp’s body is burned. The Remains.*

When the centurion saw the strife caused by the Jews, he placed the body in the middle of the fire and burned it. And so we, later on, took up his bones—more precious than costly stones and more excellent than gold—and laid them to rest in a fitting place. There, as far as it is possible for us to assemble in gladness and joy, the Lord will grant us to celebrate the "birthday" <term>birthday: original "natalem." In the early church, a martyr's "birthday" was the anniversary of their death, marking their birth into eternal life.</term> of his martyrdom, both in memory of those who have already competed in the contest, and for the training and preparation of those yet to come [to endure the same].

### XIX. *Praise of Polycarp the Martyr.*

Such is the story of the blessed Polycarp. Although he was the twelfth to suffer martyrdom in Smyrna (counting those from Philadelphia), he alone is especially remembered by everyone, so that he is spoken of even by the heathens in every place. He was not only a distinguished teacher but also an extraordinary martyr, whose martyrdom all desire to imitate, as it was in accordance with the Gospel of Christ. For, having overcome the unjust governor through endurance, and thus having received the crown of immortality, he now rejoices with the apostles and all the righteous, glorifying God the Father and blessing our Lord Jesus Christ, the savior of our souls, the helmsman of our bodies, and the shepherd of the universal <note>original: "catholicae." In this early context, it refers to the "universal" or "whole" church throughout the world.</note> church throughout the whole world.

### XX. *Send this letter to the brothers.*

You had indeed requested that these events be explained to you in greater detail; however, for the present, we have reported them in summary through our brother Marcus. When you have read these things, send the letter to the brothers further away, so that they too may glorify the Lord, who makes a choice from among His own servants. To Him, who is able to bring us all by His grace and goodness into His eternal kingdom through His only-begotten Son Jesus Christ, be glory, honor, power, and majesty forever. **Amen!** Greet all the saints. Those who are with us greet you, as does Evarestus, who wrote this, with his whole house.

<header>THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. XXI. XXII.</header>

### XXI. The time of the martyrdom.

The blessed Polycarp bore his witness on the second day of the month of Xanthicus <note>Xanthicus was a month in the Macedonian calendar, roughly corresponding to March or April.</note>, seven days before the Kalends of May <note>original: "πρὸ ἑπτὰ καλανδῶν Μαΐων". This date is traditionally calculated as February 23rd or March 26th depending on the calendar system used.</note>, on a Great Sabbath <note>A "Great Sabbath" usually refers to a Sabbath that coincides with a major festival, such as Passover or the eve of Easter.</note>, at the eighth hour. He was arrested by Herod, while Philip of Tralles was High Priest, and Statius Quadratus was Proconsul; but while Jesus Christ was reigning forever—to whom be glory, honor, majesty, and an eternal throne from generation to generation. Amen.

### XXII. Greeting. The copyists of the letter.

We bid you farewell, brothers, as you walk according to the word of the Gospel of Jesus Christ; with whom be glory to God the Father and the Holy Spirit, for the salvation of His holy elect. Even as the blessed Polycarp bore witness, in whose footsteps may we be found in the kingdom of Jesus Christ.

These things were transcribed by Gaius from the papers of Irenaeus, a disciple of Polycarp; Gaius also lived as a fellow-citizen with Irenaeus. And I, Socrates, wrote them down in Corinth from the copies made by Gaius. Grace be with you all.

And I, Pionius <note>Pionius was a later martyr (mid-3rd century) who is credited with reviving the cult of Polycarp and preserving this text.</note>, wrote them again from the previously written copy, having searched for them after the blessed Polycarp revealed them to me in a vision <note>original: "κατὰ ἀποκάλυψιν"</note>, as I will explain in what follows. I gathered them together when they were almost worn out by time, so that the Lord Jesus Christ may also gather me with His elect into His heavenly kingdom; to whom be glory, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.

---

Chapter XXI. 1) The Smyrneans began their month of Xanthicus on the 25th day of March. (Ussher). Concerning the chronology of this chapter, Hefele wishes that Ideler be consulted, *Handbook of Chronology*, Volume I, pages 419, 430.

2) A much better Codex was used by the Chronographer of Constantinople, the author of the *Sicilian Fasti* (Easter Chronicle), who reads "April." However, the true "birthday" <term>birthday: original "natalem"; the anniversary of a martyr's death into eternal life.</term> of Polycarp is to be established as March 26th; both the calculation of the Asian year and the character of the Great Sabbath

<column-break/>

prove this, even though it is celebrated among the Latins on January 26th and among the Greeks on February 23rd. From these characteristics, it is clearly perceived that his passion occurred in the year 169 of the common Christian era, and in the ninth year of the reign of Marcus Aurelius. (Ussher). This is supported by Pagi at the year 167, numbers 3 and 4. Stieren argues for the year 161 in *On the Year of Justin’s Death*, in Illgen's *Journal for Historical Theology*, 1842, issue I, page 34. <header>THE MARTYRDOM OF ST. POLYCARP. XXI. XXII.</header>

### XXI. The time of the martyrdom.

The blessed Polycarp suffered martyrdom on the second day of the beginning of the month of Xanthicus <note>A Macedonian month roughly equivalent to April.</note>, seven days before the Kalends of May <note>original: "ante septimum Calendas Maias"; this corresponds to February 23rd in the Roman calendar, though the month names vary by region.</note>, on a Great Sabbath, at the eighth hour <note>See footnote 4 regarding the calculation of time.</note>. He was captured by Herod, during the high priesthood of Philip of Tralles and the proconsulship of Statius Quadratus, but while Jesus Christ was reigning forever—to whom be glory, honor, majesty, and an eternal throne from generation to generation. Amen!

### XXII. Greeting. The transcribers of the letter.

We bid you farewell, brothers, as you walk according to the word of the Gospel of Jesus Christ; with whom be glory to God, both the Father and the Holy Spirit, for the salvation of the holy elect; just as the blessed Polycarp suffered martyrdom, in whose footsteps may we be found in the kingdom of Jesus Christ!

Gaius, who also lived with Irenaeus, transcribed these things from the papers of Irenaeus, the disciple of Polycarp. And I, Socrates of Corinth, transcribed these from the copy of Gaius. Grace be with you all.

And after this, I, Pionius <note>A martyr of the 3rd century who reportedly recovered this manuscript.</note>, wrote these things from the aforementioned copies, after I had searched for them, and the blessed Polycarp had revealed them to me through a vision, as I shall explain in the following pages. I gathered them together when they were almost worn out by the passage of time, so that the Lord Jesus Christ may also gather me with His elect into His heavenly kingdom; to whom be glory with the Father and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen!

### VISION SECOND.

(B) I. While I was traveling toward the region of the Cumaeans <note>An ancient city near Naples, Italy, often associated with the Sibyl, a prophetess</note>, at the same time as I had gone before, I remembered the previous vision as I walked. And again a spirit took me and led me to that place where I had been before. Coming therefore to that place, I knelt and began to pray to God and to praise His name, because He considered me worthy and made known to me my former sins. And when I had risen from prayer, I saw before me that elderly woman, whom I had seen before, walking and reading a book. And she said to me: “Are you able to announce these things to God’s elect?” And I said to her: “I cannot remember such great things; but give me the book itself, so that I may copy it for myself.” Taking the book, I sat in one place and wrote everything down in order. However, I could not distinguish the writing itself by syllables <note>original: "per syllabas declinare." This refers to the difficulty of reading *scriptio continua*, where ancient texts were written without spaces between words</note>. And when I had finished the entire writing of that book, suddenly the book was snatched from my hands by someone unknown.

(B) II. After fifteen days, when I was fasting and praying much to the Lord, the understanding of the writing itself was shown to me. These things were written: 
> Your offspring <note>original: "semen tuum"</note>, Hermas, have sinned against the Lord, and they have blasphemed the Lord and betrayed their parents with great wickedness. And they have listened to those who betray parents <note>referring to children who turned their Christian parents over to authorities during persecutions</note>, and by betraying them they gained nothing for themselves. But they have added to their sins lusts and mixtures of iniquities, and—

---

I shall remain silent about the things revealed in our time. Since things are so, learned men wonder why Hermas desires "syllables," since in continuous writing <note>original: "scriptione continua"</note> not even words <note>original: "voces"</note> are found separated. But in this passage, which has been much discussed by interpreters, nothing offends the one who grasps its genuine sense. For Hermas does not seek in that book what he cannot find. He understands nothing from the book, since he is unable to read it. Now, he could not read that which he was not strong enough to divide into syllables with his eyes, and at that very moment to comprehend <note>original Greek: "$\sigma\upsilon\lambda\lambda\alpha\mu\beta\acute{\alpha}\nu\epsilon\iota\nu$" (syllambanein) - to grasp or understand</note> with his mind. Thus, he notes nothing new other than that he could not express that writing syllable by syllable, neither with his mouth, nor his eyes, nor his mind. The reading of the Palatine Codex favors this interpretation: *I could not, however, distinguish the writing itself by syllables*, whether you take the word "syllable" in its proper sense or as referring to words, as in Martial 1, 62, concerning Catullus: 
*Verona loves the syllables of the learned poet,* 
*Mantua is happy with Maro [Virgil],* 
where you would understand "syllables" to mean meters and verses.

### THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK I. VISION II. (B)

Indeed, there shall be forgiveness for all who have sinned up until this day, if they repent with their whole heart and remove all doubt <term>dubietatem: a state of wavering or hesitation in faith</term> from their hearts. For the Lord has sworn by His glory concerning His elect: if sin is still committed after the appointed day, they shall not find salvation. For the repentance of the righteous has an end <note>meaning a deadline or a limit</note>. The days of repentance are fulfilled for all the saints; but for the Gentiles <note>non-Christians or pagans</note>, repentance is open until the very last day. 

Therefore, speak to the leaders of the church so that they may direct their paths toward righteousness, that they may receive the full promise with great glory, laboring perseveringly in righteousness. And do not be doubtful in any matter, so that your journey may be among the holy angels. Blessed are you who persevere in the great tribulation that is coming, and those who do not deny their own life. For the Lord has sworn by His Son that those who have denied their Lord—those who now begin to deny Him in the coming days—are to be considered cast away from their life. However, to those who denied Him previously, God will be merciful because of His great compassion.

(B) III. But as for you, do not hold a memory of the malice <note>original: "memor sis malitiae," meaning "do not hold a grudge"</note> of your children, nor neglect your sister <note>referring again to his wife</note>, so that they may be cleansed from their sins. They shall be corrected with a just correction if you are not mindful of their wrongs; for the memory of malice works eternal death. But you, Hermas, have had many personal tribulations because of the transgressions of your household, because you did not concern yourself with them, but instead you were preoccupied with your wicked business affairs and became entangled in them. Yet you shall be saved because you did not depart from the living God.

# VISION III.

->*Concerning the structure of the triumphant church and the various classes of those who are rejected.*<-

(A) I. The vision which I saw, brothers, was as follows. When I had fasted frequently and prayed to the Lord that he would show me the revelation he promised to reveal through that old woman, <note>In the previous vision, Hermas learned that this old woman is a personification of the Church, created before all things.</note> that same night she appeared to me and said: "Since you are so eager and anxious to know all things, come into the field wherever you wish, and around the sixth hour <note>Roughly noon in the ancient Roman system of counting hours from dawn.</note> I will manifest myself to you and show you what you ought to see." I asked her, saying: "Lady, in what place in the field?" "Wherever you wish," she said, "choose a good, secluded spot." Before I had begun to speak and tell her the place, she said to me: "I will come where you wish." I went, therefore, brothers, into the field and kept track of the hours, and I came to the place where I had arranged for her to come. And I saw a couch placed there; there was a linen cushion, and over the linen, a coverlet of fine flax <term>carbasinum</term> <note>original: "carbasinum," referring to a costly, fine fabric made of Spanish or Indian flax.</note> was spread. Seeing these things placed there and no one in the spot, I began to be amazed; my hair stood on end and a kind of horror seized me, since I was alone. But having come back to myself and remembered the glory of God, I took courage; kneeling down, I confessed my sins to God again, as I had done before. Behold, she arrived there with six young men whom I had seen before, and she stood behind me and listened to me as I prayed and confessed my sins to the Lord. Touching me, she said: "Stop now praying only for your sins. Pray also for righteousness, so that you may receive a portion of it in your house." And she raised me from the spot, took my hand, led me to the couch, and said to those young men: "Go and build." After the young men had departed and we were alone, she said to me: "Sit here." I said to her: "Lady, allow the elders to sit first." "Sit as I tell you," she said. And when I wished to sit on the right side, she would not allow it, but motioned to me with her hand to sit on the left. While I was thinking about this and was sad because she did not permit me to sit on the right, she said to me: "Why are you sad, Hermas? The place on the right is for those who have already earned God's favor and have suffered for the sake of His name. But for you, much remains before you may sit with them. But as you are, remain in your simplicity, <note>In this text, "simplicity" refers to a state of moral integrity and single-minded devotion to God.</note> and you shall sit with them, as will all who have performed their works and endured what they endured."

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK I. VISION III. (A)

...for the sake of the name of God; but for the rest, there are the parts on the left. I said to her: "Lady, I see nothing." "Behold, do you not see before you a great tower being built upon the waters with bright, square stones?" For the tower was being built in a square by those six young men <note>These six young men are traditionally interpreted as the six highest angels of God.</note> who had come with her. But many thousands of other men were bringing stones. Some were drawing stones from the deep <note>Representing those who have suffered for the faith, such as martyrs.</note>; while others were carrying them from the earth and handing them to those six young men. Furthermore, they were taking them and building. Now, all those stones that were pulled from the deep they placed into the structure just as they were; for they were polished and their joints fitted perfectly with the other stones, and they were so joined one to another that their seams did not appear. And in this manner, the structure of the tower appeared as if built from a single stone. But of the other stones which were brought from the earth, some they rejected, while others they fitted into the structure. Others they cut up and threw far away from the tower. But many other stones were lying around the tower, and they were not using them for the construction. For some of them were rough; others had cracks; others were white and round, not fitting into the structure of the tower. Moreover, I saw other stones being thrown far from the tower, falling onto the path and not staying on the path, but rolling from the path into a desert place; others falling into the fire and burning; others falling near the water, yet unable to roll into the water, even though they wanted to enter the water.

The tower was being built in a square shape by six men <note>In early Christian tradition, these are often interpreted as the six primary archangels.</note> who had come with her. Another multitude of men were bringing stones: some from the depths of the foundations, some from the earth itself, and they were handing them to the six men. All the stones that were pulled from the foundations were placed into the structure just as they were; for they were suitable and matched the joints of the other stones so well, and were joined one to another so closely, that no joint between them could be seen. 

The construction of the tower appeared as if it were built from a single stone. But of the other stones that had been taken from the earth, some were rejected, some were placed in the building, and others were cut down and thrown far away from the tower. Still others lay nearby and were not used in the structure. Among these were stones that were blemished <note>original: "scabiosi," literally meaning scabby or diseased, here referring to spiritual flaws.</note> or had cracks; others had become very small or stunted, and others were white and round, but were not suitable for the building. I also saw other stones thrown far from the tower, falling onto a road but not staying there, instead rolling off into another path; others were falling into fire near the water, yet they were unable to roll into the water, even though they desired greatly to reach it.

...integrity. And they believed in pretense, and all wickedness did not depart from them. For this reason, they have no salvation, because they are not useful in the structure <note>The Latin 'structura' refers to the building of the tower, a symbol for the Church</note> on account of their wickednesses. Therefore <note>original: 'Quapropter'</note> they were cut out and cast far away because of the Lord's wrath, for they provoked him to anger. Those that had cracks are they who hold discord in their hearts against one another and do not have peace among themselves; they indeed have the appearance of peace in each other's presence <note>original: 'in praesentia'</note>, but when they depart from one another, their wickedness remains in their hearts. These are the "cracks" which the stones have. Those that are stunted <note>original: 'curti', meaning shortened or mutilated</note> are they who have believed, yet have a great portion of iniquity; for this reason they are stunted and not whole." "But what of the white and round stones, Lady, which do not fit into the structure of the tower?" Responding, she said to me: "How long will you be foolish and senseless, asking everything and understanding nothing? These are they who indeed have faith, but they also have the riches of this world. When, therefore, tribulation comes, because of their riches and their business dealings they deny the Lord." I answered and said to her: "Lady, when then will they be useful to the Lord?" "When," she said, "their riches which delight them have been circumcised <note>A metaphor for cutting away worldly attachments</note>, then they will be useful to the Lord for the building. For just as a round stone, unless it is cut and casts off something of itself, cannot become square, so also they who are rich in this world, unless their riches are circumcised, cannot be useful to the Lord. Learn first from your own case. When you were rich, you were useless; but now you are useful and fit for your life; for you yourself were once one of these stones."

** (A) VII. ** "As for the other stones that you saw cast far from the tower, rolling from the road into desert places, these are they who have indeed believed, but by their doubt they have left their true way, thinking they could find a better path. But they err and are miserable, entering into desert ways. Those that fell into the fire and were burning are they who have forever departed from the living God, and it no longer enters their hearts to repent, because of the desires of their lusts and the crimes they commit." "But who are the others that fell near the waters and could not roll into the water?" "These are they who have heard the word and wish to be baptized in the name of the Lord; but when the holiness of the truth comes to their memory, they withdraw themselves and walk again after their own wicked desires." Thus she finished the explanation of the tower. I

...But,⁹ while I was still unrighteous <note>original: 'improbus' — meaning lacking in discipline or wicked</note>, I asked her: "As for all those stones¹⁰ which were cast away and did not fit into the structure of the tower—is there repentance for them, and will they have a place in this tower?"

"They have repentance," she said, "but they cannot fit into *this* tower. They will be placed in another, much lower place; and this only after they have been tormented and completed the days of their sins. And for this reason they will be transferred, because they have received¹⁴ the righteous word. Then it will happen that they are moved out of their punishments, if the wicked works they performed arise in their hearts. But if these do not arise in their hearts¹⁶, they will not be saved because of the hardness of their hearts."

### (A) VIII.

So when I stopped asking¹ her about all these things, she said to me: "Do you wish to see anything else?"² And since I was eager to see, my face became cheerful. Looking at me, she smiled and said: "Do you see seven³ women around the tower?" "I see them, Lady," I said. "This tower," she said, "is supported by them according to the command of the Lord. Listen now to their powers. The first of them, who holds with her hand, is called *faith*; through her, the elect of God shall be saved.⁷ The second, who is tucked up <note>referring to robes gathered up to allow for work or movement</note> and acts courageously, is called *abstinence* <term>Abstinence: here meaning self-control or the power to refrain from evil</term>; she is the daughter of faith.⁸ Whoever follows her will be happy in their life, because they will abstain from all evil works. Believing that if they abstain from every evil desire, they will be heirs to eternal life."

"And the others, Lady," I said,¹¹ "who are the five?" "They are daughters of one another," she said. "One is called *simplicity*, another *innocence*, another *modesty*, another *discipline*, and another *charity* <note>original: 'caritas' — meaning divine or selfless love</note>. When you have observed the works of their mother, you will be able to keep all of them."¹²

"I wanted¹³ to know, Lady, what power each of them has." "Listen," she said: "They have equal powers, but their powers are linked to one another, and they follow one another in the order they were born. From faith¹⁵ is born abstinence, from abstinence simplicity, from simplicity innocence, from innocence modesty, from modesty discipline and charity.¹⁶ Their works are holy, modest, and upright. Whoever serves these and is strong enough to hold to their works shall have a dwelling in the tower¹⁷ with the Saints of God."

I asked her¹⁸ about the times—is the end now? But she cried out with a loud voice, saying: "Senseless man! Do you not see the tower is still¹⁹ being built?"

...be sanctified? "When, therefore, the tower has been finished and built, it reaches its end; and it will be finished soon. Do not ask me anything more. Let this reminder and the renewal of your spirits be sufficient for you and all the Saints. But these things were not revealed to you alone, but so that you may show them to everyone. ### (A) IX.
"Hear me then, children: I have nurtured you in great simplicity, innocence, and modesty, because of the mercy of God, which has dripped upon you in justice, so that you might be sanctified and justified from all wickedness and all crookedness; yet you do not wish to rest from your wicked deeds. Now, therefore, hear me: have peace with one another, look after one another, and support one another. Do not enjoy God’s creatures <note>This refers to the resources and goods of the created world.</note> all by yourselves; share them abundantly with those in need. For some, by eating too much food, bring about the weakness of their own flesh and harm their bodies. But the flesh of others, who have no food, wastes away because they do not have sufficient nourishment; and because of this, their bodies are consumed. This lack of restraint is harmful to you who have much and do not share with those who are in want. Watch for the coming judgment! You who are more prominent, seek out the hungry while the tower is not yet finished. For after the tower has been completed, you will want to do good, but you will have no place. See to it then, you who glory in your riches, lest those who are in need should groan, and their groaning ascend to the Lord, and you—with all your goods—be shut out of the tower's door. Now, therefore, I say to you who lead the church and love the seats of honor: do not be like sorcerers. For sorcerers carry their poisons in boxes, but you carry your poison and your <term>pharmakon</term> <note>original: 'pharmacum' — a Greek-derived word meaning a drug, which can be either a medicine or a poison. Here it implies a corrupting influence.</note> in your hearts. You are unwilling to cleanse your hearts and mix your minds with a pure heart, so that you may receive mercy from the Great King. Take care, children, lest these dissensions of yours rob you of your life. How do you expect to instruct the elect of God, when you yourselves lack discipline? Therefore, warn one another and be at peace among yourselves, so that I, standing before your Father, may give an account for you to the Lord."

### ->THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK I. VISION III. (A)<-

**(A) X.** And when she had finished speaking with me, those six young men <note>The six young men are understood to be the highest angels who oversee the building of the Church.</note> who were building came and carried her to the tower, and four others took up the bench and they themselves also went away to the tower. I did not see their faces because they were turned away <note>original: *aversi*</note>. As she was going, I asked her to reveal to me the meaning of the three forms in which she had appeared to me. But answering me, she said: "Concerning these things, you must ask another to reveal them to you." Now, brothers, she appeared to me in the first vision, a year ago, as very old and sitting in a chair. In the second vision, she had a youthful face, but her flesh and hair were old, and she spoke to me while standing; she was more cheerful than before. In the third vision, she was entirely younger and beautiful in appearance, except that she still had old hair; she was cheerful of face and sitting on a bench. I was very sad about these things until I could understand this vision. In a vision of the night, I saw that old woman saying to me: "Every request requires humility; fast, therefore, and you shall receive from the Lord what you ask." So I fasted for one day. That same night a young man appeared to me and said: "Why do you frequently ask for revelations in prayer? Take care, lest by asking for much you harm your flesh. Let these revelations suffice for you. Can you possibly see stronger revelations than those you have seen?" I answered him, saying: "Lord, I only ask this one thing regarding the three forms of that old woman, so that the revelation may be made complete." He answered me: "You all are not foolish; but your doubts <note>The term used here refers to "double-mindedness," a key theme in this text representing a lack of total faith.</note> make you foolish, because you do not have your heart set toward the Lord." I answered him and said: "But from you we may learn these things more accurately."

**(A) XI.** "Listen," he said, "concerning the forms which you inquire about. In the first vision, why did she appear to you as an old woman sitting on a chair? Because your spirit is quite old and already withered, and having no power because of your infirmities and the doubt of your heart. For just as the elderly, who have no hope of being renewed, expect nothing else but their final sleep; so also you, weakened by worldly business, have given yourselves over to sluggishness and have not cast your care upon the Lord. Your sense has been confused, and you have grown old in your sorrows." "I wished to know, Lord, why she sat upon a chair?" He answered: "Because every weak person sits upon a chair on account of their weakness, so that the weakness of their body may be supported. Behold, you have the explanation of the first vision."

### ->THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK I. VISION III. (B)<-

**(B) X.** Now when she had finished speaking with me, six men came, who were building the tower. And they carried her to the tower, and four others carried the bench <note>original: *scamnum*; a low seat or footstool, contrasted here with the more formal chair or throne</note>. I did not see their faces, for they were turned away. As she was going, I asked her to reveal to me the nature of the three forms in which she had appeared to me. She answered and said to me: "Regarding these things, you ought to ask me later, so that they may be revealed to you." For she appeared to me, brothers, in the first vision <term>a year ago <note>original: *annotina*; referring to a vision from the previous year</note></term> as quite elderly and sitting upon a <term>chair <note>original: *cathedra*; a formal, high-backed seat associated with teachers or authority figures</note></term>. But in the second vision, she had the face of a young person, but the flesh and hair of an older woman, and she spoke to me while standing; she was more cheerful than before. In the third vision, she appeared to me entirely young and of beautiful form; only her hair was that of an elderly person. She was completely cheerful and sitting upon a bench. Because of this, I was quite sad, wanting to understand this vision. And so I saw that same elderly woman in a vision saying to me: "Every inquiry requires humility. Believe, therefore, and you shall receive from the Lord what you seek." I fasted for one day. And that very night a young man appeared and said to me: "Since you are constantly asking for visions in your prayer, see that you do not harm your flesh by asking too much. These visions are enough for you; do not think you can see visions more powerful than these which you have already seen." I answered and said to him: "Sir, I only ask this one thing regarding the three forms of the aforementioned elderly lady, so that the vision may be made complete." He answered and said to me: "How long will you all be senseless? For your very doubts make you senseless, and because you do not have your hearts ready for the Lord." I answered him: "But from you, sir, we ought to learn these things more diligently."

**(B) XI.** "Listen," he said, "concerning the forms about which you ask. In the first vision, why did she appear to you as elderly and sitting in a chair? Because your <note>original: *vestris*; plural 'your', addressed to the community of believers</note> spirit is aged and worn out, and has no power because of your self-indulgences and your doubts. For just as the elderly, having no hope of being renewed, expect nothing else but their own falling asleep <note>original: *dormitionem*; a common early Christian euphemism for death</note>, so also you, worn out by worldly affairs, have surrendered yourselves to anxieties and have not cast your care upon the Lord; thus your understanding is blunted and you have grown old in your thoughts." And I said to him: "I wish to know, sir, why she sat in a chair." And he said to me: "Because every sick person sits in a chair because of their illness, so that the weakness of their body may be supported. There you have the meaning of the first vision."

(A) XII. “In the second vision, you saw her standing, with a youthful face and more cheerful than before <gloss>1. than the previous one</gloss>; yet she had the flesh and hair of an old woman. Listen,” he said, “to this parable. When someone is already elderly, they despair of themselves <gloss>2. concerning himself</gloss> because of their weakness and poverty, and <gloss>3. and (note: omitted in some versions)</gloss> they expect nothing else except the final day of their life. Then suddenly, an inheritance is left to them <gloss>4. to him</gloss>; hearing this, they rise up and, becoming joyful, they put on strength. They no longer lie down, but stand, and are freed <gloss>5. liberated</gloss> from their former sorrows; they no longer sit, but act with manly vigor. He shows</gloss> if you have peace among yourselves with your whole heart.”

(A) XIII. “In the third vision, you saw her younger, honorable, and cheerful, with a serene countenance <gloss>1. her face</gloss>. For just as when good news comes to someone who is grieving <gloss>2. to someone sad</gloss>, they immediately forget their sorrow and expect nothing else but the announcement they have heard, and are strengthened for the future, and their spirit is renewed <gloss>3. his spirit is renewed</gloss> because of the joy they received; so you too have received the renewal of your spirits by seeing these good things. And because you saw her sitting upon a <term>bench <note>original: *subsellium*; a low seat or footstool, here symbolizing stability</note></term>, it represents a firm position <gloss>4. it is a strong position</gloss>, because a bench has four feet and stands firmly. For even the world is held together by four elements <note>The ancient view that the world is composed of Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>. Therefore, those who have repented completely will be youthful, and those who have repented with their whole heart will be well-founded <gloss>5. established</gloss>. You have the revelation in full; ask nothing more concerning what is to be revealed <gloss>6. concerning things revealed</gloss>. If anything else is necessary, it will be revealed to you.”

-># THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK I. VISION IV. (A)<-

[The Lord sent] His [angel], who is over the beasts, whose name is Hegrin <note>The name of this angel appears only here in ancient literature and its meaning is debated; see the detailed scholarly notes below.</note>, and he shut its mouth so that it would not tear you apart. You have escaped great tribulation because of your faith, and because you did not doubt in the face of such a beast. Go therefore, and declare the mighty deeds of the Lord to His elect, and tell them that this beast is a symbol of the coming persecution. If you prepare yourselves, * you will be able to escape it <note>original: "effugere illam"</note>, if your heart is pure and without blemish, and if you serve God blamelessly for the rest of the days of your life. Cast your cares upon the Lord, and He will set them right. Believe in God, you who are doubtful, for He can do all things; He can both turn His anger away from you and send you help. Woe to those doubters who hear these words and despise them; it would have been better for them not to have been born."

(A) III. I asked her <note>Hermas is speaking to a woman who represents the Church.</note> about those four colors which the beast had on its head. But she answered me, saying: "Again, you are curious, asking about such things." And I said: "Lady, show me what they are." "Listen," she said: "The black part is the world in which you live; the fiery and bloody part signifies that this age must perish through blood and fire; the golden part is you, who have escaped this age. For just as gold is tested by fire and becomes useful, so also you who live among them <note>the people of the world</note> are being tested. Therefore, those who remain, persevere, and are proven by fire will be purified by them. And just as gold is refined and loses its dross, so you also will cast away all sadness and distress, and you will be purified to be built into the structure of the tower <note>A recurring image in Hermas where the Church is envisioned as a tower made of "living stones" (the faithful).</note>. But the white part is the age to come, in which the elect of God will live; for the elect of God will be stainless and pure unto eternal life. Therefore, do not cease speaking these things into the ears of the saints. You have here the symbol of the great coming tribulation. But if you are willing, it will be nothing. Keep in mind these things that were written before." When she had said this, she departed. I did not see where she went. Then a noise broke out, and I turned back in fear, thinking that the beast was coming.

* <note>original Greek: "you will escape the power of the wild [beast], if your heart becomes [pure]"</note>

---

<columns>2</columns>
8) [A variation reads] "of whom" in the *Vatican Palatine* manuscript. Jerome <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for translating the Bible into Latin (the Vulgate).</note>, in his *Commentary on the Prophet Habakkuk* (1:14), judges that the book of Hermas should be condemned as foolish because it writes that a certain angel named Tyri is in charge of reptiles. But that angel is called Hegrin by Hermas, not Tyri, and without a doubt the word "Tyri" in Jerome’s work must have arisen from a scribal error. Cotelerius <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (1629–1686), a French scholar of early Christian texts.</note> left us two conjectures to explain the name Hegrin: 1) Perhaps it was written as *egre*, a shorthand for the Greek word *egrēgoros* <note>original: "ἐγρήγορος"</note>, meaning "watcher" or "vigilant," which corresponds to the word *ir* <note>original Hebrew: "עיר"</note> used to signify an angel in Daniel 4:10 and 20; instead of *egre*, it was written or read as *egrin*. 2) Perhaps Hermas wrote something like this: "The Lord sent His angel, who is over the beast, whose name is the Wild One" <note>original Latin/Greek: "misit Deus angelum suum super bestiam, cui nomen est τὸ ἄγριον (to agrion)"</note>, meaning fierce. This interpretation is favored by Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata* IV, 9, p. 596), and — <meta>catchword: and —</meta>

<column-break/>

Nourrius supports him; however, Lücke (*Introduction to the Revelation of John*, p. 145, note 2) defends the former view. Compare also Ittigius, in the cited work, p. 168. Compare Revelation 9:11: "the angel Abaddon." H. <note>likely the editor's initial</note>. However, Jerome does not actually name or accuse Hermas in that passage. Rather, he says that a certain apocryphal writing foolishly tells how an angel named Tyri presides over reptiles, and similarly that specific guardian angels are assigned to fish, trees, and all wild beasts. Jerome's final words match better with the *Recognitions of Clement of Rome* (I, 45). In the *Palatine Codex*, the word is *tegri*. Perhaps you have a word derived from *thēgein* <note>original Greek: "θήγειν"</note> (to sharpen, stir up, or instigate) and *agrion* <note>original Greek: "ἄγριον"</note> (wild), coined by Hermas as a Greek-Jewish Christian in the manner of the Hebrews, but mutilated by the carelessness of scribes. I propose the reading should be **Thegrin**.

# BOOK SECOND

### WHICH IS TITLED:

->*Introduction.*<-

When I had prayed at home and had sat down upon my bed, a certain man entered with a reverend face, in the garb of a shepherd, clothed in a white cloak, with a pouch on his shoulders and a staff in his hand, and he greeted me. And I greeted him in return. Immediately he sat down beside me and said to me, “I have been sent by that venerable messenger <note>original: "venerabili nuntio"; refers to a high-ranking angel, possibly representing the authority of Christ</note> to live with you for the remaining days of your life.” And I thought that he had come to tempt me. I said to him, “Who then are you? For I know to whom I have been entrusted.” He said to me, “Do you not recognize me?” “No,” I said. “I,” he said, “am that shepherd to whom you have been entrusted.” While he was still speaking, his appearance changed. When I realized that he was the one to whom I had been entrusted, I was confused; immediately fear came over me, and I was entirely overcome with distress because I had answered him so wickedly and foolishly. But he said to me, “Do not be confused, but take courage in your soul regarding my mandates which I am about to give you. For I was sent,” he said, “so that I might show you again all the things you saw before; especially those which are useful to you. First of all, write down my mandates and the forms of the parables <term>similitudines: parables or symbolic comparisons used for teaching</term>; but the rest you shall write just as I show them to you. For this reason I command you to write the mandates and parables first, so that by reading them from time to time you may more easily be able to keep them.” I therefore wrote the mandates and parables just as he commanded me. If you hear these and keep them, and walk in them, and practice them with a pure mind, you will receive from the Lord what He has promised you. But if, after hearing them, you do not repent, but instead add to your sins, you will receive the opposite from the Lord. All these things the "Shepherd," the messenger of repentance, commanded me to write.

We gather from Tertullian’s "On Prayer," chapter 12, where this passage of Hermas is cited, that it was the custom for some to sit after finishing a prayer. Tertullian, not fully seeing the reason for this, correctly notes that Hermas’s words refer to the sequence of the narrative, not to*

### HERE BEGIN THE TWELVE MANDATES OF THE SHEPHERD.

(B) When I had prayed at home and had sat down upon my bed, a certain man entered with a dignified face, in the dress of a shepherd, wrapped in a white skin <note>likely a sheepskin cloak</note>, carrying a pouch on his shoulder and a staff in his hand, and he greeted me. And I greeted him in return, and immediately he sat down beside me and said to me: "I have been sent by that venerable messenger <note>original: "venerabili nuntio"; this likely refers to a high-ranking angel or a personification of the Holy Spirit</note> to live with you for the remaining days of your life."<sup>1</sup> For I thought that he had come to test me. I said to him: "And who are you?"<sup>2</sup> For I know the one to whom I have been entrusted. He said to me: "Do you not recognize me?" "No," I replied. And he said to me: "I am that shepherd to whom you have been entrusted." And while he was still speaking, his appearance changed. When I recognized that he was the one to whom I had been entrusted, I was immediately confused; fear entered my mind, and I was completely overcome with sorrow because I had answered him so wickedly and ignorantly. And he said to me: "Do not be confused, but take courage in your soul regarding my mandates, which I am about to give you. For I have been sent," he said, "to show you again all the things you saw before, especially those which are most useful to you. First of all, write down my mandates and the forms and parables <term>similitudines: symbolic parables or "likenesses" used for moral instruction</term>; but the rest you shall write just as I show you, so that by reading them from time to time you can more easily keep them." Therefore I wrote the mandates and parables as he commanded me. If you hear these and keep them, and walk in them, and practice them with a pure mind, you will receive from the Lord whatever He has promised<sup>4</sup> you. But if, after hearing them, you do not repent, but still add to your sins, you will receive adversity from the Lord. The shepherd, that messenger of repentance, commanded me to write all these things in this way.
