# MANDATE I.
### *On faith in one God.*

(A)* „First of all, believe that there is one God, who created and completed all things, and made all things out of nothing. He alone is infinite, containing all things but contained by none <note>original: "ipse capax universorum solus immensus est"; a theological way of saying God is the only being large enough to hold the universe, while nothing is large enough to hold Him</note>, who can neither be defined by word nor conceived by the mind. Believe, therefore, in him, and fear him, and in fearing him, possess self-restraint. Keep these things, and cast away from yourself all evil desire and wickedness, and put on the virtue of righteousness, and you shall live to God, if you keep this mandate.“

# MANDATE II.
### *On avoiding slander, and on giving alms with simplicity.*

(A) † He said to me: „Have simplicity, and be innocent; and you shall be like infants who do not know the malice that destroys the lives of men. First, speak ill of no one, nor listen gladly to one who speaks ill. Otherwise, if you listen, you will be a sharer in the sin of the slanderer; and by believing it, you too will have sin, because you believed the one speaking ill of your brother. Slander is harmful; it is a restless demon; it never rests in peace, but always remains in discord. Restrain yourself from it, and always have peace with your brother. Put on holy steadfastness, in which there are no sins, but all things are joyful; and do good from your labors. Give to all the needy simply <term>simpliciter: with a sincere heart and no hidden motives</term>, not doubting to whom you should give. Give to all; for God wishes that his gifts be given to everyone. Those who receive, therefore, shall give an account to God as to why they received, and for what purpose. Those who receive under a false pretense of need shall give an account; but he who gives shall be innocent. For as he received from the Lord, he fulfilled the ministry, not doubting to whom he should give or not give; and he performed this ministry simply and gloriously to God. Keep, therefore, this mandate, just as I have spoken to you, so that your repentance may be found simple, and it may be well with your household; and keep a pure heart.“

† <note>Greek version of Mandate II</note> Have simplicity, and become harmless, and be like infants who do not know the wickedness that destroys the salvation of men. First, do not speak against anyone, nor listen gladly to one who speaks against others;

<header>THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATES I. II. (Version B)</header>

### THE FIRST MANDATE OF THE SHEPHERD.

(B) First of all, believe that there is one God, who created and perfected all things, and made all things out of nothing. He Himself is the head of all, alone immeasurable, who can neither be defined by words nor conceived by the mind. Believe in Him, therefore, and fear Him, and having accepted that fear, maintain self-restraint. Keep these things, and you will cast away <note>original Latin "abicies": a correction for "abicis"</note> from yourself all wickedness, and you will put on every virtue of justice, and you will live to God, if you keep this mandate.

---

### THE SECOND MANDATE.

(B) He said to me: hold fast to simplicity <term>simplicitas: a state of being single-minded, sincere, and without hidden motives or guile</term> and be innocent, like infants who do not know the wickedness that destroys the lives of men. Above all, think ill of no one, nor listen willingly to him who slanders the absent. For if you also listen, you will be a participant in this; for if you agree with the slanderer and believe that which was said of the absent person, you too will be like him, and harmful toward your brother, and you will be bound by the sin of that slanderer. For it is an evil thing to defame anyone; it is a restless demon <term>daemonium: in this context, a corrupting spiritual influence or a personified vice</term>, never resting in peace, but always dwelling in discord. Therefore, keep yourself from it, and you will always be at peace among all. Put on self-control, reverence, and modesty, in which there is no offense and no wickedness, but all things are smooth and joyful. Practice goodness, and from the fruit of your labors which God gives you, provide to every needy person with simplicity, not doubting to whom you should give. Give to all; for God wants it to be given to all from His own gifts. Those who receive, however, will give an account to God as to why and for what purpose they received. For whoever receives out of compulsion or some necessity will be innocent of crime; but those who receive deceitfully will give an account. But he who gives will be guiltless, for he has performed this ministry—which he received from the Lord—simply before God. Whoever, therefore, serves so simply, lives to God. Therefore, keep this mandate, as I have told you, in your repentance, and for your household with simplicity, and let your heart be pure and unfailing before God.

<note>The following is the original Greek text for the passage regarding slander and simplicity:</note>
...otherwise, you also, by hearing, will be guilty of the sin of the one speaking evil. For slander is an evil spirit, and a restless demon, never keeping peace, but always dwelling in dissensions. Therefore, keep away from it, and you will have peace with all. But put on simplicity <note>original: ἁπλότητα (haplotēta)</note> and holiness, in which there is no evil stumbling block, but all things are smooth and cheerful.

# MANDATE III.

*On fleeing from lies, and the repentance of Hermas for his pretense.*

(A) \*Again he said to me: “Love the truth, and let every word that proceeds from your mouth be true¹; so that the spirit, which the Lord has established in your flesh, may be found to be truthful in the sight of all² men, and the Lord may be magnified, who gave the spirit to you; because God is true in every word, and there is no lie in Him. \*Those, therefore,³ who lie, deny the Lord, not returning to God the deposit <term>depositum: something entrusted to one's care; here referring to the Holy Spirit</term> which⁴ they received. \*For they received a spirit free from lies. If they return this spirit as a liar,⁵ they defile the mandate of the Lord and become deceivers.⁶ Having heard these things, I wept bitterly.⁶ When he saw me weeping, he said to me: “Why do you weep?⁷ And I said: “Because, lord, I do not know if I can be saved.” “Why?” he asked. And I said: “Because, lord, I have never spoken a true word in my life,⁷ but I have always lived in pretense, and I affirmed a lie as the truth to everyone; and no one ever contradicted me, but my word was believed. How⁸ then will I be able to live, since I have acted in this way?” And he said to me: “Your perception is indeed good and true; for it was necessary for you, as a servant of God, to walk in truth,⁹ and not to join an evil conscience with the spirit of truth, nor to cause sadness to the Holy and True Spirit of God.” And I said to him:¹⁰ “Never, lord, have I heard these words so accurately.” And he said to me: “Now you hear them; take care from now on,¹¹ so that even those things which you previously spoke falsely for the sake of your business affairs may gain credit through these current words. For those past words can also find belief,¹² if you speak the truth from now on; † and if you guard the truth, you will be able to obtain life. And whoever hears this mandate, and performs it, and turns away from lying, shall live to God.”

# MANDATE THREE.

(B) Again he says to me: Love the truth, and let all truth proceed from your mouth, so that the spirit, which the Lord established in this body, may be found truthful in the sight of all men; and in this way the Lord may be honored, who dwells within you. For indeed the Lord is truthful in all His words, and there is no lie in Him. Therefore, those who lie injure Him and begin to be defrauders of the Lord, not returning to Him the spirit entrusted <term>commendatum: a deposit or something given in trust</term> to them as they received it. For they received a spirit free from any lie. If they return this spirit as a liar, they will have to give an account; they have also defiled the command of the Lord and have become defrauders against Him. Now, when I had heard these things, I wept most bitterly. When he saw me weeping, he said: Why do you shed tears? And I said: Because, lord, I do not know if I can have salvation. And he said to me: Why? And I said: Never in my whole life have I spoken a true word, but I have always lived craftily with everyone and affirmed my lie as the truth to everyone; and no one ever contradicted me, but<sup>1</sup> credit was given to my words. How can I live, since I have behaved in such a way? And he said to me: Your perception is indeed good and true. For it was necessary for you, as a servant of God, to walk with truth, and not<sup>2</sup> to join an evil conscience to the spirit of truth, nor to injure the Holy and true Spirit. And I said: Never, lord, did I hear this. And he said to me: Now you hear it. Keep these things, so that those<sup>3</sup> which you previously did wrongly may also gain credit, provided your later deeds are approved in the truth. For if these later things are found in the truth, even those earlier things will be proven as if true, if from this time forward you take care that your speech lacks lies; and if you love the truth, you will be able to acquire eternal life for yourself. And whoever obeys this precept and refrains from every lie will live to God.

...produces a great sin. <note>original: "parit peccatum magnum"</note> But you, always be mindful of the Lord at every hour, and you will never sin. For if such an evil thought enters your heart, you commit a great sin; and those who do such things follow the path of death. Therefore, watch yourself; restrain yourself from this thought. For where chastity remains in the heart of a righteous man, an evil thought should never enter there.

And I said to him: "Lord, allow me to speak a few words to you." "Speak," he said. And I said to him: "Lord, if someone has a wife who is faithful in the Lord, and he finds her in adultery, does the man sin if he continues to live with her?" 

And he said to me: "As long as he is unaware of her sin, the man living with her is without blame. But if the husband knows that his wife has transgressed, and the woman does not repent but persists in her fornication, and the husband continues to live with her, he will be guilty of her sin and a sharer in her adultery." 

And I said to him: "What then, if the woman persists in her vice?" And he said: "Let the husband dismiss her, and let the husband remain by himself. But if he dismisses his wife and marries another, he himself commits adultery." 

And I said to him: "What if the dismissed woman repents and wishes to return to her husband? Shall she not be received by her husband?" 

And he said to me: "Indeed, if the husband does not receive her, he sins and brings a great sin upon himself; but he ought to receive the sinner who has repented—though not often. For the servants of God, there is but one repentance. <note>The "one repentance" is a central, controversial theme in the Shepherd of Hermas, suggesting a single opportunity for forgiveness for serious sins committed after baptism.</note> Therefore, for the sake of repentance, a man should not marry another after dismissing his wife. This rule applies equally to both man and woman. Adultery is not only for those who defile their own flesh; but even he who makes an idol commits adultery. <note>The author equates idolatry with spiritual adultery, a common biblical metaphor.</note> If she persists in these deeds and does not repent, withdraw from her and do not live with her; otherwise, you too will be a partaker in her sin. For this reason, it is commanded to you that you should remain single, whether man or woman; for in such a case, repentance is possible. I am not providing an excuse for these things to be done in this way, but so that the one who has sinned may sin no more. As for his previous sins, God, who has the power to grant healing, will provide a remedy, for He is the one who has power over all things."

Everyone who performs penance for their sins should indeed be received with forgiveness, but not repeatedly; for to a servant of God, only one opportunity for forgiveness through penance is granted. Therefore, the husband should not marry another after the divorce of his wife, lest he take away the opportunity for penance from the woman. This rule applies equally to both the man and the woman. Now, adultery is not only committed by the one who defiles their own flesh; but also he who does things similar to the people of this age—whom we also call heathens <note>original: "ethnicos"</note>—is himself an adulterer. Therefore, if anyone remains in such acts and does not perform penance, you shall abstain from their company. But if [you do not withdraw], you yourself will come into a partnership in their sins. For this reason, it is commanded to both the husband and the wife that if they divorce, each should remain by themselves, because in such circumstances, penance⁶ can have its place. I, however," he said, "do not give an opportunity for such an act to be carried out; but rather that he who has sinned until now might cease sinning. For regarding his previous sins, it belongs to Him who can heal all things: He who has power over all things."

"...for I understand nothing, and my heart is hardened <note>original: "obturatum," literally "stopped up" or "plugged"</note> by my former way of life; open my understanding for me, because I am greatly dulled <note>The Vatican manuscript reads "foolish" (stultus) or "stunned" (intonitus) here.</note> and understand nothing at all." And responding, he said to me: "I am the one set over repentance, and I give understanding to all those who practice repentance. Does it not seem to you that to repent is itself a great wisdom? For he perceives that he has sinned and acted wickedly in the sight of the Lord, and he remembers in his mind what he has done wrong, and he repents, and now no longer works wickedly but works for good; he humbles his soul and torments it because he has sinned. You see, therefore, that <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "poenitentia." In the early Church, this often meant a formal, public process of reconciliation after a serious sin.</note> is a great understanding." (A) III. And I said to him: "Even now, Lord, I have heard from certain teachers <note>Refers to early Christian catechists or leaders providing instruction on the faith.</note> that there is no other repentance except that one, when we went down into the water <note>A reference to baptism, commonly called the "first repentance" or "remission of sins" in the early Church.</note> and received the remission of our sins, and that we are not to sin further but to remain in holiness." And he said to me: "You have heard correctly. For those who have already believed, or are about to believe, do not have 'repentance' for sins, but rather remission <note>The author distinguishes between the total "erasing" of sins at baptism and the "second chance" of repentance granted later.</note>. For to those who were called before these days, the Lord has appointed repentance; because God knows the thoughts of all hearts and knows the weakness of men and the many-sided wickedness of the devil, by which he contrives some evil against the servants of God and maliciously lays snares for them. Therefore, the merciful Lord took pity on His own creation <note>original: "figmenti sui," literally "His handiwork" or "what He fashioned."</note> and appointed this repentance, and gave the authority over this repentance to me. And therefore I say to you: after that great and holy calling, if anyone is tempted by the devil and sins, he has <term>one repentance</term> <note>The "one penance" (una poenitentia) was a famous and rigorous doctrine in the 2nd-century Church, allowing only one single chance for reconciliation after baptismal sin.</note>."

rejoicing, and honoring the Lord at all times with gentleness. ### MANDATE VI.

->*On recognizing the two spirits <note>original: "Geniis." In this context, it refers to the "Two Angels" (one of righteousness and one of wickedness) that early Christians believed accompanied every person.</note> of every man, and the inspirations of each.*<-

(A) I. "I had commanded you," he said, "in the first mandate, to keep faith, fear, and self-restraint." "Yes, Lord," I said. "And he said: 'But now I wish to show you the powers of these mandates, so that being carefree <note>original: "ἀμέριμνος"</note>, she glorifies the Lord at all times, having nothing bitter within herself, remaining always in gentleness and quiet. This long-suffering <note>original: "μακροθυμία"</note> therefore dwells whole with those who have faith; but quick-temperedness <note>original: "ὀξυχολία"</note> is first of all folly and light-headedness, then from senselessness comes bitterness, and from bitterness comes wrath, and from wrath comes anger, and from anger comes resentment <note>original: "μῆνις"</note>. Then when it departs from the man where it dwelt, that man becomes empty of the Holy Spirit, and is finally filled with evil spirits, and is completely blinded from good understanding. Thus it happens to all who are quick-tempered. Keep yourself, therefore, from the quick-temperedness of the evil one..."

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATE VI. (B) 457

freed from all anxiety, she blesses her Lord with praises, remaining at all times without any bitterness, always composed and quiet. This equanimity <note>original: "aequanimitas"</note>, therefore, dwells with those who have full faith; but anger <note>original: "iracundia"</note> is first foolish, then flighty and senseless. From it are born imprudence and worthlessness <note>original: "vilis"</note>, from worthlessness comes animosity, from animosity fury, and from fury insanity. From this, insanity, conceived from so many evils, becomes a great and insatiable sin; and when so many evil spirits have entered into the one vessel <note>A common early Christian metaphor for the human person, containing the soul and spirit.</note> of a man, where that Holy Spirit also dwells, the narrowness of the vessel begins to be unable to contain the different spirits, and so it casts out the surplus spirits. For that most tender spirit cannot inhabit one vessel with that great [evil] spirit, nor can it endure its hardness, because it shrinks from its company. It flees, therefore, from such a man and seeks a place where it may dwell quietly and peacefully. For when it has departed from the man where it once lived, that man immediately becomes empty of the righteous spirit, and being filled with other evil spirits, he becomes unstable in his mind and is led here and there, and all his prudent thoughts are blinded and deceived. This is what happens to all who are prone to anger. Remove yourself from anger, which belongs to that evil spirit, and clothe yourself in equanimity; resist all anger and bitterness, and you will be found in holiness, which is beloved by God. See that you never lose this precept through negligence. For if you master this mandate of mine, you will also be able to keep the other precepts which I am about to tell you. I will urge you to strengthen yourself in these and to be constant in mind—and not only you, but also all others who wish to keep these things, so that they too may follow the same path.

### MANDATE VII.

->*On Fearing God and Not Fearing the Demon.*<-

### [MANDATE EIGHT.]

(B) "Every creature of God," he said to me, "is twofold; for even all abstinence <term>abstinentia: self-restraint or the act of refraining from certain behaviors</term> is twofold. [...how can I] ask anything from the Lord and obtain it, since I have committed so many sins against Him? "Do not think this way," he said, "but with your whole heart turn to the Lord. See, therefore, how destructive and cruel this doubt is, and how it uproots many from the faith, even those who are very faithful and firm. ### THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATE IX. (B)

...truly, how can you ask for or obtain anything, since you have committed so many sins? Do not think such things, but return to your Lord with all your heart, and ask Him without hesitation or second-guessing, and you will immediately recognize <note>original Latin: "cognosces" - variant "cognoscis" (you recognize) found in the Palatinus manuscript</note> His great mercy: how He does not despise you, but fulfills the desire of your soul. For God is not like humans, who remember injuries; rather, He is easily moved by prayer and has mercy on His own handiwork. Therefore, now cleanse your soul from all the vanities of this world and from those things which were commanded of you a little while ago. Ask your request from the Lord with faith, and believe that you will receive everything you have asked for, and you shall obtain it. 

But if any second-guessing enters your heart, you will obtain nothing of the things you ask. For he who second-guesses God is double-minded <term>double-minded: translating the Latin "duplici animo" and Greek "dipsychos," referring to a person whose loyalty and faith are divided</term> and insincere, and he never obtains any of the things he asks for. But those who ask for everything with full and whole faith, trusting in God, shall obtain what they request, because they do not ask with hesitation or with a calculating mind. For every insincere person will find it difficult to be saved unless they repent of this offense. 

Therefore, cleanse your soul from this sin and clothe yourself in faith, which is strong, and believe that you will obtain all your desires from God. And when any request of yours is granted more slowly by the Lord, do not grow weary because you did not obtain it in the moment <note>original Latin: "ad horam" - literally "at the hour"</note>; for perhaps either because of some trial or some error of yours that you yourself do not know, you receive what you ask for more slowly. But do not cease to persevere in asking for your soul's desire, and you will obtain it; for if you hesitate in your request, blame yourself <note>The Palatinus manuscript adds: "For if you hesitate in your request, blame yourself..."</note> and not Him who is accustomed to give. 

Again he said to me: this sin—being double-minded—is evil and foolish, and it uproots many from the faith, even though they may be faithful and strong; because this hesitation is a daughter of the devil <note>original Latin: "filia diaboli"</note> and acts very wickedly toward the servants of God. Despise it, therefore, and be superior to it, and in every act of yours...

* Cleanse your heart, therefore, from double-mindedness; put on faith, for it is strong, and believe in God, that all your requests which you ask, you shall receive. And if you ever ask a request from the Lord and do not receive it, do not be double-minded because you did not receive the request of your soul quickly; for surely because of some trial or some transgression which you are unaware of, you did not receive it. Therefore, do not cease praying for the request of your soul until you receive it. But if you grow weary and become double-minded in your asking, blame yourself and not the One who gives to you...

† Despise it [double-mindedness] therefore in every matter, putting on faith that is strong and powerful; for faith promises all things and completes all things; but double-mindedness, not trusting itself, fails in all the works which it does...

### MANDATE X.

->*On sorrow of the soul, and on not grieving the Spirit of God, who is within us.*<-

(A) I. Put away all sorrow <term>sorrow: "tristitia" in Latin, "lypē" in Greek. In this context, it refers to a state of spiritual gloom or despondency that makes a person lose heart</term> far from you; for she is the sister of doubt and of anger. "In what way, Lord," I said, "is she their sister? For it seems to me that sorrow is one thing, anger another, and doubt yet another." And he said: "Because you are foolish, you do not understand. For sorrow is the most wicked of all spirits and the worst for the servants of God; it destroys the spirits of all and torments the Holy Spirit; and yet, again, it saves." <note>The idea that sorrow "saves" likely refers to the "godly sorrow" of repentance mentioned in 2 Corinthians 7:10, though the Shepherd here focuses more on its destructive side.</note> "I," I said, "Lord, am senseless and do not understand these questions: how it can torment and then again save, I do not understand." "Listen," he said, "and understand. Those who have never sought the truth, nor inquired about the Divine Majesty, but have merely believed, are entangled in the affairs of worldly people. [And there is another, a false Prophet, who ruins the minds of the servants of God—specifically those who doubt, not those who trust fully in the Lord. These doubters come to him as if to a divine Spirit and ask him what will happen to them. And that false Prophet, having no power of the divine Spirit in himself, speaks to them according to their questions, and fills their souls with promises just as they wish. But that Prophet is empty, and he gives empty answers to empty people. For whatever is asked by vain men, he answers them with vanity. Yet he speaks some true words. For the devil fills him with his own spirit, so that he might overthrow some of the righteous.]"

(B) II. "Therefore, whoever is strong in the faith of the Lord and clothed in truth does not join such spirits but stays away from them."

<header>THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATE IX. X. (B)</header>

Clothe yourself in faith <note>original: "fidem"</note>, which is valid and strong. For faith promises all things and fulfills what it promises; but hesitation <note>original: "haesitatio"</note>, which is also double-mindedness <term>double-mindedness: "dipsychia" in Greek, meaning a state of being divided in one's loyalties or thoughts, leading to spiritual paralysis</term>, does not trust itself in any matter, and therefore it fails in every act it attempts. You see, then, that heavenly faith comes from the Lord and possesses great power; but double-mindedness is an earthly spirit from the devil and has no strength. You, therefore, must serve faith, which has power, and abstain from double-mindedness, which is without any power; and you shall live to God, both you and the rest who feel the same.

## MANDATE TEN.

(B) "Remove sorrow from yourself," he said, "for she too is the sister of double-mindedness and of wrath." "How, Lord," I said, "is she the sister of these? For to me wrath seems to be one thing, double-mindedness another, and sorrow <note>original: "tristitia"</note> another." "You are an unwise man," he said, "because you do not understand that sorrow is more wicked than all the evil spirits and is most harmful to the servants of God; and this spirit subverts a person more than any other, crushing the Holy Spirit <note>original: "sanctum spiritum exterit"</note>, and yet again, it saves." And I said to him: "Lord, I am foolish and do not understand these parables. For how can sorrow crush the Holy Spirit and then again save? I do not understand." "Listen," he said. "Those who have never searched out the truth, nor sought after divinity, but have only believed, and afterwards become entangled in the varieties of business, wealth, and the friendships of various people—being implicated in the many affairs of this world—do not understand the parables of divinity. For they are darkened by these aforementioned activities, and they perish and become useless, like fields overcome by thorns and weeds. Because they have only believed, and yet wander with their whole mind among secular activities, they fail and understand nothing at all regarding righteousness. For when they hear about righteousness, their mind is occupied with their own business, and they understand nothing at all. But those who fear the Lord and search out the truth, and diligently inquire after divinity, having their hearts set on God, understand everything that is said to them and perceive it quickly, because the fear of the Lord is in them. For where the Lord dwells, there also is great wisdom. Therefore, cling to your Lord, and you will understand all things."

(B) II. "Listen now," he said, "to how sorrow vexes the Holy Spirit and how it saves again. When a person who is double-minded attempts any...

...wants to perform an act, [and when] he has fallen away from his purpose because of the vice of his <term>double-mindedness</term> <note>original: "dipsychiae," a state of wavering faith or being "double-souled"</note>, sorrow enters into him and vexes and crushes the Holy Spirit, because he was not able to accomplish that which he wanted to do. So it is also with the quick-tempered man: when he is heavily angered by something and then retreats from his anger, he repents of the iniquity which he worked. Because he did that evil thing and begins to be sorrowful, he is seen to bring sorrow to the Holy Spirit. But this¹ sorrow is hoped to have salvation, because he performs repentance for the act which was evil. Therefore, both acts of sorrow make the Holy Spirit sorrowful. Indeed, that sorrow which comes from double-mindedness—because a person did not obtain their desire—is an unjust sorrow. However, this sorrow which comes from anger—because one did what they ought not to have done—is not a bad sorrow. Therefore, the Holy Spirit is vexed by both types of sorrow, which [are] anger and double-mindedness. Take away sorrow from yourself, therefore,² and do not hurt the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, lest He petition God and depart from you. For that Spirit, which was given by God, does not endure sorrow or such distress in this body.

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATE X. XI. (A)

Therefore, take away sorrow from yourself, and do not offend the Holy Spirit who dwells in you; lest He petition the Lord and depart from you. For the Spirit of God, which was given into the flesh, does not endure sorrow. Therefore, clothe yourself in cheerfulness, which always finds favor with the Lord; and you will rejoice in it. For every cheerful man works well, and has good thoughts, and looks down upon injustice. But the sorrowful man does evil, because he makes the Holy Spirit sorrowful, who was given to man as a cheerful spirit. And again he does evil, because being sorrowful he prays to the Lord, but does not first make <term>confession</term> <note>original: "exomologesin," which can refer to a public confession of sins or a formal prayer of praise and thanksgiving</note>, and so he does not obtain from God what he asks. For the prayer of a sorrowful man never has the power to ascend to the altar of God. And I said to him: "Lord, why does the prayer of a sorrowful man not have the power to ascend to the Lord's altar?" "Because," he said, "sorrow sits in his heart. Therefore, when the prayer of a man is mixed with sorrow, it will not allow a pure prayer to ascend to the altar of God. For just as wine mixed with vinegar does not have the same sweetness; so also sorrow mixed with the Holy Spirit does not have the same pure prayer. Therefore, cleanse yourself from this evil sorrow, and you shall live to God; and all shall live to God, who cast away sorrow from themselves and clothe themselves in cheerfulness."

### MANDATE XI.

->*That spirits and prophets are to be tested by their works; and concerning the double spirit.*<-

For what is committed to empty vessels does not overflow; rather, they fit together one with another. For the Spirit of God, which was given to this flesh, does not endure fleshly sorrow or distress. — Clothe yourself, therefore, in cheerfulness, which always has favor before God and is acceptable to Him, and delight yourself in it. For every cheerful man works good things, and thinks good things, and looks down upon...

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATE X. XI. (B)

Sorrow, when joined with prayer, does not permit a pure and clean prayer to ascend into the <term>sanctuary</term> <note>original: "sacrarium," referring to the most holy part of a temple or the presence of God</note> of God. For a man who is always sorrowful offers a weak petition to the Lord, and it cannot ascend to His sanctuary. Therefore, present yourself clean from sorrow, which is wicked, and you shall live to God—both you and all those who lack that sorrow and clothe themselves in all the cheerfulness of the Lord.

Just as in a storehouse <note>original: "apotheca"</note>, if you seal up wine or oil and place an empty jar among those vessels, and later you wish to remove the seal, you will find that jar you placed there just as empty as before; so it is with **empty prophets** <note>original: "Prophetae vacui"</note>. When they come among the spirits of the righteous, they are found to be just as they were when they arrived. [The spirit of all such men is earthly and light; it has no power at all and is full of much talk. And I said: "How then can someone distinguish between them?" "Listen," he said, "concerning both types of vessels; and just as I tell you, so you shall test the Prophet of God and the false prophet. First, test the man who has the Spirit of God; because the spirit which is from above is **quiet and humble**, and it draws back from all wickedness and the vain desires of this world. He makes himself more humble than all other men, and he does not answer when he is interrogated, nor does he answer individuals. The Spirit of God does not speak to a man whenever that man wants, but only when God wills it. Therefore, when the man who has the Spirit of God comes into the **assembly of the righteous** <note>original: "ecclesiam iustorum"</note> who have faith in God, and prayer is offered to the Lord, then the holy messenger of divinity fills that man with the Holy Spirit, and he speaks to the crowd just as God wills. In this way, the spirit of divinity is recognized in whoever the spirit of divinity speaks. Listen now also concerning the earthly spirit, which is empty, foolish, and has no power. First, this man is merely *thought* to have a spirit; for he exalts himself and wishes to have the **first chair** <note>original: "primam cathedram," a seat of authority or honor</note>. He is bold and talkative, he lives in luxury and many pleasures, and he accepts **payment** for his divination. Indeed, if he does not receive payment, he does not divine. Is it possible for the Spirit of God to receive payment and divine? It is not fitting for a Prophet of God to do such things]. You have the characteristics of both—

<meta>This page continues the Eleventh Mandate of the Shepherd of Hermas from page 474. It further develops the criteria for distinguishing between a true prophet, who is filled with the Holy Spirit and acts with humility, and a false prophet, who is "empty," seeks payment, and avoids the assembly of the righteous.</meta>

<page-num>475</page-num>
->## THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATE XI. (B)<-

...they do not go to them at all. But whoever is **double-minded** <note>original: "dipsychi"; refers to those wavering in faith</note>, drawing lots just like the pagans, and frequently performing penance while remaining in their divine pursuits without any real improvement, they only acquire greater sins for themselves by serving an empty superstition. For anyone who questions a prophet about any specific action is empty of truth and is shameless. Every spirit given by God is not questioned, but having the power of divinity, it speaks all things of its own accord, because it comes from above, from the power of the Holy Spirit. 

But this spirit, which responds to questions according to the desires of individual men, is earthly and light and lacks power; it does not speak unless it is questioned. "How then, Lord," I asked, "does a person know which of them is a prophet and which is a false prophet?" "Listen," he said, "concerning both. You shall know the prophet by his speech; but the **false prophet** <note>original: "pseudoprophetam"</note>, who does not have the divine spirit, you shall test by the conduct of his life. 

For the prophet who has the divine spirit from heaven is gentle, modest, and humble. He possesses a quiet and orderly wisdom. He restrains himself from all wickedness and the vain pleasures of this world. He makes himself humbler than all other men, and he asks nothing at all. He even speaks of secret things. However, it is not within a man’s power for the spirit to speak whenever he wishes; rather, the spirit speaks only when God wants him to speak. 

Therefore, when that man who has the divine spirit enters into an **assembly** <note>original: "concilium"; a gathering of the faithful</note> of good men who have faith in the divine spirit, and a petition is made to God by that gathering, then the messenger of that prophetic spirit who rests upon him fills the man. Being filled with the Holy Spirit, he speaks to the crowd just as the Lord commands. This is how the Holy Spirit is made manifest. 

Now, these are the things that pertain to recognizing the power of that Holy Spirit. Listen now also concerning the earthly spirit, which is light, lacks power, and is full of folly. First, that man who wishes to be seen as full of the divine spirit exalts himself and desires the **chief seat** <note>original: "principatum cathedrae"; a position of authority or honor in the church</note>. He is arrogant, shameless, and talkative; he lives in great luxury and many delights. He accepts wages for his profession, and if he does not receive them, he stays silent. But a prophet who has the Holy Spirit does not accept wages; for it does not befit a prophet of God to do such things. 

Where prophets accept payment, the spirit is earthly. Such a person does not approach an assembly of proven men; rather, he joins himself to evil and vain people. He operates in corners and deludes them with his speech, talking according to the desires of their own will, giving empty answers to empty people. For an empty vessel, when joined with others equally empty, is not shattered but agrees with them in its placement. 

But when that same man comes into a gathering of proven men who have the spirit of divinity, and prayer is offered by them, that man is found to be empty. The earthly spirit that is in him flees from him in terror, and he becomes mindless and totally broken, unable to speak at all. For if you store old wine in a **cellar** <note>original: "apotheca"</note> and place an empty vessel among the full ones, later, when you empty that cellar, you will find the vessel you placed there just as empty as before. So it is with the prophets who are empty; when they come among those who have the Holy Spirit, they are found to be just as they were...

<page-num>476</page-num>
->THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK II. MANDATE XI, XII. (A)<-

...the life of the Prophets. Therefore, test the man who says he has the Holy Spirit by his life and his works. But you, believe the spirit coming from God, which has power. But do not believe the empty earthly spirit, because it is from the devil, in whom there is neither faith nor power. Listen then to a comparison that I am going to tell you. Take a stone and throw it toward heaven; or again, take a water-siphon <note>original: "siphonem"; a pump or tube used to eject water</note> and spray it toward heaven; and see if you can pierce the heaven. "How, Lord," I said, "can these things be done? For both things you have mentioned are impossible." "Just as these things are impossible," he said, "so the earthly spirit is without power and without effect. Now, understand the power coming from above through this comparison. Hail is a very small grain; yet when it falls upon a person’s head, how much pain it causes! Or again, look at a drop of water that falls from a roof tile to the ground and wears a hole in a stone. In the same way, the smallest things that fall from above onto the earth have great power. Therefore, join yourself to the one who has power, and withdraw from that empty one."

### MANDATUM XII.

->*Concerning double desire. That God’s commandments are not impossible, and the devil is not to be feared by believers.*<-

(A) I. He said to me again: <gloss>original Greek: "Remove from yourself all evil desire, put on good and holy desire. For having put on this desire, you will hate the evil desire."</gloss> "Remove all evil desire from yourself, and clothe yourself in good and holy desire. For once you are clothed in good desire, you will hate evil desire and restrain it as you wish. For evil desire is dreadful and difficult to tame. <gloss>original Greek: "For wild desire will fall into these things, into grief; if one is not wise, he is consumed by it terribly."</gloss> It is truly terrifying and wild, and in its ferocity, it consumes people; especially if a servant of God falls into it, and unless he is wise, he will be consumed by it most terribly. It consumes those who do not wear the clothing of good desire, entangles them in the affairs of this world, and delivers them to death." "What, Lord," I asked, "are the works of evil desire that deliver people to death? Show them to me so that I may withdraw from them." "Listen," he said, "to the works in which evil desire delivers the servants of God to death."

(A) II. First of all is evil desire: to covet another's wife, or for a woman to covet another's husband, and to crave luxuries.

...come, they will be of such a kind. You now have the way of life for both types of prophet. Therefore, test those who call themselves "staffs of the Holy Spirit" <note>original: "spiritus sancti baculos"; likely meaning instruments or vessels of the Spirit</note> by their lives and their human deeds. ### [THE TWELFTH MANDATE]

(B) He said to me: "Take away from yourself every desire for evil things, and clothe yourself in desire that is good and holy. For if you are clothed in that good desire, you will hate every evil desire, and you will arrive at what is good, just as you wish. For evil craving is wild <note>original: "agrestis"; meaning untamed or savage</note> and is difficult to tame, because it is cruel and violently consumes men with its ferocity—especially if it falls upon a servant of God. If one is not prudent, he is cruelly consumed by it. It destroys those who are not clothed in the desire for holiness, but are instead tangled in the vices of this world. These people it delivers over to death." "What then, Lord," I asked, "are the deeds of that evil craving which delivers men to death? Show them to me, so that I may keep away from them." "Listen," he said, "to the acts through which a wicked will brings the servants of God to death."

(B) II. First of all is the desire for another's wife, or a husband’s license <note>referring to marital infidelity or lack of restraint</note> arising from an abundance of wealth and many daily, lavish, and unnecessary meals, and other—

...forget about riches, the abundance of unnecessary foods, great drunkenness, and many luxuries. For many luxuries are foolish, and many pleasures are unnecessary for the servants of God. Therefore, this evil desire is harmful and deadly, for it delivers the servants of God over to death. Indeed, this desire is from the devil. Whoever, therefore, draws back from evil desire shall live to God. But whoever is subject to evil desire shall die forever; for this evil desire is death-bearing. You, therefore, must clothe yourself in the desire of justice, and being armed with the fear of the Lord, resist evil desire. For the fear [of the Lord] dwells within good desire. You will obtain the victory and be crowned for it, and you will attain good desire; then you will hand over the victory you have received to God, and you will serve Him by working just as He wishes. *If, however, you serve good desire and are subject to it, you will be able to master evil desire, and it will be subject to you, just as you yourself wish.’

(A) III. "I would wish <note>Latin: vellem</note> to know, Lord, in what way I ought to serve good desire." "Listen," he said: "have the fear of God and faith in God, love the truth, cherish justice, and do what is good. By performing these works, you will be a proven servant of the Lord, and you will serve God; and all who serve good desire shall live to God." When these twelve mandates were completed, he said to me: "You have these mandates; walk in them, and exhort those who hear them to perform repentance, so that their repentance may become pure for the remaining days of their lives. And fulfill this ministry which I give to you diligently; you will obtain much fruit and find favor with all who repent and believe your words. For I am with you, and I will compel them to believe." And I said to him: "Lord, these mandates are great and magnificent, and they are able to gladden the heart of the person who is able to keep them. But I do not know, Lord, if these mandates can be kept by a human being." *He said to me: "You will keep these mandates easily, and they will not be hard; but if you set it in your heart that they cannot be kept by a human, you will not keep them. But now I say to you: if you do not keep these mandates and instead neglect them, you will not be saved, nor will your children, nor your house; because you have already judged that these mandates cannot be kept by a human."

(A) IV. He spoke these things to me very angrily <note>original Latin: "iracunde"</note>, so much so that he terrified me greatly. For his appearance had changed, so that a man could not endure his anger. Turn yourselves to the Lord God, and leave behind the devil and his pleasures, because they are evil, bitter, and impure; and do not fear the devil, because he has no power over you. For I, the messenger of power <note>The "Messenger of Power" refers to the Shepherd himself, acting as God's authorized representative</note>, who rules over him, am with you. The devil creates fear, but his fear is empty. Therefore, do not fear him, and he will flee from you.”

(A) V. And I said to him: “Lord, hear me speaking a few words to you.” “Speak,” he said. “A man,” I said, “certainly desires to keep the commandments of God, and there is no one who does not ask the Lord that he might be able to observe His mandates; but the devil is hard, and by his power, he dominates over the servants of God.” And he said: “He cannot dominate over the servants of God who believe in the Lord with all their hearts. The devil can struggle against them, but he cannot conquer them. For if you resist him, he will flee from you in confusion. For whoever is not full of faith fears the devil as if he had power. The devil tests the servants of God, and if he finds them empty, he destroys them. For just as a man, when he has filled his <term>amphoras</term> <note>large ceramic storage jars used in antiquity for wine or oil</note> with good wine, and among those jars he puts a few that are half-full, and he comes to test and taste the jars, he does not test the full ones; for he knows that they are good; but he tastes the half-full ones, lest they have turned sour, for half-full jars quickly turn bitter and lose the flavor of the wine; so also the devil comes to men who are servants of God to test them. Those who are full of faith resist him bravely; and he departs from them, because he has no place to enter. Then he goes to those who are not full of faith, and because he has a place, he enters into them, and does whatever he wants to them, and they become his servants.”

(A) VI. “But I, the messenger of repentance, say to you: do not fear the devil. For I have been sent to be with you, whoever of you shall perform repentance with your whole hearts, so that I may strengthen you in faith. Believe...”

Indeed, if you later wish to return to your city, you will be excluded from it and not received if you have departed from its law. Look to it then, as one living here as a foreigner <note>original: "peregrinus"; refers to the concept of Christians as temporary residents on Earth whose true citizenship is in Heaven</note>, that you prepare no more for yourself than what is necessary and sufficient for living. Be ready so that when the master of this city <note>The "master" here represents worldly authorities or the spirit of the age</note> wishes to expel you for not following his laws, you may depart and come to your own city, where you may follow your own law with joy and without harm. 

Therefore, you who serve God and have Him in your hearts: do His works, mindful of His commandments and the promises He made to those who believe in Him and keep His word. Instead of buying fields, "redeem" souls from their distress as much as you are able. <note>original: "animos de necessitatibus redimite"; a call to use money to free others from debt or poverty rather than for personal investment</note> Care for widows and orphans; do not turn away from them. Spend all your wealth and resources on these kinds of "fields" and "houses," because this is why you received riches from God. The Lord made you wealthy for the very purpose of performing these ministries. It is much better to purchase such houses and fields, for you will find them waiting for you in your own city when you enter it. These joys are good and cheerful, free from sorrow and fear. Do not, therefore, crave the luxuries of foreign nations, for they are not fitting for the servants of the Lord; instead, practice your own kind of abundance in those things that bring true joy. Do not commit adultery, nor touch what belongs to another, nor even desire it; for it is a harmful thing to covet what is not yours. Rather, focus on your own work, and you shall find salvation.

You see, then, that the elm also bears fruit—not less than the vine, but even more. # THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDES II. III. (A)

...lying on the ground, it gives little and very poor fruit. <note>original: "in terra exiguum et pessimum fructum dat"; referring to a vine that has no support and thus rots on the ground</note> This similitude, therefore, is applied to the servants of God: to the poor man and the rich man. I responded, saying: "Lord, explain this to me." "Listen," he said: "The rich man has wealth, but toward the Lord he is poor; for he is distracted <note>original: "distrahitur"; pulled in different directions by his possessions</note> by his riches, and his prayer to the Lord is very small. What prayer he does have is weak and lacks power. But when the rich man provides for the poor man those things which he needs, the poor man prays to the Lord for the rich man, and God grants the rich man all good things. This is because the poor man is rich in prayer, and his prayer has great power before the Lord. Then, the rich man provides all things to the poor man, because he perceives that the poor man is heard by the Lord; he provides for him more gladly and without hesitation, taking care that he lacks nothing. The poor man gives thanks to God for the rich man, because they both perform their work <note>original: "opus"; referring to their mutual spiritual and material duties</note> from the Lord. Among men, the elm tree is not thought to bear fruit, and they do not know or understand that if it is joined to the vine, the vine yields a double harvest—both for itself and for the elm. In the same way, the poor, praying to the Lord for the wealthy, are heard, and the riches of the wealthy are increased because they provide for the poor from their own wealth. Thus, both become partners in good works. Whoever does these things will not be abandoned by the Lord and will be written in the Book of Life. Happy, then, are those who possess wealth and yet realize that they are enriched by the Lord; for he who realizes this will be able to perform some service <note>original: "administrare"; to manage or minister their wealth for others</note>."

### SIMILITUDE III.

->*Just as in winter green trees cannot be distinguished from dry ones, so in this age the righteous cannot be distinguished from the unrighteous.*<-

(A) He showed me many trees that had cast off their leaves, which appeared to me to be dry <note>original: "aridae"; withered or dead</note>; for they all looked the same. And he said to me: "Do you see these trees?" "I see them, Lord," I said, "they all look like they are dry." Answering me, he said: "These trees are a likeness of those who live in this age." I responded, saying: "Lord, why are they like dry trees?" "Because," he said, "in this age, neither the righteous nor the unrighteous are recognized, but are all similar. For this age is winter to the righteous, because they are not recognized while living among sinners. Just as in winter all trees are similar after shedding their leaves and it cannot be known which are dry and which are green, so in this age neither the righteous nor the unrighteous are recognized, but all appear the same."

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDES II. III. (B)

Therefore, this parable <note>original: "similitudo"; a story using a physical analogy to explain a spiritual truth</note> is set forth regarding the servants of God—the poor and the rich. "In what way, Lord?" I asked, "show me." "Listen," he said. "The rich man certainly has wealth, but toward the Lord he is poor. For, being drawn away by his riches, he possesses only a very small prayer toward the Lord, and what he has is sluggish and foolish <note>original: "inertem et fatuam"</note>, possessing no power with the Lord. But when the poor man is refreshed by the rich man, and the things he needs are provided to him, the rich man surely believes that if he works for the poor man, he will be able to find a reward for his work with God. For he understands that the prayer of the poor man is blessed, and has great power in reaching God. Therefore, the rich man provides all things to the poor man without hesitation, and the poor man, having been supplied with the necessities for his living, gives thanks to God for the one who gave to him. Just as the rich man hastens for the poor man, so that he lacks nothing in all his life, so also the poor man prays for the rich man. Both, therefore, are engaged in the work. For one works through prayer, in which he is blessed, and causes a reward to be returned from the Lord. Likewise, the rich man, from these things which he received from the Lord, provides to the poor man without hesitation. This too is a great work and acceptable to the Lord, because the rich man understood and performed the work of the Lord for the poor man. From the gifts of the Lord he acted and ministered, and rightly completed his ministry. Among men, therefore, the elm tree is not thought to bear fruit, and they do not know nor understand that when there is a drought, the elm, having water, nourishes the vine; and the vine, possessing a perennial supply of water, gives double fruit, both for itself and for the elm. So also the poor, approaching the Lord with their prayers on behalf of the wealthy, increase their riches; and in turn, the wealthy, providing for the poor whatever they need, fill their souls. Both, therefore, have been made partners in a just work. Whoever, then, shall do these things, they shall not be deserted by God, but shall be inscribed in the book of the living. Happy are they who possess wealth and sense how they are enriched by the Lord. For those who feel this will be able to perform some good work."

# SIMILITUDE IV.

*Just as in summer living trees are distinguished from dry ones by their fruit and green leaves, so in the world to come the righteous differ from the unrighteous in their blessedness.*

(A) He showed me again¹ many trees, some of which were putting out leaves, while others were dry. And he said to me: "Do you see these² trees?" I answered: "I see, Lord, that some are dry, and others are leafy."³ "These trees," he said, "which are green, are the righteous who are to inhabit the world to come.⁴ For that future world is summer to the righteous, but winter to the sinners. When, therefore, the mercy of the Lord shines forth,⁵ then those who serve God will be revealed, and they will be plain to everyone. For just as in summer⁶ the fruit of every tree appears and is revealed, so also the deeds of the righteous will be revealed and will be evident,⁷ and all will be restored, cheerful and rejoicing, in that world. But the foreign⁸ nations—namely, the sinners—will be found dry and without fruit in that world, just like the dry trees you saw; they will be burned like dry wood, and it will be made clear that they acted wickedly throughout the whole time of their lives. They will be burned for this reason: because they sinned and did not perform penance for their sins. But the other nations will also be burned because they did not acknowledge God⁹ their creator. You, therefore, produce good fruit, so that in summer your fruit may be recognized. Abstain from many affairs,¹⁰ and you will commit no sin. For whoever engages in many affairs commits many sins, because they are bound¹¹ by their business and do not serve God. For how can a person who does not serve God ask for and receive anything from God? Those who serve God¹² ask for and receive their heart's desires. But if someone handles only one business,¹³ they will be able to serve God; for their mind is not alienated from the Lord,¹⁴ but they serve God with a pure mind. If you do this, you will be able to have fruit in the world¹⁵ to come; and all who do these things will bear fruit."

But if someone performs one single work, they will also be able to serve the Lord. For their mind will not be turned away from the Lord, but they will serve Him with a pure mind. If you do these things, you will be able to have fruit in the world to come; and you and all who do these things will have the fruit of life."

The spiritual sense refers to the same thing as the watches and stations in the Roman army or navy: "A single sailor of the perpetual station lies in the boat day and night." ## II.
"Listen, therefore, to a parable <note>term: *similitudo*. A story or analogy used to illustrate a spiritual truth, similar to the parables in the Gospels.</note> which I am about to tell you regarding fasting. A certain man, who had a farm and many slaves, planted a vineyard in a portion of it. He chose a slave whom he held to be most faithful and highly regarded. As he was about to go abroad, he assigned that vineyard to him, commanding that he should tie the vines to stakes; he promised him freedom if he performed his command diligently. Indeed, he did not command him to do anything else in the vineyard. And when the master had set out abroad, the slave completed everything the master had commanded. When he had tied the vines to stakes and noticed <note>The Palatine manuscript uses the infinitive "to notice."</note> that it was filled with weeds, he began to think to himself, saying: 'I have completed these things which my master commanded me. Now I will also dig this vineyard so that it may be more beautiful; once the weeds are pulled out, it will give more fruit, no longer being choked by them.' Then he began and dug out all the weeds that were in it. Once they were pulled out, that vineyard began to be most beautiful and flourishing, no longer choked by weeds. ...that one is the Son of God. The vineyard, moreover, is the people whom <note>The Latin text here uses the masculine "quem," referring to the people as a collective body.</note> he himself preserves. **(A) VI.** "Listen," he said, "the Son of God is not placed in a servant’s condition, but in great power and authority." And I said: "How, lord? I do not understand." "Because," he said, "to those whom he delivered to his Son, the Son appointed messengers to preserve each of them; he himself, however, worked very hard and suffered much to abolish their sins. For no vineyard can be dug without labor and pain. Therefore, having deleted the sins of his people, he himself showed them the paths of life, giving them the law which he had received from the Father. You see," he said, "that he is the lord of the people, having received all power from his Father. But why did the Lord take the Son and the good angels into council regarding the inheritance? Because that Holy Spirit, which was created first of all, <note>This reflects an early Christian "Spirit-Christology" where the pre-existent Holy Spirit is closely identified with the Son.</note> goes as a messenger, having been infused into a body in which God might dwell. For his understanding <term>intellectus</term> <note>Referring to the divine mind or purpose.</note> placed it in a body as it seemed good to him. This body, therefore, into which the Holy Spirit was led, served that Spirit, walking rightly in modesty and purity, and did not defile the Spirit at all. Since that body had obeyed the Holy Spirit at all times, and had labored with it rightly and purely, and had never succumbed; that body, though it lived in a servant's manner, having been weary, yet having stood bravely with the Holy Spirit, was received by God. This powerful course pleased God; because he was not defiled on earth, he was able—

### (B) VI.

"Listen," he said. "The Son of God is not placed in a servant's condition, but in great power and authority." And I said: "How, lord? I do not understand." And he said to me: "Since God planted the vineyard—that is, he created the people—and delivered them to his Son, and the Son of God appointed messengers to preserve each one; he himself, however, labored greatly and suffered much to wipe away their sins. For no vineyard can be dug without pain or labor. Having suffered, therefore, for the sins of his people, he himself showed the people the way of life by giving them the law, which he heard from the Father. You see," he said, "that he is the lord of the people, having received all power from his Father. And listen now to why the lord invited the Son and the honorable messengers into the council regarding the inheritance. That Holy Spirit, which was created pure above all <note>This passage reflects early Christian 'Spirit Christology,' which explored the relationship between the Holy Spirit and the human body of Jesus.</note> in a body in which it might dwell, God founded and established as a chosen body, which pleased him. This body, therefore, into which the Holy Spirit was led, obeyed the same Spirit, walking rightly with modesty and chastity, and did not defile the same Spirit at all. Therefore, since this body had obeyed the same Spirit rightly and chastely, and having been exhausted by every labor, it did not succumb, but was preserved manfully and bravely by the same Spirit, it was approved by God and received together with the Holy Spirit. "For those earlier things," he said, "committed through ignorance, God alone is able to provide a remedy; for all power belongs to Him. But now, guard yourself; and since the Lord is almighty and merciful, He will give a remedy for previous faults if in the future you do not defile your body and spirit. For both are partners, and one is not polluted without the other. Therefore, keep both pure, and you will live to God."

### THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDE VI. (B)

...[substance], but feeding in one place; these are those who gave themselves over to delights and pleasures, yet spoke nothing unspeakable <note>original: *nefandi*</note> against the Lord. These therefore, though corrupted, have fallen away from the truth, and thus they still have the hope of life stored up in repentance. For a **falling away** <term>defectio|A spiritual lapse or backsliding that is not yet final.</term> has some hope of restoration; but death is held forever in destruction. And when we had gone forward a little, he showed me a **great shepherd**, appearing like a rustic figure, dressed in a white goat-skin, carrying a bag on his shoulder and a staff in his hand, knotty and exceedingly hard, and a large whip. Moreover, he had a bitter and savage look, so that he could even be dreaded. This shepherd received from that young shepherd those sheep which were indeed conducting themselves in delights, but were not exulting. And he drove them and sent them into a certain steep and thorny place, full of snares <note>original: *dolisque*</note>, to the point that they could not untangle themselves from the thorns and briars, but being entangled there, they were feeding. They were experiencing thorns and briars and heavy tortures, and he drove them here and there, nor did he give them any rest, nor did he permit them to stop in any place.

---

(b) III. When I saw them being thus whipped and experiencing miseries, I grieved for them, because they were so greatly tormented and no rest was given to them. I say to that shepherd who was with me: "Who is this shepherd, sir, so implacable and bitter, who is in no way moved by the suffering of these sheep?" And he said to me: "This shepherd," he said, "is indeed a messenger <note>original: *nuntius* / *aggelos* (angel)</note> of the righteous, but he is placed in charge of punishment. To him, therefore, are delivered those who have wandered away from God and served the desires and pleasures of this world. He therefore punishes them, just as each of them deserved, with various cruel punishments." "I wish, sir," I said, "to know these various punishments, of what kind they are." ["Hear," he said: "these various punishments and torments are"] those which men experience daily in their lives—

---

* Seeing them thus being whipped and suffering, I was grieved for them, because they were being so tormented, and had no relief at all. And I say to the angel speaking with me: "Lord, who is this shepherd, so uncompassionate and bitter?" And he says to me: "This is the **angel of punishment**; he is one of the righteous angels, but appointed over punishment. He therefore receives those who have wandered away from God, and walked in their own desires; and he punishes them, as they are worthy, with terrible and various punishments." I say to him: "I would like to know, Lord, these various punishments, of what sort they are." "Hear," he says: "the various punishments and torments are the torments of daily life."

### THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDE VI. (A)

...they suffer daily in their lives <note>original: *in vita sua*</note>. For some suffer losses, others poverty, others various hardships <note>original: *acrimonias*</note>; some suffer instability, others endure insults from those who are unworthy of them, and many other trials and troubles. For many, being unstable in their counsel, attempt many things, and nothing succeeds for them; and they say that they have no success in their actions. The things they did wickedly <note>original: *nequiter*</note> come back to them, and they blame the Lord. Therefore, when they have endured every affliction and every trouble, then they are handed over to me <note>The speaker here is the Angel of Punishment</note> for good correction, and they are strengthened in the faith of the Lord, and for the remaining days of their lives they serve the Lord with a pure mind. And when they begin to repent of their sins, then their own works, in which they wickedly occupied themselves, rise up into their hearts <note>original: *praecordia*</note>; and then they give honor to God, saying that He is a just judge, and that they have deservedly suffered everything according to their deeds. But for the future, they serve God with a pure mind, and they have success in all their affairs, receiving from the Lord whatever they ask. And then they give thanks to the Lord that they were delivered to me; and they no longer suffer any cruelty."

(A) IV. I said to him: "Even now, sir, show me." "What are you asking?" he said. I said to him: "Are those who depart from the fear of God tortured for the same length of time that they enjoyed false sweetness and pleasures?" He said to me: "They are tortured for that same length of time." And I said to him: "Then they are tortured for a very short time; for those who perceive pleasures in such a way that they forget the Lord ought to suffer seven times the amount of punishment." He said to me: "You are foolish, and you do not understand the power <note>original: *virtutem*</note> of this punishment." And I said: "If I understood it, sir, I would not ask you to show me." "Listen," he said, "to how great the power of both is—of the sweetness and of the punishment. One hour of sweetness is finished in its own space of time; but one hour of punishment possesses the power of thirty days. Whoever, therefore, enjoys deceptive sweetness and pleasure for one day, and is tortured for one day, that day of torture will be worth the space of a year. Thus, for as many days as someone enjoys pleasure, he is tortured for that many years. You see, therefore," he said, "that the time of worldly sweetness and pleasure is small, but the time of punishment and torments is greater."

<column-break/>

For when they depart from God, thinking they are in rest and wealth, then they are punished: some by being fined, others by suffering want, others falling into various illnesses, some in instabilities, others being insulted by those who are beneath them <note>original: *ἐλαττόνων*, 'lesser' or 'inferior' persons</note>, and by various other actions. For many, being unstable in their counsels, set their hands to many things, and nothing at all succeeds for them; and they are frustrated, and they do not know that it is because of the evil things they did that they do not prosper. And finally, they blame <note>original Greek reconstruction: *αἰ[τιῶνται]*</note> the Lord, and they do not endure to turn back and serve God in a pure heart for the rest of their days. But if they repent and come to their senses <note>original: *ἀνανήψωσι*, literally 'sober up' or 'become sober again'</note>, then they understand that it was because of their evil works that they did not prosper; and so they glorify the Lord, because He is a just judge, and they suffered justly, and were disciplined according to their actions.

<summary>This page explains the "mathematics of the soul" according to the Angel of Punishment: the intense spiritual toll of sin far outweighs the brief duration of worldly pleasure, with one day of indulgence resulting in a year of corrective suffering. It describes how earthly misfortunes—like poverty, illness, and failure—are often divine disciplines intended to lead a person back to a pure-hearted service of God.</summary>

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDE VI. (B)

...they suffer. For some are punished with financial losses, others with poverty, others with various illnesses, and some with mental instability. Others, enduring insults from people who are beneath them, are worn down by many inconveniences; having become unstable in their purpose, they plan many things but bring nothing to fruition. They lead themselves on, making no progress in their actions <note>original: *in actibus suis nihil proficientes*</note>; nor does it occur to them why they have acted so wickedly. Furthermore, they even blame the Lord God when they have suffered every kind of vexation and trouble. Then they are handed over to me <note>The speaker is the Angel of Punishment, whose role is to bring the sinner to a point of realization through hardship</note> for proper correction, and they are strengthened in the faith of the Lord. And for the remaining days of their lives, they serve the Lord with a pure mind once they have begun to perform penance for their sins. Then their own works, in which they occupied themselves wickedly, rise up in their hearts <note>original: *praecordiis* — literally the diaphragm or internal organs, considered the seat of emotions and conscience</note>; and then they give honor to God, saying that He is a just judge, and that each one has deservedly suffered everything according to his deeds. For the rest of their time, they serve the Lord with a pure mind and have success in all their affairs, receiving from the Lord whatever they have asked. And then they give thanks to God that they were thus handed over to me, and they no longer suffer anything cruel.

### (B) IV.

I said to him: "Even now, sir, demonstrate this to me." And he said to me: "What do you still inquire about?" And I said: "Sir, tell me, if those who fall away from the fear of God are tortured for the same length of time as they misused for the sweetness and pleasure <note>original: *dulcedinem ac voluptatem*</note> of the age." He said to me: "They are tortured for that same length of time." And I said: "That is a very short time, sir, to be tortured, when it is necessary for those who thus indulge in pleasures and forget the Lord to suffer seven times the amount of punishment." And he said to me: "You are foolish, and you do not understand the power of this punishment." And I said: "Sir, if I understood it, I would not ask you to show it to me." "Listen," he said, "to how things are. One hour of sweetness is finished in its own span; but one hour of punishment possesses the force of thirty days. Whoever, therefore, has misused sweetness and pleasure for one day—and there are twelve hours in one day’s span <note>The text calculates based on a 12-hour daylight period</note>—then his torture would be for the span of a year. Therefore, for as many days as someone has perceived pleasure, he is tortured for that many years. You see, therefore, that the time of sweetness and pleasure is small, but the time of punishment and torments is vast."

> *Listen then to the power of both: the luxury and the torment. The time of luxury and deception is but one hour; but the time of torment has the power of thirty days. If, therefore, someone lives in luxury and is deceived for one day, and is then tormented for one day, that one day of torment has the strength of an entire year. For as many days as one lives in luxury, for so many years shall he be tormented. You see, then, that the duration of luxury and deception is as nothing, but the duration of punishment and torment is great.* <note>This paragraph is a Greek version of the preceding Latin text, preserved here for comparison by scholars.</note>

<term>Similitudo</term>: A "Similitude" or "Parable," a genre used in this text to explain spiritual truths through analogies.

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDES VI. VII. (A)

(A) V. I said to him: “Lord, since I do not fully understand$^1$ these times of sweetness, pleasure, and punishment, explain them to me more clearly.” He answered me, saying: “Your foolishness clings to you persistently.$^2$ Do you not wish rather to purify your mind and serve God? See to it that perhaps, when your time is up, you are not found to be foolish.$^3$ Listen now as you desire, so that you may understand more easily. * He who gives himself over to delicacies and$^4$ pleasures for one day, and does whatever his soul desires, is filled with great folly and does not understand what he is doing; for on the next day he forgets what he did the day before. For worldly sweetness and pleasure$^5$ have no memory because of the foolishness that is inherent in them. But when torment and punishment come upon a man for one day, he is tortured for a whole year; for punishment possesses a long memory. Therefore, grieving for a whole year, he remembers, and then he recalls that vain sweetness and pleasure, and feels that he is suffering punishment because of it.$^7$ Whoever, therefore, gives themselves over to such sweetness and pleasure are punished in this way; because while they have life, they render themselves liable to death.” $\dagger$ I said to him: “What, Lord, are the harmful pleasures?$^9$” “Every act,” he said, “that a man performs gladly is a pleasure to him. For the hot-tempered man, satisfying his own character, perceives his own pleasure; and the adulterer, the drunkard, the slanderer,$^{10}$ the liar, the covetous, the deceiver, and whoever commits anything similar to these, by obeying his own disease, perceives pleasure from that thing. All these sweetnesses and pleasures are harmful$^{11}$ to the servants of God. Because of these things, therefore, they are tortured and suffer punishment. There are also pleasures that bring salvation$^{12}$ to men. For many,$^{13}$ while performing works of goodness, perceive pleasure, being drawn by their own sweetness. This pleasure, then, is useful to the servants of God,$^{14}$ and prepares life for men of this sort. But those harmful ones,$^{15}$ which were mentioned above, bring about torments and punishments. Whoever remains$^{16}$ in them and does not perform penance for their deeds shall acquire death for themselves.”

(B) V. And I said to him: "Lord, since I do not entirely understand these times of sweetness and pleasure and punishment, explain them to me more clearly." He said to me: "Your foolishness clings to you persistently, and you do not wish to be purified in your mind$^1$ <note>original: "purificari"</note> and to serve God. Take care, lest at some point, when your time is finished, you are found to be a fool. Listen now, then, as you wish, so that$^2$ you may understand more easily. He who for one day gives himself over to luxury and pleasures and does whatever his soul desires, is filled with the greatest foolishness, and does not understand what he is committing. And so, afterward, he forgets what he did the day before. For sweetness and pleasure have no memory because of the foolishness that is within them. But when torture and punishment come upon a man for a single day, he is tormented for a whole year; for punishment possesses a long memory. Grieving for the whole year, he then remembers and recalls that sweetness and pleasure, and feels for that reason that he is suffering these punishments. Whoever, therefore, has handed themselves over to sweetness and pleasures is punished in this way, because by having such a life, they have made themselves liable to death." And I said to him: "What, Lord, are the harmful pleasures of this kind?" And he said to me: "Every act of luxury, [and] whatever a luxurious man does willingly. For the hot-tempered man revels in his own deeds, as does the adulterer, the drunkard, the slanderer, the liar, the greedy man, the defrauder, and whoever does things similar to these; he satisfies his own disease. Therefore, such a one also revels in his own act. All these sweetnesses$^3$ and pleasures are harmful to the servants of God. Because of these, however, they are tortured and suffer punishments. But there are also pleasures that save men; for many who perform works of goodness find delight, led by their own will. This delight, therefore, is useful to the servants of God, and prepares life for men of this kind. But those harmful delights mentioned earlier produce torments; and those who persist in them, and do not perform penance for what they have committed, acquire death for themselves."
