Here, Hermas asks for the "Angel of Punishment" to be removed from his home, leading to a lesson on why a leader must sometimes suffer for the sake of their household's salvation.</meta>

-># THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDE VII. (A)<-
->508<-

"Lord," I said, "command that shepherd who is in charge of punishment to leave my house, because he afflicts me severely." And he, answering, said, "It is necessary for you to suffer troubles and vexations; for so that good messenger <note>original: "nuntius bonus"; here referring to a high-ranking angel</note> commanded concerning you, because he wishes to test you." "What so grave a sin have I committed, Lord," I asked, "that I should be handed over to this messenger?" "Listen," he said. "You indeed have several sins, but not so many that you should be handed over to this messenger; but your household has committed many faults and crimes, and therefore that good messenger, provoked by their deeds, commanded that you experience vexation for a certain amount of time, so that they too may perform penance for their misdeeds and wash themselves from every desire of this world. When, therefore, they have performed penance and been purified, then that messenger who is in charge of punishment will depart from you." I said to him, "Lord, if they have behaved in such a way as to provoke the good messenger, what have I done?" He answered, "They cannot suffer vexation in any other way unless you, who are the head of the entire house, undergo hardships. For whatever you suffer, they must also feel; as long as you remain well-established, they can experience no vexation." And I said, "But look, Lord, they are already now performing penance with all their hearts." "I also know," he said, "that they are performing penance with all their hearts. Do you then think," he asked, "that the faults of those who perform penance are immediately wiped out? Not at once; but it is necessary for the one who performs penance <term>poenitentiam</term> <note>This term implies both internal regret and outward acts of restitution or discipline</note> to afflict his own soul, and to show himself humble in spirit in every matter, and to endure many and varied vexations; and when he has endured all things that were appointed for him, then perhaps He who created him and formed all things will be moved by His mercy toward him and provide some remedy; and this is so if He sees that the heart of the one performing penance is pure from every wicked work. But for you and your house, it is now beneficial to be vexed, and it is necessary to suffer much vexation, just as the messenger of the Lord, who handed you over to me, commanded. Rather, give thanks to the Lord that, foreknowing the future, He deemed you worthy to predict that tribulation is imminent for those strong enough to bear it." I said to him, "And you, Lord, stay with me, and I will easily endure every vexation." "I will be with you," he said, "but I will also ask that messenger who is in charge of punishment to afflict you more lightly; yet you shall suffer adversity for a short time, and you shall be restored again to your place; only persevere in humility of mind. "I came, Lord, to ask that you command the shepherd placed in charge of punishment to depart from my house, because he afflicts me severely." And he said to me: "It is necessary for you to suffer troubles and vexations; for that honorable messenger <note>Latin: "nuntius ille honestus." In this text, "messenger" is often a synonym for an angel.</note> gave this command concerning you, because he wants to test you." And I said: "What so great a crime <note>Latin: "delictum"</note> have I committed, Lord, that I should be handed over to this messenger?" And he said to me: "You have several sins indeed, but not so many that you should be handed over to this messenger. But your household has committed many sins and crimes; therefore that honorable messenger was provoked, and he ordered you to experience trouble for a period of time, so that they too may repent <term>repentance: "poenitentia," which in a historical context refers to both the feeling of regret and the outward acts of discipline/penance</term> of their deeds and wash themselves from every desire of this world. When, therefore, they have repented and been purified, the messenger of punishment will depart from you." And I said: "Lord, if they have acted in such a way as to provoke that honorable messenger, what have I done?" He said to me: "They cannot feel the trouble unless you, who are the head of the whole house, suffer; for whatever you suffer, they must also feel. Indeed, as long as you are doing well, they will suffer no trouble." "But look, Lord," I said, "they have already repented with all their hearts." And he said to me: "I know indeed that they have repented with all their hearts, but do not think that the sins of those who repent ought to be wiped away immediately. For it is necessary for the one who repents to torment his own soul, and to carry himself with humility in every matter, and to endure many and various troubles. And when he has endured everything, perhaps He who created and established all things will be moved by His mercy toward him and give him some remedy of salvation—provided He sees that the heart of the one repenting is pure from every work of wickedness. But for now, it is beneficial for you and your house to be troubled. Why should I say more to you? It is necessary for you to suffer trouble, just as the messenger of the Lord who handed you over to me commanded. ### THE EIGHTH SIMILITUDE.

(B) He showed me a willow tree <term>willow: "salicem." In this allegory, the willow represents the Law of God given to the whole world</term> covering the plains and mountains, under whose shade came all who were called in the name of the Lord. And behold, a messenger <term>messenger: "nuntius," referring here to the Archangel Michael, who governs the people of God</term> of great honor and sublime stature was cutting branches from the same willow with a large sickle, and those people who had come under its shade received small rods, about a cubit <note>roughly 18 inches</note> in length. When everyone had received the rods, he laid down the sickle, and the tree itself remained whole, just as I had seen it before. I seemed to marvel at this in my mind. Then the shepherd said to me: "Cease to wonder that this tree remains whole after so many branches were cut away. Wait, then, and when you have seen everything, it will be demonstrated to you what it signifies." Now that messenger who had handed out the rods to the people began to demand them back. In the same order as each had received one, they were called by that name and returned their rod. And as he received each rod, he examined it. From some he received them dry and as if moth-eaten <note>original: "a tinea putridas," indicating decay caused by insects</note>, and he ordered those people to be set apart. From others he received rods that were dry, but not moth-eaten; these too he ordered to be placed aside. Others handed over rods that were "pseudo-dry" <note>appearing dry but perhaps not entirely so</note>, and they were placed separately; others even had half-dry rods with cracks in them, and they were set aside. Others handed over their rods green with cracks, and these were sequestered. Indeed, some handed over their rods where two parts were green and the third part was dry; these also were put down. Others handed over their rods almost entirely green, but with a tiny bit at the very tip being dry; and these were separated. Still others brought their rods just as they had received them from the angel. And this was the largest part...

(A) III. I said to him, "Lord, show me what this tree is; for I am deeply moved that it appears whole even though so many branches have been cut off;<sup>1</sup> and it does not seem to have lost anything at all, which amazes me greatly." "Listen," he said: "This great tree,<sup>2</sup> which covers fields and mountains and all the earth, is the Law of God given to the whole world. Moreover, by this Law, the Son of God has been preached in all the ends of the world. The people standing under the shadow are those<sup>3</sup> who heard his preaching and believed. And that magnificent and good messenger<sup>4</sup> is Michael <note>The Archangel Michael is historically viewed in this text as the guardian of the Law and the people of God</note>, who has authority over this people and governs them. For he is the one who plants the Law in the hearts of those who have believed. He visits those to whom he gave the Law,<sup>6</sup> to see if they have kept it. He looks at each person's rod, and many of them are broken. For those rods are the Law of the Lord.<sup>7</sup> He then recognizes<sup>8</sup> all those who have not kept the Law, knowing the station of each of them." I said to him, "Why, Lord, has he sent some into the tower, but left others here<sup>9</sup> for you?" "These,"<sup>10</sup> he said, "whoever transgressed the Law they received from him, have been left in my power so they may do penance for their sins; but those who satisfied the Law and kept it are under his power." "Who then, Lord," I asked,<sup>11</sup> "are those going into the tower wearing crowns?" He said to me, "Whoever struggled with the devil and defeated him,<sup>12</sup> they are the ones who are crowned. These<sup>13</sup> are the ones who suffered hardships in order to keep the Law. Those who handed over green rods with shoots but without fruit suffered affliction for the sake of the same Law,<sup>14</sup> but did not die; nor did they deny the holy Law. But those<sup>15</sup> who handed over the rods green, just as they had received them, are modest and just, and lived<sup>16</sup> with a very pure mind and kept God's commandments. You will know the rest when I have examined those rods<sup>17</sup> which I planted and watered."

(B) III. And I said to him:<gloss>1</gloss> "Show me, Lord, what this tree is. For I marvel greatly that it appears whole even though so many branches have been cut off." And he said to me: "Listen. This great tree, which covers the fields and the whole earth,<gloss>2</gloss> is the Law of God given to the whole world. Now, the Law is the Son of God, who is preached to the ends of the earth. The people standing under its shadow are those who have heard his preaching and believed. Moreover, that great and honorable messenger is Michael <note>In early Christian literature like the Shepherd of Hermas, Michael is often depicted as the celestial administrator of God's Law.</note>, who has authority over this people and governs them; it is he who plants the law in the hearts <note>original: "praecordiis", referring to the innermost seat of thought and emotion</note> of those who have believed. He visits those to whom he gave the law to see if they have kept it. For each person's rod is the law. You see, then, that many of the rods have become useless; you will recognize those who have not kept the law, and you will see the dwelling place of each of them." And I said to him: "Why did he release some, and send others into the tower, and leave others to you?" "Listen," he said. "Whoever has transgressed the law they received from God is left in my power <note>The "Shepherd" speaking here is the Angel of Repentance, who handles those who have sinned but may still repent.</note>, so that they may perform penance for their offenses. But those who have already satisfied the law and maintained their penance are under the power of another."<gloss>4</gloss> And I said to him: "Lord, who are those going into the tower wearing crowns?" He said to me: "Whoever struggled with the devil and overcame him, those are the ones crowned; that is, they are those who kept the law and endured all things. But those who had green rods with shoots but no fruit are those who gave themselves up for the sake of that same law, and though they suffered affliction, they did not deny their law, nor did they taste death. Those whom you see returned their rods just as they received them are the modest and the just, who, living with a very pure mind, kept the commandments of the Lord. Regarding the remaining rods, I will tell you about them when I have considered those rods which I planted and watered."

These, therefore, are completely dead to God, and for that reason none of them performed repentance. For even if they hear these my commandments, which I am about to show them, they will gain nothing. Life is absent from such men. But those who handed over dry and not rotten rods were close to those who had dry and rotten rods. For they were hypocrites, and they introduced perverse doctrines, subverting the servants of God, especially those who had committed sins. For they did not allow them to perform repentance completely, but held them back with foolish doctrines. You see, therefore, that many have hope of returning and performing repentance. Since you brought my commandments to them, some from among those who are like this will yet perform repentance. But whoever shall not perform repentance will lose their life. However, those who did perform repentance became good, and their seats began to be in the first walls <note>Likely referring to the outer defensive structures of the mystical Tower, which represents the Church.</note>. Some indeed even ascended into the tower. You see, therefore, that in the repentance of sinners there is life; but for those who do not perform repentance, death is prepared."

These are the doubtful ones; for they are neither living nor dead. But those who returned their rods half-dry and having cracks, are both doubtful and slanderers <note>original: maledici</note>, speaking ill of those who are absent, never having peace among themselves, and envying one another. To these, indeed, repentance <note>original: poenitentia</note> is offered; for you see some of them are repenting. However, those among them who have performed repentance quickly have their seat in the tower <term>The "Tower" is a recurring vision in this text representing the Church of the saved, built stone by stone.</term>; but those who have performed it slowly dwell within the walls. But those who have not performed repentance, but have persisted in their deeds, shall die the death.

But indeed, those who returned rods that were green but had cracks, were always faithful and good, but they had among themselves a certain envy and jealousy <note>original: zelum</note> regarding leadership and dignity. Truly, all such people are senseless and foolish who have such rivalry among themselves regarding leadership. Yet these, since they are otherwise good, if they amend their ways upon hearing these commandments and perform repentance quickly through my persuasion, shall at last begin to dwell in the tower, just like those who performed repentance worthily. But if any of them returns again to dissension, he shall be cast out from the tower and shall lose his life. For the life of those who keep the commandments of the Lord consists in the commandments, not in leadership or any special dignity. For through patience and humility of soul, men shall attain life; but through seditions and contempt for the law, they shall acquire death for themselves.

(A) VIII. "But those who had in their rods a half part dry and a half part green, these are those entangled in business affairs <note>The early Church often warned that excessive involvement in trade and secular business distracted from spiritual life.</note> and not attached to the saints; therefore, half of them lives, but half is dead. Many of them, therefore, having heard the commandments, performed repentance and began to dwell in the tower; but some of them withdrew entirely. For these, there is no place for repentance; for because of their wicked business, they spoke against the Lord and denied him. On account of this wickedness, therefore, they lost their life. From these, therefore, many performed repentance, and so began to dwell in the tower; and many withdrew from God forever. Those, therefore, have lost their life entirely. But some, having conceived a doubtful mind, stirred up dissensions; for these there is still a way back, if they perform repentance quickly and are not held back by their pleasures; but if they persist in their deeds, they shall acquire death for themselves."

(A) IX. “But those who offered their rods, of which two parts were dry <note>original: aridae</note> and a third was green, were indeed faithful; but having become enriched and satiated with worldly goods, they desired to be more famous among the foreign nations <note>original: exteras gentes; refers to the non-Christian or Gentile world</note>, and they fell into great pride, and began to have lofty ambitions, and to abandon the truth. They did not keep company with the righteous, but lived together with the foreign nations; and this life seemed sweeter to them. Nevertheless, they did not depart from God, and they remained in the faith, but they did not practice the works of faith. Therefore, many of them repented, and their places began to be in the tower. Others, however, living among the foreign nations and puffed up by their own vanities, fell away from God forever, serving the crimes and works of the nations. Men of this sort were therefore counted among the foreign nations. Others among them began to have a doubting mind, not hoping that they could attain salvation because of their own deeds; others, being made doubtful, stirred up dissensions. For these and those who began to be doubtful because of their deeds, there is still a way back; but this repentance must be swift, so that their seat may be in the tower. But for those who do not repent, but remain in their pleasures, death is near.”

(A) X. “And these, who offered green rods except for their tips <note>original: cacuminibus</note>, which alone were dry and had cracks, were always good and faithful and honest before God; but they sinned for a short time because of empty pleasures and petty thoughts which they held within themselves. Therefore, upon hearing my words, many repented quickly and began to dwell in the tower. Some of them, however, turned out to be doubtful; some added to their doubting mind the stirring up of dissensions. In these, therefore, there is even now hope of return, because they were always good; however, they will be moved with difficulty. But those who offered their rods dry, except for their tips, which alone were green—these indeed believed in God, but lived in crimes; nevertheless, they never departed from God, but always gladly bore the name of the Lord, and gladly received the servants of God into their homes <note>original: in hospitiis suis; highlighting the virtue of hospitality in the early church</note>. Hearing this, therefore, they returned and repented without delay, and practiced every equity of virtue. Some of them even met their death, and others gladly suffered adversities, mindful of their deeds.”

The Lord, in his great mercy, has sent me to announce repentance to all, even to those who do not deserve <note>original: "merentur"</note> to attain salvation because of their deeds. But the Lord is patient, and he wishes to preserve the invitation made through his Son. I said to him: “I hope, sir, that after hearing these things, everyone will repent. But those who add to their sins,” he said, “and live according to the desires of this world, shall condemn themselves to death. But you, walk in my commandments and you shall live for God; and whoever walks in them and practices them rightly shall live for God.” After he had shown me all these things, he said to me: “The remaining things I will show to you after a few days.”

That shepherd said to me: “Why do you debate within yourself and torture yourself,<note>original: "atque torqueris"</note> adding anxiety to your own heart? The virgins then carried them through the gate <note>The gate represents Jesus Christ, the only entrance to the Kingdom of God.</note> and placed them into the structure of the tower. When those stones were built in, they all became bright white and uniform, and those that had been brought earlier changed their colors. 

However, certain stones that were handed by the multitude of men for the structure of the tower did not become white; instead, they remained exactly as they were when they were placed, because they had not been carried through the gate by the virgins. Therefore, these stones looked unsightly in the building of that tower. When the six men noticed this, they ordered them to be removed and put back in their own place, from where they had been brought. After they were moved, they set each one down and said to the men who were carrying the stones: "You must not place stones in this building at all; instead, place them near the tower so that these virgins may carry them through the gate and then place them into the structure. For if they are not carried by these virgins through this gate, they cannot change their colors. Do not, therefore, labor in vain."

**V.** And the construction was finished for that day, but the tower was not yet completed; for it was destined to be built further. A delay in the building was therefore made, and the six men ordered the builders to withdraw and rest for a while. But they commanded the virgins not to leave the tower, but to guard it. After everyone had withdrawn, I said to the Shepherd: "Sir, why was the building of this tower not finished?" 

"It cannot be finished," he said, "before its Master <note>The "Master of the Tower" represents the Son of God coming to judge the quality of the believers within the Church.</note> comes and tests this structure, so that if he finds any stones that are trifles <note>original: "nugas"; referring to useless or defective material</note> in it, he may change them; for this tower is being built according to his will." 

"I wish to know, sir," I said, "what the building of this tower signifies, and also to learn about this rock and the gate, and about the mountains and the stones that came up..."

## (A) VII.

When he had commanded him these things, he departed with all those with whom he had come to the tower. The virgins, however, stood around the tower, guarding it. And I said to that Shepherd: "In what way can these stones return into the structure of this tower, since they have been rejected?" And he said to me: "I will trim the greater part from these stones and add them to the structure, and they will match with the rest." And I said: "Lord, how can they fill the same place after being trimmed <note>original: "circumcisi"</note>?" "Whichever," he said, "are found to be smaller will go into the middle of the structure; the larger ones, however, will be placed on the outside and will hold them together." When he had said these things to me, he said: "Let us go, and after three days let us return; and I will add these cleaned stones into the structure. For all things around the tower must be cleaned, lest perhaps the Master of the House <note>original: "paterfamilias"</note> should come suddenly and find the surroundings of the tower filthy, and he be offended; then these stones would not be put into the structure of this tower, and I would appear to be a negligent servant." After three days, however, when we had come to the same tower, he said to me: "Let us consider all these stones, and see which of them can go into the structure." The rest, however, could not be shaped <note>original: "deformari"; a technical term for dressing or squaring a stone</note> because of the great number of their cracks, and they were cast away from the building of the tower. Next, he examined those who were short and useless. Many among them were found to be black, others having large cracks. He ordered them also to be set aside with those who had been left behind; the rest, however, having been cleaned and shaped, he ordered to be added to the structure; these the virgins took up and fitted into the middle of the structure, because they were weaker. Then he examined those who were half-white and half-black. Many of these were found to be black; and he ordered them to be taken away and placed with those who had been rejected. The rest were found to be entirely white, and they were fitted into the structure of the tower<gloss>1</gloss> by the virgins, since they were found to be whole, and nothing had been cut away from them. They were placed on the outside, so that they might support those who had been cut down and placed in the middle. Then he examined those who were hard and rough. A few of these were cast away, because they could not be trimmed beforehand; for they were exceedingly hard. But the rest<gloss>2</gloss> were shaped, and because they were weaker, they were placed in the middle of the structure by the virgins. Then he examined those who had spots. Even from these a few turned out black, and being separated, were placed among the rest; but the others, being white and whole, were carried into the structure by the virgins and, because of their strength, were placed on the outside by the virgins.

"Whoever, then," he said, "bears the name of the Son of God, must also bear the names of these virgins; for even the Son himself bears their names. Whichever stones," he said, "you saw remaining in the building, having been passed through their hands, were clothed with their power. <note>original: "potestate vestiti sunt"; the "power" here refers to the spiritual strength of the virtues.</note> And for this reason you see the entire tower in harmony <note>original: "concordem"; referring to the unity of the Church.</note> with the rock, as if it were made from a single stone. So also those who have believed in God through His Son have been clothed in this spirit. <note>Note 14 in the original text clarifies that being clothed in the "spirit" means being clothed in "virtues."</note> Behold, there shall be one spirit, and one body, and one color for their garments; but those who bear the names of these virgins will also attain these things." And I said: "Why then, lord, were the stones cast away that were rejected, even though they had been carried through the gate and passed through the hands of these virgins into the structure of this tower?" "Since," he said, "you are concerned to inquire diligently into all things, hear about those stones that were cast away. All these received the name of the Son of God, and also the power of these virgins. Therefore, having received these spirits, they were made complete and were brought into the number of the servants of God, and there began to be one body among them and one garment; for they felt the same sense of justice, which they practiced together. But truly, after they saw those women whom you noticed were dressed in black clothing, with bare shoulders and loose hair, they began to desire to be with them because of their beauty, and they clothed themselves in their power; they threw away the robes of the virgins. Therefore, these were cast out from the house of God and handed over to those women. But those who were not corrupted by their beauty remained in the house of God. You have," he said, "the explanation for those stones which were cast away."

(A) XVII. And I said: "Now again,¹ lord, explain to me about those mountains; why are they varied, and of so many different shapes?" "Listen," he said: "these twelve mountains which you see are the twelve nations² that inhabit the whole world. The Son of God³ was preached to them by those whom he himself sent to them." "But why, lord," I asked⁴, "are the mountains varied, and of different shapes?" "Listen: these twelve nations that inhabit the whole world⁵ are twelve distinct peoples; and just as you saw the mountains varying in appearance, so too are these nations. I will teach you the character and actions of each individual mountain." "First, lord," I said, "show me this: since these mountains are so diverse, how is it that they were joined into the structure of this tower and became a single color, and are no less brilliant than those stones that ascended from the deep?⁸" "Because," he said, "all the nations under heaven heard and believed, and were called by the one name of the Son of God.⁹ Therefore, having received his <term>Seal</term> <note>original: "sigillum"; referring to the rite of baptism</note>, they all received the same wisdom and the same understanding; and they possessed one faith and one love,¹⁰ and they bore the spirits of these <term>virgins</term> <note>The "virgins" in this allegory represent the fundamental Christian virtues</note> along with his name. And so, the structure of this tower appeared to be of a single color, shining with the brightness of the sun. But after they had become unified in this way,¹¹ they began to be one single body. Yet some among them¹² defiled themselves and were cast out from the ranks of the righteous; they returned to their former state, and ended up even worse than they were before.

(A) XVIII. "How, lord,"¹ I asked, "could they become worse, having known the Lord?" And he said: "He² who does not know the Lord, if he lives wickedly, remains under the punishment of his own wickedness.³ But he who has known the Lord is strictly bound to abstain from all wickedness and to serve goodness more and more. Therefore, if the one who ought to follow goodness turns instead to the path of wickedness, does he not seem to sin more than the one who offends while being ignorant of God's power?⁵ For this reason, those who were ignorant are indeed destined for death; but⁷ those who have known the Lord and seen his wonderful works, if they live wickedly, shall be punished twice as much, and shall die forever. Just as you saw the stones that were rejected from the tower and handed over to cruel and destructive spirits; and just as you saw the tower purified until it appeared⁹ to be made of a single stone; so also shall the Church of God be, when it has been purified by casting out the evil and the hypocrites, the wicked¹⁰ and the doubters, and whoever else conducted themselves wickedly within it, through various sins of wickedness.

(B) XVII. And I said to him: "Lord, now explain to me about the mountains: why are they of various shapes and appearances?"¹ And he said to me: "Listen also to this. (B) XVIII. And I said to him: "Lord, why have those who knew God become worse?" And he said to me: "He who has not known God, if he lives wickedly, the punishment for his wickedness remains for him. But he who has known God should no longer act wickedly, but should practice goodness. If, therefore, he who ought to follow goodness does wickedly, does he not seem to you to act more wickedly than he who is ignorant of God? Therefore, those who have not known God and act wickedly are destined for death. But those who have known God, and have seen his works and wonders, yet live wickedly, shall be doubly punished and shall die forever. In this way, therefore, the Church of God is purified. Just as you saw the stones that were cast out being handed over to harmful spirits, so they too shall be cast out; but of those who remained purified, there shall be one body, just as that tower was made of a single stone after it was purified: so shall the Church of God be when it has been purified, the wicked, the hypocrites, those who think evil, and the doubters having been cast out from it; and whoever has acted wickedly shall themselves be cast out in various ways. And there shall be..."

The thistles represent the rich, and the thorns represent those bound by many affairs. These people, then, who are bound by many affairs and various matters, do not join themselves to the servants of God, but go astray, called away by those business dealings which suffocate them. Even those who are rich find it difficult to present themselves for the fellowship of the servants of God, fearing that something might be asked of them: therefore, these shall enter the kingdom of God with difficulty. For just as it is difficult to walk among thistles with bare feet, so also for these types...

...the church of God is one body and one mind, one faith and one love. And then the Son of God will rejoice in her, and will receive pleasure from his pure people being received. "Everything is great and honorable, Lord," I said. "Now show me, Lord, both the repentance and the deeds of each group, so that every soul hoping and trusting in God, having heard these things, may marvel at that great and wonderful and admirable honor and glory, and also his glorious name." "Listen now, therefore," he said, "to the variety of these mountains and the twelve nations."

**(B) XIX.** Regarding the first mountain, which is black: those who believed from it are such as are deserters, <note>original: "transfugae"; likely referring to those who abandoned the faith during Roman persecutions.</note> blasphemers, and betrayers of the servants of God. For these there is no repentance, only death; and for this reason they are black, because their kind is wicked. Regarding the second mountain, which is dry <gloss>2</gloss>, those who believed from it are hypocrites and teachers of wickedness. They are similar to the first group, having no fruit of righteousness within themselves; and just as their mountain is sterile and without fruit, so also men of this kind have the name of Christians, but are empty of faith, nor is there any fruit of truth in them. To these, therefore, repentance has been given, <gloss>2</gloss> if they follow it quickly; but if they delay, their death will be with those first ones. And I said to him: "Lord, why was repentance given to these <gloss>3</gloss> but not to the first ones? For their deeds are almost similar, Lord." "For this reason," he said, "repentance was provided for these: because they spoke nothing unspeakable against their Lord, nor were they betrayers of the servants of God; but because of a certain desire for gain <note>original: "accipiendi cupiditatem"; literally a greed for receiving things.</note>, they deceived people by teaching according to the desires of individual sinners, who will also pay the penalty for that matter. Therefore repentance was provided for them because they were not detractors of the Lord, nor betrayers of his servants."

<meta>This page continues the vision of the Shepherd regarding the twelve mountains, representing different groups of people within the Church. This section concludes the description of the ninth mountain (the corrupt ministers) and introduces the tenth mountain (the hospitable bishops).</meta>

->THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. BOOK III. SIMILITUDE IX. (B)<-

**XXVI.** Regarding the ninth mountain, which is deserted and has snakes that are deadly to humans: these are those who believed, but who have the stains of a wicked ministry. They performed their service poorly, plundering the goods of widows and even taking the property of orphans for themselves. If they persist in this greed, they shall die, and there will be no hope of life for them. But if they correct themselves and complete their ministry with purity, they will be able to live for God. Those who were found to be scabby <gloss>rough or leprous-like</gloss> are those who denied the Lord and did not look back toward God. Instead, they became wild and deserted; they do not associate with the servants of God, but living only for themselves, they lose their lives. For just as a vine left alone in a hedge <note>original: "sepe"</note> perishes without any cultivation, is choked by weeds, and over time becomes wild and ceases to be useful to its master—so also men of this kind, acting on their own whims, become wild. Having become like wild beasts <note>original: "ferae"</note>, they will be useless to their Lord. Therefore, repentance is granted to these only if they are not found to have denied the Lord from their whole hearts. But if someone is found to have denied Him from their whole heart, I do not know if they can live. And I do not say this so that someone who has denied Him may simply receive repentance; for it is impossible for those who have disowned their Lord to receive salvation. Rather, repentance is thought to be available for those who denied Him long ago. Therefore, if anyone intends to repent, they must hurry before the building of the tower <term>the Tower</term> <note>In Hermae's vision, the Tower represents the Church being built out of "living stones" or believers.</note> is finished; otherwise, they will be led to death by those women. For those are the deceitful snakes you saw on that mountain. Just as their venom is deadly, so are the words of these men, and they destroy people. These are therefore useless in the faith because of this way of life. However, some of them, having performed repentance, have attained salvation. But the rest of this kind, if they repent, can be saved; if not, they will die with those women whose power they possess.

**XXVII.** Regarding the tenth mountain, in which there were trees sheltering the livestock: these are certain believers who were hospitable bishops. They always gladly received the servants of God into their homes without any hypocrisy. They always protected the needy and widows by their ministry with perseverance and maintained a pure conduct perpetually. All such as these will be protected by God, and they have a place among the messengers <term>nuntios</term> <note>Likely referring to the rank of angels or high-status spiritual beings.</note>, if they persevere until the end in serving God. And behold, their place is with the angels of God.

(A) XXVIII. “Regarding the eleventh mountain, on which there were trees weighed down with various kinds of fruit, these are those who believed and died for the sake of the Lord’s name, and suffered with a ready mind, and gave up their lives with their whole heart.” And I said: “Why then, lord, do all these trees have fruit, yet some of them are more beautiful than others?” “Listen,” he said: “Whoever has suffered for the sake of the Lord’s name is held in honor before God; and all their transgressions are wiped away <note>original: "deleta"</note>, because they died for the sake of the name of the Son of God. But as for why their fruits are different and some among them excel, listen: for whoever was brought before the authorities <note>original: "potestates"</note> and, when questioned, did not deny the Lord but suffered with a ready mind, these are more highly honored before God; the fruits that excel belong to them. But those who were timid and hesitant, and debated in their hearts whether they should confess or deny, yet still suffered—their fruits are smaller <note>original: "exiguiores"</note>, because this thought entered into their hearts; for such a thought is evil and wicked, just as if a servant were to deny his master. Therefore, take care, you who have such thoughts, lest this mindset remain in you and you die to God. You, then, who suffer for the sake of this name, ought to honor the Lord; for the Lord considers you worthy to bear His name, and that all your sins should be redeemed. Do you not then think yourself happy? Think instead that if any of you suffers, he accomplishes a great work. For the Lord grants you life, though you do not understand it. For your sins were weighing you down; and unless you had suffered for the sake of this name, you certainly would have died to God because of your sins. I say these things to you who are debating about confession or denial. Confess, then, that you have the Lord as God, lest perhaps by denying Him you are delivered into chains. For if all the nations punish their servants who have denied their masters, what do you think the Lord, who has power over all things, will do to you? Therefore, remove these doubts and disputes from your hearts, so that you may live to God forever.”

Therefore, such people will without any doubt inhabit the kingdom of God, because they in no way stained the commandments of God, but remained in sincerity all the days of their lives, with the same state of mind. Whoever, therefore, remains,” he said, “like infants, having no malice, will be more honored than all those I have already mentioned. For all infants are honored before the Lord and are held as first. Happy are you, then, who remove malice from yourselves and put on innocence; because you first see—

(B) XXVIII. Regarding the eleventh mountain, on which there were trees filled with many different kinds of fruit: these are those who have believed, and who have suffered for the sake of the name of the Lord, and who handed over their lives with a ready mind and with their whole heart. And I questioned him, saying: "Why, lord, do all the trees indeed have fruit, but some trees are more beautiful than others?" Whoever was brought before the authorities <note>original: "potestatem"</note> and, when questioned, did not deny but suffered with a ready mind—these are more pleasing to God, and their fruit is more excellent. But whoever was timid and hesitant, and debated in their heart whether they should deny or confess, and yet suffered—their fruits are smaller <note>original: "minores"</note>, because this thought arose in their hearts; for such a thought is evil, just as a servant who denies his own master. See to it then, you who have such thoughts, that this same mind does not remain in you, and you die to God. But you, whoever are about to suffer for the name of the Lord, ought to honor God because the Lord considers you worthy <note>original: "dignos"</note> to bear this name; for all your sins will be healed. Do you not consider yourselves happy if someone among you suffers? Instead, you should think that you are performing a great work. Behold, the Lord gives you life, and you do not understand it. For your transgressions have weighed you down; and indeed, unless you had suffered for His name, you would have died to the Lord on account of your sins. These things, therefore, I say to you who hesitate between confession and denial: confess that you have a Lord, lest if you deny Him, you be delivered into chains. If the nations punish their servants who deny their master, what do you think the Lord, who has power over all things, will do to you? Remove these disputes from your heart, so that you may live to God forever."

(B) XXIX. Regarding the twelfth white mountain: these are they who have believed like little children, into whose hearts no malice has entered, nor have they known what wickedness is, but have always remained in sincerity. They, therefore, dwell without doubt in the kingdom of God, because they have in no way defiled the commandments of the Lord, but have remained in sincerity. In this same course, therefore, whoever among you shall persevere, you shall be like children, more honored before God than those who are considered first. Happy are you, therefore, whoever have removed malice from yourselves, and if you put on innocence, you shall live first of all to God.

All those stones that were taken from the plain and placed into the structure of the tower in place of those that were rejected are the 'roots' of that white mountain; because everyone from that mountain who believed was found to be good. For this reason, the lord of the tower ordered those who were from the roots of that mountain to be placed into the structure of the tower. For he knew <note>original: *scivit*</note> that if they were placed in the building itself, they would remain bright, and none of them would ever turn black. Therefore, since the Lord knew their mind—that they were born good and were able to be good—he ordered their wealth to be pruned <term>circumcidi|Literally 'to be circumcised.' The author uses this term metaphorically to describe cutting away the 'excess' of worldly wealth so the soul can fit into the spiritual building.</term>, not taken away forever, so that from the remainder <note>original: *reliquiis*</note> they might be able to do some good for the rest of their lives, and they would live for God because they were of a good kind. ...the Lord of the tower repaired the gaps which were visible after the rejection of the stones taken from the old people of God. Just as the newcomers in faith were previously contrasted with the faithful from the old people of God (Vision 3, 5), so here the children of the old faithful are distinguished from the young people among the newcomers. I would hardly believe that the author in chapter 21 inaccurately assigned the fourth mountain to the newcomers in faith, as Hilgenfeld <note>Adolf Hilgenfeld, a 19th-century biblical scholar.</note> prefers. For that "return to idols" (The Palatine manuscript <note>A significant 15th-century Latin manuscript of the Shepherd</note> says nothing about serving them again) should be referred to those whom Mandate 10, 2 had denoted. Indeed, the supplementary stones had entered into the tower's structure at the time when the meaning of the twelve mountains was being explained to Hermas; however, chapter 21 deals not with those—certainly a small part of the building—but with all who are from the fourth mountain. The fact that he distinguishes between those who are old in the faith and the newcomers is entirely characteristic of an author who has become a Christian from a Jewish background. See the Epistle of Barnabas chapters 5, 7, 13, "a new people" <note>original Greek: *laos kainos*</note>, chapters 14, 15, "the people in between" <note>original Greek: *laos ho metaxy*</note>, the 1st Epistle of Clement of Rome to the Corinthians, chapter

For when you have given a fuller <note>A "fuller" was a professional laundryman in the Roman world who cleaned, bleached, and finished cloth.</note> a new garment, you certainly wish to receive it back whole. But if the fuller returns a torn garment to you, will you accept it? Would you not rather be angry and pursue him with insults,^2 saying this to him: "I gave you a whole garment; why did you tear it and make it useless so that, because of the tear you made in it, it cannot be used?" Would you not say all these things to the fuller about the tear you found in your garment? Therefore, if you become sad and quarrel over a garment because you do not receive it back whole, what do you think the Lord will do? He gave you a whole spirit, and you have made it so entirely useless^3 that it cannot be used by its master, because the use of that spirit began to be useless and corrupted by you. And therefore, the Lord will deliver you to death on account of this deed of yours. For the Lord will punish all such people whom he finds to be keeping a memory of their sins. Not

I. II. I said to him: “Lord, ask him yourself, from the time he has been in my house, whether I have done anything out of order, or if I have offended him in any way.” “And I,” he said, “know that you have done nothing out of order and that you will not do so; and therefore I speak these things with you, so that you may persevere; for he has thought well of you in my presence. But you shall say these words to others, so that they too, who have performed or are about to perform repentance, may feel the same things as you, and so that he may interpret well of them before me, and I before the Lord.” “And I, Lord,” I said, “proclaim to every person the great things of God <note>original: "magnalia Dei"</note>; I hope, however, that all those who love them, and have sinned before, will perform repentance upon hearing these things, thus recovering life.” “Remain therefore,” he said, “in this ministry, and complete it. For whoever carries out his commands shall have life, and great honor here before the Lord. But whoever does not keep his commands, they flee from their own life and set themselves against him; and those who do not follow his commands deliver themselves to death, and each one of them will be guilty of his own blood. But I tell you to keep these commands, and you shall have a remedy for all your sins.”

III. “Moreover, I have sent these virgins <note>In this allegory, the 'virgins' are personifications of Christian virtues such as Faith, Continence, Power, and Patience. They were introduced in the previous Parable as the builders of the Tower (the Church).</note> to you, so that they may live with you; for I saw that they were very friendly toward you. You shall have them, therefore, as helpers, so that you may be better able to keep his commands; for it cannot happen that these commands be kept without these virgins. I see that they are glad to be with you; but I will also command them that they do not depart from your house at all. Only cleanse your house thoroughly; for they will gladly dwell in a clean house, because they are clean and chaste and industrious, and all of them hold grace before the Lord. Therefore, if they find your house pure, they will remain with you. But if even a little bit of defilement should occur, they will immediately depart from your house; for these virgins do not love any defilement at all.” I said to him: “I hope, Lord, that I will please them, so that they may always live gladly in my house. And just as he, to whom you delivered me, does not complain about me; so neither shall they complain.” He said to that shepherd: “I see that the servant of God wishes to see and keep these commands, and will place these virgins in a clean dwelling.” When he had said these things, he delivered me again to that shepherd, and called the virgins, and said to them: “Since I see that you gladly dwell in this man's house, I commend him and his house to you, so that you do not depart from his house at all.” And they heard these words gladly.

**II.** I said to him: "Lord, ask him yourself whether, from the time he has been in my house, I have done anything out of order <note>The Latin 'extra ordinem' suggests a breach of discipline or moral irregularity.</note> so as to offend him." And he said to me: "I also know that you have done nothing out of order, nor will you do so; for this reason I speak with you, so that you may persevere. Moreover, he has spoken well of you here in my presence. But you, tell these words to the others, so that they too, who have performed repentance, may feel the same things as you, and so that he may speak well of them here in my presence, and I [may speak well of them] before the Lord." And I said to him: "Lord, I declare to every person this magnificence of the Lord. I hope, however, that everyone, whoever hears and has previously sinned, will gladly perform repentance so as to receive life." And he said to me: "Remain in this ministry, and complete it. For whoever keeps his commands will have life, and will have the greatest honor here before God. But whoever does not keep his commands <note>original: "servaverint"</note>, they flee from their own life and despise him; they [lose] their honor here before their God. Whoever, therefore, despises him and does not keep his commands, delivers themselves to death, and each one of them becomes guilty of his own blood <note>This is a biblical idiom meaning one is responsible for their own spiritual destruction.</note>. But I tell you to serve these commands, and you will have a remedy for your former sins."

**III.** "Moreover, I have sent these virgins <note>In this allegory, the 'virgins' represent the twelve Christian virtues (such as Faith, Continence, and Simplicity). Their presence in a person's 'house' or soul is necessary for salvation.</note> to you also, so that they may live with you; for I saw that they are well-disposed toward you. You have them, therefore, as helpers, so that you may be able to keep these commands; for it is impossible to keep the commands without these virgins. I see, moreover, that they are gladly with you; and I will enjoin them never to depart from your house. Only make your house clean; for they gladly dwell in a clean house: for they are clean and chaste and diligent, and possess every grace before the Lord. If, therefore, they find your house pure, they will remain with you; but if your house is in any way filthy, they will immediately withdraw from your house: for these virgins do not love filth." And I said: "Lord, I hope I will please them so that they may gladly and always dwell in my house. And just as this man <note>Referring to the Shepherd, the Angel of Repentance.</note>, to whom you delivered me, complains of nothing regarding me, so neither will those virgins complain of anything regarding me." Then he said to that shepherd: "I know that this man keeps the commands, and will establish these virgins in a clean dwelling." When he had said these things, he again delivered me to that same shepherd. And he called those virgins and said to them: "Since I see that you gladly dwell in the house of this man, I commend him and his house to you, so that you may not depart from his house." Truly, those virgins heard these words very gladly.

**IV.** He then said to me: "Conduct yourself courageously in this ministry <note>Latin: *ministerio*; referring to Hermas’s specific role as a messenger of these revelations</note>; declare the mighty works of God to every person<sup>1</sup>, and you will find favor in this ministry. Whoever, therefore, walks in these commands shall live and be happy in his life; but whoever neglects them shall not live and shall be unhappy in his life. Tell everyone who is able to do right not to cease<sup>2</sup>; practicing good works is useful for them. Moreover, I say that every person<sup>3</sup> ought to be rescued from hardships. For he who is in need<sup>4</sup> and suffers hardships in daily life is in great torment and necessity. Whoever<sup>5</sup>, therefore, rescues such a soul from necessity acquires great joy for himself. For he<sup>6</sup> who is afflicted by such hardship is tortured by a torment equal to that of a person in chains. For many, on account of such calamities, when they cannot endure<sup>7</sup> them, bring death upon themselves <note>original: "mortem sibi consciscunt"; a literal reference to suicide resulting from extreme poverty and despair</note>. Whoever, therefore, knows the calamity of such a person and does not rescue him, commits<sup>8</sup> a great sin and becomes guilty of his blood. Therefore, perform good works, you who have received [blessings] from the Lord, lest while you delay to do them, the construction of the tower is finished; for the work of its building has been interrupted on your account<sup>9</sup>. Unless, therefore, you hurry to do right, the tower will be completed, and you will be excluded<sup>10</sup>." After he had spoken with me, he rose from the couch and, having taken the Shepherd and the virgins, he departed. But he told me that he would send back that Shepherd and those virgins to my house<sup>11</sup>.

**IV.** The shepherd said to me: "Conduct yourself courageously in this ministry <note>Latin: *ministerio*; Hermas’s specific service of sharing these revelations</note>; and show the greatness of the Lord to everyone, and you shall have favor in this ministry. Whoever, therefore, walks in these commands shall live and be happy; but whoever does not understand them shall not live, and shall be miserable in his life. Tell everyone that those who are able to do right should not stop; practicing good works is useful for them. Furthermore, I say that every person ought to be rescued from distress. For he who is in need and lives his daily life in great torment and necessity, and whoever rescues such a soul, acquires great joy for himself. For he who is afflicted by such distress is tortured just as one who is in chains. Many, in fact, because they cannot endure this kind of affliction, take their own lives <note>original: *mortem sibi adsciscunt*; highlighting the social reality of despair in the ancient world</note>. Whoever, therefore, knows the suffering of such a person and does not rescue him, commits a great sin and becomes guilty of his blood <note>a biblical idiom meaning one is responsible for another's death</note>. Do something good, all you who have received good things from the Lord. Do not be slow to act, lest the construction of the tower be finished, and you be rejected from the structure. No other tower is being built; it is for your sake that the construction of this same tower has been paused. Therefore, unless you hurry to do what is right, the tower will be finished." And after he had spoken these words, he rose from the bed, and taking that shepherd <note>the Angel of Repentance</note> and the virgins <note>symbolizing the Christian virtues</note> with him, he departed, telling me again that he would send the shepherd and the virgins to my house.

# THE BEGINNING, WITH GOD’S HELP, OF THE BOOK CALLED THE SHEPHERD.

## VISION 1.

1. The man who raised me¹ sold a certain young girl² to Rome. After many years, I recognized her—³ and I began to love her⁴ as a sister. After a long time,⁵ I saw her bathing in the river Tiber,⁶ and I gave her my hand and helped her out of the river. Seeing her beauty, I reasoned in my heart, saying, "How happy I would be if I had such a wife, both in beauty and in character." I thought only this, and nothing else. After some time, while I was traveling toward Cumae,⁸ I was glorifying God’s creations, because they are so great and powerful and beautiful. While walking, I fell asleep, and a spirit took me and carried me away through a pathless region⁹ where a person could not travel; for the place was steep and broken away¹⁰ by the waters. So, having crossed that river, I came to the level banks,¹¹ and I knelt down and began to pray to the Lord and to confess my sins. While I was praying, heaven was opened, and I saw the woman whom I had desired greeting me from heaven and saying, "Greetings, Hermas!" Looking at her, I said, "Lady, what are you doing here?" And she said, "I was taken up,¹² so that I might convict you of your sins before the Lord." I said to her, "Are you now my accuser?" "No," she said, "but listen to the words I am about to tell you. The God who dwells in the heavens, and who created out of nothing..."

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS. VISION I, 1. 2.

...who created all things out of nothing, and multiplied and increased them for the sake of his church, is angry with you because you sinned against me. Answering her, I said: "Did I sin against you? In what way? Or when did I ever speak a shameful word to you? Did I not always regard you as a daughter? Did you not always treat me with respect?" <note>The Greek text here is difficult to decipher; some versions suggest "Did you not always find fault with me?"</note> "Why, lady, do you falsely accuse me of these evil things?" Laughing, she said to me: "The desire for fornication rose up in your heart. Or does it not seem to you that it is an evil thing for a righteous man if an evil desire rises in his heart? For it is a great sin," she said. "For the righteous man purposes righteous things. By purposing righteous things, his glory is established in heaven, and he finds the Lord ready to be reconciled in every matter. But those who purpose evil in their hearts bring death and captivity upon themselves—especially those who claim this present age for themselves and boast in their wealth, and do not hold fast to the good things to come. Their souls will greatly regret it, for they have no hope, but have abandoned themselves and their own lives. But you, pray to God, and He will heal the sins of yourself, and of your whole household, and of all the saints."

II. After she had spoken these words, the heavens were closed; and I was entirely overcome with horror and grief. I began saying to myself: "If even this sin is recorded against me, how will I be able to be saved? Or how shall I appease God for my completed sins? <note>The Greek term *teleiōn* (τελείων) here refers to sins that are fully committed or "perfected," as opposed to mere thoughts.</note> With what words shall I ask the Lord to be merciful to me?" While I was debating and considering these things in my heart, I saw before me a great white chair made of white wool. Then an elderly woman <term>Elderly woman: a personification of the Church, who appears as an old woman because she was created first, before all things</term> came in most brilliant clothing, holding a book in her hands. She sat down alone and greeted me: "Hermas, greetings!" And she said: "Why is the long-suffering and quiet man, who is always laughing, so gloomy? Why are you so downcast in appearance and not cheerful?" And I said to her: "Because of a most excellent woman who says that I sinned against her." She said: "May such a thing never happen to a servant of God! But certainly, a thought about her did rise in your heart. To the servants of God, such a purpose brings sin. For it is an evil and terrifying purpose for a spirit that is holy and already proven if an evil desire or an evil deed should arise—especially in Hermas the self-controlled, who abstains from every evil desire, and who is full of all simplicity and great innocence."

Then, coming to myself and remembering the glory of God, I took courage, knelt, and began to confess my sins to the Lord, just as I had done before. But she arrived with six young men <note>original: "νεανίσκων" — these represent the six highest angels who oversee the building of the Church</note>, whom I had seen before, and she stood beside me and listened to me as I prayed and confessed my sins to the Lord. Touching me, she said, “Hermas, stop asking only about your sins; ask also about righteousness, so that you may take some portion of it with you to your home.” And she raised me up by the hand and led me to the couch, and said to the young men, “Go and build.”

After the young men had departed and we were left alone, she said to me, “Sit here.” I said to her, “Lady, let the elders <note>The leaders of the local church</note> sit first.” “Sit down as I tell you,” she said. When I wanted to sit on the right side, she would not allow me, but signaled to me with her hand that I should sit on the left. While I was thinking about this and was saddened because she did not let me sit on the right, she said to me, “Are you sad, Hermas? The place on the right is for others—for those who have already pleased God and have suffered for the sake of His name. You lack much before you can sit with them. But remain in your simplicity <term>simplicity: "ἁπλότης" (haplotēs) — a central virtue in this text meaning sincerity, single-mindedness, and lack of guile</term>, and you shall sit with them, as shall all who do what they have done and endure what they have endured.”

Others fell into the fire and were burned; and others fell near the waters, yet were unable to roll into the water.

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS.

...having overseen and taught and served purely and solemnly the word of the Lord to the servants of God—some having fallen asleep <note>A common early Christian euphemism for death.</note> and others still being present. They always agreed with one another, had peace among themselves, and listened to one another; for this reason, their joints fit together in the building of the tower. But who are those being pulled from the deep and placed into the building, fitting in with the other stones already built? These are they who have fallen asleep and suffered for the sake of the name of the Lord <note>original: "παθόντες ἕνεκα τοῦ ὀνόματος τοῦ κυρίου" — the editor notes that here and a little further on, some text is missing from the manuscript.</note>, and they have walked uprightly in His commandments. And who are those being led and placed into the building? <note>The editor notes that more text is missing here, perhaps because the scribe's eye jumped between similar words.</note> They are those who are in the faith of the Lord and are faithful. They are admonished by the angels to do good, because no wickedness was found in them. And who are those whom they were rejecting and throwing away? These are they who have sinned and wish to repent <note>original: "μεταχωρῆσαι" — the manuscript has a confused spelling here, possibly meaning to 'retreat' or 'change place,' but the editor suggests it refers to those changing their ways.</note>; for this reason, they were not thrown far outside the tower, because they will be useful for the building if they repent. Therefore, those who are about to repent <note>The bracketed text "those who... if" is a scholarly reconstruction where the manuscript had a blank space.</note>, if they indeed repent, will be strong <note>original: "ἰσχυροί" — interestingly, the manuscript copy reads "δύσχρηστοι" meaning 'difficult to use' or 'useless.'</note> in that faith <note>original: "ἐκείνῃ" — the manuscript seems to support this reading.</note> in which the tower is being built <note>original: "οἰκοδομεῖται" — the manuscript uses a past tense, 'had been built.'</note>. But if the building is finished, they will no longer have... <note>The manuscript is damaged here. The scholar Simonides suggested it meant "they will no longer have a place to rest."</note> and they will have only this: that they lie beside the tower.

VI. Those being cut up and thrown far from the tower, do you wish to know who they are? They are the sons of lawlessness <term>lawlessness: "ἀνομία" (anomia) — a state of living without regard for God's divine law or moral order</term>; they believed in hypocrisy, and all lawlessness did not depart from them. For this reason, they do not have salvation, because they are not useful <note>original: "ὠφέλιμοι" — the manuscript copy mistakenly reads "ἀδελφοί" (brothers).</note> for the building of the tower because of their wicked deeds. And the other stones which you saw lying in great numbers, not going into the building—these are the outcasts. They are those who have known the truth but did not remain in it, nor did they cling to the saints; for this reason, they are useless. And who are those having cracks? These are they who hold grudges against one another in their hearts and are not at peace among themselves. They maintain an appearance of peace, but when they depart from one another, the wickedness remains in their hearts. These, then, are the cracks they have. And those who are mutilated <note>Literally "shortened" or "stunted."</note>, these are they who have believed and for the most part live in righteousness, but they have certain parts of lawlessness; for this reason, they are mutilated and not complete. And the white and round stones, which do not fit into the building—who are they, Lady? Answering, she said to me, "How long will you be foolish and without understanding, asking about everything? <note>original: "ἐπερωτᾷς" — the manuscript had "ask," but it was corrected to "keep asking."</note>

# VISIO III, 5—8.

...and do you understand nothing? These are those who have faith, but also possess the wealth of this age as their substance. When tribulation <note>The author uses 'tribulation' (thlipsis) to refer to the pressures of social or state persecution that early Christians faced.</note> arises, because of their wealth and their business affairs, they deny their own Lord. I answered her and said, "Lady, when then will they be useful for the building?" "When," she said, "their wealth, which leads their souls astray, is trimmed away, then they will be useful to God. For just as a round stone, unless it is trimmed and loses something of itself, cannot become square, so also those who are rich in this age, unless their wealth is trimmed away, cannot become useful to the Lord. Learn first from your own case: when you were rich, you were useless; but now you are useful and profitable for life. You were all <note>The plural 'you' suggests she is addressing Hermas as a representative of a larger group here.</note> once useful to God; for you yourself are being used from these same stones."

### VII.

The other stones you saw being thrown far from the tower and falling into the road and rolling from the road into the rugged places <note>original: "ἀνοδίας" (anodias) — literally 'trackless' or 'pathless' places.</note>—these are those who have believed, but due to their double-mindedness <term>double-mindedness: from the Greek 'dipsychia,' meaning a divided heart or wavering between faith and the world</term>, they abandon the true way. Thinking they can find a better way, they wander and fall into misery, walking in the trackless places. And those falling into the fire and being burned—these are those who have finally turned away from the living God, and it no longer entered into their hearts to repent because of the desires of their licentiousness and the wickedness they committed. And the others falling near the waters and not being able to roll into the water—do you wish to know who they are? These are those who heard the word and wanted to be baptized into the name of the Lord; then, when the knowledge of the truth comes to their memory, they change their minds and go back again after their own wicked desires. 

So she finished the explanation of the tower. Becoming bold, I asked her further whether all these stones that were cast aside and do not fit into the building of the tower might have a chance for repentance, and if they might have a place in this tower. "They have the opportunity for repentance," she said, "but they cannot fit into *this* place. They will fit in another, much inferior place, and this only after they have been tormented and have fulfilled the days of their sins. And for this reason they will be moved, because they partook of the righteous word; and then it will happen that they are moved out of their torments, if it enters into their hearts to repent... <note>The editor indicates a gap in the manuscript here.</note> they are not saved because of the hardness of their hearts."

# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS.

...I became very glad to see this. She smiled at me and said, "Do you see seven women around the tower?" "I see them, Lady," I said.¹ "This tower is supported by them by command of the Lord. Hear now their powers. The first of them, the one holding hands, is called **Faith**²; through her, the elect of God are saved. The second, the one who is girded, is called **Self-Control**; she is the daughter of Faith. Whoever follows them becomes blessed in their life, because they will abstain from all evil deeds, believing that if they abstain from every evil desire, they will inherit eternal life."

"And the other five, Lady, who are they?"³ "They are daughters of one another; they are called **Simplicity**, then **Innocence**, then **Reverence**, then **Knowledge**, and finally **Love**. When, therefore, you perform all the works of their mother, you are able to live." "I wish to know, Lady," I said, "what power each of them has." "Hear," she said, "their powers. They are held by one another and follow one another, just as they were born. From Faith is born Self-Control; from Self-Control, Simplicity; from Simplicity, Innocence; from Innocence, Reverence; from Reverence, Knowledge; and from Knowledge, Love. The works of these, then, are pure and reverent and divine. Whoever serves these and prevails⁴ in holding to their works shall have a dwelling in the tower with the saints of God."

I questioned⁵ her about the time,⁶ whether the completion is already here. But she cried out with a great voice,⁷ saying, "Senseless man! Do you not see the tower still being built? As long as the tower is being built, it has its end [yet to come]; but it will be built quickly. ### VISION III, 8—10.
->583<-

...this lack of community <note>original: 'ἀσυγκρασία' (asyngrasia), meaning a failure to mix or share resources in a common life</note> is harmful to you who possess much and do not share with those in need. Look to the judgment that is coming! You, therefore, who are prominent, seek out the hungry while the tower is not yet finished. For after the tower is completed, you will want to do good, but you will have no place for it. Look³ out, then, you who boast in your wealth, lest those in want should groan, and their groaning goes up to the Lord, and you be shut out with your <margin>4) The editor Simonides suggests reading: "with the greed of your goods." But this is certainly not in the copy. Above the feminine "the" is a masculine "the," then a word written in shorthand beginning with the letters *ad*; there is also a *chi*; what that might be, I do not quite follow. The word "of the," which seems necessary, was perhaps poorly abbreviated.</margin> ... goods outside the door of the tower. Now, therefore, I say to you who are leaders of the church and to those who take the chief seats <note>original: 'πρωτοκαθεδρίταις' (protokathedritais), referring to those in positions of honor or authority in the early Christian assembly</note>: do not be like sorcerers. Sorcerers carry their charms in boxes, but you carry your charms and your poison in your heart. You are hardened <note>literally "sclerosed" or calloused</note> and do not wish to cleanse your hearts and mix your wisdom together in a pure heart, so that you may receive mercy from the Great King. Take care then, children, lest these divisions rob you of your life. How do you wish to instruct the elect of the Lord, when you yourselves have no instruction? Instruct one another then, and be at peace among them,⁵ so that I also, standing joyfully before the Father, may give an account for all of you to your Lord.

In the second vision, her face was younger, but her flesh and hair were older, and she spoke to me while standing; she was more cheerful³ than before. But in the third vision, she was entirely young and of most beautiful appearance, only her hair was old; she was joyful to the end, and was sitting on a couch. I was very distressed about these things, wanting to know this revelation. And I saw the elderly woman in a vision of the night saying: "Every request requires humility. These revelations are enough for you. Are you even able⁵ to see stronger revelations than these?"

## VISION IV.

1. This is the vision that I saw, brothers, twenty days after the previous vision occurred. It is a symbol <note>original: 'τύπον' (typon), a type or foreshadowing</note> of the coming tribulation. I was going into the countryside on the winding road <note>a note in the manuscript suggests this could also be read as the "Campanian road"</note>. From the public highway to the field is about ten stadia <note>about 1.2 miles; a stadium was a Greek unit of distance</note>, and the place is easy to travel. While walking alone, I begged the Lord to complete the revelations and visions which He showed me through His holy Church, so that He might strengthen me and grant repentance to all His servants who have stumbled, so that His great and glorious name might be glorified because He considered me worthy to be shown His wonders.

And as I was glorifying and giving thanks to Him, an echo of a voice answered me: "Do not be double-minded <note>original: 'διψυχήσεις' (dipsychēseis), referring to the state of having a divided soul or wavering faith</note>, Hermas." And I began to reason within myself and say, "How can I be double-minded, when I have been so well-founded by the Lord and have seen such glorious things?" And as I went on a little further, brothers, behold, I saw a cloud of dust rising as if toward heaven, and I began to say to myself, "Could it be cattle approaching and raising a dust cloud?" It was about one stadium away from me.

As the dust cloud became larger, I suspected it was something divine. The sun shone out briefly, and behold, I saw a massive beast, like a sea-monster <note>original: 'κῆτος' (kētos), often used for whales or legendary sea creatures</note>, and out of its mouth fiery locusts were coming. The beast was about a hundred feet long, and its head was like a pottery jar <note>original: 'κεράμου' (keramou), perhaps suggesting a hard, rounded, or hollow shape</note>. I began to weep and to ask the Lord to rescue me from it. Then I remembered the word I had heard: "Do not be double-minded, Hermas."

So, brothers, having put on the faith of God and remembering the great things He had shown me, I took courage and gave myself over to face the beast. Now the beast was coming on with such a rushing sound <note>the manuscript notes indicate this word suggests a snorting or roaring noise</note> that it could have destroyed a city. I came near to it, and that massive creature stretched itself out on the ground and did nothing except stick out its tongue; it did not move at all until I had passed by it. The beast had four colors on its head: black, then a fiery and bloody color, then golden, and finally white.
