THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS.

### MANDATE I.

First of all, believe that God is one, who created and ordered all things, and brought all things into being out of nothing, and who contains all things but is himself alone uncontainable. <note>original: 'χωρῶν, μόνος δὲ ἀχώρητος'. This is a classic early Christian description of God’s infinity: He provides the "space" for everything to exist, but nothing can limit or encompass Him.</note> Fear Him, therefore, and through this fear, practice self-control. Keep these things, and you will cast away all wickedness from yourself and clothe yourself in every virtue of righteousness; and you shall live to God, if you keep this commandment.

### MANDATE II.

He says to me: Have simplicity and be innocent,<gloss>1</gloss> and you shall be<gloss>2</gloss> like infants who do not know the wickedness that destroys<gloss>3</gloss> human life. First, speak evil of no one, nor listen gladly to one who speaks evil.<gloss>4</gloss> Otherwise, you who listen will be responsible for the sin of the one speaking evil, if you believe the slander which you hear; for by believing it, you yourself will hold a grudge against your brother. In this way, you will be guilty of the sin of the slanderer. Slander is evil; it is a restless demon, never at peace, but always dwelling in divisions. Refrain from it, and you will always have success with everyone. Clothe yourself in dignity, in which there is no evil stumbling block, but all things are smooth and joyful. Do good, and from your labors which God gives you,<gloss>6</gloss> give simply to all who are in need, not hesitating about to whom you should give or to whom you should not give. Give to all; for God wants His own gifts to be shared with everyone. Those who receive, then, will render an account to God as to why they received and for what purpose. For those who receive because they are in distress shall not be judged, but those who receive under false pretenses shall pay the penalty. Therefore, the giver is innocent; for as he received the ministry from the Lord to perform, he fulfilled it<gloss>7</gloss> without distinguishing to whom he should give. This ministry, when performed in simplicity, becomes glorious in the sight of God. He who serves God simply in this way shall live. Keep these commandments, therefore, as I have spoken to you, so that your repentance and that of your household may be found in simplicity<gloss>8</gloss> and your heart may be pure and without stain.

### MANDATE III.

Again he says to me: Love truth, and let all truth proceed from your mouth, so that the Spirit which God settled<gloss>1</gloss> in this flesh may be found true in the sight of all men; and thus the Lord who dwells in you will be glorified. For the Lord is true in every word, and there is no lie in Him. Therefore, those who lie reject the Lord and become robbers of the Lord, not returning to Him the

For the servants of God, there is only one <term>repentance</term> <note>original: "μετάνοια" (metanoia), referring to a transformative change of heart and mind.</note>. On account of this repentance, the husband ought not to marry again. This practice applies to both wife and husband. Adultery," he says, "is not only when one defiles their own flesh, but whoever acts as the heathens do also commits adultery. Therefore, if someone persists in such deeds and does not repent, stay away from them and do not live with them; otherwise, you too will be a partner in their sin. For this reason, you were commanded to remain single, whether wife or husband; for in these cases, repentance is possible. I am not," he says, "giving an excuse for this act to be carried out this way, but so that the one who has sinned may sin no more. As for their former sin, there is One <note>original: "ἔστι τοῦ δυναμένου," likely referring to God. Footnote 8 suggests the words "of God" may have fallen out of the text here.</note> who is able to provide healing—for He is the one who has authority over all things."

II. Give me understanding, for I am very foolish and perceive absolutely nothing." He answered me, saying, "I am in charge of repentance, and I give <term>understanding</term> <note>original: "σύνεσιν" (sunesis), meaning insight or comprehension.</note> to all who repent. For the one who has sinned understands that they have done evil before the Lord, and the act they committed rises into their heart; and having repented, they no longer do what is evil, but do good abundantly. They humble their soul and torture it because they sinned <note>Footnote II-1: the manuscript copy reads "I sinned."</note>. You see, then," he said, "that repentance is a great understanding. For this reason, then," I said, "Sir, I examine everything accurately from you. First, because I am a sinner, so that I may know what kind of works I must do to live, because my sins are many and varied." "You will live," he said, "if you keep my commandments and walk in them; and whoever hears these commandments and keeps them will live to God."

III. "Sir," I said, "I will add one more question." "Speak," he said. "I heard, Sir, from certain teachers, that there is no other repentance except that one, when we went down into the water and received the forgiveness of our former sins." He said to me, "You heard correctly; for that is how it is. For the person who has received forgiveness of sins should sin no more, but dwell in purity. But since you examine everything accurately, I will reveal this to you as well, without providing an excuse for those who are about to believe or those who have now believed in the Lord. For those who have now believed, or are about to believe, do not have a repentance of sins, but they have forgiveness of their former sins. ## II.

"Hear now," he said, "the activity of quick temper: how evil it is, and how it overthrows the servants of God by its own working, and how it leads them astray from righteousness. But it does not lead astray those who are full in their faith, nor can it work its power upon them, because my power is with them; rather, it leads astray those who are empty and <term>double-minded</term> <note>original: "διψύχους" (dipsychous), meaning those who waver or are hesitant in their devotion</note>. Whenever it sees such people in a state of tranquility, it inserts itself<gloss>1</gloss> into the heart of that person, and for no reason at all, the woman or the man finds themselves in bitterness over worldly matters—perhaps over food, or some petty talk, or some gift,<gloss>2</gloss> or some such foolish things. For all these things are foolish, empty, and senseless for the servants of God.

But patience is great and possesses strong power; it is robust and thrives in great expansion. It is cheerful, exultant, free from care, glorifying the Lord at all times, having nothing bitter within itself, and remaining forever meek and quiet. This patience, then, dwells with those who possess their faith in its entirety. But quick temper is first of all foolish, flighty, and senseless. Then, from foolishness comes bitterness, and from bitterness comes wrath, and from wrath comes anger, and from anger comes a grudge. Then this grudge, being composed of so many evils, becomes a great and incurable sin. For when all these spirits dwell in one vessel where the Holy Spirit also dwells, that vessel cannot contain them, but it overflows. Therefore, the tender Spirit, being unaccustomed to dwelling with an evil spirit or with harshness, departs from such a person and seeks to dwell with meekness and quiet. ## MANDATE VII.

"Fear the Lord," he said, "and keep His commandments. By keeping the commandments of God, you will be powerful in every action, and your conduct will be beyond comparison. For by fearing the Lord, you will perform everything well. This is the fear which you must have to be saved. But do not fear the Devil; for if you fear the Lord, you will have mastery over the Devil, because there is no power in him. He who has no power also inspires no fear; but he who has glorious power also inspires fear. For everyone who has power inspires fear, but he who has no power is despised by all. Fear the works of the Devil, because they are evil. By fearing the Lord, you will not perform these works, but will abstain from them.

There are, therefore, two kinds of fear. If you wish to do what is evil, fear God, and you will not do it. If you wish to do what is good, fear the Lord, and you will do it. So the fear of the Lord is strong, great, and glorious. Fear the Lord, therefore, and you shall live to Him; and as many as fear Him and keep His commandments shall live to God." "Why, sir," I asked, "did you say of those who keep His commandments, 'they shall live to God'?" ### MANDATE IX.

He said to me: "Remove from yourself¹ **double-mindedness** <term>original: "διψυχία" (dipsychia), literally 'two-souledness,' referring to a state of wavering doubt or hesitation in faith.</term> and do not doubt at all to ask anything from God, saying within yourself, 'How can I ask from the Lord and receive it, having committed so many sins against Him?' Do not reason in this way, but turn to the Lord with all your heart and ask from Him without doubting, and you will know² His great compassion, for He will not forsake you, but will fulfill the request of your soul. For He is not like men who bear grudges, but He is one who forgets offenses and has compassion on His own creation. 

You, then, cleanse your heart from all the vanities³ of this age, and from the words previously spoken to you, and ask from the Lord, and you shall receive all things; you will not lack any of your requests, provided you ask from the Lord without doubting. But if you doubt in your heart, you shall receive none of your requests. For those who doubt toward God, these are the double-minded, and they do not obtain any of their requests at all. 

But those who are complete in faith ask for all things, trusting in the Lord, and they receive them because they ask without doubting, being in no way double-minded. For every double-minded man, unless he repents, shall hardly be saved. Cleanse your heart, therefore, from double-mindedness; clothe yourself in faith, for it is strong, and believe in God that you will receive all the requests you ask. 

And if ever, after asking something from the Lord, you are somewhat slow in receiving it, do not be double-minded just because you did not receive the request of your soul quickly; for surely it is because of some temptation or some transgression of which you are unaware that you are receiving your request slowly. Do not, then, cease making the request of your soul, and you shall receive it. But if you grow weary and become double-minded in your asking, blame yourself⁴ and not Him who gives to you. 

Watch out for this double-mindedness; for it is evil and senseless, and it uproots many from the faith, even those who are very strong. For this double-mindedness is the sister of the devil, and she works great evil against the servants of God. Despise double-mindedness, therefore, and gain mastery over it⁵ in every matter, by clothing yourself in...

...it seems to lead to salvation, because after doing something evil, the person repented. Instead, clothe yourself in cheerfulness <term>original: "ἱλαρότης" (hilarotes), a state of joy or readiness of heart</term>, which always finds favor with God and is acceptable to Him; delight yourself in it. For every cheerful person does good things and thinks good thoughts, looking down upon grief. But the sorrowful person always acts wickedly. First, he acts wickedly because he grieves the Holy Spirit, who was given to humanity as a cheerful spirit. Second, by grieving the Holy Spirit, he commits lawlessness, for he neither prays effectively nor confesses to the Lord. For the intercession <term>original: "ἔντευξις" (enteuxis), meaning a petition or prayerful appeal</term> of a sorrowful person never has the power to ascend to the altar of God." "Why, sir," I asked, "does the intercession of a grieving person not ascend to the altar?" "Because," he said, "grief sits upon his heart. When grief is mixed with intercession, it does not allow the prayer to ascend pure to the altar. Just as vinegar and wine, when mixed together, do not provide the same pleasure, so also grief, when mixed with the Holy Spirit, does not allow the prayer to be the same. Cleanse yourself from this wicked grief and you shall live to God; indeed, all shall live to God who cast away grief from themselves and clothe themselves in all cheerfulness."

...and they repent frequently, they practice divination just as the nations <note>original: "ἔθνη" (ethne), often referring to pagans or non-Christians</note> do, and bring greater sin upon themselves by practicing idolatry. ...man. But seeing me entirely troubled and confused, he began to speak more gently to me. ## V.

I say to him, "Lord, hear a few words from me." "Speak what you wish," he says. "A man, Lord," I said, "is eager to keep the commandments of God, and there is no one who does not ask of the Lord that he may be strengthened in His commandments and submit to them; but the devil is hard and oppresses them." "He cannot," he says, "oppress the servants of God who hope in Him with their whole heart. The devil can wrestle against them, but he cannot throw them down. If then you resist him, he will be defeated and flee from you in shame. But those," he says, "who are empty, fear the devil as if he had power. When a man fills many jars with good wine, and among those jars a few are empty, he goes to the jars and does not consider the full ones—for he knows they are full—but he examines the empty ones, fearing they have turned sour. For empty jars quickly turn sour and the pleasure of the wine is lost. So also the devil comes to all the servants of God to test them. Those who are full in faith resist him strongly, and he departs from them because he has no place to enter. Then he goes to the empty ones, and finding a place, he enters into them, and he does what he wishes within them, and they become his subjects."

<meta>This page concludes the final chapter of the Mandates (specifically Mandate 12 in most modern editions, though here labeled XIII) and begins the "Similitudes" or Parables. The previous page featured the Angel of Repentance encouraging Hermas that God's commands are not burdensome for those who truly love Him. Here, the Angel offers a final exhortation to fear God rather than the devil, before transitioning into a famous teaching on the Christian’s status as a resident alien in the world.</meta>

<page-num>603</page-num>
<header>MANDATE XIII, 4—6. SIMILITUDE I.</header>

VI. "And I say to you," says the Angel of Repentance, "do not fear the devil. For I have been sent," he says, "to be with you who repent with all your heart and to strengthen you in the faith. Therefore, believe in God, you who have despaired of your life because of your sins, and who keep adding to your sins <gloss>1) original: "hamartias"</gloss> and weighing down your life. For if you turn back to the Lord with all your heart and practice righteousness for the remaining days of your life, and serve Him according to His will, He will provide healing for your former sins, and you will have the power to master the works of the devil. Do not fear the threat of the devil at all, for he is as weak as the sinews <note>The Greek *neura* refers to tendons or nerves; the image is of a body without life or tension.</note> of a dead man. Listen to me, then, and fear the One who is able to do all things—to save and to destroy—and keep these commandments, and you will live to God." I said to him, "Lord, now I have been strengthened in all the righteous requirements of the Lord, because you are with me. And I know that you will crush all the power of the devil, and we will master him and prevail over all his works. And I hope, Lord, to be able <gloss>2) original: "men" (perhaps a scribe's error for "me")</gloss> to keep these commandments which you have commanded, as the Lord gives me strength." "You will keep them," he says, "if your heart becomes pure toward the Lord; and indeed all who purify their hearts from the vain desires of this world <note>The term *aionos* refers to the current "age" or world-system.</note> will keep them and live to God."

## PARABLES WHICH HE SPOKE WITH ME.

He says to me: "You know," he says, "that you who are servants of God dwell in a foreign land <gloss>1) original: "hoi"</gloss>; for your city is far away from this city. If, then, you know your city in which you are destined to dwell, why do you prepare fields and costly gear and buildings and vain rooms here? Anyone, therefore, who prepares these things for this city cannot return to his own city. O foolish and double-minded and miserable man, do you not understand that all these things belong to another and are under the authority of someone else? For the lord of this city will say, 'I do not want you to dwell in my city; depart from this city, because you do not use my laws.' You, then, who have fields and dwellings and many other possessions, when you are cast out <gloss>3) original: "ekballomenos"</gloss> by him, what will you do with your field and your house and all the other things you prepared for yourself? For the lord of this region says to you justly, 'Either use my laws, or leave my region.' What then do you intend to do, since you have a law in your own city? For the sake of your fields and your other possessions, will you completely deny your own law <gloss>4) original: "ton nomon"</gloss> and walk according to the law of this—

Simply do your own work, and you will be saved.

### BEGINNING OF ANOTHER SIMILITUDE.

While I was walking in the field and observing an elm and a vine, and reflecting upon them and their fruits, the Shepherd appeared to me and said, "What are you wondering about within yourself concerning the elm and the vine?" "I am thinking, sir," I said, "that they are very well suited to one another." "These two trees," he said, "stand as a type <note>The Greek word *typos* refers to a symbolic pattern or a model that represents a spiritual reality.</note> for the servants of God." "I wish to know, sir," I said, "the meaning of the type of these trees you speak of." "Do you see," he said, "the elm and the vine?" "I see them, sir," I replied. "This vine," he said, "bears fruit, but the elm is a fruitless tree. However, if this vine does not climb up the elm, it cannot bear much fruit because it is spread out on the ground; and the fruit it does bear is rotten because it is not hanging from the elm. But when the vine is cast upon the elm, it bears fruit both from itself and because of the elm. You see, then, that the elm also gives much fruit—not less than the vine, but rather even more. For," he said, "the vine..."

hanging upon the elm tree, [the vine] gives much and beautiful fruit; but if it is cast upon the ground, it bears only a little fruit and even that is rotten. This parable, therefore, applies to the servants of God—to the poor and the wealthy alike.” “How, sir?” I asked. “Explain it to me.” “Listen,” he said. “The rich man has much wealth, but toward the Lord he is poor, being distracted by his riches. His confession <note>original: "ἐξομολόγησιν" (exomologēsin); here referring to the prayerful acknowledgment of God's goodness</note> and his prayer to the Lord are very small and they are weak <margin>1) The manuscript spells this "blichran."</margin> and <margin>2) Thus in the manuscript. And the poor man, being provided for by the rich man, prays to God for him, giving thanks <margin>4) The manuscript definitely uses an abbreviation for "giving thanks." The first printed edition of this text changed it to "and he gives thanks."</margin> for the one who gives to him. And the rich man, in turn, becomes even more zealous on behalf of the poor man, so that he may lack nothing in his life; for he knows that the prayer of the poor is acceptable and rich before God. Thus, both complete the work together. The poor man works through prayer, in which he is rich and which he received from the Lord; this he gives back to the Lord who provided for him. Likewise, the rich man provides the wealth he received from the Lord to the poor man without hesitation. This is a great work and acceptable to God, because he understood <note>The Shepherd emphasizes that the rich man's merit comes from recognizing that his wealth is a gift to be managed, not just owned.</note> the purpose of his wealth and worked for the poor using the gifts of the Lord, fulfilling his ministry correctly. To human eyes, the elm tree seems to bear no fruit, and people do not know or realize that if a drought comes, the elm—which holds water—nourishes the vine. The vine, having an uninterrupted supply of water, yields a double portion of fruit, both for itself and for the elm. In the same way, the poor, by praying to the Lord on behalf of the rich, support their wealth, and the rich, by providing the necessities to the poor, support their souls. So, both become partners in the righteous work. Whoever does these things will not be abandoned by God but will be enrolled in the books of the living. Blessed are those who possess wealth and understand that they are made rich by the Lord.”

Why then, sir," I asked, "are they as if they were dry and all alike?" "Because,"

but they are all alike. For this age is **winter** for the righteous, and

## THE BEGINNING OF ANOTHER PARABLE <note>Similitude IV</note>

He showed me many trees again, some budding and some dry, 
and he said to me, "Do you see these trees?" "I see them, sir," I said, 
"some budding and some dry." "These trees," he said, "that are budding 
are the righteous, who are going to dwell in the **age to come**; 
for the age to come is **summer** <note>The manuscript here uses the word for 'throne,' but scholars agree it should be 'summer' to fit the metaphor</note> to the righteous, but to the sinners it is 
winter. When, therefore, the mercy of the Lord shall shine forth, then 
those who serve God shall be revealed, and all shall be made manifest. For 
just as in summer the fruit of every single tree is revealed and it is 
recognized what sort they are, so also the fruit of the righteous shall be 
revealed, and all those who are flourishing <note>The original manuscript repeats the phrase 'those who are flourishing' twice</note> in that age shall be known. 
But the heathens and the sinners—the dry trees you saw—
such shall they be found: dry and fruitless in that age. Like wood 
they shall be burned up, and it shall be made manifest that their conduct 
was evil in their life. For the sinners shall be burned because 
they sinned and did not repent; and the heathens shall be burned because 
they did not know their Creator. You, therefore, bear fruit, so that in 
that summer your fruit may be known. Keep yourself from many affairs 
and you will never commit any sin; for those who engage in many affairs 
also sin much, being distracted by their affairs and not at all 
serving their own Lord. How then," he said, "can such a person 
ask anything of the Lord and receive it, while not serving the Lord? Those 
who serve Him, they shall receive their requests; but those who do not 
serve the Lord, they shall receive nothing. But if someone 
performs only one work, they can also serve the Lord; for their 
mind will not be corrupted from the Lord, but they will serve Him, having 
a pure mind. If you do these things, therefore, you are able to bear 
fruit for the age to come; and whoever does these things shall 
bear fruit."

sitting by me and saying, "Why have you come here so early in the morning?" "Because, sir," I said, "I have a **station**" <note>original: "στατίων" (station); a technical term used by early Christians, borrowed from military language, to describe a period of watching, prayer, or a half-day fast</note>. "What," he asked, "is a station?" "I am fasting, sir," I replied. "And what," he said, "is this fast that you are fasting?" "As I was accustomed, sir," I said, "so I fast." "You do not know," he said, "how to fast to the Lord, nor is this useless fast which you fast to Him truly a fast." "Why, sir," I asked, "do you say this?" "I tell you," he said, "that this is not a fast which you think you are fasting; but I will teach you what is a fast acceptable and complete to the Lord. Listen," he said.

> God does not desire such a vain fast; for by fasting to God in this way, you will perform nothing for righteousness. But fast to God a fast like this: do no evil in your life, and serve the Lord with a pure heart; keep His commandments, walking in His ordinances, and let no evil desire rise in your heart. Believe in God, and if you do these things and fear Him and restrain yourself from every evil deed, you shall live to God; and if you do these things, you perform a great fast and one acceptable to God.

II. Listen to the parable which I am going to tell you regarding fasting. A certain man had a **field** <note>original: "ἀγρὸν" (agron)</note> and many slaves, and in a part of the field he planted a **vineyard** <note>original: "ἀμπελῶνα" (ampelona)</note>. Selecting a certain slave who was faithful, well-pleasing, and held in honor, he called him and said: "Take this vineyard which I have planted and fence it until I come; but do nothing else to the vineyard. Keep this command of mine, and you shall have your freedom from me." Then the master of the slave went abroad. When he had left, the slave took and fenced the vineyard, and having finished the fencing, he saw that the vineyard was full of weeds. He reasoned within himself, saying, "I have finished this command of the master; I will now dig this vineyard, and it will be more beautiful when dug, and having no weeds it will give more fruit, not being choked by the weeds." Taking [his tools], he dug the vineyard and pulled out all the weeds that were in the vineyard; and that vineyard became very beautiful and flourishing, not having weeds choking it. After some time, the master of the slave and the field came and entered the vineyard, and seeing the vineyard beautifully fenced, and moreover dug and all the weeds pulled out and the vines flourishing, he rejoiced greatly at the works of the slave. Calling his beloved son, whom he had as an heir, and the friends whom he had as advisors, he told them what he had commanded his slave and what he found had happened. And they congratulated the slave on the testimony which the master gave him. And the master said to them, "I promised this slave freedom if he kept the command which I gave him; but he kept my command and added a good work to the vineyard, and pleased me greatly. Therefore, in return for this..."

"Because of the work he has performed, I wish to make him a co-heir with my son; for in thinking what was good, he did not neglect it, but carried it out." To this decision, the master’s son agreed with him—that the slave should become a co-heir with the son. After a few days, the master held a dinner and sent many dishes to the slave from the feast. When the slave received the dishes sent to him by the master, he took what was sufficient for himself and distributed the rest to his fellow slaves. His fellow slaves, having received the dishes, were glad and began to pray for him, that he might find even greater favor with the master because he had treated them so well. Calling together his friends and his son once more, the master reported to them the action the slave had taken regarding the dishes he had received. III. I said, "Lord, I do not know these parables of yours, nor can I understand them unless you explain them to me." "I will explain everything to you," he said, "and whatever I speak with you, I will show you. His commandments... <note>The text is fragmentary here; the Shepherd is moving from the parable to the moral application regarding 'extra' good works.</note> if you do any good thing beyond the commandment of God, you will gain for yourself greater glory, and you will be more honored in the sight of God than you would otherwise have been. If, therefore, while keeping the commandments of God, you also add these **services** <note>original: "λειτουργίας" (leitourgias); refers here to voluntary acts of devotion or charity beyond the basic requirements of the law</note>, you will rejoice, provided you observe them according to my command." I said to him, "Lord, whatever you command me, I will keep it; for I know that you are with me." "I will be with you," he said, "because you have such a readiness for doing good; and I will be with all," he said, "who have this same readiness. This **fasting** <note>original: "νηστεία" (nesteia)</note>," he said, "is very good, provided the commandments of the Lord are kept. This, then, is how you shall observe the fast you are about to keep: First of all, guard yourself from every evil word and every evil desire, and cleanse your heart from all the vanities of this world. If you keep these things, this fast will be perfect for you. And this is what you must do: after completing what is written, on the day you fast, you shall taste nothing but bread and water. Then, you shall calculate the amount of the expense for that day which you would have spent on food, and you shall give it to a widow, or an orphan, or someone in need. In this way, you will become humble-minded, so that from your humility, the one who receives it may satisfy his own soul and pray for you to the Lord. If you complete your fast in the way I have commanded you, your sacrifice will be acceptable to God, and this fast will be recorded; and the service thus performed is beautiful, joyful, and well-pleasing to the Lord. These things you shall observe in this way, you and your children and your whole household. If you observe them, you will be blessed; and as many as hear them and observe them shall be blessed, and whatever they ask from the Lord, they shall receive."

# SIMILITUDE V, 2–5. 609
## APOSTOLIC FATHERS 39

IV. I begged him many times to explain to me the parable of the field, the master, the vineyard, the servant who staked the vineyard, the stakes, the weeds pulled out from the vineyard, the son, and the friends who were advisors. For I understood that all these things were a parable. But he answered me and said, "You are very stubborn in your questioning. You ought not," he said, "to ask anything at all; for if it is necessary for it to be explained to you, it will be explained." I said to him, "Lord, whatever you show me and do not explain, I will have seen in vain, not understanding what it is. Similarly, if you speak parables to me and do not interpret them, I will have heard something from you in vain." He answered me again, saying, "Whoever is a servant of God and has his Lord in his heart, asks him for understanding and receives it, and he interprets every parable, and the words of the Lord spoken through parables become known to him. But those who are weak <note>original: "blichroi" — meaning feeble or sluggish in spirit or faith</note> and idle in prayer, they hesitate to ask from the Lord. But the Lord is very compassionate and gives unceasingly to all who ask from him. But since you have been strengthened by the holy angel and have received from him such a power of intercession, and since you are not idle, why do you not ask understanding from the Lord and receive it from him?" I said to him, "Lord, since I have you with me, I have a necessity to ask you and to question you. For you show me everything and speak with me. But if I had seen or heard these things without you, I would have asked the Lord that they might be explained to me."

V. "I told you just now," he said, "that you are meddlesome and stubborn in questioning the interpretations of the parables. But since you are so persistent, I will interpret for you the parable of the field and all the other things that follow, so that you may make them known to everyone. Listen now," he said, "and understand them. The field is this world. The Lord of the field is the one who created all things, perfected them, and gave them strength. The servant is the Son of God. The vines are this people whom he himself planted. The stakes are the holy angels of the Lord who keep the people together. The weeds pulled out from the vineyard are the lawless deeds of the servants of God. The food which he sent to him from the dinner are the commandments which he gave to his people through his Son. The friends and advisors are the holy angels who were created first. And the master’s absence from home is the time that remains until his coming." I said to him, "Lord, everything is great and wonderful and glorious. Could I then," I asked, "have understood these things? No other person, even if they were very intelligent, could understand them. Furthermore, Lord," I said, "explain to me what I am about to ask you." "Speak," he said, "if you wish <note>original: "ei ti boulei" — literally 'if you want anything'</note>." "Why, Lord," I asked, "is the Son of God represented as a servant in the parable?"

***

Chapter IV. 1) **him**: in the <term>codex | an ancient manuscript book</term> it appears to be "to him."

2) The manuscript again reads **blichroi** <note>a variant spelling for 'weak' or 'sluggish'</note>.

3) **them**: so the manuscript, not "them" (feminine) as in the <term>editio princeps | the first printed edition of a work</term>.

<column-break/>

Chapter V. 1) **them**: so again the manuscript, not "them" (feminine) as in the first edition.

2) **if anything**: it is not entirely clear whether "if anything" or "that" (as in the first edition) was written. But it seems rather to be "if anything."

3) **you wish**: as above. The first edition reads a different spelling for "you wish."

The page ends with Hermas questioning why the Son of God is depicted in the lowly status of a servant.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Fifth Similitude" of the Shepherd of Hermas. In the preceding text, the Shepherd presented a parable about a faithful servant in a vineyard. Here, the Shepherd provides the deeper theological interpretation of that servant’s identity and the relationship between the Spirit and the flesh.</meta>

<page-num>610</page-num>
# THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS.

VI. “Listen,” he said, “the Son of God is not [not]¹ placed in the condition of a servant, but is placed in great power and lordship.” “How, Lord?” I asked, “I do not understand.” “Because,” he said, “God planted the vineyard—that is, he created the people—and delivered them to his Son. And the Son appointed the angels over them to keep them. And he himself purged our² sins, having labored greatly and endured many toils; for no one can dig without toil or labor. He himself, therefore, having purged the sins of the people, showed them the paths of life, giving them the law which he received from his Father. Now, listen to why the Lord took his Son and the glorious angels as advisors regarding the inheritance of the servant. The Holy Spirit, which is pre-existent, which created the whole creation, God caused to dwell in the flesh <note>The Greek term *sarx* (flesh) here refers to the human nature or physical body that serves as a vessel for the Spirit.</note> that he desired. This flesh, therefore, in which the Holy Spirit dwelt, served the Spirit well, walking in gravity and purity, and did not defile the Spirit in any way. Because it lived well and purely, and labored with the Spirit, and worked with it in every matter with strength and bravery, he chose it as a partner <note>or "companion"</note>; for the conduct of this flesh pleased him, because it was not defiled while it held the Holy Spirit upon the earth. Therefore, he took the Son and the glorious angels as advisors, so that this flesh, having served the Spirit blamelessly, might have some place of residence, and might not seem to have lost the reward for its service; for all flesh in which the Holy Spirit has dwelt, if found undefiled and spotless, shall receive a reward. You have now the interpretation of this parable also.”

VII. “I was glad, Lord,” I said, “to hear this interpretation.” “Listen now,” he said: “Keep this flesh of yours pure and undefiled, so that the Spirit which dwells in it may bear witness to it, and your flesh may be justified. See to it that the thought never enters your heart that this flesh of yours is perishable, and that you misuse it in some defilement. If you defile your flesh, you also defile the Holy Spirit; and if you defile the flesh, you shall not live.” “But what, Lord,” I said, “if there was a prior ignorance before these words were heard? How shall the man who has defiled his flesh be saved?” “Concerning the former acts of ignorance,” he said, “it is possible for God alone to give healing; for all power is his;¹ but for the future, do not defile your flesh nor the Spirit; for both are in common, and one cannot be defiled without the other. Keep both, therefore, pure, and you shall live to God.”

I was saying to myself, “I shall be blessed if I walk in these commandments; and whoever walks in them shall be blessed.” As I was speaking these things to myself, I suddenly saw him sitting beside me, and he said this: “Why are you double-minded <note>original: *dipsycheis* — a state of doubt or being 'two-souled,' a central concern in this text</note> regarding the commandments which I have commanded you? They are good; do not be double-minded at all. Instead, clothe yourself in the faith of the Lord, and you shall walk in them; for I will strengthen you in them. These commandments are beneficial for those who intend to repent; for if they do not walk in them, their repentance is in vain. You, therefore, who are repenting, cast away<gloss>1</gloss> the wickednesses of this world which wear you down; and having clothed yourselves in every virtue of righteousness, you will be able to keep these commandments and no longer add to your sins. Walk, therefore, in these commandments of mine, and you shall live to God. All these things have been spoken to you by me.” And after he had spoken these things with me, he said to me, “Let us go into the field, and I will show you the shepherds of the sheep.” “Let us go,”<gloss>2</gloss> I said, Lord. And we came into a certain plain, and he showed me a young shepherd dressed in a suit of clothes, saffron-colored in hue. And he was feeding many sheep, and these sheep were as if living in luxury and being very wanton, and they were joyful as they skipped here and there. And the shepherd himself was joyful over his flock; and the appearance of the shepherd was very cheerful, and he ran about among the sheep.<gloss>3</gloss>

II. And he said to me, “Do you see this shepherd?” “I see him,” I said, Lord. “This,” he said, “is the angel of luxury and deceit. He wears down the souls of the servants of God who are empty, and turns them away from the truth, deceiving them with wicked desires in which they will perish;<gloss>1</gloss> for they forget the commandments of the living God, and walk in deceits and vain luxuries, and are destroyed by this angel—some to death, and others to corruption.” I said to him, “Lord, I do not know what ‘to death’ means, and what ‘to corruption’ means.” “Listen,” he said; “the sheep you saw joyful and skipping, these are those who have been torn away from God completely and have surrendered themselves to luxuries and deceits; yet they have not blasphemed against the Lord. These, then, [not]<gloss>2</gloss> have been corrupted from the truth; in them there is hope of repentance, in which they can live. Corruption, therefore, has hope of a certain renewal, but death has eternal destruction.” Again I went forward a little, and he showed me a great shepherd, wild in appearance, wrapped in a white, wild skin, and he had a certain bag upon his shoulders, and a very hard staff with knots in it, and a great whip; and his look was very bitter, so that I was afraid of him; such a look did he have. This shepherd, then, received the sheep from the young shepherd—those that were wanton and in luxury, but not skipping—and he threw<gloss>3</gloss> them into a certain place that was steep and thorny, so that from the thorns and briars they were not able—

...to be able to untangle the sheep, but instead they became entangled in the thorns and thistles. Being thus entangled, they were grazing among the thorns and thistles and were suffering greatly, being beaten<gloss>4</gloss> <note>original: *deomena* (in need), though the manuscript variant *dairemena* means "being beaten" or "flogged," which fits the context of the harsh shepherd better</note> by him; and he was driving them here and there, and gave them no rest, and those sheep were not at ease at all.

III. Seeing them, then, so lashed and suffering,<gloss>1</gloss> I was grieved for them, because they were being so tormented and had no rest at all. I say to the Shepherd who was speaking with me, “Lord, who is this shepherd who is so heartless and bitter<gloss>2</gloss> and has no compassion at all for these sheep?” “This,” he said, “is the **Angel of Punishment**; <term>Angel of Punishment (aggelos tēs timōrias): a divine messenger responsible for administering justice and corrective discipline to those who stray</term> he is one of the righteous angels, but is set over punishment. He therefore takes those who wander away from God and walk according to the desires and deceptions of this world, and he punishes them, just as they deserve, with terrible and varied punishments.” “Lord,” I said, “I wish to know these varied torments <note>original: *basanous* — while it can mean physical torture, here it refers to the spiritual and worldly hardships used as discipline</note> and punishments, and of what sort they are.” “Listen,” he said, “to the varied torments and punishments. The torments are worldly; for some are punished with losses, others with want, others with varied illnesses, others with total instability, and others by being insulted by unworthy people and suffering through many other trials. For many, being unstable in their plans, attempt many things, and nothing succeeds for them at all. And they say they are not prospering in their actions, and it does not enter their hearts that they have done evil deeds, but they blame the Lord. When, therefore, they are oppressed with every affliction, then they are handed over to me for good instruction and are strengthened in the faith of the Lord; and for the remaining days of their lives, they serve the Lord with a pure heart, and they prosper in every action, receiving from the Lord everything they ask for. And then they glorify the Lord, because they were handed over to me, and they no longer suffer any evil.”

IV. I say to him, “Lord, explain this further to me.” “What,” he says, “are you seeking?” “Whether, Lord,” I say, “those living in luxury and being deceived are tormented for the same length of time as they were living in luxury and being deceived?” He says to me, “They are tormented for the same amount of time; <gloss>2</gloss> <note>Note: The manuscript appears to be missing a small portion of text here</note> for those living in luxury and forgetting God ought to be tormented sevenfold.” He says to me, “You are foolish, and you do not understand the power of the torment.” “If I had understood it, Lord,” I said, “I would not have asked you to explain it.” “Listen,” he said, “to the power of both. The time of luxury and deception is but a single hour; but the hour of torment has the power of thirty days. If, therefore, someone lives in luxury and is deceived for a single day, and is tormented for a single day, the day of torment has the power of an entire year. For as many days as someone lives in luxury, for that many years he is tormented. You see, then,” he said, “that the time of luxury and deception is very short, but the time of punishment and torment is long.”

V. "Still," I said, "Lord, I do not at all understand about the length of time for the deception and luxury <note>original: *tryphēs* — often meaning soft living, indulgence, or revelry</note> and the punishment; reveal it to me more clearly." He answered and said to me, "Your foolishness is persistent, and you do not want to cleanse <gloss>1</gloss> your heart and serve God. See to it," he said, "lest the time be fulfilled and you be found a fool. Listen then," he said, "as you wish, <gloss>2</gloss> so that you may understand these things. The person who lives in luxury and is deceived for a single day, and does what he wants, is clothed in much foolishness; he does not understand what he is doing for the next day, for he forgets what he did the day before. For luxury and deception have no memories because of the foolishness with which a person is clothed. But when punishment and torment cling to a person for a single day, he is punished and tormented for a whole year; for punishment and torment have long memories. Thus, being tormented and punished for a whole year, a person finally remembers his luxury and deception, and knows that he suffers these evils because of them. Therefore, every person who lives in luxury and is deceived is tormented in this way, because although they have life, they have handed themselves over to death."

"What sorts of luxuries," I asked, "Lord, are harmful?" "Every action," he said, "is a luxury to a person if he does it with pleasure. For even the quick-tempered man, by satisfying his own impulse, indulges himself; and the adulterer, the drunkard, the slanderer, the liar, the greedy man, the defrauder, <term>defrauder (aposterētēs): one who withholds what is due or robs by deceit</term> and whoever does things like these, is satisfying his own disease; <note>The text views habitual sin as a 'disease' (nosos) that the sinner 'feeds' or 'satisfies'</note> therefore he indulges in his own action. All these luxuries are harmful to the servants of God. It is because of these deceptions, then, that those who are punished and tormented suffer. But there are <gloss>3</gloss> also luxuries that save people; for many who do good find pleasure in it, being carried along by their own delight. This luxury, then, is profitable to the servants of God and brings life to such a person. But the harmful luxuries mentioned before bring torments and punishments upon them. And if they persist and do not repent, they bring death upon themselves."

<meta>This page continues the "Eighth Similitude" from the Shepherd of Hermas, an early Christian allegorical work. Having previously distributed willow branches to a great multitude, the "Shepherd" (the Angel of Repentance) and the "Angel of the Lord" (Michael) are now examining the condition of these branches to judge the spiritual state of the people.</meta>

He said, "This tree is a willow, and it is a life-loving species <note>original: φιλόζωον (philozōon) – meaning it is hardy and clings to life</note>. Therefore, if these rods are planted and receive even a little moisture, many of them will live. Next, let us try to pour water over them; if any of them are able to live, I will rejoice with them; but if they do not live, I shall not be found negligent." Then the Shepherd commanded me to call the people just as each of them had stood. They came group by group and gave their rods to the Shepherd. The Shepherd took the rods and planted them according to their rank ^3^, and after planting them, he poured much water over them, so that the rods could not even be seen because of the water. And after he had watered the rods, he said to me... ^4^ and "After a few days, let us return and inspect all the rods; for he who created this tree wants all who have received branches from this tree to live. I also hope that once these little rods have received moisture and have been watered, the greater part of them will live."

### III.
I said to him, "Lord, make known to me what this tree is; for I am perplexed about it, because although so many branches have been cut from it, the tree remains healthy and nothing appears to have been cut away from it; it is in this that I am perplexed." "Listen," he said; "this great tree that overshadows plains and mountains and all the earth is the Law of God <term>Law of God: here identified with the Son of God</term> given to the whole world. And this law is the Son of God, who has been preached to the ends of the earth. The people under its shadow are those who have heard the preaching and believed in him. The great and glorious angel is Michael, who has authority over this people and governs them; for he is the one who puts the law into the hearts of those who believe. He therefore inspects those to whom he gave the law to see if they have kept it. You see the rods of each person; for the rods are the law. You see many rods rendered useless; you will recognize all of them as those who did not keep the law, and you will see the dwelling-place of each one." I said to him, "Lord, why did he dismiss some to the tower, but left others to you?" "As many," he said, "as transgressed the law which they received from him, he left to my authority for repentance. But as many as have already well-pleased the law and have kept it, he keeps them under his own authority." "Who then, Lord," I said, "are those who are crowned and are going into the tower?" "These are they who suffered for the sake of the law. And the others, who also gave back their rods green and having shoots—but not having fruit ^1^—are those who were persecuted for the law but did not suffer <note>i.e., they were not martyred</note> nor did they deny their law. And those who gave them back green just as they received them are the reverent and the righteous, who walked with a pure heart and kept the commandments of the Lord. The rest you shall know when I examine these rods that have been planted and watered."

### IV.
And after a few days we came to the place; and the Shepherd sat in the place of the angel, and I stood beside him.

### THE SHEPHERD OF HERMAS

...how many repented and were saved. "I see, sir," I said. "In order that you may see," he said, "the great mercy of the Lord, that it is great and glorious, and He has given the spirit to those who are worthy of repentance." "If then these, sir," I said, "did not all repent?" "Those whose hearts He saw were going to become pure," he said, "and serve Him with their whole heart, to these He gave repentance. But those whose deceit and wickedness He saw, who intended to repent in hypocrisy, to those He did not give repentance, lest they should profane His name."

I said to him, "Lord, now therefore show me those who gave up the rods—what kind each of them is, and their dwelling place. I ask this so that those who have believed and received the seal <note>original: σφραγῖδα (sphragida) — A term commonly used in the early Church to refer to Baptism as the 'seal' of faith.</note> and have broken it and not kept it whole, might hear and, recognizing their own deeds, repent. May they receive a seal from you and glorify the Lord, because He had mercy on them and sent you to renew their spirits."

"Listen," he said. "Those whose rods were found dry and eaten by moths <note>original: σητὸς (sētos)</note> are the apostates and traitors of the Church, who blasphemed the Lord in their sins, and were further ashamed of the name of the Lord which was called upon them. These, then, have perished utterly to God. You see that not one of them repented, even though they heard the words which I spoke to you, which I commanded you; from such as these, life has departed.

But those who gave up the dry and un-rotted <note>original: ἀσήπτους (asēptous) — meaning dry but not decayed or moth-eaten</note> rods, these also are near the first group. For they were hypocrites and brought in strange doctrines, and they perverted the servants of God—especially those who had sinned, not allowing them to repent but persuading them with foolish doctrines. These, however, have hope of repenting. You see that many of them have indeed repented since the time I spoke my commandments to them; and still more will repent. But those who do not repent have lost their lives. Those of them who did repent became good, and their dwelling was placed within the first walls; some even ascended into the tower. You see then," he said, "that repentance brings life to sinners, but not repenting brings death."

**VII.** "And those who gave up half-dry rods that had cracks in them—listen also concerning them. Those whose rods were half-dry in the same way are the double-minded <note>original: δίψυχοί (dipsychoi) — literally 'two-souled'; a key term in Hermas for those wavering between the world and God.</note>; for they are neither alive nor dead. But those who have them half-dry and with cracks, these are both double-minded and slanderers; they are never at peace among themselves but are always creating divisions. Yet even for these," he said, "repentance is possible. You see," he said, "that some of them have already repented; and there is still," he said, "hope of repentance among them."

### SIMILITUDO VIII, 6—9.

"And as many," he said, "of them as have repented, shall have their dwelling in the **tower**. But those of them who were slower to repent shall dwell within the walls. #### VIII.
"And those who gave up their rods half green and half dry, these are the ones who are entangled in <term>business affairs</term> <note>original: πραγματείαις (pragmateiais) — Referring here to worldly distractions or financial preoccupations that pull one away from spiritual life.</note> and do not cling to the saints; because of this, half of them lives, but the other half is dead. They lost their life, therefore, because of the wickedness they practiced.

Many of them, then, repented, but some of them were double-minded and fell into dissension. And when the six men saw the unseemly stones in the building, they ordered them to be removed and carried down to their own place from which they were brought..... <sup>6)</sup> they say to the men who were bringing the stones: "Do not give stones into the building at all; but place them beside the tower, so that the virgins may bring them through the gate and give them for the building. For if," they say, "they are not brought through the gate by the hands of these virgins, they cannot change their colors; do not labor then," they say, "in vain."

V. And on that day the building was finished; but the tower was not yet completed; for it was meant to be built upon further; and there was a pause in the building. And the six men ordered all those building to withdraw for a little while and rest; but they commanded the virgins not to withdraw from the tower. And it seemed to me that the virgins had been left behind to guard the tower. And after everyone had withdrawn and rested, I say to the Shepherd: "Why is it, Lord," I say, "that the building of the tower was not completed?" "It cannot yet be completed," he says, "unless its Lord comes and tests this building, so that, if any rotten stones are found, he may change them; for the tower is being built according to his will." "I would like, Lord," I say, "to know what this building of the tower is, and about the rock and the gate and the mountains, and the virgins, and the stones that rose from the abyss and were not hewn, but went into the building just as they were..."

## VI.
And behold, after a little while I see an array of many men coming; and in the midst a certain man, tall in stature, so as to overtop the tower. And the six men who had worked on the building were with him, and many other glorious ones were around him. The virgins who guarded the tower ran forward and kissed him, and began to walk near him around the tower. And that man inspected the building accurately, so that he felt each stone. Holding a certain rod in his hand, he struck each stone of the building three times. And when he struck them, some of them became black as soot, some were scabby, some had cracks, some were mutilated, some were neither white nor black, some were rough and did not fit with the other stones, and some had spots. These were the varieties of the "rotten" stones found in the building. He commanded all these to be taken out of the tower and placed beside the tower, and other stones to be brought and put in their place. And he did not command them to be brought from the mountains. But the plain was dug, and bright square stones were found, and some were round. And whatever stones were in that plain, all were brought and carried through the gate by the virgins. And the square stones were hewn and placed in the spot of those taken away. But the round stones were not placed in the building, because they were too hard to be hewn, and it happened slowly. They were placed beside the tower, as if they were going to be hewn later and placed in the building; for they were very bright.

### XII.

"How else, Lord," I asked, "could it be possible?" "If, then, you are unable to enter the city except through its gate, so," he said, "a person cannot enter the kingdom of God in any other way except through the name of his Son, who is beloved by him. Did you see," he asked, "the crowd building the tower?" "I saw them, Lord," I said. "Those," he said, "are all glorious angels. By these, the Lord is walled in. But the gate is the Son of God; this is the only entrance to the Lord. In no other way, therefore, shall anyone enter to him except through his Son. Did you see," he asked, "the six men and the glorious and great man in their midst, who walked around the tower and rejected the stones from the building?" "I saw him, Lord," I said. "The glorious man," he said, "is the Son of God, and those six are the glorious angels who support him on his right and on his left. None of these glorious angels," he said, "shall enter into the presence of God without him. Whoever does not receive the name of God shall not enter into the kingdom of God."

### XIII.
"The tower," I asked, "what is it?" "This tower," he said, "is the <term>Church <gloss>original: ἐκκλησία (ekklēsia)</gloss></term>." "And these virgins, who are they?" "They are holy spirits," he replied; "and no human can be found in the kingdom of God unless these spirits clothe them with their own garment. For if you receive the name alone, but do not receive the garment from them, you gain nothing. <note>original: ὠφελεῖς (ōpheleis)</note> For these virgins are the powers of the Son of God. If you bear the name, but do not bear His power, you will be bearing His name in vain." "And the stones," he continued, "which you saw cast away—these are the ones who indeed bore the name, but did not put on the clothing of the virgins." "What sort of clothing is theirs, Lord?" I asked. "The names themselves," he said, "are their clothing. Whoever bears the name of the Son of God ought also to bear the names of these virgins; for even the Son himself bears the names of these virgins. As many stones," he said, "as you saw go into the building, these are clothed in the power of these virgins. This is why you see the tower has become a single stone <note>meaning it appears seamless or monolithic</note> with the rock. So also those who have believed in the Lord through His Son, and clothe themselves in these spirits, shall become one spirit, one body, and the color of their garments shall be one. And the dwelling of such as bear the names of the virgins is in the tower." "The stones that were cast away, then, Lord," I asked, "why were they rejected? For they passed through the gate and were placed into the building of the tower by the hands of the virgins." "Since everything matters to you," he said, "and you examine everything accurately, hear about the rejected stones. All these," he said, "received the name of the Son of God, and they also received the power of these virgins. Having received these spirits, they were strengthened and stayed with the servants of God; they had one spirit, one body, and one garment—for they were of the same mind and practiced righteousness. But after some time, they were led astray by the women you saw dressed in black garments, with their shoulders bare and their hair loose, who were beautiful in form. When they saw these women, they desired them and put on their power, but they stripped off the power of the virgins. These, therefore, were cast out from the house of God and handed over to those women. But those who were not deceived by the beauty of these women remained in the house of God. You have here," he said, "the explanation of those who were rejected."

### XIV.
"What then, Lord," I asked, "if these men, being such as they are, should repent and cast off the desires of these women, and return to the virgins and walk in their power and in their works—will they not enter into the house of God?" "They will enter," he said, "if they cast off the works of these women, and take up again the power of the virgins and walk in their works. ## XXV.
And from the eighth mountain, where there were many springs and all the creation of the Lord was watered from these springs, those who have believed are as follows: they are apostles and teachers who preached to the whole world and who taught the word of the Lord with dignity and purity. ## XXVI.

And those who are "scabby" <note>original: <term>ἐψωριακότες <gloss>covered with sores or scabs; used here metaphorically for spiritual decay</gloss></term></note>, these are those who denied their Lord and did not return to him. For just as a vine left inside a fence and neglected is ruined and made desolate by weeds, and in time becomes wild and is no longer useful to its master, so also such people have despaired of themselves and become useless to their Lord, having grown wild. 

For these people, repentance is possible, unless they are found to have denied from the heart. But if someone is found to have denied from the heart, I do not know if he can live. And I do not say this for these present days so that someone might deny and then expect to receive repentance; for it is impossible for someone who is about to deny his Lord *now* to be saved. But for those who denied long ago, repentance seems to be available. If anyone, therefore, is about to repent, let him be quick before the tower <note>The "tower" is the central allegory of the book, representing the Church being built; once finished, the opportunity for entry closes.</note> is finished; otherwise, he will be [cast out] by the women...

Those who have done these things are glorious in the sight of God, and their place is already with the angels, if they continue serving the Lord until the end.

## XXVIII.
And from the eleventh mountain, where there were trees full of fruit, adorned with various kinds of fruit, those who have believed are these: those who suffered for the name of the Son of God, who also suffered readily with their whole heart and gave up their lives. "Why then, Lord," I say, "do all the trees have fruit, but some of their fruits are less pleasant?" "Listen," he says: "as many as ever suffered for the Name are glorious in the sight of God, and the sins of all these were taken away, because they suffered for the name of the Son of God. But why their fruits are diverse, some excelling, listen. As many," he says, "as were brought before authority and were questioned and did not deny, but suffered readily, these are more glorious before the Lord. Theirs is the excelling fruit. But as many as became cowardly and in doubt <note>The text addresses those who hesitated to confess their faith during persecutions.</note>, and reasoned in their hearts whether they should deny or confess, and yet suffered, their fruits are less, because this thought entered their heart; for it is an evil thought for a servant to deny his own Lord. See to it then, you who have such thoughts, lest this thought remain in your hearts and you die to God. But you who are suffering for the sake of the Name ought to glorify God, because God deemed you worthy to bear this Name and that all your sins might be healed. [Do you not then] count yourselves [blessed]? But you think you have performed a great work if any of you suffers for God’s sake. The Lord grants you life and you do not realize it; for your sins weighed you down, and if you had not suffered for the name of the Lord, you would have died <unclear>...</unclear> to God. I say these things to you who are doubting about denial or..."

## XXIX.
And from the twelfth mountain, the white one, those who have believed are these: they are like infant babes <note>original: <term>νήπια βρέφη <gloss>nēpia brephē</gloss></term></note>, in whose heart no evil arises, nor did they know what wickedness is, but they have always remained in a state of infancy. Such people, therefore, dwell without doubt in the kingdom of God, because in no matter did they defile the commandments of God, but remained with innocence all the days of their life in the same mindset. "All of you, then, who shall remain," he said, "and shall be like infants, having no malice, shall be more glorious than all those previously mentioned; for all infants are glorious in the sight of God and stand first in His presence. Blessed are you, therefore, as many as shall take away wickedness from yourselves and put on guiltlessness; you shall be the first of all to live unto God." After he finished the parables of the mountains, I said to him: "Lord, now explain to me about the stones taken from the plain and placed into the building instead of the stones taken from the tower, and the round stones placed into the building and those that are still round."

# ERRATA AND CORRECTIONS

"That title" <note>original: "Titulus iste"</note> — 409, 3. in the city of Rome — 412. Chapter II. note 10) From the Carmelite Codex — 413, 26. "which [fem.] happens" instead of "than happens" <note>original: "quae acc. p. quam acc."</note> — 414. note 9) Virgil and Terence — 416, note 18) "nearer" instead of "more proper" <note>original: "propius p. proprius"</note> — 421, 24. "he permitted me... he granted to me" — 423, note 14) at the end 31 instead of 32. — note 18) at the end of the London edition, 1637. — 425, Chapter IV. note 5) and the saints themselves — 429, 5. somewhat — 437, Chapter XII. note 2) "should have risen" instead of "rose" <note>original: "surrexerit p. surrexit"</note> — 442, 5. (A) When I had prayed — note 2) Matthew 10:10. — 451. note 17) has one indulgence of penance — 456, 6. this vessel — 457, 25. Behold, I have delivered — 460, note 16) most unjust (as written) <note>original: "inquissimus (sic)"</note> — 462, Mandate VIII. note 8) Hear, he says — 465, 25. write: nor ever — 468, note 8) Homily 2:15 and 3:22 following — 470, 24. is troubled — 480, 10. and; in the same note 2 Corinthians 3:14. — 17. of power — 34. by them — 482, 16. BOOK I — 485. Similitude II note 6) Origen, Homily 10, 1 on Joshua — 488, 32. and these things — 489, Similitude V. note 2) and by night he lies in a boat — 490, 17. to the successors — 494, 7. having prayed — 495, Chapter IV. note 2) in the understanding of the Palatine [Manuscript] — 496, 20. he had received. You see — 509, note 16) to press upon those able to endure it — 18. to owe — 510, 20. for — 514, 18. that they may do [penance] for their crimes — 516, 19. they had had; — 517, note 4) green Palatine [Manuscript] — 519, 9. who (the number 2 being deleted) — 10. who — 520, 23. by the commands — 521, 21. by the tower — 523, 13. this cited penance — 30. suppressed — 32. suppressed (without the number 3) — 527, 9. all [of the] kind — 532, 3. after "twenty-five", insert: then thirty-five, — 535, 2. they were (without number 7) — 3. they were — note 8) and these stones are not for the structure — 536, note 9) then "to be contained" instead of "to contain" <note>original: "continere"</note> — 537, 24. what I know — 540, note 7) that he was made younger — 542, 6. she is girded — 544, note 11) For indeed the son also [has] names — note 16) they had been rejected — 545, 5. Thus also — 548, 28. of the proclamation <note>original: "κηρύγματος"</note> — 568, note 9) in which words — 569, 23. for [the] pure — 596, 33. you should doubt <note>original: "διψυχήσῃς," meaning to be double-minded</note>. See also Prolegomena LV.

Furthermore, errors have occurred several times in the accents and breathings <note>marks used in Greek typography</note>; indeed, in several instances, they have been lost due to damage to the type-metal, which we ask the fair reader not to take offense at. Add that in some copies on page 220, "A AGINAT." was printed instead of "TO IGNATIUS" <note>original: "AD IGNAT."</note>.

**Postscript:** In a booklet very recently published: *Supplementary Remarks on Hermas* by R. Anger and W. Dindorf, the illustrious Mr. Anger has presented a "variety of readings collected from the first copy by Simonides." <note>Constantine Simonides (1820–1867) was a controversial Greek scholar and manuscript dealer, often accused of forgeries.</note> In this matter, he has applied great diligence; he has even more curiously transcribed the foolish corruption of the Simonidean writing in several places where we did not record them, since the correction was perfectly obvious\*) <note>meaning the error was so clear it didn't need noting</note>; in other places, he has silently corrected alongside us, such as at 1, 16. (page 572, 11) where the copy has "was" <note>original: "ἦν"</note> for "to be" <note>original: "ὠ"</note> (similarly at 82, 15 and 621, 14 where the copy has "the" written above for "was") 20, 13. (583, 22) "stammering" <note>original: "συμψέλλ."</note> for "συμκέλλ." 32, 17. (591, 18) "I am about to" <note>original: "μέλλω"</note> for "I care" <note>original: "μέλω"</note> 38, 26. (595, 14) "of lies" <note>original: "ψευσμάτων"</note> for "στευσμ." 

But he often passed over in silence things that should not have been neglected, such as 6, 24. "they become" [plural] for "it becomes" [singular]; 6, 25. "he promised" for "he reported"; 15, 19. "if they shall repent" for "if they repent" <note>original: "μετανοήσουσιν" instead of "μετανοήσωσιν"</note>; 16, 31. "you [plural] were useful" for "thou [singular] wert useful"; 18, 29. "I questioned"; 23, 18. "from a stadium"; 26, 3. "he sat around" for "he sat beside"; 28, 1. "justice" [singular] for "justices" [plural]; 33, 26. "you [singular] might guard" for "he might guard"; 34, 20. "complete" [neuter] for "complete" [masculine]; 49, 29. "I am able" (correct to "being able" [fem. plural]) instead of "they are able"; 91, 23. "they were carrying"; 94, 32. "being dressed" (the copy has "dressing") for "having been clothed", etc. 

Nor rarely was he mistaken about Simonides’ writing, especially where he had repeated abbreviations from the codex itself. Thus, to provide some examples: at 8, 8 (page 575, column II, line 13), instead of "he brings on" <note>original: "ἐπάγει"</note>, he notes "almost epa, above eipa (he promises)" <note>original: "ἐπαγγέλλεται"</note>; at 10, 12, instead of "I shall disappear" <note>original: "φανισθήσομαι"</note>, he gives "φανιοϑ."; at 10, 20, the copy has "flax/linen" <note>original: "λίνον"</note> (it almost looked like "of flax"), not "made of linen" <note>original: "λινοῦν"</note>; at 12, 12, the booklet has "and" <note>original: "δὲ"</note> as it seems, but it is entirely "and/also" <note>original: "τε"</note>. Likewise at 17, 4, he has "you enslave" but it is "enslaving"; 17, 18. "he finished" but the copy has "he died/ended"; 24, 29. "to be a slave" but the copy has "he shall be a slave"; 51, 13. "most distant" but the copy correctly has "difficult to pass"; 78, 6. "perhaps of sins," but it is entirely "of sinners"; at 91, 22, he brings forward "brooms" [plural], but the copy actually has "broom" [singular]; at 95, 2, it is not "with one color" <note>original: "μιᾷ χρόᾳ"</note> but "one color" <note>original: "μία χρόα"</note>. At 86, 27, he notes "again, in parenthesis again with a compound; above, straightway; it seems to underlie: sovereign/master." The matter is thus: Simonides wrote "again," with "straightway" placed above it, and at the same time added the abbreviation from the manuscript in parentheses, and that absolutely denotes "sovereign/master" <note>original: "αὐϑέντης"</note>.

\*) These following places ought rather to have been removed from that number: 597, 19 (also 600, 30) where the copy has "defiled/mixed up" rather than "poured in"; 627, 9 where the copy has "most ready" for "most becoming"; 580, 28 where "at the present time" was repeated from the first edition, but the copy provides "those, into... [corruption]" (from which Anger not badly conjectures "those into the present"). At 588 note 8, write rather that above the words "it might be found and" there has been placed (foolishly indeed) "the change might be judged."

The author critiques Rudolf Anger's recent work, highlighting specific Greek spelling and grammatical discrepancies in the transcription of ancient texts.</summary>
